The field $S/\mathfrak q$ is integral over the embedded domain $R/\mathfrak p$. For a nonzero element $a$ of this domain, its inverse in that field satisfies a monic equation. Multiplication of that equation by $a^{n-1}$ expresses $a^{-1}$ as an element of $R/\mathfrak p$. Thus $R/\mathfrak p$ is a field and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal, as in the maximal-prime criterion. ∎

Lemma. A reduced ring at a minimal prime

If $\mathfrak p$ is minimal among the primes of $R$, every element of $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ is nilpotent. When $R$ is reduced, $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a field.

Proof. Primes of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ correspond to primes of $R$ contained in $\mathfrak p$, so its maximal ideal is its only prime. It is therefore the nilradical. Equivalently, a nonnilpotent element in that maximal ideal would define a nonempty principal open by the spectrum criterion, whereas the unique point would not belong to it. If $R$ is reduced, so is its localization: a nilpotent fraction $a/s$ has $ta^n=0$ for some inverted $t$, so $(ta)^n=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$. Its maximal ideal is consequently zero, making this nonzero local ring a field. ∎

Lemma. Geometric regularity over a directed union of subfields

Suppose $k$ is the directed union of subfields $k_i$ and $A$ is a $k$-algebra. If $A$ is geometrically regular as a $k_i$-algebra for every $i$, it is geometrically regular over $k$.

Proof. The hypothesis already makes $A$ Noetherian and regular. By the finite purely inseparable test, it remains to check regularity of $A\otimes_k k'$ for a finite purely inseparable extension $k'/k$.

In positive characteristic, express this extension as a finite tower adjoining elements $\alpha_j$ with minimal polynomials $X^{p^{e_j}}-b_j$ over the preceding field. Each $b_j$ is a rational expression in the earlier $\alpha$'s with finitely many coefficients in $k$. Choose one $k_i$ containing all these coefficients, and form the corresponding tower inside $k'$ starting at $k_i$. Each displayed polynomial is still irreducible over this smaller preceding field, because a factorization there would also be a factorization over the larger preceding field. Thus the smaller tower, with final field $k_i'$, has the same successive degrees. Multiplication gives a surjection $k\otimes_{k_i}k_i'\to k'$: the image contains $k$ and all the $\alpha_j$, and is a finite-dimensional domain over $k$, hence a field. The two sides have the same dimension over $k$, so this map is an isomorphism. The extension $k_i'/k_i$ is finite purely inseparable by construction. Therefore

$$A\otimes_k k'\cong A\otimes_{k_i}k_i'$$

is regular by the hypothesis. In characteristic zero the only finite purely inseparable extension is the field itself, so the test is immediate. ∎

Lemma. Smooth ascent of geometric regularity

For a smooth homomorphism $A\to B$ of $k$-algebras, geometric regularity of $A$ over the field $k$ implies geometric regularity of $B$ over $k$.

Proof. For any finitely generated extension field $k'/k$, base change makes $A\otimes_k k'\to B\otimes_k k'$ smooth. Its source is regular by assumption, and regularity ascent makes its target regular. Noetherianity of the target follows as well from finite type over the Noetherian source. This is the defining field-extension test for geometric regularity of $B$. ∎

Definition. Formal smoothness

An $R$-algebra $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if the following lifting property holds. For every $R$-algebra $A$, every ideal $I\subset A$ with $I^2=0$, and every $R$-algebra homomorphism $u\colon S\to A/I$, there is an $R$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde u\colon S\to A$ whose composite with $A\to A/I$ is $u$. Thus the lift must respect the specified map from $R$, as well as the quotient map.

Lemma. Completion at a finitely generated ideal is complete

Historical source credit: Matlis, Theorem 15, is the citation in the original source. The proof below follows the argument credited there to Bjorn Poonen's email of 5 November 2016.

For a finitely generated ideal $I\subset R$ and an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, put $\widehat M=\varprojlim_r M/I^rM$. Then, for every $n\geq1$, the natural maps identify

$$I^n\widehat M=\ker(\widehat M\longrightarrow M/I^nM)=\widehat{I^nM}.$$

In particular, $\widehat M$ is complete for its $I$-adic filtration. Taking $M=R$ gives $I^n\widehat R=\widehat{I^n}$ and $\widehat R/I^n\widehat R=R/I^n$.

Proof. The ideal $I^n$ has a finite generating list $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. Complete the surjection

$$M^s\longrightarrow I^nM,\qquad (m_j)_j\longmapsto\sum_j a_jm_j.$$

The surjectivity theorem for completions and commutation of inverse limits with finite products give a surjection $(\widehat M)^s\to\widehat{I^nM}$. The intrinsic filtration on $I^nM$ consists of $I^{n+r}M$, so

$$\widehat{I^nM}=\varprojlim_{r\geq n}I^nM/I^rM.$$

This limit embeds naturally in $\widehat M$ and is exactly the kernel of its projection to $M/I^nM$: an element of that kernel has, at every later level $r$, a component in $I^nM/I^rM$, and conversely such compatible components give an element of the kernel. The composite from $(\widehat M)^s$ to $\widehat M$ is multiplication by the list $(a_j)$, whose image is $I^n\widehat M$. This proves all three identifications. The quotient projection is surjective, since every residue class has a representative in $M$. Hence

$$\widehat M/I^n\widehat M\cong M/I^nM.$$

These isomorphisms respect the transition maps. Taking their inverse limit identifies the canonical map from $\widehat M$ to its own completion with an isomorphism, proving completeness without any Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

Lemma. Flat ascent of the condition $(R_k)$

Let $R\to S$ be flat, with both rings Noetherian. Suppose $R$ and every fibre algebra $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ satisfy $(R_k)$, meaning regularity at primes whose local rings have dimension at most $k$. Then $S$ satisfies $(R_k)$.

Proof. Choose $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ with $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq k$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. The induced local map is flat. The dimension equality for a flat local map reads

$$\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}).$$

Both summands are nonnegative, so each is at most $k$. The assumptions make $R_{\mathfrak p}$ regular and make the displayed local fibre regular. The regular-base and regular-fibre criterion therefore makes $S_{\mathfrak q}$ regular. This checks every required prime. ∎

Lemma. Every module is a directed colimit of finitely presented modules

An arbitrary $R$-module $M$ is the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented $R$-modules.

Proof. For a finite subset $F\subset M$, let $R^F\to M$ send the basis vector $e_x$ to $x$. Choose any finite subset $E$ of its kernel and form

$$M_{F,E}=R^F/\langle E\rangle.$$

It has a presentation with finitely many generators and relations, and its evaluation map to $M$ is well-defined. Order the pairs $(F,E)$ by enlarging $F$ and enlarging $E$ after extending old relation vectors by zero in the new coordinates. The resulting coordinate inclusions induce compatible maps between these modules. Any two pairs have a common upper bound: take the union of their finite generating subsets and the union of their extended relation subsets. Thus the index set is directed.

Every $x\in M$ comes from the stage with $F=\{x\}$ and no relations, proving surjectivity of the colimit map. An element at a stage that maps to zero in $M$ is represented by a vector $v\in R^F$ in the evaluation kernel. Adjoining the single relation $v$ to $E$ kills this element at a later stage. This proves injectivity and establishes the asserted colimit, including the zero module. ∎

Lemma. Exactness of a countable Mittag–Leffler inverse limit

Let a countable directed set index short exact sequences of abelian groups

$$0\longrightarrow A_i\longrightarrow B_i\longrightarrow C_i\longrightarrow0,$$

compatible with inverse-system transition maps. If the system $(A_i)$ is Mittag–Leffler, then

$$0\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i A_i\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i B_i\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i C_i\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. The Mittag–Leffler hypothesis says that, for each $i$, the images of $A_j\to A_i$ are constant once $j$ is sufficiently large.

Proof. Limits preserve kernels, which gives exactness at the first two terms. Fix a compatible family $c=(c_i)$ in the last limit, and let $E_i\subset B_i$ be the inverse image of $c_i$. These are nonempty sets, preserved by the transition maps. A compatible family in the $E_i$ is exactly a lift of $c$.

View $A_i$ as a subgroup of $B_i$. Fix $i$ and choose $j\geq i$ for which the images of $A_k\to A_i$ have stabilized for all $k\geq j$. To prove the same stabilization for $E_k\to E_i$, choose $e_j\in E_j$ and any $e_k'\in E_k$. If $e_j'$ is the image of $e_k'$ in $B_j$, then $e_j-e_j'\in A_j$. Stabilization supplies $a_k\in A_k$ whose image in $A_i$ equals the image of $e_j-e_j'$. Thus $e_k'+a_k\in E_k$ maps to the same element of $E_i$ as $e_j$. The opposite image inclusion follows from the transition maps. Hence $(E_i)$ is a Mittag–Leffler system of nonempty sets.

Here is the nonempty-limit argument explicitly. Enumerate the countable index set and, by directedness, choose an increasing cofinal sequence dominating successive entries. Restriction to it leaves the inverse limit unchanged. For a sequence of nonempty Mittag–Leffler sets, replace each set by the eventual image of all sufficiently late sets in it. The replacement sets remain nonempty and their transition maps are surjective: for an element of an earlier eventual image, lift it from a stage late enough to realize both relevant eventual images. Starting with any element in the first replacement set, choose a preimage at each successive stage. The resulting compatible sequence gives an element of the original limit. Applying this to $(E_i)$ lifts $c$ and proves surjectivity. ∎

Lemma. Maps out of a localized module

Let $\Sigma\subset R$ be multiplicative and suppose multiplication by each $s\in\Sigma$ is an automorphism of the $R$-module $N$. For every $R$-module $M$, restriction along $M\to\Sigma^{-1}M$ gives an isomorphism

$$\operatorname{Hom}_R(\Sigma^{-1}M,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N).$$

Proof. Write $s^{-1}$ for the inverse of the multiplication operator on $N$. A map $v\colon\Sigma^{-1}M\to N$ must satisfy $v(m/s)=s^{-1}v(m/1)$, so restriction determines it uniquely.

Conversely, given $u\colon M\to N$, define $v(m/s)=s^{-1}u(m)$. If $m/s=m'/s'$, there is $t\in\Sigma$ with $t(s'm-sm')=0$. Applying $u$ and canceling the invertible operator $t$ gives $s'u(m)=su(m')$. Applying $(ss')^{-1}$ proves that the two proposed values agree. The inverse multiplication operators are $R$-linear and commute. Using a common denominator $ss'$ therefore gives

$$v(rm/s+r'm'/s')=r\,s^{-1}u(m)+r'\,(s')^{-1}u(m')$$

for $r,r'\in R$. Thus $v$ is linear and restricts to $u$. Both constructions are linear and inverse, proving the isomorphism. ∎

Lemma. Stable module isomorphism from a two-term homotopy equivalence

Let $A_1\xrightarrow{d_A}A_0$ and $B_1\xrightarrow{d_B}B_0$ be complexes of $R$-modules. If chain maps $\varphi\colon A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ and $\psi\colon B_\bullet\to A_\bullet$ are inverse up to chain homotopy, then

$$A_1\oplus B_0\cong B_1\oplus A_0.$$

Proof. Choose homotopies $h\colon A_0\to A_1$ and $h'\colon B_0\to B_1$ with

$$1-\psi_1\varphi_1=h d_A,\qquad 1-\psi_0\varphi_0=d_Ah,$$ $$1-\varphi_1\psi_1=h'd_B,\qquad 1-\varphi_0\psi_0=d_Bh'.$$

Consider the maps in the indicated direct-sum orders

$$F=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_1&-h'\\ d_A&\psi_0\end{pmatrix}\colon A_1\oplus B_0\longrightarrow B_1\oplus A_0,$$ $$G=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1&h\\ -d_B&\varphi_0\end{pmatrix}\colon B_1\oplus A_0\longrightarrow A_1\oplus B_0.$$

The homotopy equations give their diagonal entries, while the chain-map equations $d_B\varphi_1=\varphi_0d_A$ and $d_A\psi_1=\psi_0d_B$ make their lower-left entries zero. Multiplication in both orders yields

$$GF=\begin{pmatrix}1&h\psi_0-\psi_1h'\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad FG=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varphi_1h-h'\varphi_0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Each matrix is invertible, with inverse obtained by negating its upper-right entry. Thus $(GF)^{-1}G$ is a left inverse of $F$, and $G(FG)^{-1}$ is a right inverse. A left and a right inverse of the same map coincide, so $F$ is the required isomorphism. ∎

Lemma. Lifting a regular sequence from the closed fibre

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. Suppose the images of $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in S$ form a regular sequence in $S/\mathfrak mS$. Then the sequence is regular in $S$, and each $S/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$ is flat over $R$.

Proof. Regularity of the fibre sequence includes properness of its final ideal. In a local ring this places every image, and hence every $f_i$, in the maximal ideal. Use the complete injection and quotient-flatness proof in AG-CA 08, Section 5, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3. It first makes $f_1$ a nonzerodivisor in $S$ and makes $S/f_1S$ flat over $R$. This quotient is again Noetherian local, and its closed fibre is the quotient of the original closed fibre by $\overline f_1$. Apply the same assertion to $f_2$, and repeat. At each step the next fibre element is regular by hypothesis and remains in the maximal ideal, so the quotient stays nonzero. This proves both the full regular sequence and every claimed flatness statement. For $c=0$, the sequence is empty and the assertion is the given flatness. ∎

Lemma. A finite-type integer model for a relative global complete intersection

Suppose the presentation $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ is a relative global complete intersection. There is a finite-type $\mathbf Z$-subalgebra $R_0\subset R$ containing all coefficients of the $f_i$ such that the same presentation

$$S_0=R_0[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$$

is a relative global complete intersection over $R_0$.

Proof. Begin with the integer subalgebra generated by the finitely many coefficients, denoted $R_0$ provisionally. Then $S=R\otimes_{R_0}S_0$. If $S=0$, the relation $1\in(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ has finitely many polynomial coefficients in $R$. Adjoin these coefficients to $R_0$. The same relation then gives $S_0=0$, which satisfies the definition because it has no nonempty fibres.

Assume $S\ne0$. A prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ contracts to primes $\mathfrak p\subset R$, $\mathfrak q_0\subset S_0$ and $\mathfrak p_0\subset R_0$. Its fibre over $\mathfrak p$ has dimension $n-c$. This fibre is obtained from $S_0\otimes_{R_0}\kappa(\mathfrak p_0)$ by extending the field to $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The field-extension dimension theorem therefore gives dimension $n-c$ to the earlier fibre as well. The local upper bound on fibre dimension supplies a principal neighborhood $D(g)$ of $\mathfrak q_0$ on which all fibre dimensions are at most $n-c$.

As $\mathfrak q$ varies, these principal opens pull back to a cover of $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Choose finitely many of them, with elements $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in S_0$. Their images generate the unit ideal in $S$, so there are $u_i\in S$ with $\sum_i u_ig_i=1$. Represent the $u_i$ by polynomials over $R$, and represent this equality modulo $(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ by finitely many polynomial relations. Adjoin all their coefficients to $R_0$. For the resulting larger finite-type integer subalgebra, the same equality holds in $S_0$, and the $D(g_i)$ cover its entire spectrum.

The fibre bound on each chart survives this enlargement: each new fibre is an extension of the earlier residue field followed by the same localization, and field extension preserves dimension. Thus every nonempty fibre of the new $S_0/R_0$ has dimension at most $n-c$. For the reverse inequality, choose a maximal ideal in any such fibre. The polynomial local ring at its inverse image has dimension $n$, by the polynomial dimension theorem. All $c$ equations lie in its maximal ideal. Applying the one-equation dimension bound successively shows that the fibre's local ring there has dimension at least $n-c$. Thus the whole fibre also has dimension at least $n-c$. The two inequalities give the required equality on every nonempty fibre, proving the statement for this final $R_0$. ∎

Lemma. Filtered colimits commute with homology

For a directed system of three-term complexes of $R$-modules

$$L_i\xrightarrow{u_i}M_i\xrightarrow{v_i}N_i,$$

write $H_i=\ker(v_i)/\operatorname{im}(u_i)$. The colimit is a complex, and its middle homology is canonically $\varinjlim_i H_i$. In particular, directed colimits are exact. The same assertions hold for any filtered index category.

Proof. The transition maps preserve cycles and boundaries, hence induce maps on the $H_i$ and a canonical map from their colimit to the homology $H$ of the colimit complex. Composition is zero in the colimit because it is zero at every stage.

We use the element description of a directed colimit: each element has a representative at a stage, and two representatives agree exactly when they agree at a common later stage. Thus a cycle in $\varinjlim_iM_i$ has a representative $m_i\in M_i$ whose image under $v_i$ becomes zero later. Move to that later stage; the representative is now a cycle there. This proves surjectivity onto $H$.

For injectivity, suppose a cycle $m_i$ represents a class mapping to zero in $H$. Its colimit image is the image of some element represented by $l_j\in L_j$. At a common later stage, the images of $m_i$ and $u_j(l_j)$ agree. The class of $m_i$ is therefore zero in that stage's homology, so it is zero in $\varinjlim_iH_i$.

For a filtered category, the same element description holds with arrows to a common object in place of passage to a larger index. Indeed, form the equivalence relation on the disjoint union of the underlying sets by declaring two elements equivalent when arrows to a common object give equal images. Filteredness supplies common targets, and its equalization of parallel arrows makes this relation transitive and makes addition and scalar multiplication independent of all choices. It gives the module colimit. Consequently every zero or equality used in the two preceding paragraphs is again witnessed at one object. Those arguments prove the filtered assertion too. Applying homology commutation to exact complexes, including zero end terms, proves exactness of filtered colimits. ∎

Lemma. A quasi-finite polynomial model near a point

Let $S$ be a finite-type $R$-algebra, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ have fibre dimension $\dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)=n$. For some $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$, there is an $R$-algebra homomorphism $R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to S_g$ that makes $S_g$ quasi-finite over this polynomial algebra.

Proof. Put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$ and $\overline S=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The fibre point has an open neighborhood of dimension $n$, by the definition of dimension at a point. The topology of the fibre is the subspace topology from $\operatorname{Spec}S$, as described in the fundamental fibre diagram. Choose a principal neighborhood of $\mathfrak q$ whose intersection with the fibre lies inside that open. After this localization, the fibre has dimension exactly $n$: it is at most $n$ by inclusion in the chosen open, and at least $n$ because it is still a neighborhood of the given fibre point.

Choose a finite algebra generating list for this localized $S/R$. The integer-coordinate normalization theorem, applied to $\overline S$, produces $n$ elements $y_i$ that are integer polynomials in the images of these generators and make $\overline S$ finite over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[y_1,\ldots,y_n]$. The same integer polynomials lift the $y_i$ to the localized $S$, so they define a map from $R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$. Its fibre at the contraction of $\mathfrak q$ is a localization and quotient of this finite algebra, and is finite-dimensional over the corresponding residue field. Hence this map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$.

The complete proof of openness of the quasi-finite locus is AG-MO 06, Section 2A, Theorem 2A.4, based there on the pointwise algebraic Zariski Main Theorem. It gives a further principal neighborhood of $\mathfrak q$ on which the map is quasi-finite. Combining the two localizations gives $S_g$ for one $g$ in the original ring outside $\mathfrak q$: write the second denominator as a fraction in the first localization and multiply its numerator by the first denominator. This proves the assertion with the original $R$ and $S$. ∎

Lemma. Dimension bound for a quasi-finite algebra over affine space

Suppose $k$ is a field and a homomorphism $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to S$ makes $S$ a quasi-finite finite-type $P$-algebra. Then $\dim S\leq n$.

Proof. The quasi-finite integral-closure theorem supplies a finite $P$-subalgebra $D\subset S$ for which $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\operatorname{Spec}D$. The integral prime-chain dimension inequality gives $\dim D\leq\dim P=n$. Any chain in the open subset is a chain in $\operatorname{Spec}D$, yielding the conclusion.

This also makes the original local-dimension argument explicit. For $\mathfrak q\subset S$, write $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap D$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap P$. A chart of that open embedding identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ with $D_{\mathfrak r}$. A chain of primes contained in $\mathfrak r$ contracts under the integral map to a strict chain contained in $\mathfrak p$, by incomparability. Therefore $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq\dim P_{\mathfrak p}\leq n$. Taking the supremum over $\mathfrak q$ recovers the same bound. The empty spectrum causes no exception. ∎

Lemma. Dimension of a finite-type algebra after field extension

For a field extension $K/k$ and a finite-type $k$-algebra $S$, the rings $S$ and $K\otimes_kS$ have the same Krull dimension.

Proof. If $S=0$, both rings are zero. Otherwise Noether normalization gives a polynomial subalgebra $k[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset S$ with $S$ finite over it and $d=\dim S$. Flatness of the field extension preserves this inclusion, and base change preserves the finite generating list. Hence

$$K[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset K\otimes_kS$$

is a finite injective map. The dimension equality for an integral inclusion, proved by going up and incomparability, makes the right-hand dimension equal to $d$. ∎

Lemma. The surjectivity locus of a map with finite target

Let $u\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-linear map, with $N$ finitely generated. The following two subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ coincide and are open:

$$\{\mathfrak p:u_{\mathfrak p}\text{ is surjective}\}=\{\mathfrak p:u\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\text{ is surjective}\}.$$

Call this subset $U$. If $D(f)\subset U$, then $M_f\to N_f$ is surjective. No finite-generation assumption on $M$ is needed.

Proof. The cokernel $C$ is finite because it is a quotient of $N$. Right exactness identifies the two surjectivity conditions with $C_{\mathfrak p}=0$ and $C_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pC_{\mathfrak p}=0$, respectively. They are equivalent by Nakayama's lemma. If $C_{\mathfrak p}=0$, choose a finite generating list for $C$ and, for each generator, an annihilating denominator outside $\mathfrak p$. Their product $h\notin\mathfrak p$ makes $C_h=0$, so $D(h)\subset U$. This proves openness. Finally, when $D(f)\subset U$, every prime localization of $C_f$ vanishes. Local detection of a zero module gives $C_f=0$, proving the last assertion. ∎

Lemma. Five local complete-intersection criteria

Let $S$ be a local $k$-algebra essentially of finite type over a field $k$. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. The local algebra $S$ is a complete intersection over $k$.
  2. Every surjection $T\to S$ from a regular local $k$-algebra essentially of finite presentation has kernel generated by a regular sequence.
  3. For some such surjection $T\to S$, its kernel has a generating list of length $\dim T-\dim S$.
  4. There is a global complete-intersection $k$-algebra $A$ and a prime $\mathfrak a\subset A$ with $S\cong A_{\mathfrak a}$ as $k$-algebras.
  5. The same description exists with $A$ a local complete-intersection $k$-algebra.

Proof. We first supply the two comparison arguments used in changing presentations.

For surjective local maps $P\to T\to S$ with $P,T$ regular local, the kernel of $P\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence if and only if the kernel of $T\to S$ is. In either ring, this is equivalent to generation by the dimension of that ring minus $\dim S$, by the Cohen–Macaulay parameter criterion. Indeed, regular local rings are Cohen–Macaulay, and a regular quotient lowers dimension by the length of the sequence.

To compare the generator counts, put $J=\ker(P\to T)$ and $I=\ker(P\to S)$. The full regular-quotient proof in AG-CA 14, Section 1, Proposition 1.4 makes $J$ generated by part of a regular system of parameters, of length $\dim P-\dim T$. Lifting generators of $I/J$ and adjoining those of $J$ proves the implication from the expected count over $T$ to the expected count over $P$.

For the reverse implication, suppose $I$ has the expected count and $J\ne0$. If $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal of $P$, the composite

$$J/\mathfrak mJ\longrightarrow I/\mathfrak mI\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$$

is injective, because the parameter generators of $J$ are independent in the last space. Choose $x\in J$ with nonzero class there. It is part of a minimal generating list of $I$ and of a regular system of parameters of $P$. Replace $P$ by $P/xP$. Its dimension and the minimal number of generators of the new kernel $I/(x)$ both decrease by one, while $T$ and $S$ stay fixed. Induction on $\dim P-\dim T$ gives the expected count over $T$. When this difference is zero, the regular-quotient statement gives $J=0$. This proves the comparison in all cases.

The second comparison says that isomorphic local rings of finitely presented algebras over any fixed base ring come from isomorphic principal neighborhoods. Here are the finite-data and splitting steps. First consider a finitely presented map $B\to C$ inducing $B_{\mathfrak p}\cong C_{\mathfrak q}$. Choose a finite presentation for $C/B$. After inverting one element of $B\setminus\mathfrak p$, the images of all its algebra generators in $C_{\mathfrak q}$ have representatives in $B$. Subtract those representatives from the generators. Their new images vanish in $C_{\mathfrak q}$. The constant coefficients of the finitely many defining relations therefore vanish in $B_{\mathfrak p}$; a further base localization makes them zero in $B$. Evaluation of the new generators at zero now gives a retraction $\epsilon\colon C\to B$ whose kernel $H$ is generated by those generators.

Their vanishing in $C_{\mathfrak q}$ supplies one $v\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $vH=0$. The local isomorphism identifies $\mathfrak q$ with $\epsilon^{-1}(\mathfrak p)$, so $a=\epsilon(v)$ lies outside $\mathfrak p$. Invert $a$ in the base, and write $v=a+w$ with $w\in H$. Set $e=-a^{-1}w$. Then $e\in H$, and $vh=0$ gives $eh=h$ for every $h\in H$. Taking $h=e$ shows $e^2=e$, and consequently $H=eC$. The idempotent decomposition gives

$$C\cong B\times eC$$

over the localized base, with the first projection equal to $\epsilon$. The selected prime lies on the $B$ factor. Localizing at its complementary idempotent isolates that factor.

Now let $A_{\mathfrak a}\cong B_{\mathfrak b}$ as $Q$-algebras, where $A,B$ are finitely presented over a ring $Q$. Represent the images of finitely many algebra generators of $A$ by fractions in $B_{\mathfrak b}$ and clear their denominators. Clear, in addition, the finitely many witnesses that its defining relations vanish. This produces a $Q$-algebra map $A\to B_s$, with $s\notin\mathfrak b$, inducing the given local isomorphism. The map is finitely presented: a finite presentation of $B_s/Q$, together with equations specifying the images of finitely many generators of $A/Q$, is a finite presentation over $A$. Apply the preceding splitting argument. It identifies $A_t$ with a localization of $B_s$ at one further base element and the complementary idempotent. Clearing their denominators expresses the latter as $B_{s'}$ for $s'\notin\mathfrak b$. Here $t\notin\mathfrak a$. This proves the neighborhood comparison, including the prescribed local isomorphism, and applies in particular to $Q=k$.

We can now prove the five equivalences. Condition (2) implies (1) by the definition of a complete-intersection local algebra. Condition (1) gives a regular-sequence presentation, whose length is the dimension difference, proving (3). Finite type and finite presentation agree over the field and its finite-type algebras by Noetherianity. Condition (4) implies (5) by the definition of a local complete intersection.

Assume (3). Write $T=(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J)_{\mathfrak q}$ and let $I$ be the kernel of the composite polynomial map to $S$. Then

$$P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow S$$

are surjective local maps with $P,T$ regular. The first comparison gives $\dim P-\dim S$ generators for $I_{\mathfrak q}$. The five-test criterion for a polynomial presentation supplies a global complete-intersection principal neighborhood of the point in $k[x]/I$. Its local ring is $S$, proving (4).

Finally assume (5), and fix any surjection $T\to S$ as in (2). Choose the same polynomial presentation $P=k[y]_{\mathfrak q}\to T$ and write $S=(k[y]/I)_{\mathfrak q}$. The second comparison identifies a principal neighborhood in $A$ with one in $k[y]/I$. Localizing a local complete intersection preserves that property, by its defining principal cover and localization of global complete intersections. Hence the polynomial five-test criterion makes $I_{\mathfrak q}$ generated by a regular sequence in $P$. The first comparison for $P\to T\to S$ gives a regular sequence for $\ker(T\to S)$. Since the surjection was arbitrary, (2) follows. ∎

Lemma. Dimension at a point over a field

For a finite-type $k$-algebra $S$, a prime $\mathfrak p\subset S$, and the corresponding point $x$ of $X=\operatorname{Spec}S$, one has

$$\dim_xX=\dim S_{\mathfrak p}+\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak p).$$

Proof. The complete component and chain arguments are AG-CA 09, Sections 5–6, Theorem 6.1. Let $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_m$ be the minimal primes contained in $\mathfrak p$, and put $d_j=\dim(S/\mathfrak q_j)$. Every neighborhood of $x$ meets each of these components in a nonempty open subset of dimension $d_j$. Removing the other finitely many components gives a neighborhood of dimension $\max_jd_j$. Thus $\dim_xX=\max_jd_j$.

To retain the prime-chain calculation, put $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\dim(S/\mathfrak p)$. A maximal chain starting at $\mathfrak p$ and ending at a maximal ideal has length $r$. For each $j$, choose a saturated chain from $\mathfrak q_j$ to $\mathfrak p$ of length $s_j$. The catenarity proof in Section 5 shows that every such chain has that length. Concatenation gives a maximal chain in the finite-type domain $S/\mathfrak q_j$, so $d_j=s_j+r$. Localization identifies the minimal primes below $\mathfrak p$ and all their chains, giving $\dim S_{\mathfrak p}=\max_js_j$. Taking maxima in the previous equality proves the formula. ∎

Proposition. Regularity and global dimension of a polynomial algebra

Historical source: FAC, Chapter III, §4, no. 68, p. 261, uses Hilbert-syzygy vanishing for internal graded Ext over $K[t_0,\ldots,t_r]$ in degrees greater than $r+1$. The proposition here gives the ordinary global-dimension bound; the graded-to-ordinary Ext comparison is a separate input to that graded statement. FAC, Chapter III, §5, no. 74, pp. 268–269, uses the bound $r$ for finite modules at stalks of projective $r$-space. Its standard affine charts have $r$ polynomial coordinates, so that local bound follows by localization from the result below.

If $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for a field $k$, then $P$ is regular and has global dimension $n$. Every maximal localization is regular local of dimension $n$.

Proof. Polynomial regularity, including inseparable closed residue fields, is proved in AG-CA 14, Section 3, Proposition 3.3. Its argument adjoins one variable at a time, uses the flat local dimension equality, and lifts generators from the regular base and the zero- or one-dimensional fibre. The polynomial height formula and the Nullstellensatz give dimension $n$ at every maximal ideal. The homological criterion in Section 2 then gives global dimension $n$ to each of these local rings.

To pass to the global ring, take a finite $P$-module $M$. For $n\geq1$, form the first $n$ steps of a resolution by finite free modules and let $K_n$ be its $n$th syzygy. Noetherianity makes $K_n$ finite and finitely presented. At every maximal ideal, the local global-dimension bound makes $(K_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ projective, hence free. The finite-projectivity criterion therefore makes $K_n$ projective over $P$. Truncation gives $\operatorname{pd}_P M\leq n$. For $n=0$, $P=k$ and every module is a vector space, hence free.

The passage from finite modules to all modules is the full cyclic test in AG-CA 13, Section 1, Theorem 1.5. Its transfinite filtration and horseshoe construction show that a uniform bound for the cyclic quotients $P/I$ bounds the projective dimensions of arbitrary $P$-modules. Thus $\operatorname{gl.dim}P\leq n$. Conversely, localization of a projective resolution gives $\operatorname{gl.dim}P_{\mathfrak m}\leq\operatorname{gl.dim}P$: any $P_{\mathfrak m}$-module can first be regarded as a $P$-module and then localized back to itself. Choosing $\mathfrak m=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ supplies the opposite bound $n$, proving equality. ∎

Lemma. A dimension-lowering equation on a Cohen–Macaulay module

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and let $M$ be a nonzero finite Cohen–Macaulay module. Put $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M$. If $g\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies

$$\dim(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g))=d-1,$$

then multiplication by $g$ is injective on $M$, and $M/gM$ is Cohen–Macaulay of depth $d-1$.

Proof. The complete associated-prime proof is AG-CA 12, Sections 3–4, Theorem 4.2. Each associated prime of a CM module is a component of its support of dimension $d$. If $g$ were a zero divisor, it would lie in one of these primes and leave that whole $d$-dimensional component inside $\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g)$, a contradiction. The regular-element depth formula lowers depth by one, and the support identity for the quotient gives the stated dimension. This proves both conclusions.

Here is also the original proof through a regular sequence and an auxiliary equation. Fix an $M$-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_d$. Call an element $a\in\mathfrak m$ good for this list if

$$\dim\bigl(\operatorname{Supp}(M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M)\cap V(a)\bigr)=d-i-1\quad(0\leq i<d).$$

A good element is a nonzerodivisor on $M$, and $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ is a regular sequence of maximal length on $M/aM$. We verify this by induction on $d$. For $d=1$, the kernel $K$ of multiplication by $a$ is supported only at the maximal ideal, so it has finite length. Multiplication by $f_1$ is injective on $K$; finite length makes this endomorphism surjective. Nakayama then forces $K=0$. The quotient $M/aM$ is nonzero by Nakayama and has dimension zero, hence is CM of depth zero.

For use in the induction, recall explicitly the two-element permutation argument. If $u,v\in\mathfrak m$ form a regular sequence on a finite module $L$, and $K=\ker(v:L\to L)$, regularity modulo $u$ gives $K=uK$: writing $z=uz'$ for $z\in K$, injectivity of $u$ gives $vz'=0$. The finite module $K$ vanishes by Nakayama. If $uz=vw$, reduction modulo $u$ then gives $w=uw'$; cancellation of $u$ gives $z=vw'$. Thus $u$ is injective on $L/vL$. The final quotient is unchanged and nonzero, so $v,u$ is a regular sequence too.

Now suppose $d>1$ and $a$ is good. It is good for $M/f_1M$ and the remaining list. The induction hypothesis makes $a$ regular on that quotient and makes $f_2,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ regular on $M/(f_1,a)M$. Permuting $f_1,a$ by the preceding argument shows that $a$ is regular on $M$ and that $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ is regular on $M/aM$. Its support dimension is $d-1$ by goodness, so this sequence has maximal possible length and the quotient is CM. This proves the claim about good elements.

Return to the given $g$. For $d=1$, the dimension hypothesis says exactly that $g$ is good, so the claim applies. The case $d=0$ cannot satisfy the hypothesis, since $M/gM$ is nonzero and cannot have support dimension $-1$. For $d>1$, use prime avoidance to choose $h\in\mathfrak m$ outside the finitely many minimal primes of the supports

$$\operatorname{Supp}(M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M)\quad(0\leq i<d),\qquad \operatorname{Supp}(M/gM).$$

All these closed supports have positive dimension, so none of their minimal primes is the maximal ideal. The one-equation dimension bounds, applied to their support rings, show that intersecting each with $V(h)$ lowers its dimension by one. Thus $h$ is good and

$$\dim(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(h,g))=d-2.$$

The good-element claim makes $M/hM$ CM. Induction on the present lemma, applied to $g$ on that quotient, makes $g$ regular there and makes $M/(h,g)M$ CM of depth $d-2$. Permute the regular pair $h,g$ once more. This gives injectivity of $g$ on $M$ and injectivity of $h$ on $M/gM$. The regular-element depth formula yields $\operatorname{depth}(M/gM)=d-1$. Its support has dimension $d-1$ by hypothesis, completing this second proof. ∎

Lemma. Maximal prime chains in the support of a Cohen–Macaulay module

Suppose a Noetherian local ring $R$ has a finite Cohen–Macaulay module $M$ with $\operatorname{Supp}M=\operatorname{Spec}R$. Every maximal prime chain in $R$ has length $\dim R$. In particular, this holds for a Cohen–Macaulay local ring by taking $M=R$.

Proof. Write $d=\dim R$ and induct on $d$. When $d=0$, all maximal chains consist of one prime and have length zero. For $d>0$, take a maximal chain

$$\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_r.$$

It begins at a minimal prime, ends at the maximal ideal, and has no prime between consecutive entries. It has at least one strict step: the associated-component theorem for CM modules gives dimension $d$ to every minimal-prime quotient of $R$, using full support.

Choose $x\in\mathfrak p_1$ outside every minimal prime of $R$. Such a choice follows from prime avoidance, since the nonminimal prime $\mathfrak p_1$ is contained in none of those minimal primes. The one-equation dimension theorem gives $\dim R/xR=d-1$. Full support and the local Nakayama test give

$$\operatorname{Supp}(M/xM)=V(x).$$

The preceding CM equation lemma therefore makes $M/xM$ a CM module of dimension $d-1$. The same statements hold with $x^N$ for every $N\geq1$, because $V(x^N)=V(x)$.

We next choose $N$ so that $\mathfrak p_1$ is associated to $M/x^NM$, retaining the required power in this argument. The prime $\mathfrak p_0$ is associated to $M$, by the associated-component theorem, so choose a submodule $L\subset M$ isomorphic to $R/\mathfrak p_0$. Artin–Rees supplies $N$ with

$$L\cap x^NM\subset xL.$$

The image $\overline L=L/(L\cap x^NM)$ inside $M/x^NM$ therefore surjects onto $L/xL=R/(\mathfrak p_0+(x))$. Because the pair $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$ is saturated and $x\in\mathfrak p_1\setminus\mathfrak p_0$, the prime $\mathfrak p_1$ is minimal over $\mathfrak p_0+(x)$. It belongs to $\operatorname{Supp}\overline L$ by the surjection. The annihilator of $\overline L$ contains $\mathfrak p_0$ and $x^N$, so $\mathfrak p_1$ is minimal in this support. A minimal support prime of a finite module is associated; the inclusion $\overline L\subset M/x^NM$ then makes it associated to $M/x^NM$.

The complete support and associated-prime arguments used here are given in AG-CA 12, Sections 3–5. In particular, the CM module $M/x^NM$ has no embedded associated primes. Thus $\mathfrak p_1/(x^N)$ is minimal in $R/x^NR$. The remaining chain, from $\mathfrak p_1/(x^N)$ to $\mathfrak p_r/(x^N)$, is maximal in that quotient. The module $M/x^NM$ has full support over $R/x^NR$, and its depth and dimension there agree with those computed over $R$, since the action factors through the quotient. Induction gives $r-1=d-1$, hence $r=d$. ∎

Lemma. A prime containing a product of ideals

If $I,J\subset R$ are ideals and a prime $\mathfrak p$ contains $IJ$, then $I\subset\mathfrak p$ or $J\subset\mathfrak p$.

Proof. If $I$ is not contained in $\mathfrak p$, choose $a\in I\setminus\mathfrak p$. Every $b\in J$ has $ab\in IJ\subset\mathfrak p$. Primality and $a\notin\mathfrak p$ force $b\in\mathfrak p$. Thus $J\subset\mathfrak p$. ∎

Lemma. The differential sequence of a quotient

For a surjection of $R$-algebras $S\to S'=S/I$, the natural sequence of $S'$-modules

$$I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'\longrightarrow\Omega_{S'/R}\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. Its first map sends the class of $f\in I$ to $df\otimes1$. No injectivity is asserted for that map.

Proof. For $f_1,f_2\in I$, the Leibniz identity gives $d(f_1f_2)=f_1df_2+f_2df_1$, which becomes zero after tensoring with $S/I$. The first map is therefore well-defined on $I/I^2$. For $s\in S$ and $f\in I$, the identity $d(sf)=s\,df+f\,ds$ shows its $S/I$-linearity.

Let $Q$ be the quotient of $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'$ by the submodule generated by all $df\otimes1$ with $f\in I$. The rule

$$S'\longrightarrow Q,\qquad \overline s\longmapsto[ds\otimes1]$$

does not depend on the lift $s$, because changing the lift adds an element of $I$. It is an $R$-derivation by the Leibniz rule. Every $R$-derivation from $S'$ to an $S'$-module, composed with $S\to S'$, kills $I$. The universal property of $\Omega_{S/R}$ therefore factors it uniquely through this displayed derivation. Thus $Q$ represents the universal $R$-derivation of $S'$, giving the canonical identification $Q\cong\Omega_{S'/R}$. This proves exactness. Surjectivity is also visible directly: the target is generated by the differentials of elements of $S'$, all of which lift from $S$.

In terms of the original relation calculation, the kernel of $\Omega_{S/R}\to\Omega_{S'/R}$ is generated by $I\Omega_{S/R}$ and the differentials of elements of $I$. The identity $i\,ds=d(is)-s\,di$ even puts the first set of generators in the span of the second. If the differential presentation expresses a relation using an element $a\in S$ whose image in $S'$ comes from $r\in R$, then $a-\alpha(r)\in I$ and $da=d(a-\alpha(r))$, because $d\alpha(r)=0$. This recovers exactly the stated first map with the base ring fixed. ∎

Theorem. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz

Let $k$ be a field. In the polynomial ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and more generally in every finite-type $k$-algebra $A$:

  1. The residue field at a maximal ideal is a finite extension of $k$.
  2. A radical ideal is the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain it.

Proof. A complete proof of field finiteness that precedes dimension theory is AG-CA 06, Section 1, Theorem 1.3. It proves Artin–Tate, then shows that a rational function field of positive transcendence degree cannot be generated by finitely many algebra elements, because any finite list of denominators misses an irreducible polynomial. Applied to the finite-type field $A/\mathfrak m$, this proves (1). Section 2, Theorems 2.1–2.2 gives both conclusions, including their localization argument.

We retain also the polynomial induction through constructibility. It suffices for (1) to consider polynomial rings, since every finite-type algebra is their quotient. The assertion for zero variables is immediate. For the induction step, put $L=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak m$ and let $\mathfrak p$ be the contraction to $k[x_n]$. If $\mathfrak p\ne0$, it is generated by an irreducible polynomial, and $k'=k[x_n]/\mathfrak p$ is a finite field extension of $k$ embedded in $L$. The remaining images generate $L$ as an algebra over $k'$, so there is a surjection $k'[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]\to L$. Induction makes $L/k'$ finite, hence makes $L/k$ finite.

If $\mathfrak p=0$, the inclusion $k[x_n]\subset L$ is finite type and, since its base is Noetherian, finitely presented. Chevalley's theorem, with its complete affine proof in AG-MO 06, Sections 3–5, makes its spectrum image constructible. That image is the singleton containing the generic point. A constructible subset containing the generic point of this integral spectrum contains a nonempty basic open $D(f)$: in a finite union of locally closed pieces, one piece contains the generic point, and its closed part is then the whole spectrum. Such a $D(f)$ has infinitely many closed points. Indeed, the Euclidean argument gives infinitely many monic irreducibles in $k[x_n]$—a product of any finite proposed list, plus one, has a new irreducible factor—and only finitely many divide $f$. This contradicts the singleton image. The induction is complete. It is an alternative once Chevalley's theorem is available; the field-finiteness proof in AG-CA 06 supplies the result independently of that route.

For (2), let $I\subset A$ be radical and choose $f\notin I$. The ring $B=(A/I)_f$ is nonzero: otherwise some power of $f$ would lie in $I$, contradicting radicality. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $B$ and put $L=B/\mathfrak n$. Part (1) makes $L/k$ finite. The contraction $\mathfrak m\subset A$ contains $I$ and avoids $f$, since $f$ is invertible in $B$. The domain $A/\mathfrak m$ is a $k$-subalgebra of the finite-dimensional field $L$, hence is itself finite-dimensional over $k$. Multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism of this domain and therefore surjective. It has an inverse in the domain, showing that $A/\mathfrak m$ is a field. Thus $\mathfrak m$ is maximal.

Every element outside $I$ is consequently excluded by some maximal ideal containing $I$, proving the required intersection equality. The reverse inclusion is immediate. For $I=A$, the intersection is empty and is interpreted as $A$, so this case is included as well. ∎

Lemma. Transporting the local flatness criterion

Consider a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc} R&\longrightarrow&R'\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ S&\longrightarrow&S' \end{array}$$

whose rings are Noetherian and local and whose homomorphisms are local. Suppose $S'$ is a localization of $S\otimes_RR'$. Let $I$ be a proper ideal of $R$, let $M$ be a finite $S$-module, and put

$$I'=IR',\qquad M'=M\otimes_SS'.$$

If $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the natural map

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',R'/I')$$

is zero, then $M'$ is flat over $R'$.

Proof. Write $B=R/I$, $B'=R'/I'$, $A=S\otimes_RR'$ and $N=M\otimes_RR'$. The ideal $I'$ is proper because $R\to R'$ is local. The module $M'$ is the localization of $N$ corresponding to $A\to S'$. Before this localization,

$$N/I'N\cong(M/IM)\otimes_BB'$$

is flat over $B'$ by base change. Localization in the acting algebra preserves this flatness: tensor an injection of $B'$-modules with $N/I'N$ and then apply the exact localization functor. Thus $M'/I'M'$ is flat over $B'$. The local flatness criterion for a proper ideal reduces the problem to vanishing of $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',B')$.

We prove the two surjections needed for that vanishing. Choose a free $R$-module $F$ mapping onto $M$, with kernel $K$, and put

$$T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B),\qquad L=\operatorname{im}(K/IK\longrightarrow F/IF).$$

The sequence $0\to L\to F/IF\to M/IM\to0$ stays exact after tensoring with any $B$-module, since its last term is flat. Tensoring $T\to K/IK\to L\to0$ with $B'$ is right exact. It follows that the kernel of $K\otimes_RB'\to F\otimes_RB'$ is the image of $T\otimes_BB'$. The kernel is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B')$, so we obtain

$$T\otimes_RR'=T\otimes_BB' \twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B').$$

For the second map, let $K'$ be the kernel of $F\otimes_RR'\to N$. There is a surjection $K\otimes_RR'\to K'$. After tensoring over $R'$ with $B'$, every element of

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B') =\ker(K'\otimes_{R'}B'\longrightarrow F\otimes_RB')$$

therefore has a lift in $K\otimes_RB'$. That lift has zero image in $F\otimes_RB'$, so belongs to $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B')$. Hence

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B') \twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B').$$

These maps are the natural comparison maps, as is apparent from the free presentation. Neither argument assumes flatness of $R\to R'$.

Tor in the last display commutes with localization of its $A$-module argument. Indeed, compute it by a free $R'$-resolution of $B'$; tensoring that resolution with $N$ gives a complex of $A$-modules, and exact localization commutes with its homology. Consequently,

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B')\otimes_AS' \cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',B').$$

The two surjections show that the localized target is generated, over $S'$, by the natural images of elements of $T$. Those images are all zero by hypothesis. Thus the target vanishes, and the ideal criterion gives the required flatness. This is also the transport argument used in the eventual-flatness lemma. ∎

Lemma. Detecting faithful flatness on fibres

For a flat $R$-module $M$, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. Tensoring with $M$ is faithfully flat: it preserves and reflects exactness of complexes of $R$-modules.
  2. If $N$ is a nonzero $R$-module, then $M\otimes_RN\ne0$.
  3. For each prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$, one has $M\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\ne0$.
  4. For each maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$, one has $M/\mathfrak mM\ne0$.

Proof. Under (1), the identity of a nonzero module cannot become zero after tensoring. Equivalently, reflection of exactness applied to the complex $0\to N\to0$ prevents its middle term from becoming zero. This proves (2). Residue fields are nonzero modules, so (2) implies (3), and restricting to maximal primes proves (3)$\Rightarrow$(4).

Suppose (4) holds. Let $N_1\to N_2\to N_3$ be a complex that becomes exact at its middle term after tensoring with $M$. Its middle homology $H$ satisfies $H\otimes_RM=0$: flatness identifies the tensor of its kernel and image with the kernel and image of the tensored complex. If $x\in H$ is nonzero, its annihilator $I$ is proper, and the cyclic submodule it generates gives an injection $R/I\hookrightarrow H$. Flatness would then give

$$M/IM\hookrightarrow H\otimes_RM=0.$$

Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supset I$. The quotient map $M/IM\to M/\mathfrak mM$ would force the latter module to be zero, contradicting (4). Hence $H=0$. Tensoring already preserves exactness by flatness, and now also reflects it, proving (1). No finite-generation condition on any of these modules is used. ∎

Remark. Quotient and localization descriptions of a fibre

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring map and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. Write $S_{\mathfrak p}=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}S$ and

$$\begin{aligned} C&=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\otimes_RS\\ &\cong S_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}\\ &\cong(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}(S/\mathfrak pS). \end{aligned}$$

The canonical diagram has the following two halves, joined along the column $R\to S$:

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} C&\longleftarrow&S_{\mathfrak p}&\longleftarrow&S\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\ \kappa(\mathfrak p)&\longleftarrow&R_{\mathfrak p}&\longleftarrow&R \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{ccccc} S&\longrightarrow&S/\mathfrak pS&\longrightarrow&C\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\ R&\longrightarrow&R/\mathfrak p&\longrightarrow&\kappa(\mathfrak p). \end{array}$$

For example, the first horizontal arrow in the upper row is quotient by $\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}$, while the last is localization by $R\setminus\mathfrak p$. The displayed identifications of $C$ identify the two outer columns, including their structure maps. Every square commutes.

The localization description of spectra and the quotient description show that each horizontal arrow induces a homeomorphism from the spectrum of its target onto a subspace of the spectrum of its source. After applying $\operatorname{Spec}$, all four squares are fibre squares of topological spaces. For localization the relevant subspace consists of primes avoiding the multiplicative set, and its inverse image is the same avoidance condition upstairs. For quotient it consists of primes containing the ideal, and its inverse image is the containment condition for the extended ideal. These descriptions verify both the sets and their subspace topologies.

In particular, primes of $C$ correspond exactly to primes of $S$ whose contraction is $\mathfrak p$. A commutative unital ring has a prime ideal precisely when it is nonzero. Thus

$$\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}(S)\to \operatorname{Spec}(R)) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\ne0.$$

If $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$, extend the two halves by placing, respectively, the rows

$$\kappa(\mathfrak q)\ \longleftarrow\ S_{\mathfrak q}\ \longleftarrow\ S$$ $$S\ \longrightarrow\ S/\mathfrak q\ \longrightarrow\ \kappa(\mathfrak q)$$

above the $S$-row. The vertical maps from that row, from left to right across the joined diagram, are

$$\begin{gathered} C\to\kappa(\mathfrak q),\qquad S_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q},\qquad 1_S,\\ S/\mathfrak pS\to S/\mathfrak q,\qquad C\to\kappa(\mathfrak q). \end{gathered}$$

They exist because $\varphi(R\setminus\mathfrak p)$ avoids $\mathfrak q$, and because $\mathfrak pS\subset\mathfrak q$. The two maps from $C$ agree under its canonical identifications. This gives the extended commutative diagram with identical outer columns. Its new horizontal maps, too, are quotients or localizations and induce homeomorphisms onto their images on spectra.

Lemma. Six descriptions of an isolated point

Let $S$ be a finite-type algebra over a field $k$, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. The singleton $\{\mathfrak q\}$ is open in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$.
  2. The $k$-vector space $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is finite dimensional.
  3. There is $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$.
  4. The dimension $\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ of the space at this point is zero.
  5. The point $\mathfrak q$ is closed and $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=0$.
  6. The residue extension $\kappa(\mathfrak q)/k$ is finite and $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=0$.

When these hold, there is a product decomposition

$$S\cong S_{\mathfrak q}\times S'$$

with $S'$ a finite-type $k$-algebra, whose first projection is localization at $\mathfrak q$. Moreover, every $g$ as in (3) gives the canonical isomorphism $S_g\cong S_{\mathfrak q}$.

Proof. First assume (1). Choose a principal neighborhood $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$. Its only prime is maximal in $S_g$. Since $S_g$ is finite type over $k$, the Nullstellensatz makes its residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ finite over $k$. The subalgebra $S/\mathfrak q\subset\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is then a finite-dimensional domain over $k$. Multiplication by any nonzero element is injective on that finite-dimensional space and hence surjective, so the subalgebra is a field. Thus $\mathfrak q$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ as well as open.

The clopen product decomposition gives $S=S_1\times S'$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(S_1)$ the single point $\mathfrak q$. The factor $S_1$ is local and equals $S_{\mathfrak q}$ canonically. It is a finite-type, zero-dimensional $k$-algebra. Noether normalization makes it finite over a polynomial subalgebra with zero variables, hence finite over $k$. This proves (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) and the asserted product decomposition. Both factors are quotients of $S$, so are finite type.

Assume (2). The ring $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is Artinian and local, hence has only one prime. For the localization map, write

$$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0.$$

The ring $S$ is Noetherian, so $K$ is finite over $S$. The module $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is finite over $S$ because any finite $k$-basis also generates it as an $S$-module; thus $Q$ is finite as well. Both $K$ and $Q$ vanish after localization at $\mathfrak q$. Choose a common $g\notin\mathfrak q$ killing finite generating sets of both modules after localization. Then $S_g\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism, so $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$. This proves (2)$\Rightarrow$(3), while (3)$\Rightarrow$(1) follows from the definition of a principal open.

An open singleton has dimension zero, giving (1)$\Rightarrow$(4). Conversely, (4) supplies a principal neighborhood $D(g)$ of dimension zero. Its ring $S_g$ is Noetherian, so the zero-dimensional ring theorem makes its spectrum a finite discrete space. The point $\mathfrak q$ is isolated there, and hence in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$. This proves (4)$\Rightarrow$(1).

The dimension formula at a point reads

$$\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}(S) =\dim S_{\mathfrak q}+\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak q).$$

For a closed point the Nullstellensatz makes the transcendence degree zero, so (5) implies (4). Under (4), both nonnegative terms on the right vanish. The residue field is a finitely generated field extension of $k$, so transcendence degree zero makes it finite; this gives (6). Finally, under (6) the finite-dimensional-domain argument in the first paragraph makes $S/\mathfrak q$ a field, proving (5).

The product assertion was obtained above. For any $g$ satisfying (3), the ring $S_g$ has exactly one prime and is consequently local. Its localization at that prime changes nothing, and equals $S_{\mathfrak q}$. This proves the assertion for every such $g$. ∎

Lemma. Finiteness after arbitrary base change

Given $R\to S$, an $S$-module $M$, and $R\to R'$, put

$$S'=S\otimes_RR',\qquad M'=M\otimes_RR'.$$

Then:

  1. If $M$ is finite over $S$, then $M'$ is finite over $S'$.
  2. If $M$ is finitely presented over $S$, then $M'$ is finitely presented over $S'$.
  3. If $S$ is a finite-type $R$-algebra, then $S'$ is a finite-type $R'$-algebra.
  4. If $S$ is a finitely presented $R$-algebra, then $S'$ is a finitely presented $R'$-algebra.

Proof. The canonical identification

$$M\otimes_SS'\cong M\otimes_RR'$$

sends $m\otimes(s\otimes r')$ to $sm\otimes r'$. Its inverse sends $m\otimes r'$ to $m\otimes(1\otimes r')$; the balancing relations verify that both maps are well-defined. Tensoring a finite generating surjection $S^n\to M$ with $S'$ gives a surjection $(S')^n\to M'$. Tensoring a finite presentation $S^a\to S^b\to M\to0$ gives the right exact sequence $(S')^a\to(S')^b\to M'\to0$. These prove (1) and (2).

For the algebra assertions, take any polynomial presentation

$$S=R[x_i\mid i\in E]/(f_j\mid j\in F).$$

The universal property of polynomial algebras and quotients identifies its base change with

$$S'=R'[x_i\mid i\in E]/(f'_j\mid j\in F),$$

where $f'_j$ is obtained by mapping every coefficient to $R'$. Equivalently, a map from this displayed algebra to an $R'$-algebra is exactly an $R$-algebra map from $S$ compatible with its $R'$-structure, which is the tensor-product universal property. If $E$ is finite, the resulting algebra is finite type. If both $E$ and $F$ are finite, its presentation is finite. This proves (3) and (4), with no flatness assumption on the base change. ∎

Lemma. Formal smoothness from a square-zero section

Let $P\to S$ be a surjection of $R$-algebras with kernel $J$, where $P$ is a polynomial algebra on any set of variables. Then $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if and only if $P/J^2\to S$ admits an $R$-algebra section.

Proof. The kernel of $P/J^2\to S$ is $J/J^2$ and has square zero. If $S$ is formally smooth, lift the identity map of $S$ across this surjection. The lift is the required section.

Conversely, fix a section $\sigma\colon S\to P/J^2$. Test formal smoothness against an $R$-algebra $A$, an ideal $I\subset A$ with $I^2=0$, and an $R$-algebra map $u\colon S\to A/I$. Lift the image under $u$ of each polynomial variable independently to $A$. Those choices define an $R$-algebra map $\psi\colon P\to A$ lifting $P\to S\to A/I$, even if the variable set is infinite. For each $j\in J$, one has $\psi(j)\in I$, so $\psi(J^2)=0$. The induced map $\bar\psi\colon P/J^2\to A$, composed with $\sigma$, lifts $u$. This proves the lifting property. ∎

Lemma. The split conormal criterion

For a polynomial presentation $P\twoheadrightarrow S$ over $R$ with kernel $J$, formal smoothness of $S$ over $R$ is equivalent to split exactness of

$$0\longrightarrow J/J^2\xrightarrow{\ d\ } E\longrightarrow\Omega_{S/R}\longrightarrow0,$$

where $E=\Omega_{P/R}\otimes_PS$.

Here $d$ sends $j\bmod J^2$ to $dj\otimes1$, and splitting is as a sequence of $S$-modules. The assertion permits an arbitrary variable set.

Proof. Right exactness is the quotient differential sequence. Suppose first that $S$ is formally smooth, and take the section $\sigma\colon S\to C=P/J^2$ supplied by the preceding lemma. If $\pi\colon C\to S$ is the quotient map, then

$$D(c)=c-\sigma(\pi(c))\in J/J^2$$

defines an $R$-derivation from $C$ to the $S$-module $J/J^2$. In fact, write $c=\sigma(s)+n$ and $c'=\sigma(s')+n'$ with $n,n'\in J/J^2$. Their product has nilpotent part $sn'+s'n$, since $nn'=0$. This is exactly the product rule, and $D$ vanishes on the image of $R$. Its restriction to $J/J^2$ is the identity.

For clarity, the canonical map

$$\Omega_{P/R}\otimes_PS \longrightarrow\Omega_{C/R}\otimes_CS$$

is an isomorphism. Applying the quotient differential sequence to $P\to P/J^2$ shows that its possible kernel is generated by $d(J^2)$. Every such differential is a sum of terms $j\,dj'$ with $j,j'\in J$, which vanish after tensoring with $S$. The derivation $D$ therefore induces an $S$-linear retraction $E\to J/J^2$ of the first arrow. This proves both its injectivity and the splitting of the sequence.

For the reverse implication, choose an $S$-linear section

$$\tau\colon\Omega_{S/R}\longrightarrow E.$$

For each $\lambda\in S$, choose a lift $x_\lambda\in P$. Exactness gives $f_\lambda\in J$ with

$$df_\lambda=dx_\lambda-\tau(d\lambda)\quad\text{in }E.$$

Set $y_\lambda=x_\lambda-f_\lambda$, so $dy_\lambda=\tau(d\lambda)$ in $E$ and $y_\lambda$ maps to $\lambda$. We claim that

$$s\colon S\longrightarrow P/J^2,\qquad \lambda\longmapsto y_\lambda\bmod J^2$$

is an $R$-algebra section. The injectivity of $J/J^2\to E$ says that whenever $h\in J$ and $dh=0$ in $E$, one has $h\in J^2$. This observation verifies every required identity.

First, another pair of choices for the same $\lambda$ gives a difference $h\in J$ whose differential is zero, since both corrected lifts have differential $\tau(d\lambda)$. Thus the value of $s$ is independent of the choices. Next,

$$y_\lambda+y_\mu-y_{\lambda+\mu}\in J,\qquad d(y_\lambda+y_\mu-y_{\lambda+\mu}) =\tau(d\lambda+d\mu-d(\lambda+\mu))=0.$$

The difference belongs to $J^2$, so $s$ is additive. For multiplication, the coefficients of $y_\lambda$ and $y_\mu$ in $E$ are their images $\lambda$ and $\mu$ in $S$. Hence

$$\begin{aligned} d(y_\lambda y_\mu-y_{\lambda\mu}) &=\lambda\tau(d\mu)+\mu\tau(d\lambda)-\tau(d(\lambda\mu))\\ &=0. \end{aligned}$$

The element being differentiated lies in $J$, and hence in $J^2$. This proves $s(\lambda)s(\mu)=s(\lambda\mu)$. Written in the original lifts, the same calculation uses

$$y_\lambda y_\mu-y_{\lambda\mu} \equiv x_\lambda x_\mu-x_{\lambda\mu} -x_\mu f_\lambda-x_\lambda f_\mu+f_{\lambda\mu} \pmod{J^2},$$

because $f_\lambda f_\mu\in J^2$.

Finally, if $\lambda$ is the image of $r\in R$, then $y_\lambda-r\in J$ and $d(y_\lambda-r)=\tau(d\lambda)=0$. Thus $s(\lambda)$ is the image of $r$ in $P/J^2$. This proves compatibility with the base ring and, taking $r=1$, preservation of the unit. The composite $S\xrightarrow{s}P/J^2\to S$ is the identity by construction. The preceding square-zero-section criterion now proves formal smoothness. ∎

Lemma. The naive cotangent complex of a quotient

For a surjection $A\twoheadrightarrow B$ with kernel $I$, there is a homotopy equivalence

$$\mathrm{NL}_{B/A}\simeq[I/I^2\longrightarrow0],$$

where the conormal module occupies homological degree one. In particular,

$$H_1(L_{B/A})=I/I^2.$$

Proof. The algebra $A$, viewed over itself, is a polynomial algebra on the empty set. Thus $A\twoheadrightarrow B$ is an allowed polynomial presentation. Its conormal complex has terms $I/I^2$ and $\Omega_{A/A}\otimes_AB=0$. The complete comparison-of-presentations theorem, AG-CA 16, Theorem 7.1 identifies this complex with the canonical presentation complex up to homotopy. Its proof constructs polynomial lifts in both directions and a derivation homotopy between each composite and the identity; it applies equally to an empty or infinite variable set.

Taking degree-one homology gives the asserted module. Here $H_1(L_{B/A})$ is the notation for $H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{B/A})$ used in these algebraic criteria. The assertion about the two-term complex makes no claim that the full cotangent complex has no higher homology. ∎

Lemma. Finite modules over a Noetherian ring

If $R$ is Noetherian and $M$ is a finite $R$-module, then every submodule of $M$ is finite, the module $M$ is finitely presented, and each increasing sequence of submodules of $M$ stabilizes.

Proof. We prove the submodule assertion by induction on the size of a generating list for $M$. The zero module is immediate. A cyclic module has the form $R/I$; its submodules are $J/I$ with $I\subset J$, and each such $J$ has a finite generating list.

For a list of length $n>1$, let $M_0$ be the submodule generated by its first $n-1$ members. The quotient $M/M_0$ is cyclic. Given $N\subset M$, the sequence

$$0\longrightarrow N\cap M_0\longrightarrow N \longrightarrow\operatorname{im}(N\to M/M_0)\longrightarrow0$$

has finitely generated end terms by induction. A finite generating list of the first term, together with lifts of a generating list of the last, generates $N$. This proves the assertion.

Now choose a finite free surjection $R^n\to M$. Its kernel is a submodule of a finite module and is therefore finite. A generating list of that kernel gives a finite presentation of $M$.

Finally, if $N_1\subset N_2\subset\cdots\subset M$, their union $N$ is a submodule, hence has finitely many generators. All these generators occur in one $N_j$, so $N_i=N_j$ for every $i\geq j$. More generally, this explains the equivalence between the ascending chain condition and finite generation of every submodule: if a submodule were not finite, repeatedly choosing an element outside the submodule generated by the previous choices would give a strictly increasing chain. ∎

Lemma. Spectrum embeddings from unit multiples

Historical source: EGA I, Corollary 1.2.4.

Suppose $\varphi\colon R\to S$ has the property that every $g\in S$ can be expressed as $u\varphi(f)$, where $f\in R$ and $u$ is a unit of $S$. Then contraction gives a homeomorphism

$$\operatorname{Spec}(S)\longrightarrow \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}(S)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)).$$

Proof. Write $j$ for the contraction map. It is continuous, since $j^{-1}(D(f))=D(\varphi(f))$. If primes $\mathfrak q_1,\mathfrak q_2$ have the same contraction, membership of $g=u\varphi(f)$ in either prime is equivalent to membership of $f$ in that common contraction. The primes therefore have exactly the same elements, proving injectivity.

For the same expression of $g$, the unit $u$ does not affect its principal open, so

$$D(g)=j^{-1}(D(f)),\qquad j(D(g))=j(\operatorname{Spec}S)\cap D(f).$$

Principal opens form a basis. Thus the continuous bijection onto the image sends each basic open to an open of that image, and its inverse is continuous. ∎

Lemma. A product ring gives a disjoint spectrum

The projections from $R=R_1\times R_2$ induce a homeomorphism

$$\operatorname{Spec}(R_1)\amalg\operatorname{Spec}(R_2) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(R).$$

Proof. Let $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$. Their sum is one, their product is zero, and each is idempotent. Inverting $e_1$ makes it equal to one and makes $e_2$ zero. The first projection consequently induces

$$R_{e_1}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R_1,\qquad (a,b)/e_1^n\longmapsto a.$$

Its inverse is $a\mapsto(a,0)/1$; the identity $(1,0)/1=1$ verifies that this is a unital homomorphism. The same construction identifies $R_{e_2}$ with $R_2$.

Every prime of $R$ contains one of $e_1,e_2$, because their product is zero, and cannot contain both, because their sum is one. Hence $D(e_1)$ and $D(e_2)$ form a disjoint open cover. Each is also closed, being the complement of the other. The spectrum-localization homeomorphisms identify these two pieces with the two displayed spectra, and agree with the original projections. Their union is the required homeomorphism. This also covers a zero factor. ∎

Lemma. The equalizer for a finite principal cover

If $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ generate the unit ideal of $R$, then

$$0\longrightarrow R\xrightarrow{\alpha}\bigoplus_iR_{f_i} \xrightarrow{\beta}\bigoplus_{i,j}R_{f_if_j}$$

is exact. The first map sends $r$ to its local images. The $(i,j)$ component of the second is the difference between the images of the $i$th and $j$th entries on their common localization.

Proof. We prove the same assertion with an arbitrary $R$-module $M$ in place of $R$:

$$0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow\bigoplus_iM_{f_i} \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{i,j}M_{f_if_j}.$$

The maps are $m\mapsto(m/1)_i$ and $(s_i)_i\mapsto(s_i-s_j)_{i,j}$ after passing to the indicated localizations. Their composite is zero.

Exactness can be checked at maximal ideals. To recall why, localization is exact and so commutes with the homology modules of this complex. A nonzero element $h$ of a module has a proper annihilator; in a maximal ideal containing that annihilator, $h/1$ remains nonzero, since no element outside that ideal can kill $h$. Thus vanishing of every maximal localization forces a module to be zero.

At a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, at least one $f_a$ is a unit in $R_{\mathfrak m}$. Localization twice identifies the $a$th term with $M_{\mathfrak m}$ and the $(a,i)$ overlap with $(M_{\mathfrak m})_{f_i}$. The first map is injective because its $a$th component is the identity. If a tuple belongs to the kernel of the difference map, its $a$th entry is an element $s$ of $M_{\mathfrak m}$, and the $(a,i)$ equality says that its $i$th entry is exactly the image of $s$. The tuple therefore comes from the first map. This proves exactness at each maximal localization, hence globally. Taking $M=R$ proves the stated ring sequence. If the cover is empty, its unit-ideal hypothesis forces $R=0$, and the sequence is again exact. ∎

Definition. Formally étale algebras

An $R$-algebra $S$ is formally étale if, for every $R$-algebra $A$ and every ideal $I\subset A$ satisfying $I^2=0$, reduction gives a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-alg}}(S,A) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-alg}}(S,A/I).$$

Thus each $R$-algebra map from $S$ to a square-zero quotient lifts to $A$ in exactly one way.

Lemma. Right exactness of tensor products

For an exact sequence of $R$-modules

$$M_1\xrightarrow{f}M_2\xrightarrow{g}M_3\longrightarrow0$$

and any $R$-module $N$, the sequence

$$M_1\otimes_RN\xrightarrow{f\otimes1}M_2\otimes_RN \xrightarrow{g\otimes1}M_3\otimes_RN\longrightarrow0$$

is exact.

Proof. We give the tensor–Hom argument, including the adjunction it uses. For arbitrary $R$-modules $U,N,P$, an $R$-linear map $a\colon U\otimes_RN\to P$ determines

$$U\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P),\qquad u\longmapsto(n\longmapsto a(u\otimes n)).$$

Additivity and the scalar relation in a tensor product make this map $R$-linear. Conversely, an $R$-linear map $b\colon U\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)$ gives the bilinear function $(u,n)\mapsto b(u)(n)$, and hence a unique map $U\otimes_RN\to P$. The two constructions are inverse, are linear on the Hom modules, and commute with maps in each argument. They prove the natural adjunction.

A map $M_2\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)$ that vanishes on $f(M_1)$ factors uniquely through $M_3$, because $M_3$ is the cokernel of $f$. Under this adjunction, it follows that a map $M_2\otimes_RN\to P$ vanishing on the image of $f\otimes1$ factors uniquely through $M_3\otimes_RN$. This proves that $M_3\otimes_RN$ is the cokernel of $f\otimes1$. Explicitly, if $Q$ is that cokernel, the factorization property constructs maps $Q\to M_3\otimes_RN$ and back; uniqueness makes their composites the identities. The first map is the one induced by $g\otimes1$. It is also visibly surjective, since each generator $m_3\otimes n$ lifts by choosing a preimage of $m_3$ under $g$. These facts prove the displayed exact sequence. ∎

Lemma. When an element vanishes in a directed colimit

Let $(M_i,\mu_{ij})$ be a system of modules over a directed preordered set, and let $\mu_i\colon M_i\to M=\operatorname{colim}_iM_i$ be its structure maps. Then

$$\mu_i(x)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mu_{ij}(x)=0\text{ for some }j\geq i.$$

Proof. Here is the explicit colimit construction. Start with the disjoint union of the sets $M_i$ and declare $x\in M_i$ equivalent to $y\in M_j$ when their images agree in some $M_k$ with $k\geq i,j$. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. For transitivity, move the two witnessing equalities to a common upper index; the middle representatives then agree there, giving equality of the first and last representatives.

Add two classes by moving their representatives to any common upper index and adding there. Define scalar multiplication using any representative. To check independence of representatives or of the upper index, move the finitely many equality witnesses to one further upper index. The proposed results agree at that index. The same procedure reduces all module axioms to the corresponding axioms in one $M_k$. The maps $M_i\to M$ are linear and compatible. Every compatible family of maps $M_i\to Q$ has a unique induced linear map on these classes, because equivalent representatives have the same image. This proves the universal property of the colimit.

All stage zeros represent the same class. Applying the equivalence relation to $x\in M_i$ and $0\in M_i$ gives exactly the criterion stated above. Neither the preorder nor the module transition maps are required to be injective. ∎

Lemma. Integral algebras over a field

Let $S$ be an algebra over a field $k$.

  1. A finite-dimensional $k$-algebra that is a domain is a field.
  2. An integral $k$-algebra that is a domain is a field.
  3. In any integral $k$-algebra, every prime ideal is maximal.

Proof. For (1), take $0\ne s\in S$. Multiplication by $s$ is injective since $S$ is a domain. It is therefore surjective on the finite-dimensional $k$-space $S$, so some $t$ satisfies $st=1$.

For (2), any $s\in S$ belongs to the finite-dimensional subalgebra $k[s]$: a monic equation for $s$ expresses every sufficiently high power in terms of lower powers. This subalgebra is a domain, so (1) makes it a field. Each nonzero $s$ thus has an inverse already in $k[s]$, and hence in $S$.

For (3), take a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$. The domain $S/\mathfrak q$ is integral over $k$, because monic equations descend to quotients. Part (2) makes it a field, so $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. If $S$ has no primes the assertion is vacuous. ∎

Lemma. A flat local map is faithfully flat

Every flat local homomorphism $R\to S$ of local rings is faithfully flat.

Proof. If $\mathfrak m$ and $\mathfrak n$ are their maximal ideals, locality gives $\mathfrak mS\subset\mathfrak n$, so $S/\mathfrak mS\ne0$. This is the only maximal fibre of the base. The maximal-fibre test for a flat module, applied to the $R$-module $S$, proves faithfulness. No finiteness or Noetherian hypothesis is needed. ∎

Lemma. Faithful flatness and surjectivity on spectra

For a flat ring map $R\to S$, the following are equivalent:

  1. The map is faithfully flat.
  2. Every prime of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.
  3. Every maximal ideal of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.

Proof. The fibre diagram identifies primes above $\mathfrak p$ with primes of $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Thus $\mathfrak p$ has a preimage exactly when that fibre ring is nonzero. The all-prime and maximal-prime fibre conditions are precisely the two equivalent tests in the faithfully flat module lemma. This proves all three equivalences, including the empty-spectrum case. ∎

Lemma. Isolating one finite branch by an étale neighborhood

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ contract to $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$, and suppose the map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$. There exist an étale $R$-algebra $R'$, a prime $\mathfrak p'$ above $\mathfrak p$, and a product decomposition

$$S\otimes_RR'=A\times B$$

such that:

  1. The canonical residue map $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak p')$ is an isomorphism.
  2. The algebra $A$ is finite over $R'$.
  3. There is exactly one prime $\mathfrak r$ of $A$ above $\mathfrak p'$.
  4. This prime contracts to $\mathfrak q$ in $S$.
  5. No prime of $B$ contracts both to $\mathfrak q$ in $S$ and to $\mathfrak p'$ in $R'$.

Proof. Let $C\subset S$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $S$, and set $\mathfrak q_C=\mathfrak q\cap C$. The complete arbitrary-base algebraic Zariski Main theorem is AG-MO 06, Theorem 2A.1. It supplies $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q_C$ with $C_g=S_g$. This is a pointwise theorem and requires only finite type.

Put $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and consider $F=S\otimes_Rk$ and $F_C=C\otimes_Rk$. The chosen point $\bar{\mathfrak q}\in\operatorname{Spec}(F)$ is isolated by the quasi-finite fibre criterion. Its image $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ lies in the open on which $(F_C)_g=F_g$, so it too is isolated. It is closed because $F_C$ is integral over $k$, and every prime in an integral algebra over a field is maximal. Moreover, $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ is the only point of $\operatorname{Spec}(F)$ above $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$: any point above it avoids $g$ and must correspond under that localization isomorphism.

The clopen singleton gives

$$F_C=F_1\times F_2,\qquad \operatorname{Spec}(F_1)=\{\bar{\mathfrak q}_C\}.$$

Let $e=(1,0)$. Since $F_C=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}(C/\mathfrak pC)$, write $e$ as $c/r$ with $c\in C$ and $r\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$. Thus the image of $c$ is $(\bar r,0)$. In particular, $c$ avoids $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ and belongs to every other prime of $F_C$.

Choose a monic equation $f(c)=0$ over $R$. In $k[T]$ write

$$\bar f=T^a\bar h,\qquad \bar h(0)\ne0.$$

Both factors are monic. Multiplying $f$ by $T$ if necessary ensures $a\geq1$ while keeping $f(c)=0$.

We spell out the étale factor-lifting construction. For any monic $f\in R[T]$ and coprime monic factors $\bar h,\bar i$ over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, the case $f=1$ has the immediate lifts $h=i=1$ over $R$. Otherwise introduce coefficient variables for monic polynomials $H,I$ of their respective degrees. The coefficient equations $HI=f$ define an $R$-algebra $U$ with equally many variables and equations. Evaluating at $\bar h,\bar i$ gives $U\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The coefficient Jacobian represents

$$k[T]_{<\deg\bar h}\oplus k[T]_{<\deg\bar i} \longrightarrow k[T]_{<\deg f},$$ $$ (v,w)\longmapsto\bar i\,v+\bar h\,w.$$

It is invertible: reduce modulo $\bar h$ to determine $v$ uniquely using the inverse of $\bar i$, then divide the remainder by the monic $\bar h$ to determine $w$. Consequently its determinant $\Delta$ has nonzero value at the chosen evaluation. The coefficient-Jacobian construction makes $R'=U_\Delta$ étale over $R$. The kernel $\mathfrak p'$ of its evaluation in $k$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$.
