The fraction field of the image contains $\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)=k$ and is contained in $k$, so its residue field is canonically $k$, even when $\mathfrak p$ is not maximal.

The same coefficient matrix over $U_\Delta$ is invertible. Solving it with target polynomial $1$ gives a Bézout identity for $H,I$. Their images $h,i\in R'[T]$ therefore satisfy

$$f=hi,\qquad \alpha h+\beta i=1$$

for suitable polynomials $\alpha,\beta$, and have the prescribed reductions. This construction also permits prescribed factors which are not monic. If their leading coefficients are $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{-1}$, first invert a base element outside $\mathfrak p$ so that $\lambda$ lifts to a unit $u$. Apply the monic construction to $\lambda^{-1}\bar h$ and $\lambda\bar i$, and then multiply the lifts by $u$ and $u^{-1}$. The product, Bézout property and specified reductions are preserved. This preliminary principal localization is étale and keeps the same residue field.

Apply the construction with $\bar i=T^a$ and the above $\bar h$. In $C\otimes_RR'$, the elements $h(c),i(c)$ have product zero and generate the unit ideal. Their principal opens are disjoint and cover the spectrum, giving

$$C\otimes_RR'=C_1\times C_2,$$ $$C_1=(C\otimes_RR')_{i(c)},\qquad C_2=(C\otimes_RR')_{h(c)}.$$

The corresponding decomposition of the target is

$$S\otimes_RR'=S_1\times S_2,$$ $$S_1=(S\otimes_RR')_{i(c)},\qquad S_2=(S\otimes_RR')_{h(c)}.$$

The marked fibres are still $F_C$ and $F$. On the first factor of $F_C$, the element $i(c)$ becomes $\bar r^a$, a unit; on the second it is zero. The factor $C_1$ therefore has precisely $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ in its marked fibre. The unique-preimage property proved above shows that $S_1$ has precisely $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ in its marked fibre, while $S_2$ has no point over it. As a direct factor, $C_1$ is a quotient of the integral $R'$-algebra $C\otimes_RR'$, hence is integral over $R'$. Similarly, $S_1$ is finite type over $R'$. Base change and localization of $C_g=S_g$ give

$$(C_1)_g\cong(S_1)_g.$$

It remains to make $S_1$ finite by shrinking the base. We give the general argument. Suppose $T\to D\to E$ are ring maps, $D$ is integral over $T$, $E$ is finite type over $T$, and $D_g\to E_g$ is an isomorphism. If $g$ is a unit in $D\otimes_T\kappa(\mathfrak t)$, then the image of $V(g)\subset\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ under the integral map is a closed set missing $\mathfrak t$. Choose $b\in T\setminus\mathfrak t$ whose principal open avoids that image. No prime of $D_b$ contains $g$, so $g$ is a unit there, and also in $E_b$. The localization isomorphism then gives $D_b\cong E_b$. Thus $E_b$ is integral and finite type over $T_b$, hence finite: monic equations for a finite algebra generating list bound the powers needed to generate it as a module.

For $D=C_1$, the image of $g$ avoids the unique prime of its marked fibre, so is a unit in that fibre. Apply this argument at $\mathfrak p'$, using the closed-image property of integral maps. Replace $R'$ by the resulting principal localization, and localize both product factors. The first factor is now finite. Étaleness and the canonical residue-field isomorphism persist, and the marked fibres have not changed. Taking $A=(S_1)_b$ and $B=(S_2)_b$ proves all five assertions. ∎

Lemma. Fibrewise injectivity over an arbitrary local base

Let $R\to S$ be local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset R$, and let $u\colon M\to N$ be $S$-linear. Assume that $S$ is essentially of finite presentation over $R$, that $M,N$ are finitely presented over $S$, that $N$ is flat over $R$, and that

$$M/\mathfrak mM\longrightarrow N/\mathfrak mN$$

is injective. Then $u$ is injective and $\operatorname{coker}u$ is flat over $R$.

Proof. The finite local-model construction gives a directed system

$$R_\lambda\longrightarrow S_\lambda,\qquad u_\lambda\colon M_\lambda\longrightarrow N_\lambda$$

with colimit the given data. To include the map, descend finite presentations of both modules, images of the finitely many source generators, and the finitely many relations which these images satisfy. At one common stage this defines $u_\lambda$, and later maps are its base changes. Each $R_\lambda$ is essentially finite type over $\mathbb Z$, each $S_\lambda$ is a local localization of a finite-type $R_\lambda$-algebra, and both modules are finite over $S_\lambda$. In particular these rings are Noetherian. For $\mu\geq\lambda$, the ring $S_\mu$ is a localization of $S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu$, and the modules change by the same base change and localization.

By eventual flatness, choose a stage at which $N_\lambda$ is $R_\lambda$-flat. It remains flat at every later stage: first make the arbitrary base change on $R_\lambda$, then localize in the acting algebra. We restrict to this cofinal tail.

Write $\mathfrak m_\lambda$ for the maximal ideal of $R_\lambda$, $\kappa_\lambda=R_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda$, and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. The local transition maps give embeddings of these residue fields, with colimit $\kappa$. Put $\bar M_\lambda=M_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda M_\lambda$ and $\bar M=M/\mathfrak mM$. We must make the residue map $u_\lambda$ injective at a finite stage.

Fix one index $\lambda$ and consider

$$E_\lambda=\bar M_\lambda\otimes_{\kappa_\lambda}\kappa, \qquad \Psi_\lambda\colon E_\lambda\longrightarrow\bar M.$$

The ring

$$T_\lambda=(S_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda S_\lambda) \otimes_{\kappa_\lambda}\kappa$$

is a localization of a finite-type $\kappa$-algebra, hence Noetherian. The module $E_\lambda$ is finite over it, so $\ker\Psi_\lambda$ has a finite generating list $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r$.

Each $\xi_i$ uses only finitely many coefficients in $\kappa$. Represent these at a residue-field stage $\kappa_\mu$, with $\mu\geq\lambda$. Its image in $\bar M_\mu$ becomes zero in $\bar M=\operatorname{colim}_\nu\bar M_\nu$. The directed-colimit zero criterion makes that image zero at some later index. After taking one common upper index for the finite list, all the $\xi_i$ map to zero in $E_\mu$. This includes the case of an empty generating list.

For any $\nu\geq\mu$, the model base-change property gives

$$E_\nu=W_\nu^{-1}E_\lambda$$

for the image of a multiplicative set from $S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\nu$ in $T_\lambda$. Every element of $W_\nu$ maps to a unit in $S/\mathfrak mS$, because it was inverted in the ring $S_\nu$ mapping to $S$. If $x=y/w\in E_\nu$ maps to zero in $\bar M$, then $\Psi_\lambda(y)=0$. Express $y$ as a $T_\lambda$-linear combination of the $\xi_i$. These generators already vanish in $E_\mu$, and thus in $E_\nu$, so $x=0$. We have proved that $\Psi_\nu$ is injective for all $\nu\geq\mu$.

Since $\kappa_\nu\to\kappa$ is a field extension, $\bar M_\nu\to E_\nu$ is injective as well. Hence $\bar M_\nu\to\bar M$ is injective. Its composite with the assumed injection $\bar u\colon\bar M\to\bar N$ factors through the residue map $\bar u_\nu$. If an element is killed by $\bar u_\nu$, this composite kills it, so it is zero. Therefore $\bar u_\nu$ is injective.

At such a stage, the complete Noetherian fibre-injectivity theorem is AG-CA 08, Lemma 5.1, with its local flatness proof in Section 4. It applies to the finite $S_\nu$-modules $M_\nu,N_\nu$ and the $R_\nu$-flat target. It proves that $u_\nu$ is injective and its cokernel $Q_\nu$ is flat over $R_\nu$. Its proof first obtains injection modulo every power of the maximal ideal, uses Krull intersection over $S_\nu$, and then applies the Tor form of the local criterion to the cokernel.

Directed colimits preserve these injections: an element mapping to zero in the target colimit does so at a finite later stage, where the corresponding map is injective. Cokernels commute with the colimit, so $\operatorname{coker}u=\operatorname{colim}_\nu Q_\nu$. The flatness theorem for varying-ring colimits makes this an $R$-flat module. Thus both conclusions hold without a Noetherian assumption on the original rings. ∎

Remark. A cyclic flat module that is not projective

Finite generation does not suffice for the implication from flatness to projectivity. Let $R=C^\infty(\mathbb R)$, let $\mathfrak m$ be the kernel of evaluation at $0$, and put

$$I=\{f\in R:f\text{ vanishes on some open interval containing }0\}.$$

Then the localization $R_{\mathfrak m}$ is the cyclic module $R/I$, and it is flat but not projective.

To identify this localization, use smooth cutoff functions: for any neighborhood $U$ of $0$, there is a smooth function $\chi$ supported in $U$ and equal to $1$ on a smaller neighborhood. Such functions follow, for example, from $\rho(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $\rho(t)=0$ for $t\leq0$. For $0<a<b$ with $[-b,b]\subset U$, one may take

$$\chi(x)= \frac{\rho(b^2-x^2)} {\rho(b^2-x^2)+\rho(x^2-a^2)}.$$

The denominator is positive everywhere, so this formula has the stated properties.

If $f$ becomes zero in $R_{\mathfrak m}$, some $s$ with $s(0)\ne0$ satisfies $sf=0$. On a neighborhood where $s$ is nonzero, $f$ vanishes. Conversely, if $f\in I$, choose a cutoff supported where $f$ vanishes. Then $\chi f=0$ and $\chi(0)=1$, which kills $f$ in the localization. Thus the kernel of $R\to R_{\mathfrak m}$ is exactly $I$. This map is surjective: for $f/h$ with $h(0)\ne0$, multiply the smooth function $f/h$ on a neighborhood of $0$ by a cutoff supported there, and extend by zero. The resulting global function represents the given fraction. This proves $R_{\mathfrak m}\cong R/I$.

Localization is flat. The ideal $I$ is nonzero, since it contains a nonzero smooth function supported away from $0$, and is proper, since it does not contain $1$. If $R/I$ were projective, the quotient map would split as an $R$-module map. The associated projection $R\to I$ is multiplication by an idempotent $e$, so $I=eR$. A smooth idempotent takes values only in $\{0,1\}$ and is constant on the connected space $\mathbb R$. It generates either zero or all of $R$, contradicting the two properties of $I$. This proves nonprojectivity.

Lemma. Exact finite-module completion and flatness of the completed ring

Fix an ideal $I$ in a Noetherian ring $R$, and use a hat for $I$-adic completion. The map $R\to\widehat R$ is flat, and completion preserves exact sequences of finite $R$-modules.

Proof. The complete filtration and inverse-limit argument is Completion, §§1–3, Theorems 3.1–3.2. In an exact sequence $0\to N\to M\to L\to0$ of finite modules, Artin–Rees makes the filtrations $I^nN$ and $N\cap I^nM$ cofinal. The quotient sequences have surjective transitions on their left terms, so their inverse limits are exact. Comparing the two filtrations identifies the left limit with $\widehat N$. This proves exactness of completion on these modules.

The same proof, applied to a finite presentation, identifies $M\otimes_R\widehat R$ with $\widehat M$: both are the cokernel of the original presentation matrix acting on finite free $\widehat R$-modules. In particular, for every ideal $J\subset R$, the map

$$J\otimes_R\widehat R\longrightarrow\widehat R$$

identifies with the injective map $\widehat J\to\widehat R$. Here $J$ is finite because $R$ is Noetherian. The ideal criterion for flatness therefore proves that $\widehat R$ is flat over $R$. ∎

Lemma. Composition of flatness and faithful flatness

Suppose $R\to R'$ is flat and $M'$ is flat as an $R'$-module. Then $M'$ is flat over $R$. If both given flatness assertions are faithful, the resulting one is faithful too. Taking $M'$ to be an $R'$-algebra gives the corresponding assertions for compositions of ring maps.

Proof. For every $R$-module $N$ there is a natural isomorphism

$$M'\otimes_{R'}(R'\otimes_RN)\ \longrightarrow\ M'\otimes_RN.$$

It sends $m'\otimes(r'\otimes n)$ to $r'm'\otimes n$. Its inverse sends $m'\otimes n$ to $m'\otimes(1\otimes n)$. The balancing relations make both maps well-defined; those same relations show that the two composites fix every elementary tensor. Naturality follows by applying a homomorphism to $n$.

An injection of $R$-modules stays injective after tensoring first with $R'$ and then with $M'$. Under this natural identification, their composite is tensoring over $R$ with $M'$. Hence $M'$ is $R$-flat. If the first two functors also detect nonzero modules, their composite does: a nonzero $N$ gives a nonzero $R'\otimes_RN$, then a nonzero $M'\otimes_{R'}(R'\otimes_RN)$. The faithful-flatness criterion gives the last assertion. ∎

Lemma. Completeness after completing an arbitrary module

For a Noetherian ring $R$, an ideal $I$, and any $R$-module $M$, its completion is $I$-adically complete. For every $n\geq0$, the canonical maps identify

$$I^n\widehat M=\widehat{I^nM}, \qquad \widehat M/I^n\widehat M=M/I^nM.$$

The completion on $I^nM$ uses its own $I$-adic filtration.

Proof. Noetherianity makes $I$ finitely generated. Apply the completion-kernel theorem for a finitely generated ideal, which proves these identities and completeness without requiring $M$ to be finite. Its filtration comparison uses $I^a(I^nM)=I^{a+n}M$. Thus its canonical injection of $\widehat{I^nM}$ into $\widehat M$ has image exactly $I^n\widehat M$, as asserted. ∎

Lemma. Flat terms of a universally exact sequence

Let $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ remain exact after tensoring with every $R$-module. If $M_2$ is flat, then $M_1$ and $M_3$ are flat.

Proof. Fix an injection $N\to N'$ and write $N''=N'/N$. Tensor the given sequence with each of $N,N',N''$. This gives three short exact rows, and the maps between them commute with every row map.

First, $M_1\otimes_RN\to M_1\otimes_RN'$ is injective: its composite into $M_2\otimes_RN'$ factors as the injective row map into $M_2\otimes_RN$ followed by the injection supplied by flatness of $M_2$. This proves flatness of $M_1$.

For the other end, suppose $z\in M_3\otimes_RN$ dies in $M_3\otimes_RN'$. Lift $z$ to $x\in M_2\otimes_RN$. In the middle row the image of $x$ comes from some $y\in M_1\otimes_RN'$. Its image in $M_2\otimes_RN''$ is zero, so injectivity of the bottom row forces the image of $y$ in $M_1\otimes_RN''$ to be zero. Right exactness of tensor products now lifts $y$ from an element $y_0\in M_1\otimes_RN$. Subtract the row image of $y_0$ from $x$. The difference dies in $M_2\otimes_RN'$, hence is zero by flatness of $M_2$. Its image in $M_3\otimes_RN$ was $z$, so $z=0$. Thus tensoring with $M_3$ preserves every injection, proving its flatness. ∎

Proposition. Coherence detected by products of flat modules

Historical source: Chase, Theorem 2.1.

For a commutative ring $R$, the following are equivalent:

  1. Every finitely generated ideal of $R$ is finitely presented; that is, $R$ is coherent.
  2. The product of every family of flat $R$-modules is flat.
  3. The module $R^A=\prod_{\alpha\in A}R$ is flat for every set $A$.

Proof. We first establish the two tensor-product criteria used in both directions. For an $R$-module $M$ and a family $(Q_\alpha)$, the projections define

$$\theta_{M,(Q_\alpha)}\colon M\otimes_R\prod_\alpha Q_\alpha \longrightarrow \prod_\alpha(M\otimes_RQ_\alpha).$$

The following four properties are equivalent: $M$ is finitely generated; this map is surjective for every family; it is surjective for every constant family $Q_\alpha=Q$ and every index set; and it is surjective for the families $Q_\alpha=R$ alone. Replacing “finitely generated” by “finitely presented” and “surjective” by “bijective” gives another four equivalent properties.

For finite generation, take generators $m_1,\ldots,m_s$. Any tuple on the right has coordinates expressible as $\sum_{j=1}^s m_j\otimes q_{\alpha j}$. It is the image of $\sum_jm_j\otimes(q_{\alpha j})_\alpha$. Thus finite generation gives surjectivity for every family. Restricting families gives the next two implications. Conversely take the index set to be the underlying set of $M$, and consider the tuple whose coordinate indexed by $m$ is $m$. If $\theta_{M,(R)}$ is surjective, this tuple comes from a finite sum

$$\sum_{j=1}^s m_j\otimes(r_{j,m})_{m\in M}.$$

Coordinate comparison gives $m=\sum_jr_{j,m}m_j$ for every $m\in M$. Hence the displayed finite list generates $M$.

For finite presentation, choose $R^u\to R^v\to M\to0$ with $u,v$ finite. Tensoring with $\prod Q_\alpha$ gives a cokernel presentation. Tensoring with each $Q_\alpha$ and then taking the product gives a second cokernel presentation: products of module surjections are surjective, and kernels and images are computed coordinatewise. Finite free modules commute with products, by rearranging the finitely many coordinates. Thus the first two terms and their maps in these presentations agree, and their cokernels agree. This proves bijectivity of $\theta$ for every family.

For the converse it suffices to assume bijectivity for the families $Q_\alpha=R$. The finite-generation result supplies a surjection $F=R^v\to M$ with $v$ finite; let $K$ be its kernel. Fix a set $A$ and a tuple in $K^A$. View it in $F^A$, and lift it through the isomorphism $F\otimes_RR^A\cong F^A$. Its image in $M\otimes_RR^A$ is zero, because its image in $M^A$ is zero and $\theta_{M,(R)}$ is injective. The right-exact tensor sequence therefore lifts it from $K\otimes_RR^A$. This proves that

$$K\otimes_RR^A\longrightarrow K^A$$

is surjective for every $A$. The criterion just proved makes $K$ finitely generated. A finite generating list for $K$ completes a finite presentation of $M$. The intervening constant-family conditions follow by restriction, so all four finite-presentation criteria are established.

Now assume (1), and write $Q=\prod_\alpha Q_\alpha$ with each $Q_\alpha$ flat. For a finitely generated ideal $J$, coherence and the product criterion identify

$$J\otimes_RQ\ \cong\ \prod_\alpha(J\otimes_RQ_\alpha).$$

Each map $J\otimes_RQ_\alpha\to Q_\alpha$ is injective. Their product is injective, so the canonical map $J\otimes_RQ\to Q$ is injective. The ideal flatness test proves (2). Taking every factor equal to $R$ gives (3).

Finally assume (3). For a finitely generated ideal $J$, flatness of $R^A$ makes $J\otimes_RR^A\to R^A$ injective. The finite-generation criterion says its image is $J^A$, so $\theta_{J,(R)}$ is bijective for every $A$. The finite-presentation criterion makes $J$ finitely presented. This gives (1) and completes the proof. ∎

Lemma. Noetherian rings are coherent

Every Noetherian ring is coherent.

Proof. Each ideal is a finite module, and every finite module over a Noetherian ring is finitely presented, by the finite-module theorem. In particular each finitely generated ideal has the presentation required in the definition of coherence. ∎

Remark. Strict henselization as a union of finite étale local extensions

Let $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be local, fix $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, and identify the residue field of $R^h$ with $\kappa$. For each finite intermediate extension $\kappa\subset L\subset\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, the finite étale equivalence gives a finite étale local $R^h$-algebra $A_L$ with its specified residue identification $\kappa(A_L)=L$. This marked algebra is unique up to unique marked isomorphism. The marking is necessary: the unmarked extension may have automorphisms.

Every inclusion $L\subset L'$ lifts uniquely to $A_L\to A_{L'}$, by full faithfulness of that equivalence. Uniqueness makes these arrows compose compatibly. They are local, since their residue maps are the prescribed field inclusions, and they are étale by the theorem on maps between étale algebras. In particular they are flat local maps, hence faithfully flat and injective. We may therefore write their colimit as a union:

$$H=\bigcup_{\kappa\subset L\subset\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}},\ [L:\kappa]<\infty}A_L.$$

Each $A_L$ is henselian, by the finite-local-algebra result in Henselian local rings and henselization, Proposition 3.1. The residue maps give $H\to\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Its kernel consists of the union of the stage maximal ideals, and every element outside this kernel is already a unit at a stage. Thus $H$ is local with residue field $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. To check henselianity, take a monic polynomial over $H$ with a specified simple root in that residue field. Its coefficients and that root lie at a common finite stage. The root equation and nonzero derivative hold in that stage's residue field, which embeds in $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Henselianity there lifts the root. Hence $H$ is strictly henselian.

Here is the identification with the strict henselization, including the required compatibility. Given a local map $R\to T$ to a henselian local ring and a compatible embedding $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}\to\kappa(T)$, the ordinary henselization property extends it uniquely to $R^h\to T$. For each $L$, henselian evaluation then gives a unique map $A_L\to T$ inducing the chosen embedding of $L$. These maps are compatible by uniqueness. They yield a local map $H\to T$ with the prescribed residue embedding, and every such map has those same restrictions, so is unique.

This is precisely the marked universal property of the strict henselization in Theorem 5.1. Apply the two universal properties to $H$ and $R^{sh}$ to obtain inverse marked local maps. Thus $H\cong R^{sh}$. The same theorem constructs $R^{sh}$ as a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras; this identification proves that property for the displayed union as well.

Lemma. Evaluating an ind-étale algebra in a henselian local ring

Let $R\to S$ be any homomorphism with $S$ henselian local, and put $\mathfrak p=R\cap\mathfrak m_S$. Suppose $A$ is a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras. Choose a prime $\mathfrak q\subset A$ over $\mathfrak p$ and a $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-embedding

$$\tau\colon\kappa(\mathfrak q)\longrightarrow\kappa(S).$$

There is exactly one $R$-algebra map $f\colon A\to S$ whose inverse image of $\mathfrak m_S$ is $\mathfrak q$ and whose residue map is $\tau$.

Proof. Write $A=\operatorname{colim}_iA_i$ and let $\mathfrak q_i$ be the contraction of $\mathfrak q$. The local map $(A_i)_{\mathfrak q_i}\to A_{\mathfrak q}$ induces an embedding $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. Compose with $\tau$. The étale evaluation theorem supplies a unique map $f_i\colon A_i\to S$ with precisely that prime and residue embedding. For every transition arrow, the two possible evaluations of its source have the same residues and therefore agree. The maps $f_i$ consequently define $f\colon A\to S$.

For an element represented in $A_i$, membership in $\mathfrak q$ is equivalent to membership in $\mathfrak q_i$, and hence to its image under $f_i$ lying in $\mathfrak m_S$. Thus $f^{-1}(\mathfrak m_S)=\mathfrak q$. Every element of $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is represented by a quotient of two elements of $A$, with denominator outside $\mathfrak q$; these elements occur at a common stage. The residue formula there shows that $f$ induces $\tau$ on this quotient. Finally, any other map with the prescribed data restricts to each $f_i$ by uniqueness of étale evaluation. It equals $f$ on the colimit. ∎

Proposition. Two successive localizations

For multiplicative subsets $S,T$ of a ring $A$, let $\overline S$ be the image of $S$ in $T^{-1}A$. There is a canonical isomorphism

$$\overline S^{-1}(T^{-1}A)\ \cong\ (ST)^{-1}A.$$

Proof. The localization at $ST$ inverts both $S$ and $T$, since each multiplicative subset contains $1$. Its structure map therefore factors through the two successive localizations. Conversely, the successive localization inverts every product $st$, so its structure map factors through $(ST)^{-1}A$. The resulting maps have the formulas

$$\frac{a/t}{s/1}\longmapsto\frac{a}{st}, \qquad \frac{a}{st}\longmapsto\frac{a/t}{s/1}.$$

The universal properties prove they are well-defined. Their composites are the unique endomorphisms extending the original structure map from $A$, hence are identities. The argument includes multiplicative subsets containing zero, when the corresponding rings are zero. ∎

Proposition. Localization preserves exact sequences

Historical source: FAC, Chapter II, §4, no. 48, Lemma 1, p. 241. The fraction construction there assumes $0\notin S$; the zero localization is included below.

For any multiplicative subset $S\subset A$, localization is an exact functor on $A$-modules.

Proof. Recall that $m/s=m'/s'$ precisely when some $t\in S$ kills $s'm-sm'$. Addition and scalar multiplication use common denominators. These relations identify localization with extension of scalars by the inverse maps

$$ \begin{aligned} S^{-1}A\otimes_AM&\longrightarrow S^{-1}M,\\ (a/s)\otimes m&\longmapsto am/s,\\ S^{-1}M&\longrightarrow S^{-1}A\otimes_AM,\\ m/s&\longmapsto (1/s)\otimes m. \end{aligned} $$

The fraction relation makes the first formula independent of representatives and balanced over $A$. For the second, the relation $t(s'm-sm')=0$ becomes $s'm-sm'=0$ after extending scalars, since $t$ is invertible; division by $ss'$ then proves independence. The elementary tensor identities prove that these maps are inverse.

Take an exact sequence $L\xrightarrow{u}M\xrightarrow{v}N$. Its localization is a complex. If $m/s$ is in the localized kernel, there is $t\in S$ with $tv(m)=0$. Choose $\ell\in L$ with $u(\ell)=tm$. Then

$$m/s=u(\ell)/(ts),$$

which lies in the localized image. The reverse inclusion follows from $vu=0$. Applying this to sequences with a zero end also preserves injections and surjections, proving exactness. If $0\in S$, every localized module is zero and the conclusion holds directly. ∎

Lemma. Descent of finite projectivity along a flat local map

Let $R\to S$ be flat and local, with both rings local. For a finite $R$-module $M$,

$$M\text{ is finite projective over }R \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M\otimes_RS\text{ is finite projective over }S.$$

No finite-presentation assumption on $M$ is needed.

Proof. Finite projectivity is preserved by base change, since a splitting from a finite free module remains a splitting after tensoring. Conversely, suppose $M_S=M\otimes_RS$ is finite projective. It is finite free, by the finite-projective criteria. Choose lifts $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of a basis of $M/\mathfrak m_RM$. They generate $M$ by Nakayama. The identification

$$M_S/\mathfrak m_SM_S \cong(M/\mathfrak m_RM)\otimes_{\kappa(R)}\kappa(S)$$

shows that $M_S$ has rank $r$ and that the images of these lifts are a basis modulo $\mathfrak m_S$. Relative to any free basis of $M_S$, the square matrix of the lifts has determinant nonzero in $\kappa(S)$ and thus a unit in $S$. They are therefore an $S$-basis.

The surjection $R^r\to M$ defined by the lifts becomes an isomorphism over $S$. The map $R\to S$ is faithfully flat because it is flat and local. Flatness identifies the base change of the kernel with zero; faithful flatness forces the kernel to be zero. Thus $M\cong R^r$. This also covers $r=0$: Nakayama gives $M=0$. ∎

Lemma. Openness of the Cohen–Macaulay fibre locus of fixed dimension

Suppose $R\to S$ is flat and finitely presented. For $d\geq0$, consider the primes $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ such that, on putting $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$,

$$\begin{gathered} S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q} \text{ is Cohen–Macaulay},\\ \dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)=d. \end{gathered}$$

This subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is open. Here $\dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)$ is dimension at the point of the fibre scheme, rather than the dimension of its local ring alone.

Proof. We first prove the field calculation used twice below. Let $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\to T$ be quasi-finite, with $T$ a finite-type $k$-algebra. At a prime $\mathfrak r\subset T$, write $\mathfrak a$ for its contraction and set

$$A=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]_{\mathfrak a}, \qquad B=T_{\mathfrak r}, \qquad e=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak r).$$

The residue extension $\kappa(\mathfrak a)\subset\kappa(\mathfrak r)$ is finite, and the local closed fibre of $A\to B$ has dimension zero, by quasi-finiteness. In particular $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak a)=e$. The polynomial local ring $A$ is regular; a full proof over arbitrary fields is Regular local rings, Proposition 3.3. The field dimension formula at a point gives

$$\dim A=d-e, \qquad \dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=\dim B+e.$$

If $B$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$, these identities give $\dim B=\dim A$. Since the local closed fibre has dimension zero, the Cohen–Macaulay flatness criterion over a regular base makes $B$ flat over $A$.

Conversely, suppose $B$ is flat over $A$. The flat local dimension formula gives $\dim B=\dim A$. A regular system of parameters $a_1,\ldots,a_h$ of $A$ is regular, where $h=\dim A$, by the regular-local parameter theorem. It stays regular in $B$: after the first $j$ parameters, the quotient of $B$ is flat over the corresponding quotient of $A$, and tensoring the injection defined by $a_{j+1}$ preserves injectivity. All successive quotients of $B$ are nonzero since these parameters lie in its maximal ideal. Thus $B$ has depth at least $h=\dim B$, and hence is Cohen–Macaulay. The second dimension identity gives $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$. This proves the equivalence in full, including nonclosed points and $d=0$.

Now fix a point $\mathfrak q$ in the asserted locus. By the quasi-finite polynomial model, after a principal localization of $S$ away from $\mathfrak q$ there is a quasi-finite map

$$P=R[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\longrightarrow S.$$

Keep this localization in the notation. If $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q\cap P$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$, the induced local map in the fibre is

$$P_{\mathfrak q'}/\mathfrak pP_{\mathfrak q'} \longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}.$$

These are precisely the relevant localizations of the polynomial and source algebras over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The field equivalence proves that this map is flat.

Apply the general fibrewise flatness criterion to

$$R_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow P_{\mathfrak q'} \longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q},\qquad M=S_{\mathfrak q}.$$

The last algebra is essentially finitely presented over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, the middle is essentially of finite type, $M$ is a nonzero finitely presented module over itself, and it is $R_{\mathfrak p}$-flat by the assumed flatness of $S$. The fibre condition has just been proved. Thus $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $P_{\mathfrak q'}$.

The algebra $S$ is finitely presented over $P$: take its finite presentation over $R$ and add the $d$ relations identifying the variables of $P$ with their chosen images. Therefore general openness of flatness, Theorem 6.4, gives $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_g$ is flat over $P$. The proof of that theorem includes the finite-model flatness argument and the Noetherian flat-locus theorem; the latter uses the full generic-freeness proof in Flat morphisms, §5. Thus no Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ has been introduced.

For any $\mathfrak r\in\operatorname{Spec}S_g$, base change this flat, quasi-finite map from $P$ to the residue field at $\mathfrak r\cap R$. The resulting map is again flat and quasi-finite over a polynomial ring in $d$ variables. The converse half of the field equivalence shows that its local source ring is Cohen–Macaulay and its dimension at $\mathfrak r$ is $d$. Hence every point of $D(g)$ is in the specified locus. Together with the initial localization, this gives an open neighborhood of the original $\mathfrak q$ inside the locus. ∎

Lemma. Coefficients of a monic divisor

Let $K$ be a field and suppose the monic polynomial

$$f=x^n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_ix^i$$

divides

$$g=x^m+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_jx^j$$

in $K[x]$. Then:

  1. Every $a_i$ is integral over any subring $R_0\subset K$ containing all the $b_j$.
  2. For any subring $R\subset K$ containing both lists of coefficients, every $a_i$ belongs to $\sqrt{(b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1})R}$.

Proof. Pass to a splitting field for $g$ and list its roots with multiplicity. Each root satisfies the monic equation $g=0$ over $R_0$, hence is integral over $R_0$. The roots of $f$ form a sublist, and its coefficients are signed elementary symmetric polynomials in that sublist. The closure of integral elements under addition and multiplication makes these coefficients integral, proving (1).

For (2), the monic quotient $h=g/f$ has degree $m-n$. Comparing coefficients from the highest degree downward expresses each coefficient of $h$ as a coefficient of $g$ minus a sum of products of coefficients of $f$ and coefficients of $h$ already found. Induction puts all of them in $R$. This also covers $m=n$, when $h=1$.

Set $J=\sqrt{(b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1})R}$ and $\overline R=R/J$. It is reduced, and reduction of $fh=g$ gives a product of monic polynomials equal to $x^m$. At a minimal prime $\mathfrak l$ of $\overline R$, its localization is a field, by the minimal-prime localization lemma. In that field a monic divisor of $x^m$ of degree $n$ is $x^n$. Hence every image $\overline a_i$ is zero in $\overline R_{\mathfrak l}$. The zero criterion for localization supplies $s_i\notin\mathfrak l$ with $s_i\overline a_i=0$, so primality implies $\overline a_i\in\mathfrak l$.

The intersection of the minimal primes equals the nilradical: every prime contains a minimal prime, and the nilradical is the intersection of all primes. Since $\overline R$ is reduced, this intersection is zero. Thus each $\overline a_i=0$, or $a_i\in J$, as claimed. If $\overline R=0$ the conclusion is immediate; if $n=0$ there are no coefficients $a_i$ to check. ∎

Lemma. A finite algebra containing prescribed integral elements

Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism and let $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in S$. These elements are all integral over $R$ if and only if some $R$-subalgebra of $S$ is finite as an $R$-module and contains every $s_i$.

Proof. Suppose $s_i$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $d_i\geq1$. In $R[s_1,\ldots,s_n]$, that equation expresses every power $s_i^{d_i}$ as a combination of lower powers. Repeated reduction in each variable shows that the finitely many monomials

$$s_1^{e_1}\cdots s_n^{e_n}, \qquad 0\leq e_i<d_i,$$

span this algebra as an $R$-module. This is the required finite subalgebra. For an empty list, the image of $R$ itself is cyclic and suffices.

Conversely, every element of an algebra finite over $R$ is integral over $R$, by the finite-algebra integrality theorem. Apply this to the proposed subalgebra and its elements $s_i$. The argument uses the image of $R$ in $S$ and does not require injectivity. ∎

Lemma. The clopen partition defined by an idempotent

An idempotent $e\in R$ gives the disjoint decomposition

$$\operatorname{Spec}R=D(e)\amalg D(1-e).$$

Both parts are open and closed.

Proof. In each residue field the equation $e^2=e$ forces the image of $e$ to be either $0$ or $1$. Thus

$$ \begin{aligned} D(e)&=\{\mathfrak p:e=1\text{ in }\kappa(\mathfrak p)\} =V(1-e),\\ D(1-e)&=\{\mathfrak p:e=0\text{ in }\kappa(\mathfrak p)\} =V(e). \end{aligned} $$

Exactly one of these alternatives holds at every prime. The displayed equalities also identify each open set as the closed complement of the other. They include $e=0$, $e=1$, and the empty spectrum of the zero ring. ∎

Lemma. A principal open is the spectrum of a localization

For $f\in R$, contraction identifies $\operatorname{Spec}R_f$ homeomorphically with $D(f)\subset\operatorname{Spec}R$. The inverse sends $\mathfrak p\in D(f)$ to $\mathfrak pR_f$.

Proof. In the spectrum-localization theorem, take the multiplicative set of powers of $f$. Its disjointness from a prime is exactly $f\notin\mathfrak p$. That theorem proves the contraction-extension bijection and identifies principal-open bases on both sides, so it proves the asserted homeomorphism and inverse. ∎

Theorem. Chevalley’s theorem on constructible images

Let $R\to S$ be finitely presented. The image of every constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is constructible in $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

Proof by polynomial elimination. We supply the affine-set reductions and both terminal cases of the degree induction.

On an affine spectrum, a retrocompact open is the same as a quasi-compact open. Indeed the whole spectrum is quasi-compact, so retrocompactness implies quasi-compactness. Conversely a quasi-compact open is a finite union of principal opens; its intersection with another such union is again a finite union of principal opens, using $D(a)\cap D(b)=D(ab)$. Consequently the definition of constructibility as finite unions of differences of retrocompact opens gives the following description:

$$E=\bigcup_{\nu=1}^r \bigl(D(f_\nu)\cap V(g_{\nu1},\ldots,g_{\nu m_\nu})\bigr).$$

These sets form the Boolean algebra generated by principal opens. The converse is immediate from the same finite-union description. The Zariski-topology construction gives the principal-open basis, and the affine quasi-compactness lemma supplies the required finiteness of principal covers.

This description also proves two image rules. Under $\operatorname{Spec}R_c\cong D(c)$, clear powers of $c$ from each element defining a basic constructible piece. Its image has the form

$$D(ca)\cap V(b_1,\ldots,b_m),$$

where $a,b_j\in R$. Under $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\cong V(I)$, with $I=(h_1,\ldots,h_\ell)$ finitely generated, lift all defining elements to $R$. The corresponding image is

$$D(a)\cap V(h_1,\ldots,h_\ell,b_1,\ldots,b_m).$$

Finite unions prove both rules for every constructible subset of the localized or quotient spectrum.

We now treat $R[x]$. First, if $f=\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i$, a prime $\mathfrak p$ belongs to the image of $D(f)$ exactly when

$$\kappa(\mathfrak p)[x]_{\overline f}\ne0.$$

This polynomial ring is a domain, so its localization is nonzero exactly when $\overline f\ne0$, or equivalently some $a_i\notin\mathfrak p$. Therefore

$$\operatorname{image}(D(f))=\bigcup_{i=0}^nD(a_i).$$

This is quasi-compact open. Since arbitrary opens are unions of principal opens, the projection $\operatorname{Spec}R[x]\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is open as well.

The second terminal case is $D(f)\cap V(g)$ when the leading coefficient of $g$ is invertible. Divide by that unit, making $g$ monic of degree $d$. If $d=0$, the set is empty. Otherwise $A=R[x]/(g)$ is free over $R$ on $1,x,\ldots,x^{d-1}$: monic division gives both spanning and uniqueness. Let the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $f$ on $A$ be

$$P(T)=T^d+r_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+r_0.$$

Its formation commutes with passage to $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, since the multiplication matrix and its determinant reduce coefficientwise. Over this field, multiplication by $\overline f$ is nilpotent if and only if the reduced characteristic polynomial is $T^d$. In one direction a basis adapted to the kernels of successive powers gives a triangular matrix with zero diagonal. In the other direction Cayley–Hamilton makes its $d$th power zero. Multiplication is nilpotent precisely when the element $\overline f$ is nilpotent, by evaluating a power of the operator on $1$. Thus

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathfrak p\in\operatorname{image}(D(f)\cap V(g)) &\Longleftrightarrow (A\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p))_{\overline f}\ne0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \mathfrak p\in\bigcup_{i=0}^{d-1}D(r_i). \end{aligned} $$

Here a localization at one element is zero exactly when some power of that element is zero. A nonzero fibre algebra has a prime, which supplies the point upstairs. This proves the second terminal case with an explicit finite list of coefficients.

For a general basic piece

$$D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subset\operatorname{Spec}R[x],$$

discard zero equations and order the remaining ones by degree. Induct, for all coefficient rings at once, on the integer

$$N=\sum_{g_i\ne0}(\deg g_i+1).$$

If there are no equations, the first terminal case applies. Otherwise write $c$ for the nonzero leading coefficient of a least-degree equation $g_1$. Split the base into $V(c)$ and $D(c)$. On the closed part, pass to $R/(c)$: the degree of $g_1$ drops, or it becomes zero, so $N$ decreases. The closed-image rule returns the resulting constructible image to $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

On $D(c)$, the leading coefficient of $g_1$ is a unit. If this ring is zero, the part is empty; if $g_1$ is constant, its vanishing set is empty. If localization lowers the degree of any equation or makes one zero, $N$ has already decreased and induction applies. Otherwise the degree order is unchanged. If $g_1$ is the sole equation, the second terminal case applies. If another equation $g_j$ remains, its degree is at least that of $g_1$; subtract a suitable multiple $a x^{\deg g_j-\deg g_1}g_1$ to cancel its leading term. This leaves the defining ideal unchanged and strictly lowers $\deg g_j$, or removes a zero equation. Thus each nonterminal branch reduces $N$. The localization image rule brings its constructible image back to the original base. Combining the two parts completes the induction.

Finally write $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J$ with $J$ finitely generated. The closed-image rule first regards the chosen constructible set as one in polynomial affine space. Project away one variable at a time, applying the one-variable theorem over each intervening coefficient ring. After all $n$ projections its image in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is constructible. This includes $n=0$, when only the closed-image rule is needed. ∎

There is also a complete proof by finite models in Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley’s theorem, §§3–5, Theorem 5.1. It descends the finite algebra presentation and the finitely many Boolean conditions to a finite-type $\mathbb Z$-subalgebra. Sections 3–4 prove Noetherian Chevalley using the irreducible-closed constructibility criterion and a normalization argument for the generic image. The general proof checks equality of images after base change through the nonzero tensor product of the two residue fields over their common field. This proves the same arbitrary-ring statement.

Lemma. Specialization and generization of constructible subsets

Let $E$ be a constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$. If $E$ is stable under specialization, it is closed. If it is stable under generization, it is open.

First proof, by realizing an affine image. Each basic piece

$$D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$$

is the image of the spectrum of the finitely presented algebra

$$B=(R/(g_1,\ldots,g_m))_f \cong R[z]/(g_1,\ldots,g_m,fz-1).$$

A finite union of such images is the image of $\operatorname{Spec}(\prod_\nu B_\nu)$, by the product-spectrum theorem.

This product is again finitely presented. One explicit presentation adjoins finitely many orthogonal idempotents $e_\nu$ summing to $1$, and variables $z_\nu$ with

$$ \begin{gathered} e_\nu z_\nu=z_\nu,\qquad e_\nu g_{\nu j}=0,\qquad f_\nu z_\nu=e_\nu. \end{gathered} $$

Together with $e_\nu^2=e_\nu$, $e_\nu e_\mu=0$ for $\nu\ne\mu$, and $\sum e_\nu=1$, these relations split the presented algebra into the factors $B_\nu$. On the $\nu$th factor only $z_\nu$ survives, and its remaining equations are exactly those for $B_\nu$. Thus the displayed finite presentation has the required product. The empty union is the spectrum of the zero algebra, which has the presentation $R/(1)$.

We have realized $E$ as an affine-spectrum image. If it is specialization-stable, the closed-image lemma makes it closed. If it is generization-stable, its constructible complement is specialization-stable, hence closed by what was just proved. Then $E$ is open.

Second proof, using the spectral topology. The affine spectrum is spectral: it is quasi-compact and has the quasi-compact basis $D(f)$ closed under finite intersections; distinct primes are distinguished by such opens; and every nonempty irreducible closed subset has a unique generic point, by the irreducibility theorem. Indeed an irreducible $V(I)$ has prime radical, and is the closure of that prime.

For completeness, its constructible topology, generated by the opens $D(f)$ and their complements $V(f)$, is compact. Given an ultrafilter $\mathscr U$ of subsets of the spectrum, put

$$\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}=\{f\in R:V(f)\in\mathscr U\}.$$

The identities $V(0)=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $V(1)=\varnothing$, $V(-f)=V(f)$, and $V(f)\cap V(g)\subset V(f+g)$ show that this is a proper additive subgroup. The inclusion $V(f)\subset V(af)$ gives ideal stability. Finally $V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g)$ and the ultrafilter alternative give primality. Every basic constructible neighborhood of $\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$ belongs to $\mathscr U$: for a condition $D(f)$ use $f\notin\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$, and for $V(g)$ use $g\in\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$. Finite intersections preserve membership. Thus every ultrafilter converges, proving compactness. The empty spectrum is compact directly.

A constructible set is open and closed in this topology, hence compact. If $\mathfrak p$ is in the Zariski closure of $E$, then

$$\{E\cap D(f):f\notin\mathfrak p\}$$

has the finite intersection property: a finite intersection is $E\cap D(\prod f)$, and this Zariski neighborhood of $\mathfrak p$ meets $E$. These are closed subsets in the constructible topology on $E$, so compactness gives a prime $\mathfrak q\in E$ lying in all of them. This means $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$. If $E$ is specialization-stable, it follows that $\mathfrak p\in E$. Hence $E$ is closed. The complement argument again proves the generization assertion. This is the spectral-space argument in affine form; the complete compactness route also appears in Flat morphisms, §3, Lemma 3.1. ∎

Lemma. Integral elements form a subalgebra

For any ring map $R\to S$, the elements of $S$ integral over $R$ form an $R$-subalgebra.

Proof. Given two integral elements $a,b$, the finite-subalgebra criterion places them in the finite algebra $R[a,b]\subset S$. This algebra contains $a+b$, $ab$, and $-a$, all integral by the converse direction of that criterion. It also contains the image of every element of $R$, which is integral since it satisfies a monic linear equation. Thus the integral elements contain the structural image and are closed under the algebra operations. ∎

Lemma. Integrality over an ideal and its graded algebra

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a homomorphism, let $I\subset R$ be any ideal, and form

$$\mathcal R(I)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nt^n\subset R[t].$$

An element $s\in S$ is integral over $I$ if and only if $st\in S[t]$ is integral over $\mathcal R(I)$.

Proof. If

$$s^d+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\varphi(a_j)s^j=0, \qquad a_j\in I^{d-j},$$

then multiplication by $t^d$ gives a monic equation for $st$, with coefficient of $(st)^j$ equal to $\varphi(a_j)t^{d-j}$. That coefficient comes from $\mathcal R(I)$.

Conversely, suppose $(st)^d+\sum_{j<d}b_j(st)^j=0$ with $b_j\in\mathcal R(I)$, interpreted through its map to $S[t]$. Take the homogeneous component of degree $d$ in this equality. Only the degree-$d-j$ component of $b_j$ contributes to the term indexed by $j$; it has the form $a_jt^{d-j}$ for some $a_j\in I^{d-j}$. Comparing the coefficient of $t^d$ gives the displayed equation for $s$. This comparison takes place in $S[t]$ and remains valid when $\varphi$ is not injective. ∎

Lemma. Five tests for a point to lie in the image

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$. The following are equivalent:

  1. Some prime of $S$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$.
  2. $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is nonzero.
  3. $S_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}$ is nonzero.
  4. $(S/\mathfrak pS)_{\mathfrak p}$ is nonzero.
  5. $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak pS)=\mathfrak p$.

In these expressions the subscript $\mathfrak p$ means localization using $R\setminus\mathfrak p$.

Proof. The fibre-ring identifications identify the three rings in (2)–(4), and identify their spectra with the primes of $S$ lying over $\mathfrak p$. A ring has a prime exactly when it is nonzero. This proves equivalence of (1)–(4).

For the last condition, a localization of $S/\mathfrak pS$ is zero exactly when some element of the multiplicative set becomes zero there: equivalently, some $a\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ has $\varphi(a)\in\mathfrak pS$. Thus (4) says that no such $a$ exists. The contraction of $\mathfrak pS$ always contains $\mathfrak p$, so the absence of such an $a$ is precisely (5). ∎

Lemma. Localizing the integral closure

Let $A\to B$ be any ring map, let $T\subset A$ be multiplicative, and let $B'\subset B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. Then the integral closure of $T^{-1}A$ in $T^{-1}B$ is $T^{-1}B'$.

Proof. Exactness of localization embeds $T^{-1}B'$ into $T^{-1}B$. If $b\in B'$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $n$, division by $t^n$ shows that $b/t$ satisfies a monic equation over $T^{-1}A$. This gives one inclusion.

For the converse take $z=b/t\in T^{-1}B$ integral over $T^{-1}A$. Choose an equation

$$\begin{gathered} z^n+\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i/t_i)z^{n-i}=0,\\ a_i\in A,\qquad t_i\in T. \end{gathered}$$

Put $u=t\prod_i t_i\in T$. Then $y=uz$ is represented by the actual element $(\prod_i t_i)b$ of $B$, and $c_i=u^ia_i/t_i$ is an element of $A$. Multiplying the equation by $u^n$ gives

$$P(y)=y^n+\sum_{i=1}^nc_i y^{n-i}=0 \quad\text{in }T^{-1}B.$$

The element $P(y)\in B$ need not yet be zero. The localization zero criterion gives $v\in T$ with $vP(y)=0$ in $B$. Set $w=vy$. Then in $B$,

$$w^n+\sum_{i=1}^nv^ic_iw^{n-i}=v^nP(y)=0.$$

This is monic, so $w\in B'$. Finally $z=w/(vu)$ belongs to $T^{-1}B'$. The proof clears both the coefficient denominators and the possible localization zero witness, without a torsion-free assumption. ∎

Lemma. Base change preserves integral and finite maps

Given $R\to S$ and $R\to R'$, set $S'=R'\otimes_RS$. If $S$ is integral over $R$, then $S'$ is integral over $R'$. If $S$ is finite over $R$, then $S'$ is finite over $R'$.

Proof. Choose any algebra generating family $(s_\lambda)$ for $S$. In the integral case each generator satisfies a monic equation over $R$. The images $1\otimes s_\lambda$ satisfy the same equations after applying $R\to R'$ to the coefficients. They generate $S'$ as an $R'$-algebra. Since integral elements form a subalgebra, all of $S'$ is integral over $R'$.

In the finite case choose module generators $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. If $s=\sum_i a_is_i$, then

$$r'\otimes s=\sum_i r'\varphi'(a_i)(1\otimes s_i).$$

Every tensor is a finite sum of such elementary tensors, so the $1\otimes s_i$ span $S'$ over $R'$. This proves finiteness. Neither assertion needs flatness of the base change. ∎

Lemma. Prime lifting is specialization lifting

A ring map $R\to S$ has going down exactly when the induced spectrum map lifts generizations. It has going up exactly when that map lifts specializations.

Proof. The closure of a prime $\mathfrak p$ as a point of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is $V(\mathfrak p)$. Thus $\mathfrak p_1$ specializes $\mathfrak p_0$ exactly when $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$, and it is a generization exactly when the inclusion is reversed.

For going down, begin with $\mathfrak q_1\subset S$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ and a generization $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$. Lifting that generization means finding $\mathfrak q_0\subset\mathfrak q_1$ over $\mathfrak p_0$, which is precisely the going-down requirement. Conversely a going-down lift supplies that point for every such pair. For going up, start with $\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak p_0$ and $\mathfrak p_1\supset\mathfrak p_0$; the required specialization is a prime $\mathfrak q_1\supset\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak p_1$. These are exactly the going-up data in both directions. ∎

Lemma. An injective ring map reaches every minimal prime

If $R\to S$ is injective, each minimal prime of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.

Proof. Fix a minimal prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$. Exact localization gives an injection $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak p}$. The source is nonzero, so the target is nonzero and has a prime. Its contraction to $R_{\mathfrak p}$ must be the unique prime of that ring: primes there correspond to primes of $R$ contained in the minimal prime $\mathfrak p$. Pulling the chosen prime back to $S$ therefore gives a prime contracting to $\mathfrak p$, as required. ∎

Lemma. Modules over a localization

For a multiplicative set $T\subset R$, restriction of scalars identifies the category of $T^{-1}R$-modules with the full subcategory of $R$-modules on which every $t\in T$ acts invertibly.

Proof. Restriction has this property since $t/1$ is a unit of the localized ring. Conversely suppose $N$ has the stated invertible operators. Write $r_N$ for multiplication by $r$, and define the action of a fraction by

$$\frac r t\ \longmapsto\ r_Nt_N^{-1}.$$

All multiplication operators commute, and their inverses commute with them as well. If $r/t=r'/t'$, some $u\in T$ kills $t'r-tr'$. Its action is invertible, so

$$t'_Nr_N=t_Nr'_N.$$

Multiplying by the two inverse denominator operators proves that the proposed action is independent of the fraction representative.

The usual common-denominator formulas for addition and multiplication now give addition and multiplication of these operators. The fraction $1/1$ acts as the identity, so they define a $T^{-1}R$-module structure. It is the only extension: $1/t$ must act by $t_N^{-1}$. Every $R$-linear map between two such modules commutes with each $t$ and therefore with its inverse, so it is automatically linear for this extended action. The extension and restriction functors leave underlying groups and maps unchanged, and uniqueness of the extended action makes them inverse. If $0\in T$, its invertibility forces $N=0$, agreeing with the category of modules over the zero ring. ∎

Lemma. Exact sequences detected by Hom

For maps $M_1\xrightarrow{u}M_2\xrightarrow{v}M_3$ of $R$-modules:

(1) The sequence $M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ is exact if and only if, for every $N$, the sequence

$$0\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_3,N) \to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_2,N) \to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_1,N)$$

is exact.

(2) The sequence $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3$ is exact if and only if, for every $N$, the sequence

$$0\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_1) \to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_2) \to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_3)$$

is exact.

All Hom maps are induced by $u$ and $v$; no projectivity hypothesis is imposed.

Proof of (1). If the original sequence is exact, a map from $M_3$ is determined by its composite with the surjection $v$. A map $M_2\to N$ kills $u$ precisely when it descends uniquely through $M_2/\operatorname{im}u\cong M_3$. These two observations prove the stated Hom exactness.

Conversely assume the Hom sequences are exact. With $N=M_3$, the image of $\operatorname{id}_{M_3}$ is $v$, and the complex condition forces $vu=0$. Let $q\colon M_2\to C=\operatorname{coker}u$. The relation $vu=0$ factors $v$ as $bq$ for a map $b\colon C\to M_3$. Apply exactness with $N=C$ to $q$, which kills $u$: it gives $a\colon M_3\to C$ with $av=q$. Hence $abq=q$, and surjectivity of $q$ gives $ab=\operatorname{id}_C$. Also $bav=bq=v$. Injectivity of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_3,M_3)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_2,M_3)$ gives $ba=\operatorname{id}_{M_3}$. Thus $b$ is an isomorphism and $v$ is the cokernel of $u$, proving the required exactness.

Proof of (2). If the original sequence is exact, the injection $u$ gives an injection on Hom sets. A map $N\to M_2$ killed by $v$ has image in $\ker v=\operatorname{im}u$ and factors uniquely through $M_1$. This gives exactness.

Conversely, the complex condition for $N=M_1$, applied to the identity, yields $vu=0$. Let $K=\ker u$. Its inclusion into $M_1$ maps to zero in $M_2$, so injectivity of the Hom map with $N=K$ forces this inclusion to be zero; therefore $u$ is injective. Let $L=\ker v$, with its inclusion $j\colon L\to M_2$. Exactness with $N=L$ supplies $h\colon L\to M_1$ with $uh=j$. Hence every element of $\ker v$ is in $\operatorname{im}u$. The opposite containment follows from $vu=0$, completing the proof. ∎

Lemma. Module maps and finite witnesses in a directed algebra colimit

Let $(R_i)$ be a directed system of $A$-algebras with colimit $R$, and let $M,N$ be $A$-modules.

  1. If $M$ is finite and two maps $u,u'\colon M\to N$ become equal after tensoring with $R$, they become equal after tensoring with some $R_i$.
  2. If $N$ is finite and $u\colon M\to N$ becomes surjective over $R$, it is surjective after tensoring with some $R_i$.
  3. If $N$ is finitely presented, every $R$-linear map $v\colon N\otimes_AR\to M\otimes_AR$ is the base change of an $R_i$-linear map $v_i\colon N\otimes_AR_i\to M\otimes_AR_i$ for some $i$.
  4. If $M$ is finite, $N$ is finitely presented, and $u\colon M\to N$ becomes an isomorphism over $R$, it becomes an isomorphism over some $R_i$.

No transition map is assumed injective or flat.

Proof. For every $A$-module $L$, there is a natural identification

$$L\otimes_AR\cong\operatorname{colim}_i(L\otimes_AR_i).$$

One can obtain it from the tensor universal property: compatible balanced maps at all stages are exactly a balanced map with the colimit algebra. The element criterion for a directed colimit therefore applies. Finitely many representatives occur at a common stage, and finitely many elements zero in the colimit become zero together at some later stage.

For (1), choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_s$ of $M$. The finitely many differences $(u-u')(m_j)\otimes1$ vanish in $N\otimes_AR$, hence vanish in $N\otimes_AR_i$ at one stage. The tensors $m_j\otimes1$ generate the base-changed source, so the two maps agree there.

For (2), choose generators $n_1,\ldots,n_t$ of $N$ and preimages of $n_j\otimes1$ in $M\otimes_AR$. Represent these preimages at one stage. Their images under $u$ need not yet equal $n_j\otimes1$ at that stage, but the finitely many differences vanish in the colimit. Enlarge the stage once more to kill all these differences. The images now contain a generating list of $N\otimes_AR_i$, proving surjectivity.

For (3), choose a finite presentation $A^s\to A^t\to N\to0$, with images $n_1,\ldots,n_t$ of the standard generators and relation vectors $(a_{\ell1},\ldots,a_{\ell t})$ for $1\leq\ell\leq s$. At a common stage choose $z_j\in M\otimes_AR_i$ representing $v(n_j\otimes1)$. Each relation image

$$\sum_{j=1}^t a_{\ell j}z_j$$

is zero in the colimit. Enlarge $i$ until all are zero. Right exactness of tensoring the chosen presentation shows that the assignment $n_j\otimes1\mapsto z_j$ now defines $v_i$, whose base change is $v$.

For (4), apply (3) to the inverse of $u\otimes_AR$, obtaining $v_i$. The composites of $v_i$ with the base-changed $u$ agree with the identity after passing to $R$. Both source modules at this stage are finite: $M$ is finite, and finite presentation makes $N$ finite. On the directed tail above $i$, the finite-generator argument of (1), now over $R_i$, kills both lists of differences at one common later stage. The resulting maps are inverse there. This argument allows the descended $v_i$ to be defined only over $R_i$; it need not arise from an $A$-linear map. ∎

Lemma. Removing initial terms of a quasi-regular sequence

Let $M$ be a module over any ring $R$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ be $M$-quasi-regular. For $0\leq i\leq c$, put

$$\begin{gathered} \overline R=R/(f_1,\ldots,f_i),\\ \overline M=M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M. \end{gathered}$$

Then the remaining images $\overline f_{i+1},\ldots,\overline f_c$ are $\overline M$-quasi-regular over $\overline R$.

Proof. It is enough to remove $f_1$ and repeat. Put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ and write $\overline J$ for the ideal generated by the remaining elements in $R/(f_1)$. The quasi-regularity isomorphism identifies the associated graded module with

$$\operatorname{gr}_J(M)\cong(M/JM)[X_1,\ldots,X_c],$$

where the initial form of multiplication by $f_1$ is multiplication by $X_1$.

For every $n\geq1$ we claim

$$J^nM\cap f_1M=f_1J^{n-1}M.$$

One inclusion follows from $f_1\in J$. For the other suppose $f_1m\in J^nM$. If $n=1$, the conclusion $m\in J^0M$ needs no argument. If $n\geq2$ and $m\notin J^{n-1}M$, choose the largest $j$ in the finite range $0\leq j\leq n-2$ for which $m\in J^jM$. Then $m$ has nonzero class in $J^jM/J^{j+1}M$. Multiplication by $X_1$ is injective on a polynomial module, so $f_1m$ has nonzero class in $J^{j+1}M/J^{j+2}M$. This contradicts $f_1m\in J^nM\subseteq J^{j+2}M$. Hence $m\in J^{n-1}M$, proving the claim. The argument chooses a degree in a finite range and does not require separation of the $J$-adic filtration.

Now for $n\geq1$,

$$ \begin{aligned} \overline J^n\overline M/\overline J^{n+1}\overline M &\cong J^nM\big/\bigl(J^{n+1}M+(J^nM\cap f_1M)\bigr)\\ &=J^nM\big/\bigl(J^{n+1}M+f_1J^{n-1}M\bigr). \end{aligned} $$

In degree zero the quotient is $M/JM$. The resulting graded module is therefore obtained by setting $X_1=0$ in the polynomial module above:

$$\operatorname{gr}_{\overline J}(\overline M) \cong(M/JM)[X_2,\ldots,X_c].$$

The isomorphism has the prescribed generator images, so it is the quasi-regularity map for the remaining sequence. Its final quotient is still $M/JM$. Iterating proves the statement, including the original and empty remaining sequences. ∎

Lemma. The dimension formula in a Cohen–Macaulay local ring

If $R$ is Noetherian local and Cohen–Macaulay, then for every prime $\mathfrak p$,

$$\dim R=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(R/\mathfrak p).$$

Proof. Choose a prime chain of maximum length below $\mathfrak p$ and one of maximum length from $\mathfrak p$ to the maximal ideal. Their lengths are $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\dim(R/\mathfrak p)$, respectively. Each is saturated in its interval. The first begins at a minimal prime, since otherwise it could be extended, and the second ends at the maximal ideal. Concatenation is consequently a maximal chain in $\operatorname{Spec}R$. The Cohen–Macaulay maximal-chain theorem says its length is $\dim R$, proving the equality. The same conclusion follows from the full-support Cohen–Macaulay module version, taking the module to be $R$. ∎

Lemma. One nonzero relation eliminates one polynomial variable

Let $k$ be a field and let $0\ne I\subsetneq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. There are polynomials $y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}$ such that

$$k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I$$

is finite over the subalgebra generated by their images. Moreover the $y_i$ may lie in the image of $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

Proof. Choose a nonzero $F\in I$. A nonzero constant cannot belong to the proper ideal, so $F$ has positive degree and $n\geq1$. It suffices to prove the assertion for the quotient by $(F)$.

Choose an integer $B$ larger than every exponent appearing in a monomial of $F$. For $1\leq i<n$ put

$$e_i=B^i,\qquad y_i=x_i-x_n^{e_i}.$$

For the exponent vector $\alpha$ of any monomial occurring in $F$, the integer

$$w(\alpha)=\alpha_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}B^i\alpha_i$$

is its base-$B$ encoding, so these weights are distinct. In

$$F(y_1+T^{e_1},\ldots,y_{n-1}+T^{e_{n-1}},T),$$

the highest power of $T$ comes uniquely from the highest-weight original monomial, taking its highest $T$-term in every factor. Its coefficient is the nonzero coefficient of that original monomial, an element of $k^\times$. Divide by this coefficient. The resulting polynomial is monic in $T$ with coefficients in $k[y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}]$, and it vanishes at the class of $x_n$.

Thus $x_n$ is integral over the subalgebra generated by the $y_i$. Every other $x_i$ equals $y_i+x_n^{e_i}$, so the quotient by $(F)$ is generated over that subalgebra by this single integral element and is finite. Passing to the quotient by $I$ preserves finiteness. The formulas for $y_i$ have integer coefficients. For $n=1$ the list is empty and the argument is simply monic normalization of the one-variable polynomial $F$. ∎

Lemma. An integral overring has the same dimension

If $R\subset S$ is an integral extension, then $\dim R=\dim S$, with no Noetherian assumption.

Proof. Every prime of $R$ has a prime above it by lying over for integral overrings. Starting above the first prime of a finite chain in $R$, repeated going up lifts the whole chain to $S$. Distinct contractions ensure that all its inclusions remain strict. This proves $\dim R\leq\dim S$.

Conversely, contract any finite strict chain in $S$ to $R$. Two comparable primes over the same base prime must coincide, by integral incomparability. Hence every contracted inclusion is strict, giving $\dim S\leq\dim R$. Taking suprema over all finite chains covers infinite dimensions as well. If $R=0$, its unital overring is also zero and the two spectra are empty. ∎

Lemma. Five tests for dimension one

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$, the following conditions are equivalent.

  1. The dimension of $R$ is one.
  2. Its Hilbert–Samuel degree $d(R)$ is one.
  3. Some nonnilpotent $x\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies $V(x)=\{\mathfrak m\}$.
  4. Some nonnilpotent $x\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies $\sqrt{xR}=\mathfrak m$.
  5. A principal ideal is an ideal of definition, whereas the zero ideal is not.

Here an ideal of definition means an ideal with radical $\mathfrak m$.

Proof. Suppose (1). The finiteness of minimal primes and prime avoidance give an element of $\mathfrak m$ outside every minimal prime: each minimal prime is strictly smaller than $\mathfrak m$. Any other prime must be $\mathfrak m$, since a nonminimal prime strictly below $\mathfrak m$ would give a chain of length two. The chosen element therefore belongs to exactly one prime, namely $\mathfrak m$. It is not nilpotent, since nilpotents belong to every prime. This proves (3).

The radical description of closed subsets identifies (3) with (4). If $\sqrt{xR}=\mathfrak m$ and $x$ is nilpotent, then $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$. Conversely, if $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$, every element of $\mathfrak m$ is nilpotent. Thus (4) and (5) are equivalent.

Assume (5), and write $I=xR$ for the principal ideal of definition. Multiplication by $x^j$ maps $R/I$ onto $I^j/I^{j+1}$. Consequently

$$\ell_R(R/I^{n+1})\leq(n+1)\ell_R(R/I).$$

The eventual polynomial has degree at most one. The dimension-zero criterion, proved just below, says that degree zero would make the zero ideal an ideal of definition. Hence the degree is one, proving (2).

For the remaining implication, suppose $d(R)=1$. If a chain of length two exists, extend its upper endpoint to $\mathfrak m$ and retain a chain

$$\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak m.$$

Put $B=R/\mathfrak p$. The Hilbert-function exact-sequence lemma gives $d(B)\leq1$. Since $B$ has a nonzero prime strictly below its maximal ideal, the dimension-zero criterion excludes $d(B)=0$. Choose $x\in\mathfrak q\setminus\mathfrak p$. Multiplication by its image in the domain $B$ gives

$$0\longrightarrow B\xrightarrow{x}B\longrightarrow B/xB\longrightarrow0.$$

The same exact-sequence lemma says that $\chi_{I,B/xB}$ has degree strictly less than one: the two copies of $\chi_{I,B}$ cancel. Thus $B/xB$ is zero-dimensional. But the images of $\mathfrak q$ and $\mathfrak m$ are two distinct primes of that quotient, a contradiction. Therefore $\dim R\leq1$; degree one excludes dimension zero, so (1) holds.

The general dimension, growth and parameter theorem also yields (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(5). The argument above retains the direct prime-avoidance and Hilbert-growth proof in dimension one. ∎

Lemma. Dimension zero and constant Hilbert growth

A Noetherian local ring $R$ has dimension zero precisely when $d(R)=0$.

Proof. If the lengths $\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^{n+1})$ are eventually constant, then $\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}=0$ for large $n$. Nakayama applied to the finite module $\mathfrak m^n$ gives $\mathfrak m^n=0$. The filtration by powers of $\mathfrak m$ now proves that $R$ has finite length, and its only prime is $\mathfrak m$.

Conversely, dimension zero means $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$. In a Noetherian ring the nilradical is nilpotent: take finitely many generators of it, choose a nilpotence exponent for each, and use the pigeonhole principle on sufficiently long products of generators. Hence some power of $\mathfrak m$ vanishes. The finite filtration again gives finite length, and the Hilbert function $\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^{n+1})$ is eventually the positive constant $\ell_R(R)$. Its degree is zero. This also proves the finite-length characterization used above. ∎

Lemma. Hilbert polynomials in an exact sequence

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $I$ have radical $\mathfrak m$, and consider finite modules in an exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0.$$

Write $\chi_Q(n)=\ell_R(Q/I^{n+1}Q)$, using the same notation for its eventual numerical polynomial. Set $\deg0=-\infty$ and $d(0)=-\infty$. Then:

  1. If $M'$ has infinite length, the polynomial $\chi_M-\chi_{M''}-\chi_{M'}$ has degree strictly below $\deg\chi_{M'}$.
  2. The degree of $\chi_M$ is $\max\{\deg\chi_{M'},\deg\chi_{M''}\}$.
  3. One has $d(M)=\max\{d(M'),d(M'')\}$.

Proof. We first supply both finite-colength comparisons needed in the argument. Identify $M'$ with its image in $M$. By Artin–Rees, there is $c\geq0$ such that, for $n\geq c$,

$$M'\cap I^nM=I^{n-c}N,\qquad N=M'\cap I^cM.$$

Since $I^cM'\subset N$, the quotient $M'/N$ has finite length $l$. Taking lengths in the quotient exact sequence gives

$$\chi_M(n)=\chi_{M''}(n)+\chi_N(n-c)+l\qquad(n\geq c).$$

Indeed the kernel of $M/I^{n+1}M\to M''/I^{n+1}M''$ is $M'/I^{n+1-c}N$, whose length is $l+\chi_N(n-c)$. The same identity is valid at $n=c-1$ if $\chi_Q(-1)=0$. Subtracting consecutive identities therefore also proves

$$\varphi_M(n)=\varphi_{M''}(n)+\varphi_N(n-c)\qquad(n\geq c),$$

where $\varphi_Q(n)=\ell_R(I^nQ/I^{n+1}Q)$. These are the full shifted equalities, not just a comparison of leading terms.

Next let $Q'\subset Q$ be any finite-colength inclusion of finite modules, and put $a=\ell_R(Q/Q')$. Choose $b\geq0$ with $I^bQ\subset Q'$. For $n\geq b$, the inclusions

$$I^{n+1}Q'\subset I^{n+1}Q\subset I^{n+1-b}Q'$$

give

$$a+\chi_{Q'}(n-b)\leq\chi_Q(n)\leq a+\chi_{Q'}(n).$$

If $Q$ has infinite length, so does $Q'$. Their eventual polynomials have positive degree: degree zero would imply stabilization of the lengths, then $I^nQ=I^{n+1}Q$, and Nakayama would force $I^nQ=0$ and finite length. The displayed bounds show that the two polynomials have the same degree and leading coefficient. Their difference consequently has smaller degree. This proves the full finite-colength assertion for arbitrary $Q'\subset Q$.

Apply this comparison to $N\subset M'$ when $M'$ has infinite length. The shifted equality expresses the desired error polynomial as the sum

$$\begin{aligned} \chi_M-\chi_{M''}-\chi_{M'} ={}&l+\bigl(\chi_N(n-c)-\chi_N(n)\bigr)\\ &+\bigl(\chi_N(n)-\chi_{M'}(n)\bigr). \end{aligned}$$

The second line has smaller degree by the finite-colength comparison. Translating a positive-degree polynomial changes only terms below its leading degree, so the first line does too. This proves (1). Nonzero Hilbert polynomials have positive leading coefficients. Thus adding $\chi_{M'}$ and $\chi_{M''}$ cannot cancel their highest terms, and (1) yields (2) in this case.

If $M'$ has finite length, a power of $I$ annihilates it. Artin–Rees then gives $M'\cap I^nM=0$ for sufficiently large $n$. Hence

$$\chi_M(n)=\chi_{M''}(n)+\ell_R(M')\qquad(n\gg0).$$

If $M'\ne0$ the added constant is positive; if $M'=0$ it is zero. This proves (2), including the case $M''=0$. For a nonzero finite module the degree in (2) is its invariant $d$, independent of the chosen ideal of definition. If $M'=0$ or $M''=0$, exactness identifies $M$ with the other module; if $M=0$, both end modules vanish. The convention $d(0)=-\infty$ therefore proves (3) in every remaining case. ∎

Lemma. Reduced algebras after separable scalar extension

Suppose $S$ is a reduced algebra over a field $k$. If $K/k$ is separable, or if it is separably generated, then $K\otimes_kS$ is reduced. Neither $S$ nor $K$ is required to be finitely generated.

Proof for a separable extension. A tensor and a proposed nilpotence relation involve finitely many elements of $K$ and $S$. Choose a finitely generated intermediate field $K_0/k$ and a finite type subalgebra $S_0\subset S$ containing them. The map

$$K_0\otimes_kS_0\longrightarrow K\otimes_kS$$

is injective: first tensor the injection $S_0\subset S$ with the vector space $K_0$, then tensor $K_0\subset K$ with $S$. Thus it suffices to prove reducedness for $K_0\otimes_kS_0$. The algebra $S_0$ is reduced, and the definition of separability makes $K_0/k$ separably generated. We may therefore assume these two finiteness conditions.

There are finitely many minimal primes $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$ of $S$. The map

$$S\longrightarrow\prod_{\nu=1}^t\operatorname{Frac}(S/\mathfrak p_\nu)$$

is injective: its kernel is the intersection of the minimal primes, which is zero. Equivalently, this is the embedding into the finite product of fields supplied by the total-fraction-ring description. Tensoring preserves the injection, and it commutes with this finite product. The zero algebra causes no difficulty; otherwise it is enough to prove the assertion for a domain $S$.

Choose a separating transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ and a primitive element $\alpha$ as in the field-generation lemma. Put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ and let $P\in F[T]$ be the monic separable minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. The ring

$$A=F\otimes_kS$$

is a localization of the domain $S[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$, so it is a domain. Moreover

$$K\otimes_kS\cong A[T]/(P).$$

Monicity makes the right side free over $A$, on the powers of $T$ below $\deg P$. It therefore embeds into $E[T]/(P)$, where $E=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. A Bézout identity between $P$ and $P'$ over $F$ remains valid over $E$. Thus $P$ factors over $E$ into distinct irreducible polynomials, and the Chinese remainder theorem makes $E[T]/(P)$ a finite product of fields. Its subring $A[T]/(P)$ is reduced. This proves the claim.

Proof for a separably generated extension. This route does not first assume that every such extension is separable. Choose a separating transcendence basis $\{x_i\}_{i\in J}$, so $K$ is separable algebraic over $k(x_i\mid i\in J)$. Given a finite list $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s\in K$, choose for each $\lambda_j$ a monic separable annihilating polynomial over that rational field. Only finitely many variables occur in its coefficients and in a Bézout identity with its derivative. All these data therefore lie in $F_T=k(x_i\mid i\in T)$ for some finite $T\subset J$. The minimal polynomial of each $\lambda_j$ over $F_T$ divides the chosen separable polynomial; it is consequently separable. Hence

$$F_T(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s)/F_T$$

is finite separable. Such subfields form a directed family: for two of them, include both finite variable sets and both generator lists, and enlarge $T$ to include all the needed coefficients. Their union is $K$.

Each member is finitely generated and separably generated over $k$, so the domain-and-separable-polynomial argument above applies to it and every finite type reduced subalgebra of $S$. The tensor injections and finite nilpotence witnesses from the first paragraph then prove reducedness for the entire tensor product. ∎

Lemma. Exchanging one element to obtain a separating basis

Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$, and suppose

$$K=k(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})$$

with $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ a transcendence basis. Assume that taking $p$-th powers carries every finite $k$-linearly independent family in $K$ to a $k$-linearly independent family. Some index $j\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$ then has the following property: the $n$ elements obtained by omitting $x_j$ form a separating transcendence basis.

Proof. A nonzero polynomial relation among the $n+1$ generators exists. Choose one, $F\in k[X_1,\ldots,X_{n+1}]$, with smallest total degree. Its degree is positive. If $F$ factored into two nonconstant polynomials, one factor would vanish at the generators, contradicting minimality. Thus $F$ is irreducible.

Suppose every exponent in every monomial of $F$ were divisible by $p$. Write

$$F=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha X^{p\alpha}.$$

The corresponding elements $x^\alpha$ are pairwise distinct: equality between two would already give a nonzero polynomial relation of total degree at most $\deg(F)/p<\deg(F)$. The relation

$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(x^\alpha)^p=0$$

and the hypothesis therefore force the family $(x^\alpha)_\alpha$ to be linearly dependent. A nontrivial dependence gives a polynomial relation of total degree at most $\deg(F)/p$, again impossible. Hence $\partial F/\partial X_j\ne0$ for some $j$.

Regard $F$ as a polynomial in $X_j$. Choose a nonzero coefficient of a positive power of $X_j$. Its total degree is smaller than $\deg F$, so it cannot vanish upon evaluation at the other generators. The evaluated polynomial is therefore nonconstant, and $x_j$ is algebraic over

$$L=k(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_j},\ldots,x_{n+1}).$$

Since $K/L$ is algebraic, $L$ has transcendence degree $n$. It is generated by the displayed $n$ elements, so they are algebraically independent. Evaluation therefore identifies their polynomial ring with $k[X_i\mid i\ne j]$.

Gauss' lemma now transfers the irreducibility of $F$ to $L[T]$. Its derivative in $T$ is nonzero, since $\partial F/\partial X_j\ne0$ and the other variables remain algebraically independent. An irreducible polynomial with nonzero derivative is separable. It follows that $K=L(x_j)$ is finite separable over $L$, proving the assertion. For $n=0$ the remaining list is empty and $L=k$, so the same argument includes that case. ∎

Lemma. Split transitivity for a formally smooth map

For ring maps $A\to B\to C$ with $C$ formally smooth over $B$, the canonical sequence

$$0\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BC \longrightarrow\Omega_{C/A} \longrightarrow\Omega_{C/B}\longrightarrow0$$

is split exact as a sequence of $C$-modules.

Proof. Right exactness is the differential transitivity sequence. Put $V=\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BC$, and give the square-zero extension $C\oplus V$ its $B$-algebra structure

$$b\longmapsto\bigl(b,db\otimes1\bigr).$$

Formal smoothness lifts the identity $C\to C$ across the $B$-algebra surjection $C\oplus V\to C$. Write this lift as $c\mapsto(c,Dc)$. Its second component is an $A$-derivation with $D(b)=db\otimes1$. Universality gives a $C$-linear map $\Omega_{C/A}\to V$ whose composite with $V\to\Omega_{C/A}$ is the identity. The first arrow is consequently a split injection; right exactness identifies its complement with $\Omega_{C/B}$.

One can also use the original cotangent-complex argument. The formal-smoothness criterion makes $H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{C/B})$ zero and $\Omega_{C/B}$ projective. The cotangent transitivity sequence then gives injectivity on the left, and projectivity splits the resulting short exact sequence. ∎

Lemma. Differentials commute with directed colimits

Let $(R_i\to S_i)_{i\in I}$ be a compatible system indexed by a directed set, with colimit $R\to S$. There is a canonical isomorphism

$$\Omega_{S/R}\cong\operatorname*{colim}_{i\in I}\Omega_{S_i/R_i}.$$

The colimit on the right carries its natural $S$-module structure; the transition maps of differential modules are linear over the corresponding ring maps.

Proof. Denote that colimit by $V$. For $s\in S$, choose a representative $s_i\in S_i$ and let $\delta(s)$ be the image of $ds_i$ in $V$. Two representatives become equal at a later index, and functoriality of differentials then makes their images equal. Thus $\delta$ is well-defined. Move finitely many representatives to a common index to check additivity and the Leibniz rule. An element of $R$ comes from some $R_i$, where its image has zero differential; hence $\delta$ is an $R$-derivation.

If $N$ is an $S$-module and $D\colon S\to N$ is an $R$-derivation, its restriction to each $S_i$ annihilates $R_i$. The resulting maps $\Omega_{S_i/R_i}\to N$ are compatible and induce a unique $S$-linear map $V\to N$ carrying $\delta(s)$ to $D(s)$. Conversely every such linear map produces a derivation.
