Uniqueness follows because the elements $ds_i$ generate every differential module. Thus $(V,\delta)$ represents precisely the universal derivation of $S$ over $R$.

In terms of the defining presentation, the same argument says that every generator $ds$ and every relation expressing additivity, the product rule, or vanishing on a base element is represented at some index; a finite collection of such relations is represented at a common later index. This is the presentation proof of the same canonical isomorphism. ∎

Lemma. A separating basis and one additional generator

Suppose $K/k$ is both finitely generated and separably generated, and put $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_kK$. There are $x_1,\ldots,x_{r+1}\in K$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ form a transcendence basis,

$$K=k(x_1,\ldots,x_{r+1}),$$

and $x_{r+1}$ is separable over $k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$.

Proof. Choose a separating transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ and put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$. The extension $K/F$ is algebraic and separable. It is finite, since a finite list of generators of $K/k$ also generates it over $F$, and each such generator is algebraic.

Here is the needed primitive-element argument. If $F$ is infinite, choose generators $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_s$ of a nontrivial finite separable extension $E/F$. There are $[E:F]$ distinct embeddings of $E$ into an algebraic closure fixing $F$. This count follows along a tower of simple extensions: each embedding extends once for each distinct root of the next separable minimal polynomial, so the counts multiply by the successive degrees.

For each pair of distinct embeddings $\sigma,\tau$, the polynomial

$$\sum_{i=1}^s T^{i-1}\bigl(\sigma(\alpha_i)-\tau(\alpha_i)\bigr)$$

is nonzero, because the embeddings differ on a generator. There are only finitely many pairs and finitely many roots to avoid. Choose $c\in F$ avoiding all of them, and set $\theta=\sum_i c^{i-1}\alpha_i$. Its images under all $[E:F]$ embeddings are distinct. Hence its minimal polynomial has at least $[E:F]$ roots, and therefore degree exactly $[E:F]$. This forces $E=F(\theta)$.

If $F$ is finite, $E$ is a finite field. Its multiplicative group is cyclic, as follows. In a finite abelian group the least common multiple $e$ of all element orders is itself the order of an element: for each prime dividing $e$, choose an element whose order contains the largest required power of that prime, take its component of that prime-power order, and multiply these commuting components. In $E^\times$ every element is a root of $T^e-1$, so $|E^\times|\leq e$. The reverse inequality follows from the existence of the element of order $e$. Thus this element generates $E^\times$, and in particular generates $E$ as a field over $F$.

Apply these arguments to $E=K$. A primitive generator is separable over $F$ because $K/F$ is separable. If $K=F$, take the additional generator to be zero. This proves all three assertions, including $r=0$. ∎

Lemma. Localizing the base or the target of differentials

For a ring map $A\to B$, the following canonical identifications hold.

  1. If a multiplicative subset $U\subset A$ maps to units of $B$, then $\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{B/U^{-1}A}$.
  2. For a multiplicative subset $U\subset B$, one has $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}$.

Proof. For (1), an $A$-derivation into a $B$-module vanishes on the image of $a\in A$. If $u\in U$, differentiating $u\,u^{-1}=1$ shows that it vanishes on $u^{-1}$ as well, since $u$ acts invertibly. It therefore vanishes on the entire image of $U^{-1}A$. The two types of derivations coincide for every target module, which proves the canonical identification.

For (2), put $N=U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}$ and define

$$\delta(b/u)=u^{-1}db-bu^{-2}du.$$

We check the fraction relation explicitly. If $b/u=b'/u'$, there is $v\in U$ with $v(bu'-b'u)=0$. Differentiating this equality in $N$, and using the fact that $bu'-b'u$ is zero after localization, gives

$$u'\,db+b\,du'-u\,db'-b'\,du=0.$$

Divide by $uu'$, and write $q=b/u=b'/u'$. The resulting equation is

$$\frac{db}{u}-\frac{db'}{u'} =q\left(\frac{du}{u}-\frac{du'}{u'}\right),$$

which is exactly the equality of the two proposed values of $\delta$. In this argument $v$ is invertible in $U^{-1}B$, so cancellation of its action on $N$ is justified.

For addition, expand the formula at $(bu'+b'u)/(uu')$ and use

$$d(uu')=u\,du'+u'\,du.$$

The cross terms cancel, leaving $\delta(b/u)+\delta(b'/u')$. For multiplication the same expansion gives

$$\delta\left(\frac{bb'}{uu'}\right) =\frac{b}{u}\delta\left(\frac{b'}{u'}\right) +\frac{b'}{u'}\delta\left(\frac{b}{u}\right).$$

The formula vanishes on the image of $A$ and sends $1$ to zero. Thus it is an $A$-derivation, inducing a map $\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}\to N$.

In the other direction the derivation $B\to\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}$ induces the canonical map from $N$. The two composites fix every $db$, and in the target localization the product rule forces

$$d(b/u)=u^{-1}db-bu^{-2}du.$$

Since these differentials generate the respective modules, both composites are identities. The proof also covers a multiplicative set containing zero, when the localized ring and both modules are zero. ∎

Definition. Perfect fields

A field $k$ is called perfect when every extension field of $k$ is separable over $k$.

Lemma. Finite purely inseparable enlargement

Given a finitely generated field extension $K/k$, there are finite purely inseparable extensions $k'/k$ and $K'/K$ fitting into a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc} k&\longrightarrow&K\\ \big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\ k'&\longrightarrow&K' \end{array}$$

such that $K'/k'$ is separably generated.

Proof. In characteristic zero the identity extensions work. Suppose the characteristic is $p>0$. Choose a transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of $K/k$, and put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$. The extension $K/F$ is finite.

We use its separable-then-purely-inseparable decomposition, with the following justification. The elements of $K$ separable over $F$ form a subfield $E$: any finite list of separable elements generates a finite separable extension, and hence its sums, products and inverses are separable. For any algebraic element $a$, write its irreducible polynomial in the form $g(T^{p^e})$, with $g'\ne0$, by repeatedly dividing all exponents by $p$ while the derivative is zero. The polynomial $g$ is irreducible, so $a^{p^e}$ is separable over $F$. Thus $K/E$ is purely inseparable. This also proves uniqueness: an element separable over a field and purely inseparable over it must belong to that field, since its minimal polynomial cannot have both distinct roots and only one distinct root. Consequently any separable intermediate field over which $K$ is purely inseparable contains every element separable over $F$ and equals $E$.

Induct on $d=[K:E]$, simultaneously for all finitely generated extensions with a chosen transcendence basis. If $d=1$, the basis already separates and no enlargement is needed. Otherwise choose $\beta\in K\setminus E$ with $\beta^p=\alpha\in E$. Such a choice follows by taking the penultimate member of a shortest chain of successive $p$-th powers taking an element of $K\setminus E$ into $E$. Let

$$P(T)=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\in F[T]$$

be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. It is separable.

Write each $a_i$ as a quotient of two polynomials in $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ with coefficients in $k$. Only finitely many coefficients occur. In an algebraic closure containing $K$, adjoin their $p$-th roots to $k$ to obtain a finite purely inseparable extension $k_1/k$. Also put $y_i=x_i^{1/p}$ and

$$F_1=k_1(y_1,\ldots,y_r),\qquad L=KF_1.$$

Each $a_i$ is a $p$-th power in $F_1$: replace each coefficient of its numerator and denominator by its chosen root and replace each monomial $x^\gamma$ by $y^\gamma$. Frobenius recovers the original rational function. Its denominator is nonzero because its $p$-th power is the original nonzero denominator.

The extension $F_1/F$ is finite purely inseparable, as is $L/K$. The elements $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ are algebraically independent over $k_1$. Indeed a hypothetical relation can be raised to a sufficiently large $p$-power to put its coefficients in $k$; its monomials then become distinct monomials in the algebraically independent $x_i$. This would give a nonzero relation over $k$. Thus $F_1$ is a rational function field over $k_1$.

Let $E_1=EF_1$. The extension $E_1/F_1$ is separable, because the separable equations for generators of $E/F$ remain separable after extending scalars. The extension $L/E_1$ is purely inseparable. By the uniqueness argument above, $E_1$ is exactly the maximal separable subfield of $L/F_1$.

Choose $b_i\in F_1$ with $b_i^p=a_i$, and form

$$Q(T)=T^n+b_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n.$$

Then $Q(T)^p=P(T^p)$, and $Q(\beta)^p=P(\alpha)=0$, so $Q(\beta)=0$. Moreover $Q$ is separable. In an algebraic closure Frobenius is bijective, and its bijection from the roots of $Q$ to the roots of $P$ preserves their multiplicities, as the displayed polynomial identity shows. Since $P$ has distinct roots, so does $Q$. Therefore $\beta$ is separable over $F_1$, and hence $\beta\in E_1$.

This proves the strict decrease:

$$[L:E_1]\leq[K:E(\beta)] <[K:E]=d.$$

For the first inequality, a basis of $K$ over $E(\beta)$ spans the compositum $KE_1=L$ over $E_1$. The second inequality holds because $\beta\notin E$. The inclusions and identifications used here are summarized by

$$\begin{array}{ccc} K&\longrightarrow&L\\ \big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\ E(\beta)&\longrightarrow&E_1\\ \big\uparrow&&\big\Vert\\ E&\longrightarrow&E_1\\ \big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\ F&\longrightarrow&F_1\\ \big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\ k&\longrightarrow&k_1. \end{array}$$

Every square commutes inside the chosen algebraic closure. In particular the repeated right-hand entry records the newly obtained inclusion of $\beta$ in the separable subfield.

Apply induction to the finitely generated extension $L/k_1$, with transcendence basis $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ and smaller inseparable degree. It supplies finite purely inseparable extensions $k_2/k_1$ and $L'/L$ with $L'/k_2$ separably generated. Their composites $k_2/k$ and $L'/K$ are finite purely inseparable. Taking $k'=k_2$ and $K'=L'$ gives the required square. ∎

Lemma. Separating transcendence bases imply separability

Every separably generated extension $K/k$ is separable.

Proof. In characteristic zero every finitely generated intermediate field has a transcendence basis over which its finite algebraic extension is separable, since irreducible polynomials have nonzero derivative. Hence the assertion follows from the definition of separability.

In characteristic $p>0$, apply the separably generated scalar-extension proof to the reduced $k$-algebra $k^{1/p}$. It shows that $K\otimes_k k^{1/p}$ is reduced. The separability criterion then gives separability of $K/k$. That proof of reducedness uses a separating basis directly, so this implication does not assume the conclusion it is proving. ∎

Lemma. Separability passes to intermediate fields

If $K/k$ is separable and $k\subset K'\subset K$, then $K'/k$ is separable.

Proof. Any intermediate field finitely generated over $k$ inside $K'$ is also such an intermediate field inside $K$. By separability of $K/k$, it is separably generated over $k$. This is precisely the definition of separability for $K'/k$.

Equivalently, for every field extension $L/k$, the vector-space injection $K'\subset K$ remains injective after tensoring with $L$. Thus $K'\otimes_kL$ embeds into the reduced ring $K\otimes_kL$ and is reduced. The geometric reducedness criterion gives the same conclusion. ∎

Lemma. Flatness through Tor

For an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, the following five tests are equivalent.

  1. Tensoring with $M$ is exact.
  2. $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M,N)=0$ for every $R$-module $N$ and every $i>0$.
  3. $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,N)=0$ for every $R$-module $N$.
  4. $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)=0$ for every ideal $I$ of $R$.
  5. The equality in (4) holds for every finitely generated ideal $I$.

Proof. If $M$ is flat, tensoring a free resolution of $N$ with $M$ preserves exactness in positive degrees. Computing Tor from this resolution proves (2). The implications (2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(4)$\Rightarrow$(5) simply restrict the indices or modules being tested.

Suppose (5). For a finitely generated ideal $I$, the sequence $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$ gives

$$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I) \longrightarrow M\otimes_RI\longrightarrow M.$$

This is the relevant portion of the long exact Tor sequence; the preceding term is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R)=0$. One obtains that sequence by tensoring the short exact sequence with a free resolution of $M$. Each free term preserves its exactness, and the resulting short exact sequence of complexes has the usual connecting maps on homology. Thus the vanishing in (5) makes $I\otimes_RM\to M$ injective for every finitely generated ideal. The full ideal criterion for flatness implies (1). No finiteness assumption on $M$ or Noetherian assumption on $R$ enters this argument. ∎

Lemma. Generators remain generators after enlarging scalars

Let $R\to S$ be a ring map and let $M$ be an $S$-module. If $M$ is finite over $R$, it is finite over $S$.

Proof. Choose $R$-module generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$. Every expression $\sum r_im_i$ is also an $S$-linear expression, using the images of the coefficients $r_i$ in $S$. The same list therefore generates over $S$. This includes the empty list when $M=0$. ∎

Lemma. Simple modules and length one

For an $R$-module $M$, these assertions are equivalent: $M$ is simple; $\ell_R(M)=1$; and $M\cong R/\mathfrak m$ for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.

Proof. A simple module is nonzero and has no submodules besides zero and itself. This says exactly that its only strict chain from zero to the whole module has length one. If $\mathfrak m$ is maximal, the submodules of $R/\mathfrak m$ correspond to ideals containing $\mathfrak m$, so this quotient is simple.

Conversely, take $0\ne x\in M$ when $M$ is simple. The nonzero submodule $Rx$ is all of $M$, so the map $R\to M$, $r\mapsto rx$, identifies $M$ with $R/I$, where $I=\operatorname{Ann}_R(x)$. The ideal is proper because $x\ne0$. An ideal $I\subsetneq J\subsetneq R$ would give a nonzero proper submodule $J/I$ of $R/I$. No such $J$ exists, so $I$ is maximal. ∎

Lemma. Comparing length under restriction of scalars

For an $S$-module $M$ and a ring map $R\to S$,

$$\ell_R(M)\geq\ell_S(M).$$

Equality holds when the ring map is surjective. Length is allowed to be infinite.

Proof. Every strict chain of $S$-submodules is a strict chain of $R$-submodules. Taking suprema of the possible chain lengths proves the inequality, also when these lengths are unbounded. If $R\to S$ is onto, an $R$-submodule is closed under every scalar of $S$, since that scalar has a lift in $R$. The two collections of submodules coincide, giving equality. ∎

Lemma. Localization and polynomials preserve geometric reducedness

If a $k$-algebra $R$ is geometrically reduced, then so are every localization $U^{-1}R$ and the polynomial algebra $R[x]$.

Proof. A localization of a reduced ring is reduced. Indeed, if $(a/u)^n=0$, some $v\in U$ satisfies $va^n=0$. Then $(va)^n=0$, so $va=0$ and $a/u=0$. A polynomial ring over a reduced ring is also reduced: the injections into the product of the domains $R/\mathfrak p$, over all prime ideals $\mathfrak p$, induce an injection on polynomial rings. Each target polynomial ring is a domain, and a subring of their product has no nonzero nilpotents.

For any extension field $K/k$, the canonical tensor identifications give

$$\begin{aligned} K\otimes_k U^{-1}R&\cong U^{-1}(K\otimes_kR),\\ K\otimes_k R[x]&\cong(K\otimes_kR)[x]. \end{aligned}$$

The ring $K\otimes_kR$ is reduced by hypothesis. Apply the two preceding observations to conclude. In the first line $U$ denotes its image in the tensor algebra; even if that image contains zero, the conclusion still holds. ∎

Lemma. Generic finite presentation for an inclusion of domains

Let $R\subset S$ be domains with $S$ finite type over $R$. There are nonzero elements $f\in R$ and $g\in S$ such that $S_{fg}$ is finitely presented over $R_f$.

Proof. Induct on the number of chosen algebra generators. With no generators $S=R$, and $f=g=1$ works.

For one generator, write $S=R[t]\cong R[T]/Q$. If $Q=0$, this is already a polynomial presentation. Otherwise choose $0\ne h\in Q$ of smallest degree $d$ and let $f\ne0$ be its leading coefficient. The inclusion $R\subset S$ implies $d\geq1$. Inverting $f$ makes $f^{-1}h$ monic. Division by it shows that

$$R_f[T]/(f^{-1}h)\longrightarrow S_f$$

is an isomorphism. To justify injectivity, any element of its kernel has a representative of degree below $d$. Clear the finitely many powers of $f$ in its coefficients. Since $S$ is a domain and $f\ne0$, vanishing in $S_f$ implies vanishing of the resulting polynomial in $S$. A nonzero such polynomial would contradict the minimal choice of $d$. Thus the remainder is zero. This gives a finite presentation, with $g=1$.

Now take $n>1$ generators $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ and set $S_0=R[t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}]\subset S$. By induction, choose $0\ne f\in R$ and $0\ne g_0\in S_0$ with

$$R_f\longrightarrow B=(S_0)_{fg_0}$$

finitely presented. The algebra $S_{fg_0}$ is generated over the domain $B$ by the single element $t_n$. The one-generator argument supplies $0\ne a\in B$ such that

$$B_a\longrightarrow(S_{fg_0})_a$$

is finitely presented. Write $a=b/(fg_0)^N$ with $0\ne b\in S_0$. Localizing $B$ at $a$ is the same as localizing it at $b$.

A principal localization is finitely presented, using one variable and the relation $aZ-1$; finite presentation is preserved under composition. Hence the composite from $R_f$ to $(S_{fg_0})_a=S_{fg_0b}$ is finitely presented. Taking $g=g_0b\ne0$ proves the assertion. This explicitly returns the intermediate denominator to an element of the original algebra $S$. ∎

Lemma. Smoothness and regularity with separable residue field

Let $S$ be a finite type algebra over a field $k$, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ have residue field separable over $k$. Then $S$ is smooth over $k$ at $\mathfrak q$ if and only if $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is regular.

Proof. Write $R=S_{\mathfrak q}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak qR$ and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. We first give the conormal calculation in its full useful scope: for any Noetherian local $k$-algebra $R$ with finitely generated separable residue field, the natural map

$$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$$

is injective.

Put $A=R/\mathfrak m^2$ and $N=\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. Choose a separating transcendence basis $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$ of $\kappa/k$ and a separable primitive element $\bar y$ over $F=k(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r)$, using the field-generation lemma. Lifts $x_i\in A$ define a map $F\to A$: every nonzero polynomial in the $\bar x_i$ is nonzero in the residue field, so its value at the lifts is a unit of the local ring $A$.

Let $P\in F[T]$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\bar y$, and choose any lift $y\in A$. Evaluating coefficients through $F\to A$, one has $P(y)\in N$ and $P'(y)\in A^\times$. Since $N^2=0$, the correction

$$y'=y-\frac{P(y)}{P'(y)}$$

satisfies $P(y')=0$. It therefore extends $F\to A$ to a $k$-algebra section $\sigma\colon\kappa=F[T]/(P)\to A$ of the residue map. In the trivial primitive extension take $\bar y=0$ and $P=T$.

The map $D\colon A\to N$ defined by $D(a)=a-\sigma(\bar a)$ is a $k$-derivation when $N$ is viewed as an $A$-module through $\kappa$. Indeed the product of two elements of $N$ vanishes, giving the Leibniz rule, and $D$ vanishes on $k$. It restricts to the identity on $N$. Thus the conormal map into $\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_A\kappa$ has a retraction and is injective. The quotient $R\to A$ does not change this differential fibre: every differential of a product of two elements of $\mathfrak m$ vanishes after tensoring with $\kappa$. This proves the claimed injection and the split exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa \longrightarrow\Omega_{\kappa/k}\longrightarrow0.$$

Alternatively, formal smoothness of $\kappa/k$ supplies the section $\kappa\to R/\mathfrak m^2$ directly; the same derivation then proves the injection. This is the full subargument in Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion, §3, Theorem 3.2.

Now set $t=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa$. The differentials of a separating basis form a basis of $\Omega_{\kappa/k}$. To see the effect of the additional primitive generator, its defining separable equation has invertible derivative in that generator; differentiating it solves uniquely for that generator's differential and imposes no relation on the basis differentials. Thus $\dim_\kappa\Omega_{\kappa/k}=t$. By differential localization, the middle term of the exact sequence is $\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa$. Consequently

$$\begin{aligned} \dim_\kappa(\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa) &=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)+t\\ &\geq\dim R+t\\ &=\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}S. \end{aligned}$$

The last equality is the pointwise dimension formula. Equality in the middle inequality holds exactly when the Noetherian local ring $R$ is regular. The differential criterion, proved in full in §§1–2 of the same Jacobian-criterion lesson, identifies equality between differential dimension and point dimension with smoothness. This proves both implications. ∎

Theorem. Zariski's Main Theorem in affine algebra

Let $S$ be finite type over an arbitrary ring $R$, let $C\subset S$ be the subring of elements integral over $R$, and suppose $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$. Then some $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ makes the canonical map

$$C_g\longrightarrow S_g$$

an isomorphism.

Proof. We retain the monogenic calculation, the conductor step and the induction through a finite intermediate algebra. The complete argument also appears in Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley's theorem, §2A, Theorem 2A.1. Its two conductor inputs have complete proofs in The theorem on formal functions, Appendix Z, at the exact locators used below.

We first record the pointwise operations used in the proof. The isolated-fibre criterion characterizes quasi-finiteness for finite type maps by isolation of the selected point in its fibre. For $A\to B\to D$ with $D$ finite type over $A$, the same algebra generators generate $D$ over $B$. A principal open isolating a prime of $D$ in its fibre over $A$ still isolates it in the smaller fibre over $B$. Thus enlarging the intermediate base preserves quasi-finiteness at that prime, without any finiteness assumption on $B/A$. Localizing the base and source away from their selected primes also preserves and reflects the property: the local fibre is unchanged, and in the fibre topology the source localization is an open neighborhood of the point.

We also need the full four-ring assertion. In a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc} A&\longrightarrow&B\\ \big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\ A'&\longrightarrow&B' \end{array}$$

suppose $A\to B$ is finite type and $B\otimes_AA'\to B'$ is surjective. Let $\mathfrak q'$ contract to $\mathfrak q\subset B$ and to $\mathfrak p'\subset A'$, with $\mathfrak p\subset A$ their common contraction. Quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak q$ implies it at $\mathfrak q'$. Indeed the isolated closed point $\mathfrak q$ in $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ gives a product decomposition $H_1\times H_2$, where $H_1$ is the finite-dimensional local fibre algebra at that point. After extending to $\kappa(\mathfrak p')$ and taking the quotient defining the new fibre, its idempotent gives a factor $H'_1$, a quotient of $H_1\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak p')$. This factor is finite-dimensional. The chosen prime lies in it, since the idempotent of $H_1$ maps to one in its residue field. The spectrum of a finite-dimensional algebra over a field is finite and discrete, so $\mathfrak q'$ is isolated in its fibre. The quotient map also ensures finite type over $A'$. This proves the assertion with all four rings arbitrary.

The monogenic case. Suppose $S=R[x]=R[X]/I$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. Some polynomial in $I$ has a coefficient outside $\mathfrak p$. Otherwise the fibre would be $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[X]$, which has no isolated points: its zero prime has transcendental residue field, and every nonzero prime contains that zero prime as a distinct generization. Thus we have a relation

$$a_mx^m+\cdots+a_0=0$$

with coefficients in $C$, at least one outside $\mathfrak q$. Initially the coefficients come from $R$; allowing $C$ permits the following degree reduction.

For $m\geq1$, the element $a_mx$ is integral over $C$. Multiplying the relation by $a_m^{m-1}$ gives a monic equation in $a_mx$. Transitivity puts $a_mx$ in $C$, since $C$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $S$. If $a_m\notin\mathfrak q$, then $x=(a_mx)/a_m\in C_{a_m}$, and $C_{a_m}=S_{a_m}$. If $a_m\in\mathfrak q$, replace the leading two terms by

$$\bigl(a_mx+a_{m-1}\bigr)x^{m-1}.$$

This reduces the degree while retaining a coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$, because $a_mx\in\mathfrak q$. A degree-zero relation with its coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$ is impossible. The process therefore reaches a leading coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$ and proves the monogenic case. All localized inclusions used here are injective by exactness of localization.

The conductor step. Now suppose $R\subset S$, that $R$ is integrally closed in $S$, and that $S$ is finite over $R[x]$ for an element $x\in S$. The map from the polynomial ring $R[X]$ need not be injective. Let

$$J=\{u\in S:uS\subset R[x]\}.$$

It is an ideal of $S$, contained in $R[x]$. The complete coefficient lemma is Appendix Z, Lemma Z.6, including the monic-denominator and leading-coefficient arguments in Z.1–Z.5. It says that

$$\begin{gathered} u\sum_{i=0}^m a_ix^i\in\sqrt J\\ \Longrightarrow\quad ua_i\in\sqrt J\quad(0\leq i\leq m), \end{gathered}$$

for $u\in S$ and $a_i\in R$. These hypotheses allow zero divisors and a noninjective map $R[X]\to S$.

Set $\bar S=S/\sqrt J$ and $\bar R=R/(R\cap\sqrt J)$. The canonical maps form the commutative diagram

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} R&\longrightarrow&R[X]&\longrightarrow&S\\ \big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\ \bar R&\longrightarrow&\bar R[X]&\longrightarrow&\bar S. \end{array}$$

Here $\bar R$ embeds in $\bar S$, the horizontal composites are the structural maps, and $\bar S$ is finite over the image $\bar R[\bar x]$ of $\bar R[X]$. Both $\bar R$ and $\bar S$ are reduced. The coefficient lemma says that $\bar x$ is strongly transcendental over $\bar R$: an equation $\bar u\sum\bar a_i\bar x^i=0$ forces every $\bar u\bar a_i=0$.

The complete strong-transcendence theorem, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.11, with Z.8–Z.10 and the polynomial-normality proof in §0, now says that $\bar R\to\bar S$ has no quasi-finite points. Its proof passes to one minimal component and then to a normal domain by integral extension; it makes no Noetherian or finiteness-of-normalization assumption. If $J\subset\mathfrak q$, the four-ring assertion above would carry quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak q$ to $\mathfrak q/\sqrt J$, a contradiction. Hence choose $u\in J\setminus\mathfrak q$.

The definition of the conductor gives $R[x]_u=S_u$: for $s\in S$, one has $s=(us)/u$ and $us\in R[x]$. The contracted point of $R[x]$ is quasi-finite over $R$, because the local fibre ring is the same as that of $S$. The integral closure of $R$ inside $R[x]$ is still $R$. The monogenic case therefore supplies $a\in R\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $R_a=R[x]_a$. Write the image of $u$ there as $b/a^N$, with $b\in R$. Since $u$ and $a$ avoid the chosen prime, so does $b$. Inverting $h=ab$ makes both $a$ and $u$ units, and yields

$$R_h=R[x]_h=S_h.$$

This proves the finite-over-one-generator case when the base is integrally closed in the target.

Induction. Replace $R$ by its image in $S$ if necessary. This preserves the fibre at the selected point, finite type and the integral closure. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in S$ such that $S$ is finite over $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and induct on $n$. Such a list exists because a finite algebra-generating list works.

If $n=0$, then $S$ is integral over $R$, so $C=S$. If $n=1$, replace the base by $C$. Quasi-finiteness persists by the intermediate-base observation. The same finite module generators span $S$ over $C[x_1]$, and transitivity makes $C$ integrally closed in $S$. The conductor step supplies the required element of $C$.

For $n>1$, let $D$ be the integral closure of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]$ in $S$. Again $D\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, $D$ is integrally closed in $S$, and $S$ is finite over $D[x_n]$. The conductor step gives $v\in D\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $D_v=S_v$.

To use induction, a finite type intermediate algebra is essential. Choose a finite $R$-algebra generating list of $S_v$, and write its members as $y_j/v^{e_j}$ with $y_j\in D$. Let

$$E=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},v,y_1,\ldots,y_t]\subset D.$$

Then $E_v=S_v$: surjectivity follows from the chosen generators, and injectivity from localization of inclusions. Every added generator is integral over $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]$, so $E$ is finite over that ring. At $\mathfrak q_E=E\cap\mathfrak q$, its local ring and local fibre agree with those of $S$, proving quasi-finiteness of $E/R$ at $\mathfrak q_E$.

Let $F$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $E$. Induction gives $w\in F\setminus\mathfrak q_E$ with $F_w=E_w$. Express $v=c/w^N$ in that ring, with $c\in F$. The equality implies $c\notin\mathfrak q_E$, since $v,w$ avoid the prime. Put $g=wc$. Inverting $g$ makes $w$ and $v$ units, so

$$F_g=E_g=S_g.$$

Finally $F\subset C\subset S$, and localization of these inclusions is injective. The outer equality forces $C_g=S_g$. The element $g$ belongs to $C\setminus\mathfrak q$, completing the proof. ∎

Lemma. Finite-dimensional algebras are Artinian

An algebra finite-dimensional over a field is an Artinian ring.

Proof. Its ideals are vector subspaces. Every strict descent of ideals strictly decreases their nonnegative integer dimensions, so a descending chain must stop. This is the Artinian condition. ∎

Lemma. Artinian rings and zero-dimensional Noetherian rings

Every Noetherian ring of dimension zero is Artinian. Conversely, an Artinian ring is Noetherian and has dimension at most zero.

Proof. Let $R$ be Noetherian of dimension zero. Its finitely many minimal primes are also all of its maximal ideals; write them as $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$. Thus the spectrum is a finite discrete space. Its nilradical

$$N=\bigcap_{i=1}^t\mathfrak p_i$$

is nilpotent, since it has finitely many generators, each nilpotent. Choose $e\geq1$ with $N^e=0$. Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, and so are their $e$-th powers: from $a+b=1$ with $a,b$ in the two ideals, expand $(a+b)^{2e-1}$.

For pairwise comaximal ideals intersection equals product. The Chinese remainder theorem therefore gives

$$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^tR/\mathfrak p_i^e,$$

because $\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^e=N^e=0$. Each factor has just one prime, hence is local with nilpotent maximal ideal, and it identifies canonically with $R_{\mathfrak p_i}$. This is also the local-factor decomposition obtained from the open-and-closed points of the spectrum.

In each factor the filtration by powers of its maximal ideal has finitely many nonzero terms. Its layers are finite-dimensional over the residue field, since the factor is Noetherian. Consequently each factor, and then their finite product, has finite length as an $R$-module. A descending chain of ideals strictly decreases length whenever it changes, so $R$ is Artinian. This retains the local-factor proof and supplies the finite-length step.

Now suppose $R$ is Artinian. The finite-length theorem for Artinian rings gives finite length of the module $R$, hence the ascending chain condition and Noetherianity. Every prime is maximal: its quotient is an Artinian domain, and such a domain is a field. Indeed, for $0\ne a$ its descending chain $(a^n)$ stabilizes, giving $a^n=a^{n+1}b$ for some $b$; cancellation yields $ab=1$. Thus no chain of distinct prime ideals has positive length.

The original decomposition route gives the same conclusion: an Artinian ring has finitely many maximal ideals and nilpotent Jacobson radical, so its local factors each have only their maximal prime. The zero ring is Artinian and Noetherian with empty spectrum; this explains the phrase “at most zero” in the converse. ∎

Proposition. Regular local rings and global dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. $\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa$ is finite.
  2. The global dimension of $R$, taken over all $R$-modules, is finite.
  3. $R$ is regular.

When these conditions hold,

$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa =\dim R=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2).$$

Proof. Put $d=\dim R$ and $e=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)$. For a regular local ring the resolution theorem gives global dimension at most $d$, including arbitrary modules. Thus (3) implies (2), and (2) immediately implies (1).

If $p=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa$ is finite, the embedding-dimension bound and the depth bound give

$$e\leq p\leq d.$$

The number of generators of the maximal ideal always bounds dimension, so $d\leq e$. Equality follows, which is precisely regularity. Finally, under these equivalent conditions,

$$e\leq\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa \leq\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq d=e.$$

The complete homological argument, including the characteristic-free Koszul comparison for the first inequality, is Regular local rings, Section 2. The unrestricted global-dimension step uses the cyclic-module test and its transfinite proof in Projective dimension, Sections 1–2. ∎

Lemma. Projective syzygies do not depend on the chosen resolution

Let $M$ have finite projective dimension $d$ over a ring $R$. Suppose

$$F_e\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0 \longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0$$

is exact, every $F_i$ is projective, and $e\geq0$, $e\geq d-1$. The kernel at $F_e$ is projective; when $e=0$ this means $\ker(F_0\to M)$. No finiteness condition on these modules is required.

Proof. Induct on $d$, allowing every eligible $e$. If $d=0$, the surjection onto $M$ splits. Its kernel is a direct summand of $F_0$, hence projective. Repeat this splitting along the given sequence to reach its last kernel.

Suppose $d>0$ and choose a projective resolution of length $d$,

$$0\longrightarrow P_d\longrightarrow\cdots \longrightarrow P_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.$$

Write $K=\ker(F_0\to M)$ and $L=\ker(P_0\to M)$. Schanuel's construction gives

$$P_0\oplus K\cong F_0\oplus L.$$

If $e=0$, the inequality forces $d=1$. Then $L\cong P_1$, so $P_0\oplus K$ is projective, and its summand $K$ is projective.

For $e>0$, the module $F_0\oplus L$ has a projective resolution of length at most $d-1$: add $F_0$ to the final surjection $P_1\to L$ and use the identity on that summand. Through the displayed isomorphism, the other sequence provides

$$F_e\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_2 \longrightarrow P_0\oplus F_1 \longrightarrow P_0\oplus K\longrightarrow0.$$

The final map is the identity on $P_0$ together with the map $F_1\to K$; the preceding map has zero $P_0$ component. Apply the induction hypothesis to the actual projective dimension, which is at most $d-1$, and to the index $e-1$. For $e\geq2$ its last kernel is the original kernel. For $e=1$ it is

$$\ker(P_0\oplus F_1\longrightarrow P_0\oplus K) =0\oplus\ker(F_1\longrightarrow K),$$

and $K\hookrightarrow F_0$ identifies this with the kernel of $F_1\to F_0$. Both cases prove the claim. ∎

Lemma. Length after restricting scalars

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be local, and let $B$ be semilocal with maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_n$. Suppose a map $A\to B$ contracts each $\mathfrak m_i$ to $\mathfrak m$ and gives finite extensions $\kappa_i=\kappa(\mathfrak m_i)$ of $\kappa$. For a $B$-module $M$ of finite length,

$$\ell_A(M)=\sum_{i=1}^n[\kappa_i:\kappa]\, \ell_{B_{\mathfrak m_i}}(M_{\mathfrak m_i}).$$

In particular, restriction of scalars gives a module of finite length.

Proof. Take a composition series of $M$. Each simple quotient is $B/\mathfrak m_i$ for exactly one $i$, by the description of simple modules. As an $A$-module it is a $\kappa$-vector space of dimension $[\kappa_i:\kappa]$, and this equals its length.

Localizing the series at $\mathfrak m_i$ kills every quotient belonging to another maximal ideal: an element in that other ideal but outside $\mathfrak m_i$ becomes a unit. The quotients belonging to $\mathfrak m_i$ become the simple $B_{\mathfrak m_i}$-module $\kappa_i$. Thus their number is $\ell_{B_{\mathfrak m_i}}(M_{\mathfrak m_i})$. Add the $A$-lengths of all the factors to obtain the formula. An empty composition series covers $M=0$; if $B=0$, the empty sum does as well. ∎

Lemma. Finite ring maps are integral

If $S$ is finite as an $R$-module, every element of $S$ is integral over $R$.

Proof. Choose module generators $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ of $S$. For $s\in S$, write $sv_i=\sum_j a_{ij}v_j$ with $a_{ij}\in R$. Multiplication by the adjugate of $sI_t-(a_{ij})$ shows that the monic polynomial

$$P(T)=\det(TI_t-(a_{ij}))$$

satisfies $P(s)v_i=0$ for every $i$. The generators span $1$, so $P(s)=0$ in $S$. This determinant argument does not require a basis. If $S=0$, the polynomial $1$, or the degree-one polynomial $T$, gives the assertion directly. This is the faithful finite-module test in the integrality criterion. ∎

Lemma. Finite algebras and integral generators

For a ring map $R\to S$, the following are equivalent:

  1. $S$ is a finite $R$-module.
  2. $S$ is integral over $R$ and finitely generated as an $R$-algebra.
  3. Some finite list of algebra generators of $S$ consists of elements integral over $R$.

Proof. Module generators also generate as an algebra, and the preceding lemma proves their integrality, giving (1) implies (2). The implication (2) implies (3) follows by choosing algebra generators.

For (3), write $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_t]$ and choose monic equations for the $x_i$, of positive degrees $d_i$. Replacing a power $x_i^{d_i}$ with a combination of smaller powers repeatedly expresses every polynomial in the $x_i$ as a linear combination of

$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_t^{a_t}, \qquad 0\leq a_i<d_i.$$

This is a finite spanning set over $R$, proving (1). With no generators, its sole monomial is $1$. The argument also proves the finite-list assertion of the integrality criterion. ∎

Lemma. Surjectivity and exactness for completion

Fix an ideal $I$ of an arbitrary ring $R$, and write

$$\widehat X=\varprojlim_{n\geq1}X/I^nX$$

for an $R$-module $X$. The following statements hold.

  1. If $\varphi\colon M\to N$ is surjective modulo $I$, then $\widehat\varphi$ is surjective.
  2. Every surjective module map remains surjective on completion.
  3. If $0\to K\to M\to N\to0$ is exact and $N$ is flat, its completed sequence is exact, including both zero endpoints.
  4. For finite $M$, the canonical map $M\otimes_R\widehat R\to\widehat M$ is surjective.

Neither $I$ nor the modules in the first three statements need be finitely generated.

Proof. For (1), the cokernel $C$ of $\varphi$ satisfies $C=IC$, and hence $C=I^nC$ for every $n$. Thus each map $M/I^nM\to N/I^nN$ is onto. Equivalently, this is the nilpotent-ideal form of Nakayama's lemma over $R/I^n$; it does not use finite generation.

Set $K_n=\varphi^{-1}(I^nN)$. We have compatible exact sequences

$$0\longrightarrow K_n/I^nM \longrightarrow M/I^nM \longrightarrow N/I^nN\longrightarrow0.$$

Their left transition maps are also onto. Indeed, take $x\in K_n$ and express

$$\varphi(x)=\sum_j z_jy_j,\qquad z_j\in I^n.$$

Surjectivity modulo $I$ supplies $m_j\in M$ such that $y_j-\varphi(m_j)\in IN$. Then

$$x'=x-\sum_jz_jm_j,\qquad \varphi(x')=\sum_jz_j\bigl(y_j-\varphi(m_j)\bigr)\in I^{n+1}N.$$

Thus $x'\in K_{n+1}$ and $x'-x\in I^nM$, as required. All sums here are finite, by the definition of an ideal times a module.

The countable inverse-limit exactness lemma now proves (1). In this surjective-transition case its lifting argument is especially direct: lift the first component of a compatible element of $\widehat N$; after lifting its next component, the discrepancy from the previous lift lies in $K_n/I^nM$. Lift that discrepancy to $K_{n+1}/I^{n+1}M$ and subtract it. Induction constructs a compatible lift in $\widehat M$. Statement (2) is an immediate instance.

For (3), tensor the given short exact sequence with $R/I^n$. Flatness of $N$ kills its first Tor and gives

$$0\longrightarrow K/I^nK\longrightarrow M/I^nM \longrightarrow N/I^nN\longrightarrow0.$$

The left transitions are quotient maps, so the same lifting argument gives surjectivity on inverse limits. Kernel equality and injectivity are checked component by component, proving the whole completed sequence exact.

For (4), choose a surjection $R^t\to M$ with $t$ finite. By (2), completion gives an onto map $\widehat R^{\,t}\to\widehat M$. On a tuple $(a_i)$ this map is $\sum_i a_iv_i$, where the $v_i$ are the chosen generators of $M$. It factors through the canonical map $M\otimes_R\widehat R\to\widehat M$, so that map is onto. ∎

Lemma. Separated finite modules over complete rings

Suppose $R\to\widehat R$ is an isomorphism for the $I$-adic topology. If $M$ is finite and $\bigcap_{n\geq1}I^nM=0$, then $M\to\widehat M$ is an isomorphism.

Proof. The preceding lemma makes

$$M\cong M\otimes_R\widehat R\longrightarrow\widehat M$$

surjective. An element has zero image exactly when it belongs to every $I^nM$. The assumed intersection is zero, giving injectivity as well. ∎

Lemma. Going up and maximal ideals

For a ring map having the going-up property, the contraction of every maximal ideal is maximal.

Proof. Let $\mathfrak q$ be maximal in the target and $\mathfrak p$ its contraction. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak p$ in the source. Going up gives a prime $\mathfrak q'\supseteq\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak m$. Maximality forces $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q$, hence $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak p$. ∎

Lemma. Reducedness descends through faithful flatness

If $R\to S$ is faithfully flat and $S$ is reduced, then $R$ is reduced.

Proof. A faithfully flat map is injective. A nilpotent element of $R$ therefore embeds as a nilpotent element of $S$, which is zero. Injectivity makes the original element zero. ∎

Lemma. Smooth algebras over reduced rings are reduced

If $R$ is reduced and $R\to S$ is smooth, then $S$ is reduced.

Proof. First assume $R$ is Noetherian. The finite presentation makes $S$ Noetherian. Smoothness gives flatness and regular fibres, hence reduced fibres. The Noetherian flat-ascent lemma then shows that $S$ is reduced.

For arbitrary reduced $R$, use finite smooth models: there is a finitely generated $\mathbf Z$-subalgebra $R_0\subset R$ and a smooth $R_0$-algebra $S_0$ with $S\cong R\otimes_{R_0}S_0$. The larger finitely generated subalgebras of $R$ form a directed system; base-changing $S_0$ along them keeps it smooth.

Let $x\in S$ satisfy $x^2=0$. Its expression uses finitely many coefficients from $R$, so at some larger stage it comes from an element $x_0$ of the corresponding smooth algebra. The equality $x^2=0$ also holds at a sufficiently large stage, by the finite-witness property of a directed colimit. Replace the stage so that $x_0^2=0$ there. Its base ring, being a subring of $R$, is reduced and Noetherian. The first paragraph makes that smooth algebra reduced, so $x_0=0$ and hence $x=0$. Finally, if a nonzero nilpotent had least vanishing exponent $r\geq2$, its nonzero power of exponent $r-1$ would have square zero. Therefore exclusion of nonzero square-zero elements proves reducedness. ∎

Lemma. A regular quotient cuts out part of a parameter system

Source credit: FAC, Chapter III, §5, no. 75, proof of Theorem 3, pp. 269–270.

In the cited geometric setting, the ideal of a nonsingular subvariety in a local ring of projective space is generated by as many equations as its codimension. The successive colon equalities recorded there express regularity of those equations. The following local argument identifies the generators intrinsically.

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be regular local, and suppose $R/I$ is regular local. There is a minimal generating list $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ for $\mathfrak m$ such that $I=(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ for some $0\leq c\leq d$.

Proof. Put $d=\dim R$, $\dim(R/I)=d-c$, and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. Since $I$ is proper, $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$. The cotangent-space quotient gives an exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow (I+\mathfrak m^2)/\mathfrak m^2 \longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \longrightarrow\mathfrak m/(I+\mathfrak m^2) \longrightarrow0.$$

Regularity of both rings says that the middle and final dimensions are $d$ and $d-c$. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ in $I$ representing a basis of the kernel, and extend it to a basis using $x_{c+1},\ldots,x_d\in\mathfrak m$. Nakayama makes this a minimal generating system.

The regular-parameter quotient theorem, equivalently the parameter assertion in regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay, shows that

$$A=R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$$

is a regular local domain of dimension $d-c$. It surjects onto $R/I$. If its kernel were nonzero, choose a nonzero element $g$ in that kernel. It is a nonunit and a nonzerodivisor in the domain $A$. The one-equation dimension result would give

$$\dim(R/I)\leq\dim(A/gA)=\dim A-1,$$

contrary to their equal dimensions. Thus the kernel is zero and $I=(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$.

This argument includes $c=0$, with an empty initial list, and dimension zero, when $A$ is a field and cannot have a nonzero proper kernel. Because a regular parameter system is a regular sequence, the source's colon assertions are exactly

$$(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}):x_j=(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}), \qquad 1\leq j\leq c.$$

They say that multiplication by $x_j$ is injective after dividing by its predecessors. ∎

Lemma. Fibrewise injectivity over a Noetherian target

Let $R\to S$ be local, with $S$ Noetherian, and let $\mathfrak m$ be the maximal ideal of $R$. Suppose $N$ is finite over $S$, $M$ is flat over $R$, and $u\colon N\to M$ is $R$-linear. If

$$N/\mathfrak mN\longrightarrow M/\mathfrak mM$$

is injective, then $u$ is injective and its cokernel is $R$-flat. The base ring $R$ need not be Noetherian, and no $S$-module structure on $M$ is required.

Proof. We first prove that $u_n\colon N/\mathfrak m^nN\to M/\mathfrak m^nM$ is injective for every $n\geq1$. The case $n=1$ is assumed. Set $V_n=\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$ and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. Tensoring the quotient sequence gives right-exact rows

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} N\otimes_R V_n&\longrightarrow&N/\mathfrak m^{n+1}N&\longrightarrow&N/\mathfrak m^nN\longrightarrow0\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow u_{n+1}&&\downarrow u_n\\ M\otimes_R V_n&\longrightarrow&M/\mathfrak m^{n+1}M&\longrightarrow&M/\mathfrak m^nM\longrightarrow0 . \end{array}$$

The lower left horizontal map is injective by flatness of $M$. The left vertical map is the tensor product over $\kappa$ of $u_1$ with $V_n$, since $V_n$ is killed by $\mathfrak m$; it is injective too. No injectivity of the upper left horizontal map is assumed.

If $z\in\ker u_{n+1}$, its image on the top right is zero by the induction hypothesis. Write $z$ as the image of $y\in N\otimes_R V_n$. Its image along the bottom row is zero. Injectivity of the bottom horizontal map, followed by that of the left vertical map, gives $y=0$ and hence $z=0$. This proves the induction.

The ideal $\mathfrak mS$ lies in the maximal ideal of $S$. Krull intersection, applied to the finite $S$-module $N$, gives $\bigcap_n\mathfrak m^nN=0$. Any element of $\ker u$ belongs to that intersection, so $u$ is injective.

Put $Q=M/u(N)$. The Tor sequence and flatness of $M$ identify

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(Q,R/J) \cong\ker(N/JN\longrightarrow M/JM)$$

for every ideal $J\subset R$. If $J$ is proper, it lies in $\mathfrak m$, and $R/J\to S/JS$ is local with Noetherian target. The source module $N/JN$ is finite over $S/JS$, the target $M/JM$ is flat over $R/J$, and the map on residue quotients is the given $u_1$. The injectivity already proved, applied over $R/J$, makes this kernel zero. For $J=R$ it is zero directly. The Tor criterion for flatness now gives flatness of $Q$. ∎

Lemma. The universal derivation represents derivations

For a ring map $R\to S$ and an $S$-module $M$, composition with the universal derivation gives a natural isomorphism

$$\operatorname{Hom}_S(\Omega_{S/R},M) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_R(S,M), \qquad \alpha\longmapsto\alpha\circ d.$$

Proof. Start with the free $S$-module having symbols $[s]$ for all $s\in S$. Its quotient defining $\Omega_{S/R}$ imposes precisely

$$[s+t]-[s]-[t],\qquad [st]-s[t]-t[s],\qquad [r]\quad(r\in R),$$

where $r$ in the final expression denotes its image in $S$. A function $D\colon S\to M$ extends uniquely to a linear map from the free module. It annihilates these relations exactly when $D$ is additive, obeys the Leibniz rule, and vanishes on $R$. Those are the conditions for an $R$-derivation. Thus it factors uniquely through $\Omega_{S/R}$ exactly in that case. Composition with a homomorphism of target modules commutes with this construction, proving naturality. ∎

Lemma. Noetherianity of an adic completion

Let $I$ be a finitely generated ideal of a ring $R$. If $R/I$ is Noetherian, then $\widehat R=\varprojlim_nR/I^n$ is Noetherian and complete for the ideal $I\widehat R$.

Proof. The completion-kernel theorem for finite ideals gives

$$\widehat R/I^n\widehat R\cong R/I^n$$

and completeness of $\widehat R$ for $I\widehat R$. We may therefore replace $R$ by $\widehat R$ and prove that a complete ring with the two stated finiteness properties is Noetherian.

Choose generators $f_1,\ldots,f_t$ of $I$. Sending $T_i$ to the initial class of $f_i$ gives a surjective graded map

$$(R/I)[T_1,\ldots,T_t]\longrightarrow \operatorname{gr}_I(R)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^n/I^{n+1}.$$

The polynomial ring is Noetherian, so the graded ring is too. For an arbitrary ideal $J\subset R$, its initial ideal is

$$\bigoplus_{n\geq0}(J\cap I^n)/(J\cap I^{n+1}) \ \subseteq\ \operatorname{gr}_I(R).$$

Choose finitely many homogeneous generators and lift them to $g_j\in J\cap I^{d_j}$, where $d_j$ is the degree of the corresponding generator.

If $x\in J\cap I^n$, its initial class is a sum of these generators with coefficients of degrees $n-d_j$, using only $d_j\leq n$. Lifting those coefficients gives $a_j\in I^{n-d_j}$ for these indices; use $a_j=0$ for the others. Then

$$x-\sum_j a_jg_j\in J\cap I^{n+1}.$$

Beginning at $n=0$ and applying this to each successive remainder constructs coefficients $a_{j,n}\in I^{\max(0,n-d_j)}$ such that

$$x-\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_j a_{j,n}g_j\in I^{N+1}.$$

For fixed $j$, the coefficients tend to zero $I$-adically, so completeness defines $A_j=\sum_{n\geq0}a_{j,n}\in R$. Multiplication by $g_j$ and addition of finitely many terms are continuous. Separatedness therefore gives $x=\sum_jA_jg_j$. Thus the $g_j$ generate $J$.

If the initial ideal is zero, the same argument puts $J$ in every $I^n$, so $J=0$. Hence every ideal is finitely generated, proving Noetherianity. ∎

Lemma. Flatness detected by every ideal-power quotient

Let $R\to S$ be a map of Noetherian rings, let $I\subset R$, and let $M$ be finite over $S$. Suppose $M/I^nM$ is flat over $R/I^n$ for all $n\geq1$. Then $M_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R$ whenever $\mathfrak q\supseteq IS$. In particular $M$ is flat over $R$ if $S$ is local and $IS$ lies in its maximal ideal.

Proof. Let

$$K=\ker(I\otimes_RM\longrightarrow M).$$

For every $n$, the inclusion $I/I^n\hookrightarrow R/I^n$ remains injective on tensoring with the assumed flat module $M/I^nM$. Thus the image of $K$ in

$$\begin{aligned} (I/I^n)\otimes_{R/I^n}(M/I^nM) &\cong(I/I^n)\otimes_RM\\ &\cong(I\otimes_RM)/I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM) \end{aligned}$$

is zero. The last identification follows by tensoring $I^n\to I\to I/I^n\to0$: the image of $I^n\otimes_RM$ is $I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM)$. Consequently

$$K\subseteq I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM)\quad(n\geq1).$$

The module $I\otimes_RM$ is finite over $S$, because $I$ is finite over the Noetherian ring $R$. At a chosen $\mathfrak q\supseteq IS$, localizing these inclusions and applying Krull intersection over $S_{\mathfrak q}$ gives $K_{\mathfrak q}=0$. This is the intersection consequence of Artin–Rees used in the original argument.

Put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. The localized module $M_{\mathfrak q}/IM_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}/IR_{\mathfrak p}$, by the case $n=1$ and localization of flat modules. Also $K_{\mathfrak q}=0$ is the vanishing of

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_{\mathfrak p}} (M_{\mathfrak q},R_{\mathfrak p}/IR_{\mathfrak p}).$$

The ideal variant of the local flatness criterion for $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ now makes $M_{\mathfrak q}$ flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Since $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat over $R$, it is flat over $R$ as well. Taking $\mathfrak q$ to be the maximal ideal proves the final assertion. ∎

Lemma. A countable Mittag–Leffler system has an element in its limit

Let $(X_i)$ be an inverse system of nonempty sets over a countable directed index set. If the images in each fixed $X_i$ stabilize for sufficiently large indices, then $\varprojlim_iX_i$ is nonempty.

Proof. Enumerate the indices and recursively choose an increasing sequence $j_n$ dominating the first $n$ indices and the previously chosen $j_{n-1}$. It is cofinal. Restriction to this sequence does not change the limit: a compatible sequence supplies a value at any original index by mapping down from a $j_n$ above it, independently of which such $n$ is used.

We can thus work with a system indexed by the positive integers. Replace $X_n$ by the eventual image $Y_n$ of its later terms. Stabilization and nonemptiness give $Y_n\ne\varnothing$. The transition $Y_{n+1}\to Y_n$ is surjective: for $y\in Y_n$, choose a stage late enough that the images at both $n$ and $n+1$ have stabilized, and lift $y$ from that stage. Its image in $X_{n+1}$ lies in $Y_{n+1}$ and maps to $y$.

Choose an element of $Y_1$ and then a preimage at each successive stage. Countable choice, as supplied by the axiom of choice, produces a compatible sequence. Its images in the $X_n$ give the required element of the inverse limit. ∎

[^1]: A set-sized collection of representatives suffices: restrict the objects $A'\to A$ to algebras $A'$ presented as quotients of $R[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$. This keeps the same finite-presentation constructions.

[^2]: In the notation of the flatness argument, right exactness applied to $K\to N_2\to Q\to0$ identifies the kernel of $N_2\otimes_RM\to Q\otimes_RM$ with the image of $K\otimes_RM$. The surjection $N_1\to K$ identifies this image with that of $N_1\otimes_RM$. Injectivity of $Q\otimes_RM\to N_3\otimes_RM$ then leaves this kernel unchanged on composing into $N_3\otimes_RM$. Hence the original three-term sequence is exact after tensoring. These are precisely the roles of the second and fourth arrows' injectivity in that argument.

[^3]: The injective maps $L\otimes_RM\to M^{\oplus n}$ and $L'\otimes_RM\to M^{\oplus n}$ identify both source modules with submodules of the same module, compatibly with $L\subseteq L'$. Their quotient therefore injects into $(M^{\oplus n})/(L\otimes_RM)$. Right exactness identifies the source quotient with $(L'/L)\otimes_RM=K\otimes_RM$, giving the claimed injection.

[^4]: If $I=0$, generators of $S^{-1}M$ already generate $M_f$ for some $f\in S$. If $I=\mathfrak p$ is prime and $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$, generators of the residue fibre $M\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ generate $M_f$ for some $f\notin\mathfrak p$. In this second case every element of $S+I$ is still outside $\mathfrak p$.

Infinitesimal lifting and completed local rings

Definition. Local complete-intersection maps

A finite-type ring map $A\to B$ is a local complete intersection when, in a finite polynomial presentation $B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J$, the kernel $J$ is a Koszul-regular ideal. The condition can be checked in one such presentation and then holds in every one.

Lemma. Noetherian henselizations and their completions

Source credit: EGA IV, Theorem 18.6.6 and Proposition 18.8.8.

For a local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$, fix a separable closure of $\kappa$ for the strict henselization. The following are equivalent: $R$ is Noetherian; $R^h$ is Noetherian; $R^{sh}$ is Noetherian. Under these conditions:

  1. The maximal-ideal completions $\widehat{R^h}$ and $\widehat{R^{sh}}$ are Noetherian complete local rings.
  2. The canonical map $\widehat R\to\widehat{R^h}$ is an isomorphism.
  3. Both maps $R^h\to\widehat{R^h}$ and $R^{sh}\to\widehat{R^{sh}}$ are flat.
  4. The map $\widehat R\to\widehat{R^{sh}}$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of its target.
  5. With the compatible residue-field marking,
$$(\widehat R)^{sh}\cong\widehat R\otimes_{R^h}R^{sh}.$$
  1. The canonical comparison gives
$$\widehat{(\widehat R)^{sh}}\cong\widehat{R^{sh}}.$$

Proof. The maps $R\to R^h\to R^{sh}$ are faithfully flat, their maximal ideals are extended from $\mathfrak m$, and their residue fields are $\kappa$ and the chosen $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. These properties and the marked universal constructions are proved in Henselian local rings, Sections 4–5. Thus Noetherian descent proves the reverse implications.

Assume $R$ is Noetherian. For $B=R^h$ or $R^{sh}$, the ideal $\mathfrak mB$ is finite and $B/\mathfrak mB$ is a field. The Noetherian completion lemma therefore makes $C=\widehat B$ Noetherian and complete. It is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mC$: this follows from its quotients $C/\mathfrak m^nC=B/\mathfrak m^nB$, whose maximal ideals are nilpotent. Equivalently, an element with nonzero residue is inverted at every quotient level, and the compatible inverses give an inverse in $C$. This proves (1) before assuming Noetherianity of $B$.

For the ordinary henselization, its universal property gives compatible isomorphisms

$$R/\mathfrak m^n\cong R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h.$$

Indeed, $R/\mathfrak m^n$ is henselian because its maximal ideal is nilpotent. The induced map from $R^h$ gives an inverse to the displayed map. The other composite is the identity by uniqueness for the henselian quotient $R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h$. Taking limits proves (2), as in Proposition 6.1.

We next prove (3) without assuming that $B$ is Noetherian. The pointed étale construction expresses $B$ as a filtered colimit of local étale neighborhoods $R_i$, each Noetherian, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i=\mathfrak mR_i$. Their transition maps and maps into $B$ are flat and local. In the ordinary case $R_i^h=R^h$, so (2) applied to $R_i$ identifies $C$ with $\widehat{R_i}$. Noetherian completion flatness makes $C$ flat over every $R_i$.

For the strict case, choose a basis of $B/\mathfrak mB$ over $R_i/\mathfrak m_i$ and lift its elements once to $e_\alpha\in B$. The same lifts give, for all $n$, isomorphisms

$$\bigoplus_\alpha R_i/\mathfrak m_i^n \ \cong\ B/\mathfrak m_i^nB.$$

Here is why an infinite basis causes no problem. The module on the right is flat over the Artinian local ring on the left's coefficient side. The cokernel of the indicated free-module map vanishes modulo its nilpotent maximal ideal, hence is zero. Flatness of the target makes the kernel inject after residue tensoring; because the residue map is a basis isomorphism, the kernel also equals its maximal-ideal multiple, and nilpotence makes it zero. These isomorphisms are compatible in $n$ because the lifts were fixed. Hence $C$ is the completion of a free $R_i$-module, of possibly infinite rank, and completed direct sums are flat.

In both cases $C$ is flat over every stage. A finite relation with coefficients in $B$ has its coefficients at one stage. The equational flatness criterion there trivializes the relation, and the same finite expressions work over $B$. This is also the flat-colimit criterion, so $B\to C$ is flat. It is local with nonzero residue field, hence faithfully flat. Descent from the already Noetherian $C$ proves that both henselizations are Noetherian. The complete stagewise argument, including the arbitrary-rank basis construction, is Theorem 6.3.

The formal étaleness of henselization implies the required adic formal smoothness of $R\to R^{sh}$. The completion comparison for formal smoothness then proves (4).

A complete local ring is henselian, so the marked map $R^h\to\widehat R$ exists. Apply the strict henselization tensor comparison, with $(\widehat R)^h=\widehat R$, to obtain (5).

For (6), put $A=\widehat R$, $B=R^{sh}$ and $T=A^{sh}=A\otimes_{R^h}B$. The map $B\to T$ induces $\alpha\colon\widehat B\to\widehat T$. On the other hand, $\widehat B$ is complete local with residue field $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, hence strictly henselian. Its canonical local map from $A$, with this residue marking, extends uniquely to $T\to\widehat B$. Completion gives $\beta\colon\widehat T\to\widehat B$.

To check these maps are inverse, the tensor presentation and (2) give, compatibly in $n$,

$$\begin{aligned} T/\mathfrak m^nT &\cong(A/\mathfrak m^nA)\otimes_{R^h}B\\ &\cong(R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h)\otimes_{R^h}B\\ &\cong B/\mathfrak m^nB. \end{aligned}$$

The first map is induced by $B\to T$. The map $T\to\widehat B$ gives its inverse: on the tensor factors it uses the canonical maps from $A$ and $B$, and these become precisely the displayed quotient identifications. The maximal ideals of $T$ and $B$ are both generated by $\mathfrak m$, so these quotients compute their completions. Passing to inverse limits proves $\beta\alpha=1$ and $\alpha\beta=1$, establishing the omitted inverse check. ∎

Lemma. Making a lift of a unit invertible

If $\bar u$ is a unit of $A/I$, there is an étale map $A\to A'$ inducing $A/I\cong A'/IA'$ and a unit $u'\in A'$ whose residue is $\bar u$.

Proof. Lift $\bar u$ to $f\in A$ and take $A'=A_f$. This principal localization is étale, and the image $u'=f/1$ is invertible. Its reduction is

$$A_f/IA_f\cong(A/I)_{\bar u}=A/I,$$

since $\bar u$ was already a unit. Under this identification $u'$ reduces to the prescribed element. ∎

Lemma. An intersection identity from first Koszul homology

Let $I\subset A$, and suppose the images of $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ in $A/I$ have vanishing first Koszul homology. For $J=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$,

$$I\cap J=IJ.$$

Proof. The Koszul terms are free, so the quotient $A\to A/I$ gives a short exact sequence of complexes

$$0\to I\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g) \to K_\bullet(A,g)\to K_\bullet(A/I,\bar g)\to0.$$

The homology sequence, together with the assumed $H_1=0$, makes

$$H_0(I\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g))=I/IJ \longrightarrow H_0(K_\bullet(A,g))=A/J$$

injective. Its kernel is $(I\cap J)/IJ$, proving the equality. Empty lists give $J=0$ and the same conclusion. ∎

Lemma. Complete-intersection maps are local on the target

Suppose $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ generate the unit ideal in $S$. If each map $R\to S_{g_j}$ is a local complete intersection, then so is $R\to S$.

Proof. A Koszul-regular ideal is locally finitely generated along its vanishing set, by definition; off that set it is the unit ideal locally. A finite affine cover therefore makes it finitely generated. Consequently a local complete-intersection algebra has a finite presentation. The finite-cover finiteness criterion now makes $S$ finitely presented over $R$. Choose $S=P/I$ with $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $I$ finite.

Fix $\mathfrak q\supseteq I$ in $P$. Choose a lift $h_j\in P$ of some $g_j$ with $h_j\notin\mathfrak q$, and set

$$Q=P[T],\qquad z=Th_j-1,\qquad I_j=(I,z),\qquad\mathfrak q_j=(\mathfrak q,z).$$

The quotient $Q/\mathfrak q_j=(P/\mathfrak q)_{h_j}$ is a domain, so $\mathfrak q_j$ is prime. Also $Q/I_j=S_{g_j}$, making $I_j$ Koszul-regular.

Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I$ whose classes form a basis of the conormal fibre $(I/I^2)\otimes_S\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. The principal-localization conormal calculation identifies the conormal fibre of $I_j$ with this fibre plus the line generated by $z$. Thus $z,f_1,\ldots,f_r$ give a basis at $\mathfrak q_j$.

Since $I_j$ is finite, Nakayama makes these elements generate it in the local ring $Q_{\mathfrak q_j}$; the finite cokernel vanishes on some principal neighborhood. Shrink that neighborhood further so that $I_j$ also has a Koszul-regular generating list. Such a list is quasi-regular, and its conormal classes form a basis. Its length is therefore $r+1$. By independence of generators of fixed length, the particular list $z,f_1,\ldots,f_r$ is Koszul-regular on a principal neighborhood $Q_h$ with $h\notin\mathfrak q_j$.

Multiplication by $z=Th_j-1$ is injective on $Q$: if $z\sum a_iT^i=0$, the constant coefficient gives $a_0=0$, then successive coefficients give every $a_i=0$. It remains injective after localization. Thus the one-element sequence $z$ is Koszul-regular. Koszul truncation makes the images of $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ a Koszul-regular generating list of the image of $I$ in

$$Q_h/(z)\cong(P_{h_j})_{\bar h}.$$

Write $\bar h=a/h_j^N$. Because $h\notin\mathfrak q_j$, we have $a\notin\mathfrak q$. The displayed ring is $P_{ah_j}$, with $ah_j\notin\mathfrak q$. We have therefore found the required principal neighborhood in the original polynomial ring. Since this works for every $\mathfrak q\supseteq I$, the ideal $I$ is Koszul-regular. ∎

Lemma. Global complete intersections give Koszul-regular equations

If $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ is a relative global complete intersection, its displayed equations form a Koszul-regular sequence.

Proof. Put $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$. Multiplication by each $f_i$ on the Koszul complex is null-homotopic, so $J$ annihilates its homology. At a prime not containing $J$, a generator becomes a unit and all homology vanishes. At a prime containing $J$, the global-CI regular-sequence theorem makes the displayed equations a regular sequence in the localized polynomial ring. Regular sequences are Koszul-regular, so their positive homology vanishes there too. A module vanishing at every prime is zero, proving the claim. ∎

Definition. Four regularity conditions on an ideal

For an ideal $I$ of a ring $R$, each condition below is imposed locally along $V(I)$. For every $\mathfrak p\supseteq I$, there must be a $g\notin\mathfrak p$ and a finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ of $I_g$ in $R_g$ of the specified kind:

  1. A regular ideal admits a regular generating sequence.
  2. A Koszul-regular ideal admits a Koszul-regular generating sequence.
  3. An $H_1$-regular ideal admits a generating sequence with zero first Koszul homology.
  4. A quasi-regular ideal admits a quasi-regular generating sequence.

The neighborhood and list may depend on $\mathfrak p$. If $V(I)$ is empty, these conditions are vacuous.

Lemma. Relative regularity under arbitrary base change

Let $A\to B$ and $A\to A'$ be ring maps, put $B'=B\otimes_AA'$, and set $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subset B$. Assume $B/J$ is flat over $A$. Then quasi-regularity of the list $f_i$ implies quasi-regularity of its image in $B'$, and $H_1$-regularity implies $H_1$-regularity of its image.

Proof. Suppose the list is quasi-regular. Each graded piece $J^n/J^{n+1}$ is the direct sum of copies of $B/J$ indexed by degree-$n$ monomials, and is therefore $A$-flat. The sequences

$$0\to J^n/J^{n+1}\to B/J^{n+1}\to B/J^n\to0$$

prove by induction that every $B/J^n$ is $A$-flat. Tensoring $0\to J^n\to B\to B/J^n\to0$ then identifies $J^n\otimes_AA'$ with its image in $B'$, namely $(J')^n$. Tensoring the sequence between two successive powers identifies

$$ (J')^n/(J')^{n+1} \cong(J^n/J^{n+1})\otimes_AA'.$$

The monomial descriptions and their multiplication maps thus base-change to the same descriptions over $B'/J'$. This is quasi-regularity of the specified images.

For the second assertion, the first-homology base-change surjection gives

$$H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))\otimes_AA' \longrightarrow H_1(K_\bullet(B',f'))\longrightarrow0.$$

Its proof uses flatness only of $B/J$, as assumed here. Vanishing of the source forces vanishing of the target. ∎

Lemma. The regularity notions agree for finite local modules

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M\ne0$ be finite, and take $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in\mathfrak m$. The following are equivalent: the list is $M$-regular; it is $M$-Koszul-regular; it is $M$-$H_1$-regular; it is $M$-quasi-regular. In particular the four notions agree for lists in $\mathfrak m$ acting on $R$.

Proof. Successive injectivity gives positive Koszul exactness. Positive exactness includes vanishing in degree one. The first-homology argument then gives quasi-regularity, including its arbitrary-module formulation. Finally the Noetherian local quasi-regularity theorem gives regularity for this finite module. Its nonzero quotient condition is satisfied: an ideal generated inside $\mathfrak m$ cannot kill $M$ by Nakayama. These implications close the cycle. ∎

Lemma. Completion preserves and detects regularity

A Noetherian local ring $A$ is regular exactly when its maximal-ideal completion $\widehat A$ is regular.

Proof. If $\widehat A$ is regular, the faithfully flat local completion map and descent of regularity imply that $A$ is regular.

Conversely, assume $A$ regular and put $d=\dim A$. A minimal list of $d$ generators of its maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ generates the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\widehat A$ of the completion. The dimension comparison says $\dim\widehat A=d$. Thus its embedding dimension is at most its dimension; the reverse inequality always holds, so $\widehat A$ is regular.

Alternatively, the completion map is flat and local with closed fibre $A/\mathfrak m$, a field. The regular-base, regular-fibre ascent theorem proves the same conclusion. ∎

Lemma. A derivation detects a non-pth-power element

Let $B$ be a domain of characteristic $p>0$ that is a finite-type algebra over a Noetherian complete local ring. If $f\in B$ does not belong to $\operatorname{Frac}(B)^p$, there is a derivation $D\colon B\to B$ with $D(f)\ne0$.

Proof. Choose a finite-type map $R\to B$ with $R$ Noetherian complete local. Its image is a quotient of $R$, so it is again Noetherian complete local; it is a domain of characteristic $p$ because it embeds in $B$. Replace $R$ by that image. The complete-domain normalization theorem gives a finite subring extension $k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]\subset R$. Replacing the base by this power-series ring still makes $B$ a finite-type algebra.

Normalization over a domain now provides

$$R\subset A=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\subset B'\subset B,$$

where $B'$ is finite over $A$ and $B'_g=B_g$ for some $0\ne g\in R$. The fraction fields of $B'$ and $B$ agree. Choose $N\geq0$ with $f'=g^{pN}f\in B'$. This element is still not a $p$th power in that field. If a derivation $D'$ of $B'$ detects $f'$, the extension lemma below extends $g^MD'$ to $B$ for a suitable $M$. In the common fraction field its value on $f$ is

$$g^{M-pN}D'(f')\ne0,$$

because derivations in characteristic $p$ kill $g^{pN}$. It is therefore enough to treat a finite extension of domains $A\subset B$.

Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$; then $L/K$ is finite. Use the coefficient rings $A_J$ and their fields $K_J$ from the power-series subfield lemma. They satisfy $\bigcap_JK_J=K^p$ and are downward directed. The finite-extension conclusion of the field-intersection lemma gives

$$\bigcap_J L^pK_J=L^p.$$

Since $f\notin L^p$, some $J$ has $f\notin L^pK_J$. By the p-basis constant-field test, $df$ is then nonzero in $\Omega_{L/K_J}$. A linear functional on this $L$-vector space that does not kill $df$ gives a $K_J$-derivation $\delta\colon L\to L$ with $\delta(f)\ne0$.

The extensions $A_J\subset A\subset B$ are finite, so choose finitely many $A_J$-module generators $b_1,\ldots,b_t$ of $B$. Express each $\delta(b_i)$ as a fraction in $B$ and let $h\ne0$ be the product of their denominators. Since $\delta$ kills $A_J$, the derivation $h\delta$ sends every $A_J$-linear combination of the $b_i$ into $B$. Its restriction is the required derivation, and its value on $f$ is nonzero. ∎

Lemma. Extension of derivations

Let $D\colon R\to R$ be a derivation of a ring.

  1. For any ideal $I$, there is a canonical extension $\widehat D\colon\widehat R\to\widehat R$ to the $I$-adic completion.
  2. For any multiplicative subset $S$, there is a unique extension to $S^{-1}R$.
  3. Suppose $R\subset R'$ is a finite-type extension, $g\in R$ is a nonzerodivisor on $R'$, and $R_g=R'_g$. Some $g^ND$ extends to a derivation of $R'$.

Proof. The product rule gives $D(I^{n+1})\subset I^n$. Thus applying $D$ to a representative defines compatible additive maps

$$R/I^{n+1}\longrightarrow R/I^n.$$

Passing to their inverse limit, and identifying a sequence with its shifted tail, defines $\widehat D$. At level $n$, compute the product of two inputs using representatives at level $n+1$. The product rule in $R$, reduced modulo $I^n$, gives the product rule for the output. The same computation proves additivity and that $1$ maps to zero. These maps also commute with $R\to\widehat R$. The construction is continuous, lowering the filtration index by at most one, and is unique among continuous extensions because the image of $R$ is dense and $\widehat R$ is separated. No finiteness hypothesis on $I$ or $R$ is used.

For localization the only possible formula is

$$D(r/s)=\frac{D(r)}s-\frac{rD(s)}{s^2}.$$

It is well defined even in the presence of zero divisors. Indeed, equality of two fractions means that $t(s'r-sr')=0$ for some $t\in S$. After differentiating this equality and localizing, the factor $t$ is a unit and $s'r-sr'=0$, so $D(s'r-sr')=0$. These two equalities give equality of the proposed values after bringing them to a common denominator.

For the algebra laws, the map $r\mapsto r+\varepsilon D(r)$ is a ring homomorphism to $(S^{-1}R)[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. It sends each $s\in S$ to a unit, whose inverse is $s^{-1}-\varepsilon s^{-2}D(s)$. The localization universal property extends this homomorphism, and its $\varepsilon$-coefficient is exactly the displayed formula. Comparing coefficients proves additivity and Leibniz. Finally, differentiating $s\cdot s^{-1}=1$ forces that formula, proving uniqueness.

For the third assertion, choose algebra generators $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of $R'$ and a common $a\geq0$ with $g^ax_i\in R$. Localize $D$ and set $E=g^{a+1}D$. Then

$$E(x_i)=gD(g^ax_i)-a(g^ax_i)D(g)\in R.$$

Also $E(R)\subset R$. Applying Leibniz to a polynomial in the $x_i$, including its coefficients in $R$, now shows that $E$ maps $R'$ into $R'$. The nonzerodivisor condition identifies $R'$ with its image in $R'_g$, so this restriction is an actual derivation of $R'$ extending $g^{a+1}D$. ∎

Lemma. Regularity of polynomial root extensions

Suppose $R$ is regular and a derivation $D\colon R\to R$ sends $f\in R$ to a unit. Then

$$R[Z]/(P(Z)-f)$$

is regular for every $P\in\mathbf Z[Z]$. In particular this holds for $P(Z)=Z^n$ for every $n\geq1$.

Proof. The polynomial ring $R[Z]$ is regular by regular ascent. Extend $D$ coefficientwise, putting $D(Z)=0$. It annihilates $P(Z)$, including when $P$ is constant, so it sends $P(Z)-f$ to the unit $-D(f)$. Apply the derivation criterion for a regular hypersurface. No monicity condition on $P$ is needed. ∎

Lemma. The fibres of henselization

Let $R$ be Noetherian local and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. There are finitely many primes $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_t$ of $R^h$ above $\mathfrak p$, and finitely many primes $\mathfrak r_1,\ldots,\mathfrak r_s$ of $R^{sh}$ above it. The canonical maps identify

$$R^h\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong \prod_{i=1}^t\kappa(\mathfrak q_i), \qquad R^{sh}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong \prod_{j=1}^s\kappa(\mathfrak r_j).$$

Every displayed residue field is algebraic separable over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

Proof. Both henselizations are Noetherian by the henselization comparison theorem. As they are filtered colimits of étale $R$-algebras, all the assertions follow from the Noetherian ind-étale fibre lemma.

Here is also the direct proof through a domain. Henselization commutes with quotient by $\mathfrak p$:

$$R^h/\mathfrak pR^h\cong(R/\mathfrak p)^h,\qquad R^{sh}/\mathfrak pR^{sh}\cong(R/\mathfrak p)^{sh}.$$

For the first equality the quotient on the left is henselian, and a local map from $R/\mathfrak p$ to a henselian local ring extends uniquely from $R$ to $R^h$; the extension kills $\mathfrak pR^h$. This proves the universal property. The same argument with the chosen separable residue-field marking proves the strict version: the quotient is strictly henselian and has the same marked residue field. The quotient permanence and both universal properties are proved in Henselian local rings and henselization, Sections 3–5; Section 6, Proposition 6.1 gives the associated maximal-ideal-power comparisons.

Replace $R$ by $R/\mathfrak p$, so it is a domain and the fibre in question is the generic fibre. Write $T$ for either henselization. It has finitely many minimal primes, and flat going down shows that every minimal prime contracts to $(0)$: a nonzero contraction would have the smaller prime $(0)$ beneath it, forcing a smaller prime in $T$. Conversely every prime over $(0)$ is minimal. To justify this converse, primes in a fibre of an ind-étale map are incomparable: after base change to the fraction field, a strict inclusion would contract to a strict inclusion at a finite étale stage, a product of fields. A minimal prime contained in a prime over $(0)$ must therefore equal it.

Since $R$ is reduced, so is $T$ by reducedness of henselizations. Its generic fibre is thus a reduced Noetherian ring whose primes are precisely the finitely many minimal primes just found, all maximal. The dimension-zero theorem and the localization description at reduced minimal primes identify it with the product of its residue fields. These are canonically the residue fields of the corresponding primes of $T$. Each field is a filtered union of images of finite separable field factors from the étale stages; consequently it is algebraic separable over the fraction field of $R$. This proves the original assertions after undoing the quotient. ∎

Proposition. Formal smoothness and regular maps of complete local rings

Let $A\to B$ be a local homomorphism of Noetherian complete local rings. Write $k=A/\mathfrak m_A$ and $\bar B=B/\mathfrak m_AB$. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. $A\to B$ is a regular map.
  2. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $\bar B$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
  3. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $k\to\bar B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $\bar B$.
  4. $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

Proof. The flatness and closed-fibre criterion identifies (2), (3) and (4). A regular map has a geometrically regular closed fibre, so (1) implies (2). Assume the other three conditions and fix a prime $\mathfrak p\subset A$. We must prove geometric regularity of $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

By formal-smoothness base change, replace $A\to B$ by $A/\mathfrak p\to B/\mathfrak pB$. Quotients of these complete Noetherian local rings remain complete, and the induced map is formally smooth for the quotient maximal-ideal topology. We may therefore assume that $A$ is a domain and the chosen prime is zero.

The complete-domain normalization theorem gives a regular subring $A_0\subset A$, finite in $A$, with the same residue field as $A$.
