The ring $A_0$ is a power-series ring over a field, or over a Cohen ring. Apply the closed-fibre equation-lifting construction to $A_0\to A\to B$. It supplies a Noetherian complete local $A_0$-algebra $C$, formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, with

$$B\cong C\widehat\otimes_{A_0}A=C\otimes_{A_0}A.$$

The first equality uses flatness of $B/A$. For the second, $A$ is finite over $A_0$, so the tensor product is finite over $C$ and already complete for the relevant ideal-adic topology. If $K_0=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, the desired fibre is obtained from $C\otimes_{A_0}K_0$ by the field extension $K_0\subset K$. Geometric regularity is preserved by field extension. It suffices to prove the assertion with regular power-series base $A_0$ and target $C$.

Rename that pair $A\to B$. Flatness, the regular base, and the regular closed fibre imply that $B$ is regular by regular local ascent. Its localization $B\otimes_A K$, where $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, is therefore regular. If $K$ has characteristic zero, the field criterion for geometric regularity finishes the proof.

In the remaining case $A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ in characteristic $p>0$. It is enough to test finite purely inseparable extensions $L/K$. Induct on their degrees. The case $L=K$ was just proved. For a nontrivial extension choose $K\subset M\subset L$ with $[L:M]=p$, and write

$$L=M(u),\qquad u^p=f\in M\setminus M^p.$$

There is a finite $A$-subalgebra $A'\subset M$ with fraction field $M$: take finitely many algebraic generators of $M/K$ and multiply each by a nonzero element of $A$ so that its monic equation has coefficients in $A$. If necessary replace $u$ by $bu$ for a nonzero denominator $b\in A'$ of $f$. Then the new $f=b^pf$ belongs to $A'$ and is still outside $M^p$, while the extension $L/M$ is unchanged. Thus

$$A''=A'[Z]/(Z^p-f)$$

is a finite domain extension with fraction field $L$.

The ring $A'$ is Noetherian complete local. Indeed it is finite over the complete henselian local ring $A$, so it decomposes as a finite product of complete local rings; being a domain leaves exactly one factor. The non-pth-power derivation lemma gives a derivation $D\colon A'\to A'$ with $D(f)\ne0$.

Set $T=B\otimes_A A'$. It is finite over $B$, hence a product of Noetherian complete local rings $T_\nu$. Each $A'\to T_\nu$ is local: the contraction of its maximal ideal lies over $\mathfrak m_A$, and $A'$ has only one such maximal ideal. Base change gives formal smoothness of $A'\to T$ for $\mathfrak m_BT$. Passage to each local factor preserves the lifting property, since idempotents lift uniquely across square-zero ideals. The induced topology on $T_\nu$ is its maximal-ideal topology: its closed fibre over $B$ is local Artinian, so the two defining ideals have cofinal powers.

Apply derivation lifting to each factor and combine the resulting derivations to extend $D$ to $T$. Localizing gives a derivation of

$$T\otimes_{A'}M=B\otimes_A M$$

whose value on $f$ is a unit, because $D(f)$ is a nonzero element of the field $M$. By induction $B\otimes_A M$ is regular. The polynomial root-extension criterion now makes

$$B\otimes_A L\cong (B\otimes_A M)[Z]/(Z^p-f)$$

regular. This completes the purely inseparable induction, proves geometric regularity of every fibre, and establishes (1). ∎

Lemma. Algebraic and adic formal smoothness

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring map.

  1. Suppose $\varphi$ is algebraically formally smooth. Give $R$ a linear topology and $S$ a pre-adic topology, subject only to continuity of $\varphi$. The resulting map has the topological formal-smoothness property.
  2. Suppose $\varphi$ is continuous for the $\mathfrak m$-adic and $\mathfrak n$-adic topologies. Formal smoothness for these topologies is equivalent to formal smoothness with $R$ discrete and $S$ still $\mathfrak n$-adic.

Here topological formal smoothness tests continuous maps to discrete rings across square-zero quotients.

Proof. For (1), take a square-zero ideal $J$ in a discrete ring $D$ and a lifting diagram

$$\begin{array}{ccc} S&\longrightarrow&D/J\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow\\ R&\longrightarrow&D . \end{array}$$

Algebraic formal smoothness supplies an $R$-algebra lift $\psi\colon S\to D$. Since the topology on $S$ is pre-adic, choose a defining ideal $\mathfrak n$. Continuity of its given map to $D/J$ means that $\mathfrak n^k$ has zero image for some $k$. Thus $\psi(\mathfrak n^k)\subseteq J$ and $\psi(\mathfrak n^{2k})\subseteq J^2=0$. The lift is continuous, proving (1).

For (2), formal smoothness with the discrete base immediately supplies lifts for the diagrams with continuous $\mathfrak m$-adic base map. Conversely, consider a diagram with the base viewed as discrete. Continuity of $\varphi$ supplies $r$ with $\varphi(\mathfrak m^r)\subseteq\mathfrak n$, and continuity of the top map supplies $k$ with $\mathfrak n^k$ killed in $D/J$. Commutativity puts the image of $\mathfrak m^{rk}$ under $R\to D$ in $J$, so $\mathfrak m^{2rk}$ is killed in $D$. That base map is therefore already $\mathfrak m$-adically continuous. The assumed adic lifting property applies and gives the desired continuous lift. ∎

Lemma. Formal smoothness is unchanged by adic completion

Equip $R,S$ with topologies defined by finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak m,\mathfrak n$, and suppose $R\to S$ is continuous. Write $\widehat R,\widehat S$ for these completions and $\widehat{\mathfrak n}=\mathfrak n\widehat S$. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. $R\to S$ is formally smooth for the specified adic topologies.
  2. $R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for the $\widehat{\mathfrak n}$-adic target topology.
  3. $\widehat R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for the completed adic topologies.

Proof. Finite generation of the ideals gives the canonical quotient identities

$$\widehat R/\mathfrak m^n\widehat R\cong R/\mathfrak m^n, \qquad \widehat S/\mathfrak n^n\widehat S\cong S/\mathfrak n^n,$$

as well as completeness for the extended ideals. A continuous map from either original ring to a discrete ring factors through one of these quotients. The quotient identities therefore extend it uniquely to a continuous map from its completion; restriction is the inverse operation.

Apply this correspondence to the maps into a discrete ring $D$ and into $D/J$, for any square-zero ideal $J$. It identifies the lifting diagrams for (1), (2) and (3), and also identifies their continuous lifts. Compatibility with the base map follows either on each quotient or by uniqueness of extension from the dense original ring. The completed map $\widehat R\to\widehat S$ is defined by this same continuous-extension construction. Thus existence of a lift in any one of the three forms is equivalent to existence in the others. The preceding lemma allows the base topology to be viewed as discrete whenever that convention is used. ∎

Lemma. A derivation criterion for a regular hypersurface

Let $R$ be regular and $f\in R$. If there is a derivation $D\colon R\to R$ whose value $D(f)$ becomes a unit in $R/(f)$, then $R/(f)$ is regular.

Proof. Check the claim at any prime $\mathfrak q$ of $R$ containing $f$. The localization rule for derivations extends $D$ to $R_{\mathfrak q}$. The hypothesis implies $D(f)\notin\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q}$. But Leibniz sends the square of the maximal ideal into that ideal. Hence

$$f\notin(\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q})^2.$$

In the regular local ring $R_{\mathfrak q}$, the element $f$ is therefore part of a minimal generating system for the maximal ideal. Such a system is a regular sequence, by regular local Cohen–Macaulayness. Quotienting by its first element gives dimension and embedding dimension both one less, so $R_{\mathfrak q}/(f)$ is regular local. This proves regularity at every prime of $R/(f)$; if the quotient is zero, there are no primes to check. ∎

Lemma. Completion of an arbitrary direct sum is flat

Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $I\subset R$ be any ideal, and let $\Lambda$ be any set. Then

$$\widehat{\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R}$$

is flat over $R$.

Proof. Put $A=\widehat R$. The quotient identities for Noetherian completion identify

$$\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda R} \cong\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda A},$$

where the right completion is for $IA$. The ring $A$ is Noetherian, complete and flat over $R$. Flatness over $A$ therefore suffices. Replace $R$ by $A$.

The completed-sum inclusion is universally injective:

$$\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda R} \ \hookrightarrow\ \prod_\lambda R.$$

The product is flat because a Noetherian ring is coherent and the coherence criterion for products makes every product of copies of $R$ flat. A universally injective submodule of a flat module is flat. These two facts prove the assertion, with no restriction on the size of $\Lambda$.

There is also a direct equational proof in Henselian local rings, Lemma 6.2. In the description by coefficient families tending to zero, a finite relation has columns in a finite syzygy module. Artin–Rees writes these columns using its generators with coefficients still tending to zero. Those coefficient families trivialize the relation in the completed sum, proving flatness by the equational criterion. This proof has the same arbitrary-rank scope. ∎

Lemma. Formal étaleness and adic smoothness of henselizations

For a local ring $R$, the three maps

$$R\longrightarrow R^h,\qquad R^h\longrightarrow R^{sh},\qquad R\longrightarrow R^{sh}$$

are formally étale. Each is also formally smooth when its target is given its maximal-ideal topology.

Proof. The ordinary and strict pointed-neighborhood constructions write these maps as filtered colimits of étale algebras. For the middle map, one may use the marked finite étale extensions of the henselian ring $R^h$; their residue fields run through the finite subextensions of the chosen separable closure. The constructions and their universal properties are in Henselian local rings, Sections 4–5.

Étale algebras are formally étale. Given a square-zero lifting problem for such a colimit, lift its map on each stage. Existence comes from formal étaleness of the stages, and uniqueness makes their lifts compatible with every transition. The universal property of the colimit gives the unique lift. This is the formal-étale colimit lemma.

In particular the three maps are algebraically formally smooth. A continuous map from one of these targets to a square-zero quotient kills some power $\mathfrak n^k$ of its maximal ideal modulo the square-zero ideal. Any algebraic lift then kills $\mathfrak n^{2k}$, hence is continuous. Thus algebraic-to-adic formal smoothness gives the second assertion. No Noetherian hypothesis is used. ∎

Lemma. Replacing ideal generators without changing regularity

Let $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ in a ring $R$. If $I$ has a quasi-regular, $H_1$-regular, or Koszul-regular generating list of length $r$, respectively, then $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ has the same property.

Proof. Start with a quasi-regular generating list $g_1,\ldots,g_r$. It identifies $I/I^2$ with $(R/I)^r$ and makes the canonical maps

$$\operatorname{Sym}_{R/I}^n(I/I^2)\longrightarrow I^n/I^{n+1}$$

isomorphisms. The classes of the $f_i$ give a surjection $(R/I)^r\to I/I^2$. After the first identification this is a surjective square matrix. It has a right inverse because its target is free; taking determinants proves its determinant a unit, so it is invertible. Hence the $f_i$ also give a basis, and the displayed intrinsic graded maps prove their quasi-regularity.

Write $g_j=\sum_i a_{ij}f_i$ and put $\Delta=\det(a_{ij})$. Both sets of classes are bases of $I/I^2$, so $\Delta$ is invertible modulo $I$. On degree-one generators, the map

$$e_j^{\,g}\longmapsto\sum_i a_{ij}e_i^{\,f}$$

extends by exterior powers to a chain map $K_\bullet(g)\to K_\bullet(f)$: applying the differential gives exactly the chosen expression for $g_j$. It becomes an isomorphism after inverting $\Delta$.

Koszul homology is killed by $I$, since exterior multiplication by $e_i$ is a homotopy for multiplication by the corresponding generator. Thus $\Delta$, being invertible modulo $I$, already acts invertibly on this homology. The map on homology is consequently an isomorphism before localization as well.

An $H_1$-regular list is quasi-regular, and a Koszul-regular list is $H_1$-regular. Applying the preceding comparison to either kind of list $g$ transfers the required homology vanishing to $f$. This proves all three assertions. ∎

Lemma. Removing a Koszul-regular initial segment

Suppose both $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ and $f_1,\ldots,f_n,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ are Koszul-regular in $A$. Then the images of the $g_j$ are Koszul-regular in $A/(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$.

Proof. Put $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$. The augmented complex $K_\bullet(A,f)\to A/I$ is a finite free resolution. The exterior decomposition for a direct sum identifies

$$K_\bullet(A,f,g) =\operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K_\bullet(A,f)\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g)\bigr).$$

On a pure tensor in degrees $p,q$, the differential is $d\otimes1+(-1)^p1\otimes d$, which is the Koszul differential for the concatenated list.

Tensor the augmentation $K_\bullet(A,f)\to A/I$ with this bounded free complex $K_\bullet(A,g)$. The resulting total-complex map is a quasi-isomorphism. To see this directly, its cone is the total complex of a bounded double complex whose columns are exact: each column is the acyclic augmentation cone tensored with a finite free module. Filter the total complex by the degree in $K_\bullet(A,g)$. The successive quotients are shifts of these exact columns; induction through the finite filtration proves the total cone acyclic. Hence

$$K_\bullet(A,f,g)\ \simeq\ (A/I)\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g) =K_\bullet(A/I,\bar g).$$

The left complex has no positive homology by hypothesis, and the right complex therefore has none either. Empty initial or final lists are covered by the same argument. ∎

Lemma. Successive injectivity gives Koszul exactness

Source credit: FAC, Chapter III, §3, no. 62, Proposition 1, pp. 254–255; §4, no. 69, Lemma 1, p. 262; §5, no. 75, proof of Theorem 3, pp. 269–270.

Let $M$ be any module over a ring $R$. If multiplication by $f_i$ is injective on $M/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})M$ for each $i$, then $K_\bullet(R,f_1,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_RM$ has zero homology in every positive degree. No nonvanishing condition on the final quotient is needed. In particular every module-regular sequence, and every ring-regular sequence, is Koszul-regular.

Proof. For an empty list there are no positive terms. For one element the assertion is precisely injectivity of its multiplication map. For a longer list, multiplication by $f_1$ gives a termwise injective map on $K_\bullet(R,f_2,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_RM$. Its cokernel is

$$K_\bullet(R/(f_1),\bar f_2,\ldots,\bar f_r) \otimes_{R/(f_1)}(M/f_1M).$$

The mapping cone of that injective map is quasi-isomorphic to its cokernel: the kernel of the natural cone-to-cokernel map is the contractible cone of the identity on the source. The cone itself is the Koszul complex of the whole list, after the usual exterior decomposition and degree signs. The hypotheses descend to the shorter list acting on $M/f_1M$, so induction makes the cokernel complex acyclic in positive degrees. The same holds for the original complex. ∎

In no. 62 the required hypothesis is exactly successive injectivity, applied there to $t_0^k,\ldots,t_r^k$. The positive cochain Koszul exactness used in that text follows from this argument with the corresponding degree convention; it identifies the degree-zero cocycles and removes the intermediate cohomology.

No. 69 specializes to powers of polynomial variables. For $k\geq1$ those powers form a regular sequence; for $k=0$ they are units, so a one-variable contraction makes the Koszul complex contractible. Removing its final ring term gives the indicated graded resolution of the ideal generated by the powers.

No. 75 uses the exterior basis indexed by increasing tuples for the equations of a nonsingular subvariety. Its augmented complex resolves the local quotient. The printed general differential has sign $(-1)^j$, while its degree-one formula sends $e\langle i\rangle$ to $f_i$. To agree with that formula, the general differential is

$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_q}) =\sum_{j=1}^q(-1)^{j+1}f_{i_j} \,e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_q}.$$

If every positive differential instead receives the opposite sign, multiplication by $(-1)^q$ in homological degree $q$ gives a chain isomorphism. Thus the printed inconsistency is corrected without changing the exactness conclusion.

Lemma. The first Koszul homology has a base-change surjection

Let $A\to B$, let $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subset B$, and suppose $B/J$ is $A$-flat. For any map $A\to A'$, put $B'=B\otimes_AA'$ and let $f'_i$ be the images. The canonical map

$$H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))\otimes_AA' \longrightarrow H_1(K_\bullet(B',f'))$$

is surjective.

Proof. Let $Z=\ker(B^r\xrightarrow{(f_i)}B)$ and $H=H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))$. Split the low-degree Koszul complex into

$$\begin{gathered} 0\to J\to B\to B/J\to0,\\ 0\to Z\to B^r\to J\to0,\\ \bigwedge^2 B^r\to Z\to H\to0. \end{gathered}$$

After tensoring over $A$, the first sequence remains short exact because its quotient is flat. Thus $J\otimes_AA'$ injects into $B'$ with image $J'$. Right exactness of the second sequence makes

$$Z\otimes_AA'\longrightarrow \ker((B')^r\longrightarrow B')$$

surjective. The third sequence identifies $H\otimes_AA'$ with the cokernel of the map from $(\bigwedge^2B^r)\otimes_AA'$. Exterior powers of this finite free $B$-module commute with the indicated base change; its image is exactly the Koszul boundary image in the target kernel. Passing to cokernels yields the claimed surjection. Neither flatness of $B$ over $A$ nor flatness of $A'$ over $A$ was used. ∎

Lemma. Positive Koszul exactness includes degree one

An $M$-Koszul-regular list is $M$-$H_1$-regular. Taking $M=R$ gives the ring version.

Proof. The first property asks for zero homology in every positive degree; the second asks only for degree one. ∎

Lemma. Vanishing of first Koszul homology implies quasi-regularity

For an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, an $M$-$H_1$-regular list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ is $M$-quasi-regular.

Proof. Write $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. The assertion is that, for every $n\geq0$, the monomial map

$$\bigoplus_{\substack{\nu\in\mathbf N^r\\|\nu|=n}}M/JM \longrightarrow J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad (\bar m_\nu)\longmapsto\sum_\nu m_\nu f^\nu$$

is an isomorphism. It is always surjective. The cases $r=0$ and $n=0$ are immediate.

The hypothesis gives exactness of

$$\bigwedge^2R^r\otimes_RM \longrightarrow R^r\otimes_RM \longrightarrow JM\longrightarrow0,$$

where $(e_i\wedge e_j)\otimes m$ maps to $(f_ie_j-f_je_i)\otimes m$. Tensor with $R/J$. The first map becomes zero, giving

$$JM/J^2M\cong(M/JM)^r.$$

This proves the degree-one assertion. The right side is a direct sum of copies of $M/JM$; no freeness of $M/JM$ is asserted.

For $n\geq2$, suppose $\xi=\sum_{|\nu|=n}m_\nu f^\nu$ belongs to $J^{n+1}M$. First consider the coefficient $m_*=m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}$. Collect all other monomials according to one of the factors $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}$, obtaining

$$\xi=\sum_{i<r}b_if_i+m_*f_r^n.$$

Because $\xi\in J^{n+1}M$, it also admits a decomposition

$$\xi=\sum_{i\leq j<r}c_{ij}f_if_j +\sum_{i<r}c'_if_if_r^n+c''f_r^{n+1}.$$

Indeed, a degree-$(n+1)$ monomial either has at least two factors from the first $r-1$ entries, has exactly one, or has none; the remaining factors are absorbed into the module coefficients. Subtracting the two expressions gives a relation among

$$f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f_r^n$$

whose last coefficient is $m_*-c''f_r$. This list is $M$-$H_1$-regular by the multiplication lemma, applied repeatedly to the last entry. Every relation is therefore a Koszul boundary. Its last coordinate lies in $\sum_{i<r}f_iM$, so $m_*\in JM$. This also covers $r=1$, when the indicated sum is zero.

To obtain every coefficient, pass to the faithfully flat Laurent polynomial ring

$$T=R[X_1,\ldots,X_r,X_r^{-1}].$$

Flat base change preserves the exact sequence defining first-homology vanishing. The invertible change of generators

$$g_i=f_i-\frac{X_i}{X_r}f_r\quad(i<r), \qquad g_r=\frac{f_r}{X_r}$$

therefore gives another $M\otimes_RT$-$H_1$-regular list generating $JT$. Express $\xi$ through $f_i=g_i+X_ig_r$ for $i<r$ and $f_r=X_rg_r$. Its coefficient of $g_r^n$ is

$$\sum_{|\nu|=n}m_\nu X^\nu.$$

The case just proved puts this element in $J(M\otimes_RT)$. The Laurent monomials form an $R$-basis of $T$, and the displayed monomials are distinct. After passage to $(M/JM)\otimes_RT$, coefficient uniqueness makes every $\bar m_\nu$ zero. Thus every $m_\nu\in JM$, proving injectivity of the monomial map in degree $n$. ∎

Lemma. Completion does not change local dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(A,\mathfrak m)$,

$$\dim A=\dim\widehat A.$$

Proof. The completion has maximal ideal $\widehat{\mathfrak m}=\mathfrak m\widehat A$, the same residue field as $A$, and compatible quotient isomorphisms

$$A/\mathfrak m^n\cong\widehat A/\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,n} \qquad(n\geq1).$$

The restriction-of-scalars length formula, with its residue degree equal to one, gives equality of their lengths over $A$ and $\widehat A$, respectively. Their local Hilbert functions thus coincide. The dimension-growth theorem identifies the degree of each eventual length polynomial with the dimension of the corresponding ring, proving the equality.

Alternatively, $A\to\widehat A$ is flat and local, and its closed fibre is the common residue field. The local flat dimension formula gives the dimension of the target as $\dim A$ plus the fibre dimension zero. ∎

Lemma. Coefficient subfields of power-series fraction fields

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, with $p$-basis $(b_i)_{i\in I}$. For $n,m\geq0$, set

$$A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]][Y_1,\ldots,Y_m], \qquad K=\operatorname{Frac}(A).$$

For each finite subset $J\subset I$, define

$$k_J=k^p(b_i:i\notin J),\qquad A_J=k_J[[X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]][Y_1^p,\ldots,Y_m^p], \qquad K_J=\operatorname{Frac}(A_J).$$

Then $A$ is finite over $A_J$, and these fields satisfy

$$K^p\subset K_J,\qquad \bigcap_JK_J=K^p,\qquad K_{J\cup J'}\subset K_J\cap K_{J'}.$$

Thus they have all the properties required in the field-intersection lemma.

Proof. The bounded-exponent monomials in the $b_j$, $j\in J$, form a basis of $k$ over $k_J$, of size $p^{|J|}$. One can check this directly in the full $p$-basis expansion: the span of the monomials supported outside $J$ is already the field $k_J$, and grouping exponents in and outside $J$ proves both spanning and independence.

An explicit $A_J$-basis of $A$ is

$$\left\{ \prod_{j\in J}b_j^{e_j}\prod_{\nu=1}^nX_\nu^{a_\nu} \prod_{\mu=1}^mY_\mu^{c_\mu}: 0\leq e_j,a_\nu,c_\mu<p \right\}.$$

Expand each coefficient in the finite $k_J$-basis and group all variable exponents modulo $p$. This gives the asserted expansion even for formal series, and uniqueness follows coefficient by coefficient. Equivalently, finiteness of the coefficient extension and the finite-completion theorem first give finiteness for the formal-series rings; adjoining the polynomial variables and their $p$th powers gives the displayed finite extension.

Frobenius sends every element of $A$ into $A_J$, so it sends every fraction into $K_J$. This remains true for formal series because each coefficient of a sum or product involves only finitely many terms. The refinement inclusion follows directly from $k_{J\cup J'}\subset k_J\cap k_{J'}$.

It remains to compute the intersection. Write any $z\in K$ as $f/g^p$, with $f,g\in A$ and $g\ne0$; for an initial fraction $a/b$, use $f=ab^{p-1}$ and $g=b$. Suppose $z$ belongs to every $K_J$, and fix $J$. Choose $a,c\in A_J$, $c\ne0$, with $z=a/c=ac^{p-1}/c^p$. Then

$$c^pf=ac^{p-1}g^p\in A_J.$$

Every $A_J$-derivation of $A$ kills $c^p$ and the right side, so it kills $f$, since $A$ is a domain. The formal partial derivatives in the $X_\nu$ and the ordinary partial derivatives in the $Y_\mu$ are such derivations. Their vanishing on $f$ means that all its exponents are multiples of $p$.

For each $j\in J$, the coordinate derivation on $k$ over $k_J$ extends coefficientwise to $A$, fixing the variables. It is a derivation on formal series by the finite coefficient formula for products, and it is zero on $A_J$. The constant-field test for a p-basis says that their common kernel in $k$ is $k_J$. Hence every coefficient of $f$ belongs to $k_J$, and $f\in A_J$.

Finally $\bigcap_Jk_J=k^p$. Indeed an element of $k$ has a unique finite expansion in the full $p$-basis monomials; membership in $k_{\{j\}}$ removes every monomial with positive $j$th exponent. Doing this for all $j$ leaves only the constant coefficient in $k^p$. It follows that

$$\bigcap_J A_J=A^p.$$

Here an element with all coefficients in $k^p$ and all exponents divisible by $p$ has a $p$th root obtained coefficientwise, with divided exponents; the polynomial variables still have finite support. We conclude that $f=h^p$ for some $h\in A$, and $z=(h/g)^p$. This proves the remaining inclusion. ∎

Lemma. Noetherian fibres of ind-étale algebras

Suppose $B$ is a filtered colimit of étale algebras over a ring $A$, and $B$ is Noetherian. For every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ there are finitely many primes $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_r$ of $B$ above $\mathfrak p$, and the canonical residue maps give

$$B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong \prod_{i=1}^r\kappa(\mathfrak q_i).$$

Each factor is an algebraic separable extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. An empty fibre is allowed, with the empty product interpreted as the zero ring.

Proof. Put $F=B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. This is a localization of $B/\mathfrak pB$, hence Noetherian. Writing $B=\operatorname{colim}_\lambda B_\lambda$ expresses $F$ as the filtered colimit of the étale $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebras $F_\lambda=B_\lambda\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Each $F_\lambda$ is a finite product of finite separable field extensions, by Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Section 7, Theorem 7.2, whose complete proof includes the local field calculation and finite product decomposition.

Reducedness passes to this colimit without any injectivity assumption on its transitions. A nilpotent element is represented at one stage, and its vanishing power becomes zero at a later stage. That later ring is reduced, so the element itself becomes zero there.

There are also no strict inclusions between primes of $F$. If $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak q'$ existed, an element of their difference would be represented at a stage. Contracting both primes to that stage would give distinct comparable primes of a product of fields, which is impossible. Thus $F$ is reduced and has dimension zero. The Noetherian dimension-zero theorem makes it Artinian, and its finite local decomposition is a product of fields. The factors are its residue fields, equivalently the $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)$ for primes of $B$ over $\mathfrak p$.

For any such factor, an element is represented by an element of some $F_\lambda$: the factor is $F/\mathfrak q$ because $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. The map from $F_\lambda$ to this field factors through one of its finite separable field factors. Thus every element is algebraic and separable over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, proving the final assertion. ∎

Lemma. Reducedness and henselization

For any local ring $R$, the following three conditions are equivalent: $R$ is reduced; its henselization $R^h$ is reduced; its strict henselization $R^{sh}$ is reduced.

Proof. The maps $R\to R^h\to R^{sh}$ are faithfully flat. In particular they are injective, so reducedness of either target implies reducedness of the preceding rings; this is also the faithfully flat descent argument.

If $R$ is reduced, every étale $R$-algebra is reduced by ascent of reducedness under smooth maps. Both henselizations are filtered colimits of such algebras. The finite-witness argument from the preceding proof applies: a power vanishing in the colimit vanishes at some stage, where reducedness forces the original element to vanish. Both colimits are therefore reduced. ∎

Proposition. Flatness and a formally smooth closed fibre

Let $A\to B$ be a local map of Noetherian local rings, let $k=A/\mathfrak m_A$, and put $\bar B=B/\mathfrak m_AB$. The following are equivalent:

  1. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $\bar B$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
  2. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $k\to\bar B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $\bar B$.
  3. $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

Proof. The field theorem identifies (1) with (2). Condition (3) implies flatness by the adic flatness lemma, and base change to $k$ gives the other assertion of (2).

Assume (2). We may complete both local rings. Indeed, the formal-smoothness comparison with completions applies to the closed fibre and to the desired conclusion. Flatness also passes to $\widehat A\to\widehat B$: first $\widehat B$ is flat over $A$, and then every quotient $\widehat B/\mathfrak m_A^n\widehat B$ is flat over $A/\mathfrak m_A^n=\widehat A/\mathfrak m_A^n\widehat A$. The all-powers flatness criterion gives the assertion over $\widehat A$. The closed fibre of the completed map is the completion of $\bar B$. Hence assume $A$ and $B$ complete.

Choose compatible regular coefficient presentations

$$\begin{array}{ccc}R&\longrightarrow&S\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ A&\longrightarrow&B.\end{array}$$

The vertical maps are surjective. Choose parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ of $R$, with $t_1=p$ in positive residue characteristic. They form part of a parameter system in $S$, and $\bar S=S/\mathfrak m_RS$ is regular. The ring $\bar B$ is also regular. By the regular quotient theorem, the kernel of $\bar S\to\bar B$ is generated by a parameter subsequence $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$.

Lift the $\bar x_i$ into $\ker(S\to B)$ and quotient $S$ by these lifts. The list $t_1,\ldots,t_d,x_1,\ldots,x_r$ is part of a regular system, so the parameter-substitution lemma shows that the new $S$ is still a power-series ring over a field or Cohen ring. The $t_i$ remain part of its parameters, $R\to S$ stays flat, and now $\bar S=\bar B$.

Set $I=\ker(R\to A)$. The surjection $S/IS\to B$ is a closed-fibre isomorphism and both rings are flat over $A$. It is injective by the fibrewise injectivity criterion. Equivalently, if $H$ is its kernel, tensor the exact sequence with $k$: flatness of $B$ gives $H/\mathfrak m_AH=0$. The ideal $H$ is finite over the Noetherian local ring $S/IS$, so Nakayama gives $H=0$. We have proved

$$B=S\otimes_R A.$$

It is enough to prove formal smoothness of $R\to S$.

Write $K=S/\mathfrak m_S$. Extend the $t_i$ to parameters by $y_1,\ldots,y_m$. Parameter substitution presents $S$ as

$$K[[t_1,\ldots,t_d,y_1,\ldots,y_m]]$$

in residue characteristic zero, or as

$$\Lambda[[t_2,\ldots,t_d,y_1,\ldots,y_m]]$$

over a Cohen ring with residue field $K$ in positive residue characteristic, where $t_1=p$.

Take a discrete square-zero test $T\to T/J$, a map $\varphi\colon R\to T$, and a compatible continuous $\bar\psi\colon S\to T/J$. A power of $\mathfrak m_S$ kills $J$. Filtering $J$ by its powers under this action, exactly as in the field theorem, reduces the lifting problem to $\mathfrak m_SJ=0$. Thus $J$ is a $K$-vector space.

Formal smoothness over the prime ring first gives a continuous lift $\psi\colon S\to T$ over $\mathbf Q$ or $\mathbf Z$, as appropriate. Keep its coefficient map and the images of the $y_i$, but replace the images of the power-series variables $t_i$ by $\varphi(t_i)$. Their reductions agree with the old ones. Their generated ideal is still nilpotent in $T$, so power-series evaluation defines a continuous lift after this replacement. In the Cohen case the equality on $t_1=p$ is automatic.

The difference $D=\psi|_R-\varphi$ is a derivation into $J$, zero on every $t_i$. Since $\mathfrak m_RJ=0$, it vanishes on all of $\mathfrak m_R$ and factors through a derivation of $k$. It therefore corresponds to a $K$-linear map

$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf Z}\otimes_k K\longrightarrow J.$$

The map

$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf Z}\otimes_k K \longrightarrow\Omega_{\bar S/\mathbf Z}\otimes_{\bar S}K$$

is injective. In characteristic $p$ this is condition (5) of the field theorem, since $\bar S/k$ is formally smooth. In characteristic zero its composite to $\Omega_{K/\mathbf Z}$ is injective by separability of $K/k$, so the displayed map itself is injective.

Extend the linear functional to the larger vector space and compose with $S\to\bar S$ and the universal differential. This gives a derivation $D'\colon S\to J$ restricting to $D$ on $R$. The map $\psi-D'$ is multiplicative because $J^2=0$ and $D'$ satisfies Leibniz; it preserves $1$, has the correct reduction, and is an $R$-map. Also $D'(\mathfrak m_S^2)=0$, proving continuity of the correction. This solves each filtered lifting step and proves formal smoothness of $R\to S$. Base change gives (3). ∎

Lemma. Base change of adic formal smoothness

Suppose $R\to S$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak n$-adic topology of $S$. For any ring map $R\to R'$, the map

$$R'\longrightarrow S'=S\otimes_R R'$$

is formally smooth for the topology defined by $\mathfrak n'=\mathfrak nS'$.

Proof. Restrict a continuous square-zero test for $S'/R'$ along $S\to S'$. Formal smoothness gives an $R$-algebra lift $S\to T$. Together with the specified $R'\to T$, tensor universality gives the required $R'$-algebra lift $S'\to T$. If the first lift kills $\mathfrak n^a$, the tensor lift kills $(\mathfrak nS')^a$. Thus the constructed lift is continuous. ∎

Remark. Lifting the equations from the closed fibre

Suppose $A\to A'\to B$ are local maps of Noetherian complete local rings, and $A\to A'$ identifies their residue fields with $k$. Assume $B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$ is formally smooth over $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology. There is a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc}C&\longrightarrow&B\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow\\ A&\longrightarrow&A'\end{array}$$

in which $C$ is Noetherian complete local, $A\to C$ is formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, and the induced map

$$C/\mathfrak m_AC\longrightarrow B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$$

is an isomorphism.

Let $D=C\otimes_A A'$ and let $E=C\widehat\otimes_A A'$ be its completion along $I=\mathfrak m_{A'}D$. Then $E$ is Noetherian complete local and flat over $A'$. The square has the following additional properties:

  1. The induced map $E\to B$ is surjective.
  2. If $A\to A'$ is surjective, then $C\to B$ is surjective.
  3. If $A'$ is finite over $A$, then $B$ is finite over $C$.
  4. If $B$ is flat over $A'$, then $E\to B$ is an isomorphism.

Proof. The closed-fibre lifting lemma constructs $A\to C$. Its prescribed fibre map lifts to $C\to B$ by continuous lifting, applied to the closed ideal $\mathfrak m_{A'}B\subset\mathfrak m_B$. The lift is local because its residue map is the specified isomorphism.

The ideal $I$ is finitely generated, and $D/I=C/\mathfrak m_AC$ is Noetherian. The Noetherian completion theorem and the ideal-power completion identities give

$$E/I^nE=C\otimes_A(A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n)=:E_n.$$

Each $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ has finite length with factors $k$, and is therefore finite over $A$. Thus $E_n$ is finite over $C$. It is a complete local ring: modulo $\mathfrak m_C$ it is a local Artinian algebra with residue field $C/\mathfrak m_C$, since the finite filtration of $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ has residue field $k$. Completeness of finite modules over $C$ and cofinality of the corresponding maximal-ideal powers give the assertion.

The ideal $IE$ lies in the Jacobson radical of the $I$-adically complete ring $E$, so locality of $E/IE$ makes $E$ local. It is also complete for its maximal ideal. To check this explicitly, a compatible sequence modulo its maximal-ideal powers determines an element of every $E_n$, because each $E_n$ is already complete in that topology. These elements are compatible in $n$, hence come from $E=\varprojlim E_n$. They represent the original sequence: for a fixed maximal-ideal power, choose $n$ at least that large and use $I^nE$ contained in that power. Injectivity follows from Krull intersection in the Noetherian local ring $E$.

The ring $C$ is flat over $A$ by adic formal smoothness. Hence $E_n$ is flat over $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ for every $n$. The all-powers criterion applied to the Noetherian local target $E$ proves flatness over $A'$.

The map $D\to B$ extends to $E\to B$, since a Noetherian complete local ring is complete along every ideal contained in its maximal ideal. Modulo $\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$, the map to $B/\mathfrak m_{A'}^nB$ is surjective: its cokernel has zero reduction modulo the nilpotent ideal generated by $\mathfrak m_{A'}$, and nilpotent Nakayama applies without a finiteness assumption. In particular, $E/IE\to B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$ is the chosen isomorphism. It follows that the residue fields of $E$ and $B$ agree and that $\mathfrak m_EB=\mathfrak m_B$. Successively lift a residue and then each homogeneous maximal-ideal error, using finitely many generators of $\mathfrak m_E$. The corrections in $\mathfrak m_E^n$ converge in $E$ and map to the prescribed element of $B$. This proves (1), without assuming that inverse limits preserve arbitrary surjections.

If $A\to A'$ is surjective, $D$ is a quotient of $C$, hence complete along $I$; thus $C\to E\to B$ is surjective. If $A'$ is finite over $A$, $D$ is a finite $C$-module and already complete along the image of $\mathfrak m_A$. The $\mathfrak m_A$- and $\mathfrak m_{A'}$-adic topologies on $A'$ are cofinal, since $A'$ is finite local over $A$. Consequently $D=E$, and the surjection in (1) proves (3).

Finally let $H=\ker(E\to B)$ and assume $B$ flat over $A'$. Tensoring $0\to H\to E\to B\to0$ with $k$ gives $H/\mathfrak m_{A'}H=0$, because the fibre map is an isomorphism. The ideal $H$ is finite over $E$, and $\mathfrak m_{A'}E\subset\mathfrak m_E$, so Nakayama gives $H=0$. This is also the fibrewise injectivity criterion, and proves (4). ∎

Lemma. Descent along a split module extension

Let $R\to R'$ identify $R$ with an $R$-module direct summand of $R'$. For an $R$-algebra $S$ and an ideal $\mathfrak n\subset S$, put

$$S'=S\otimes_R R',\qquad\mathfrak n'=\mathfrak nS'.$$

Continuous square-zero lifting for $S'/R'$ with its $\mathfrak n'$-adic topology implies the corresponding formal smoothness of $S/R$ with its $\mathfrak n$-adic topology.

Proof. Take a discrete square-zero test $S\to T/J$ over $R$. Put $T'=T\otimes_R R'$ and let $J'$ be the image of $J\otimes_R R'$ in $T'$. This ideal has square zero, and $T'/J'=(T/J)\otimes_R R'$. The base-changed test has a continuous lift $S'\to T'$.

Choose an $R$-module decomposition $R'=R\oplus M$. It gives

$$T'=T\oplus(T\otimes_R M),\qquad J'=J\oplus J'',\qquad J''=\operatorname{im}(J\otimes_R M\to T\otimes_R M).$$

The composite $S\to S'\to T'$ reduces to the original map into the embedded copy of $T/J$. Its image therefore lies in

$$T+J'=T\oplus J''.$$

Although $M$ need not be an ideal of $R'$, the submodule $J''$ is an ideal of this last subring: it is stable under $T$, and its products with $J'$ vanish because $(J')^2=0$. Quotienting by $J''$ gives a ring map $S\to T$ that solves the original test. It is continuous, since the lift from $S'$ kills a power of $\mathfrak n'$ and restriction followed by quotient kills the corresponding power of $\mathfrak n$. ∎

Lemma. Extending a derivation across a formally smooth map

Let $A\to B$ be a local map of Noetherian local rings, with $B$ complete. If $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$, every derivation $D\colon A\to A$ extends to a derivation $D'\colon B\to B$.

Proof. Give $T=B[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ its complete local topology and define its $A$-algebra structure by

$$a\longmapsto a+\varepsilon D(a),$$

where both terms are read in $B$. This is a ring map by Leibniz. It is local and continuous for the maximal-ideal topologies: the maximal ideal of $T$ is $\mathfrak m_B+\varepsilon B$, and the image of $\mathfrak m_A$ lies there.

The quotient $T/(\varepsilon)$ is $B$. Its identity map is continuous, the ideal $(\varepsilon)$ is closed and square-zero, and $T$ is complete because it is finite over $B$. The continuous lifting theorem provides an $A$-algebra map $\phi\colon B\to T$ reducing to the identity. Write $\phi(b)=b+\varepsilon D'(b)$. Comparing constant and $\varepsilon$ coefficients proves additivity, Leibniz and $D'|_A=D$, as required. ∎

Definition. Formal smoothness for linearly topologized rings

Let $R\to S$ be a continuous homomorphism of linearly topologized rings. It is formally smooth if every commutative square of continuous ring maps

$$\begin{array}{ccc} R&\longrightarrow&T\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ S&\longrightarrow&T/J \end{array}$$

with $T$ discrete and $J^2=0$ admits a continuous diagonal lift $S\to T$, compatible with both given maps. Base rings in an ideal-adic lifting assertion are given the discrete topology unless a different base topology is specified.

Lemma. Continuity for ideal-adic topologies

Give $R$ the $I$-adic topology and $S$ the $J$-adic topology. A ring map $\phi\colon R\to S$ is continuous exactly when

$$\phi(I^a)\subset J$$

for some integer $a\geq1$.

Proof. Continuity at zero gives this condition by taking the neighborhood $J$. Conversely, the condition implies $\phi(I^{ab})\subset J^b$ for every $b\geq1$. These are neighborhood bases at zero; translation gives continuity at all points. ∎

Lemma. The completed sum embeds universally into the product

Let $R$ be Noetherian and complete for an ideal $I$, and let $\Lambda$ be any set. The natural map

$$C=\widehat{\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R} \longrightarrow P=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R$$

stays injective after tensoring with any $R$-module.

Proof. A compatible element of the quotients $\bigoplus_\lambda R/I^n$ specifies a unique family $(c_\lambda)\in P$, by completeness in each coordinate. At each fixed $n$, only finitely many coordinates are nonzero modulo $I^n$. Conversely, every family with this property gives such a compatible element. Thus

$$C=\{(c_\lambda)\in P: \text{ for each }n,\ c_\lambda\in I^n \text{ outside a finite set}\},$$

and the natural map is an inclusion.

First tensor with a finite module $Q$. Choose a finite presentation

$$R^s\xrightarrow{A}R^t\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0,$$

which exists because $R$ is Noetherian. Put $L=\operatorname{im}A\subset R^t$. Artin–Rees gives $c\geq0$ such that

$$L\cap I^{n+c}R^t\subseteq I^nL =A(I^nR^s)\qquad(n\geq0).$$

Consider the canonical diagram with right-exact rows:

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} C^s&\xrightarrow{A}&C^t&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes_RC\longrightarrow0\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ P^s&\xrightarrow{A}&P^t&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes_RP\longrightarrow0 . \end{array}$$

All vertical maps are induced by $C\subseteq P$, and the two matrices have the same entries.

Take an element in the kernel of the right vertical map and lift it to $v\in C^t$. Write its coordinate columns as $v_\lambda\in R^t$. Applying the coordinate evaluations of $Q\otimes_RP$ shows that every $v_\lambda$ lies in $L$. These columns tend to zero in the finite-exception sense above.

We can lift the columns through $A$ while retaining that property. For a nonzero $v_\lambda$, choose the largest $n\geq0$ for which $v_\lambda\in I^{n+c}R^t$, if such $n$ exists. It is finite because $\bigcap_n I^nR^t=0$. The displayed inclusion supplies a lift $w_\lambda\in I^nR^s$. If no such $n$ exists, take any lift; if $v_\lambda=0$, choose the zero lift. For each fixed $n$, all but finitely many columns belong to $I^{n+c}R^t$, so these choices put all but finitely many $w_\lambda$ in $I^nR^s$. Consequently $(w_\lambda)$ defines $w\in C^s$ and $Aw=v$.

Right exactness of the upper row now makes the chosen element of $Q\otimes_RC$ zero. Thus the right vertical map is injective for every finite $Q$. Finally, any module is the directed union of its finite submodules. Tensor products commute with these colimits, and filtered colimits of module sequences are exact. Passing to the colimit preserves the proved injections and gives injectivity for every module. ∎

Lemma. Functoriality of the Koszul construction

Suppose $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $\varphi'\colon E'\to R$ are module maps and $\psi\colon E\to E'$ satisfies $\varphi'\psi=\varphi$. The exterior powers of $\psi$ define a morphism of differential graded algebras

$$K_\bullet(\varphi)\longrightarrow K_\bullet(\varphi').$$

Proof. In degree $q$ the map sends $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q$ to $\psi(e_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge\psi(e_q)$. It preserves exterior products and the unit. In the differential of this image, the coefficient obtained by removing its $i$th factor is $\varphi'(\psi(e_i))=\varphi(e_i)$, with sign $(-1)^{i-1}$. Thus applying the differential before or after the map gives the same sum. No freeness assumption on either module is needed. ∎

Lemma. Koszul homology is killed by the defining ideal

For a finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in R$, multiplication by each $f_j$ on $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ is chain-homotopic to zero. Consequently every homology module of this complex is annihilated by $(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$.

Proof. If $e_j$ denotes the $j$th degree-one generator, define $h_j(a)=e_j\wedge a$. The product rule gives

$$d h_j(a)+h_jd(a)=f_ja.$$

Thus $h_j$ is the required degree-one homotopy. An element homotopic to zero acts as zero on homology; linear combinations show that the whole ideal acts as zero. This is the abstract Koszul homotopy. ∎

Lemma. Joining two Koszul lists

For lists $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$ there is a natural isomorphism

$$K_\bullet(f,g)\cong \operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K_\bullet(f)\otimes_RK_\bullet(g)\bigr).$$

Proof. Send the generators for the first list to $e_i\otimes1$ and those for the second to $1\otimes u_j$. The exterior direct-sum identity identifies their ordered wedge monomials with a basis on each side. In the tensor product the multiplication rule on homogeneous elements is

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b') =(-1)^{\deg(b)\deg(a')}(a\wedge a')\otimes(b\wedge b'),$$

so this map respects all exterior relations, including squares of degree-one elements in characteristic two. The total differential is

$$d(a\otimes b)=da\otimes b+(-1)^{\deg(a)}a\otimes db.$$

It takes the first generators to $f_i$ and the second to $g_j$. Its product rule therefore agrees with the Koszul differential on every wedge monomial, proving the isomorphism. Empty lists give the degree-zero factor $R$ and cause no exception. ∎

Definition. The Koszul differential

For an $R$-linear map $\varphi\colon E\to R$, the Koszul complex has degree-$q$ term $\bigwedge^q_RE$, with $\bigwedge^0_RE=R$. Its multiplication is exterior multiplication, and its degree-minus-one differential is

$$d(e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q) =\sum_{i=1}^q(-1)^{i-1}\varphi(e_i) e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat e_i\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q.$$

In degree zero the differential is zero. This is the unique graded derivation with $d(e)=\varphi(e)$ in degree one.

The formula is alternating and multilinear, so it is defined on the exterior power even when $E$ is not free. Applying it twice removes each pair of distinct factors in two orders with opposite signs; hence $d^2=0$. It satisfies

$$d(a\wedge b)=da\wedge b+(-1)^{\deg(a)}a\wedge db.$$

Thus the exterior algebra is a graded-commutative differential algebra. The notation $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ means $E=R^r$ with its standard basis sent to the indicated elements.

Lemma. Appending a Koszul entry gives a cone

For $r\geq1$, set $C=K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})$. There is an isomorphism

$$K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\cong \operatorname{Cone}(f_r\colon C\to C).$$

Proof. Use the homological cone convention

$$\operatorname{Cone}(u)_n=B_n\oplus A_{n-1},\qquad d(b,a)=(d_Bb+u(a),-d_Aa)$$

for a chain map $u\colon A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$. If $e_r$ is the newly adjoined generator, send $(a,b)\in C_n\oplus C_{n-1}$ to $a+e_r\wedge b$. The exterior direct-sum decomposition makes this a degreewise isomorphism, and

$$d(a+e_r\wedge b)=da+f_rb-e_r\wedge db$$

proves compatibility with differentials. This also proves the case $r=1$, and is the free-module specialization of the abstract cone identification. ∎

Lemma. Multiplying the last entry of a Koszul sequence

Fix a list $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}$ in $R$, two elements $f,g\in R$, and an $R$-module $M$.

  1. If appending $f$ and appending $g$ each give an $M$-$H_1$-regular list, then appending $fg$ does too.
  2. The same assertion holds for $M$-Koszul-regular lists.

Proof. Put $C=K_\bullet(R,f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})\otimes_RM$. Appending an element $a$ gives its multiplication cone. The short exact sequence from that cone to the shifted complex gives

$$H_i(C)\xrightarrow{a}H_i(C) \longrightarrow H_i(K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},a)\otimes_RM) \longrightarrow H_{i-1}(C)\xrightarrow{a}H_{i-1}(C).$$

Thus vanishing of the middle homology says exactly that multiplication by $a$ is surjective on $H_i(C)$ and injective on $H_{i-1}(C)$. If both $a=f$ and $a=g$ have these properties, their composite $fg$ has them as well. Use $i=1$ for (1), and all $i>0$ for (2).

Equivalently, the multiplication comparison of Koszul complexes gives the original exact segment from the homology for the list ending in $f$, through that ending in $fg$, to that ending in $g$. Vanishing of both outer terms gives the same conclusion. Repeated application permits replacing any last entry by a positive power. ∎

Lemma. Flat scalar extension preserves Koszul regularity

Let $\rho\colon R\to S$ be flat, let $M$ be any $R$-module, and set $N=M\otimes_RS$. For every finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$:

  1. $M$-$H_1$-regularity of the list implies $N$-$H_1$-regularity of $\rho(f_1),\ldots,\rho(f_r)$.
  2. $M$-Koszul-regularity implies $N$-Koszul-regularity of the image list.

Proof. Base extension identifies the exterior generators and their differentials, giving

$$\bigl(K_\bullet(R,f)\otimes_RM\bigr)\otimes_RS \cong K_\bullet(S,\rho(f))\otimes_SN.$$

Tensoring with a flat module preserves the kernels, images and quotients defining homology. Consequently the $i$th homology on the right is $H_i(K_\bullet(R,f)\otimes_RM)\otimes_RS$. Vanishing for $i=1$ gives the first assertion, and vanishing for every $i>0$ gives the second. There is no finiteness assumption on $M$. ∎

Lemma. An invertible change of generators

Let $X=(x_{ij})\in\operatorname{GL}_r(R)$ and set $g_i=\sum_jx_{ij}f_j$. Then $K_\bullet(g_1,\ldots,g_r)$ and $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ are isomorphic as differential graded algebras.

Proof. Let $e'_i$ denote the generators for $g$ and $e_j$ those for $f$. The map

$$e'_i\longmapsto\sum_jx_{ij}e_j$$

has column matrix $X^{\mathsf T}$ and intertwines the two maps to $R$. Its exterior extension is therefore a chain map by Koszul functoriality. The inverse matrix gives its inverse in every degree. This specifies both the direction of the map and the transpose required by the row-indexed formula for the $g_i$. ∎

Lemma. Differential and Frobenius consequences of field intersections

Let $K$ have characteristic $p>0$. Suppose that intermediate fields $K^p\subset K_\alpha\subset K$ satisfy

$$\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha=K^p,$$

and that any two contain a third member of the family. Then

$$\bigcap_\alpha \ker\bigl(\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/K_\alpha}\bigr)=0.$$

For every finite extension $L/K$ one also has

$$\bigcap_\alpha L^pK_\alpha=L^p.$$

Proof. First assume the family is nonempty. Choose a $p$-basis of $K$ over $\mathbf F_p$ using the differential basis theorem. A nonzero differential has an expression

$$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^r c_i\,du_i$$

using finitely many distinct elements of that basis, with not all $c_i$ zero. If $\eta$ vanishes after passing to $\Omega_{K/K_\alpha}$, those $du_i$ are dependent there. The same theorem says that the $p^r$ monomials $u^E$, with $0\leq e_i<p$, have a nontrivial relation over $K_\alpha$, since $K_\alpha K^p=K_\alpha$.

Let $V\subset K^{p^r}$ be the kernel of the linear map $(a_E)\mapsto\sum_E a_Eu^E$. If $\eta$ lies in every displayed kernel, each $V\cap K_\alpha^{p^r}$ is nonzero. Subspace descent, with ground field $K^p$, supplies a nonzero vector in $V\cap(K^p)^{p^r}$. This contradicts the original $p$-independence of the $u_i$, proving the differential assertion.

For the finite-extension assertion, the result passes up a tower $K\subset M\subset L$. Once it holds for $M/K$, the fields $M_\alpha=M^pK_\alpha$ have intersection $M^p$ and are again downward directed. Moreover

$$L^pM_\alpha=L^pK_\alpha.$$

One may therefore prove the assertion successively along a tower of finite extensions with no proper intermediate fields. Such a tower exists by induction on the degree, choosing a proper intermediate field whenever one exists.

Each nontrivial step without intermediate fields is either separable or purely inseparable of degree $p$. To see this, choose a generator $u$; its minimal polynomial has the form $Q(T^{p^e})$ with $Q$ separable. The intermediate field generated by $u^{p^e}$ is separable over the base. If the step is inseparable, that intermediate field must be the base, so the step is purely inseparable. The absence of intermediate fields then forces its degree to be $p$.

Consider first a finite separable extension $L/K$. Choose a primitive element $u$ and put $\theta=u^p$. The extension $L/K(\theta)$ is both separable and purely inseparable, so $L=K(\theta)$. If $d=[L:K]$, then $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{d-1}$ is a $K$-basis of $L$ and a $K^p$-basis of $L^p$: the latter assertion follows by applying Frobenius to the basis $1,u,\ldots,u^{d-1}$. Since $K^p\subset K_\alpha\subset K$, the same powers form a $K_\alpha$-basis of $L^pK_\alpha$. In fact their span is the algebra generated by $\theta$ over $K_\alpha$, reduced using its degree-$d$ equation over $K^p$; being a finite-dimensional domain, it is a field. A vector lying in every $L^pK_\alpha$ has unique coordinates in this common $K$-basis. Those coordinates lie in every $K_\alpha$, hence in $K^p$, proving the assertion.

For a purely inseparable step of degree $p$, write $L=K(u)$ with $u^p=t\in K\setminus K^p$. Then

$$L^p=K^p(t),\qquad L^pK_\alpha=K_\alpha(t).$$

The powers $1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}$ are independent over $K^p$ and span $K_\alpha(t)$ over $K_\alpha$. They need not be independent over $K_\alpha$; for example, $t$ may already belong to that field. Take $z\in\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha(t)\subset K$, and form the $K$-linear relation space

$$V=\left\{(a_0,\ldots,a_{p-1},b)\in K^{p+1}: \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_it^i-bz=0\right\}.$$

Every $V\cap K_\alpha^{p+1}$ contains a vector with last coordinate $1$. Subspace descent gives a nonzero vector in $V\cap(K^p)^{p+1}$. Its last coordinate cannot vanish, because the powers of $t$ are independent over $K^p$. Dividing by that coordinate expresses $z$ in $K^p(t)=L^p$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. This completes the tower argument.

If the family is empty, interpret intersections inside $K$, $\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}$ and $L$, respectively. The hypothesis then gives $K=K^p$. Such a field is perfect, so its absolute differentials vanish and every finite extension $L$ is perfect. Both conclusions follow in this case as well. ∎

Theorem. Formal smoothness over a field

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a Noetherian local algebra over a field $k$. In characteristic zero, $A$ is regular if and only if $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.

If $k$ has characteristic $p>0$, the following five conditions are equivalent:

  1. $A$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
  2. $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.
  3. $A\otimes_k k'$ is regular for every finite intermediate extension $k\subset k'\subset k^{1/p}$.
  4. $A$ is regular and the boundary map $H_1(L_{K/k})\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ is injective.
  5. $A$ is regular and the natural map
$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_k K \longrightarrow\Omega_{A/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_A K$$

is injective.

Proof. The characteristic-zero assertion follows from formal smoothness implying regularity and the converse with separable residue extension: all extensions of a characteristic-zero field are separable.

In characteristic $p$, the complete geometric-regularity comparison proves the equivalence of (1), (3), (4) and (5). If (2) holds, base change to a finite purely inseparable $k'/k$ gives formal smoothness of $A'=A\otimes_k k'$ for the extended ideal $\mathfrak mA'$. This finite extension has one prime above $\mathfrak m$, and $\mathfrak mA'$ has maximal-ideal radical, so its powers define the maximal-ideal topology of $A'$. The formal-smoothness-to-regularity lemma makes $A'$ regular. The purely inseparable criterion then gives (1).

It remains to derive (2) from (5). Consider a square-zero extension $T\to T/J$, a $k$-algebra structure $\varphi\colon k\to T$, and a continuous compatible map $\bar\psi\colon A\to T/J$, with $T$ discrete. Via $\bar\psi$, the ideal $J$ is an $A$-module annihilated by some $\mathfrak m^n$. Filter it by

$$0=\mathfrak m^nJ\subset\mathfrak m^{n-1}J \subset\cdots\subset J.$$

These are ideals of $T$, and each successive quotient is annihilated by $\mathfrak m$. Lifting through the corresponding successive square-zero quotients reduces the problem to the case $\mathfrak mJ=0$. The action on every layer is independent of the intervening lifts because $J^2=0$. Thus this reduction applies without a finite-generation assumption on $J$.

In the reduced case $J$ is a $K$-vector space. Since $A$ is regular and $K/\mathbf F_p$ is separable, the converse lemma supplies a continuous $\mathbf F_p$-algebra lift $\psi\colon A\to T$. Its failure to respect $k$ is the derivation

$$D=\psi|_k-\varphi\colon k\longrightarrow J.$$

The universal property of differentials gives a $k$-linear map $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\to J$, hence a $K$-linear map from $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_k K$. Condition (5) lets us extend it to a $K$-linear map

$$\xi\colon\Omega_{A/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_A K\longrightarrow J.$$

Compose $\xi$ with the universal differential to obtain a derivation $D'\colon A\to J$ restricting to $D$ on $k$. Then $\psi-D'$ is a ring map: expanding a product gives the required identity by Leibniz, and the product of two values of $D'$ vanishes in $J^2$. It fixes the unit, reduces to $\bar\psi$, and restricts to $\varphi$. It is continuous as well: $D'(\mathfrak m^2)=0$ because $\mathfrak mJ=0$, and $\psi$ already kills some power of $\mathfrak m$. This constructs the desired lift at each layer and proves (2). ∎

Lemma. Adic formal smoothness implies flatness

A local map $A\to B$ of Noetherian local rings is flat if it is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

Proof. The completion comparison preserves the formal lifting property. It is enough to show flatness of $\widehat A\to\widehat B$: the composite $A\to\widehat B$ is then flat, and faithful flatness of $B\to\widehat B$ descends flatness to $A\to B$. Thus assume both rings complete.

Take the regular coefficient presentations $R\to A$ and $S\to B$ of the next lemma, with $R\to S$ flat. If $I=\ker(R\to A)$, then $S/IS$ is flat over $A$. It is a complete Noetherian local ring, and the surjection $S/IS\to B$ has a closed kernel contained in its maximal ideal. The continuous lifting theorem, applied to the identity map of $B$, gives an $A$-algebra section $B\to S/IS$. Consequently $B$ is an $A$-module direct summand of a flat module, and is flat. ∎

Lemma. Compatible regular coefficient presentations

For a local map $A\to B$ between Noetherian complete local rings there is a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc} R&\longrightarrow&S\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ A&\longrightarrow&B \end{array}$$

whose vertical maps are surjective and with these properties. In residue characteristic zero, $R$ and $S$ are finite-variable power-series rings over fields. In positive residue characteristic $p$, they are such rings over Cohen rings. The images in $S$ of a parameter system for $R$ extend to a regular system of parameters there. Consequently $R\to S$ is flat, with regular closed fibre $S/\mathfrak m_RS$.

Proof. The Cohen structure theorem, with its coefficient-ring construction in Sections 4–5, supplies surjections

$$R=\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_a]]\longrightarrow A, \qquad S_0\longrightarrow B.$$

Choose fields as coefficient rings in residue characteristic zero, and Cohen rings in positive residue characteristic, including when $A$ or $B$ itself has characteristic $p$.

The prime-ring formal smoothness proved below and continuous lifting through the closed kernel of $S_0\to B$ lift $R\to A\to B$ to $\phi\colon R\to S_0$. This lift is local: an element of $\mathfrak m_R$ has image in $\mathfrak m_B$, and the preimage of $\mathfrak m_B$ under the local surjection is $\mathfrak m_{S_0}$.

Set $S=S_0[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_a]]$. Keep $\phi$ on $\Lambda$ and send $X_i$ to $\phi(X_i)+Y_i$; send each $Y_i$ to zero in $B$. These substitutions converge in the maximal-ideal topology and preserve the square. The classes of $\phi(X_i)+Y_i$ are independent in the cotangent space because their $Y_i$ coordinates form the identity matrix. In positive residue characteristic, include $p$ as the first parameter: its class is nonzero in the cotangent space of the Cohen power-series ring $S_0$ and independent of the new $Y_i$ coordinates. Thus the images of the parameters of $R$ extend to a cotangent basis of $S$, hence to a regular system of parameters.

The flatness criterion over a regular local base now gives flatness, and quotient by this parameter subsequence is regular by regular local Cohen–Macaulayness. ∎

Lemma. Changing parameters in complete power-series rings

Let $F$ be a field and $\Lambda$ a Cohen ring with uniformizer $p$.

  1. A regular system of parameters $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ in $F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ gives an isomorphism $F[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]]\to F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ by $Y_i\mapsto y_i$.
  2. If $z_1,\ldots,z_r$ is part of a regular system of parameters in that ring, then $r\leq n$ and its quotient by these elements is a power-series ring in $n-r$ variables over $F$.
  3. If $p,y_1,\ldots,y_n$ is a regular system of parameters in $\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$, substitution gives an isomorphism $\Lambda[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]]\to\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$.
  4. If $p,z_1,\ldots,z_r$ is part of a regular system of parameters there, then $r\leq n$ and the quotient by the $z_i$ is a power-series ring in $n-r$ variables over $\Lambda$.

Proof. For (1), substitution is continuous and induces an isomorphism on residue fields and on degree-one cotangent spaces. The associated graded rings of the source and target power-series rings are polynomial rings on their standard parameters: group series terms by variable degree, and in the Cohen case include the $p$-adic orders of their coefficients. Thus the induced graded map is the invertible linear substitution specified in degree one, and is an isomorphism in every degree. Induction in the short exact sequences between successive maximal-ideal quotients gives an isomorphism on every such quotient. Completeness and separatedness give the asserted ring isomorphism.

The same proof gives (3), using $p$ together with the variables in degree one; the coefficient map fixes $p$. For (2), extend the $z_i$ to a regular system of parameters and apply (1). Quotienting its source by the first $r$ variables leaves the claimed power-series ring. For (4), extend $p,z_1,\ldots,z_r$ to a regular system and use (3), again killing only the $r$ indicated variables and retaining $p$. ∎

Lemma. Formal smoothness over the prime ring

The maps

$$\mathbf Q\to F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]],\qquad \mathbf F_p\to L[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]],\qquad \mathbf Z\to\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$$

are formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology, where $F$ has characteristic zero, $L$ has characteristic $p$, and $\Lambda$ is any Cohen ring of residue characteristic $p$.

Proof. The coefficient fields are formally smooth over their prime fields by the separability criterion. For a Cohen ring, Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 4, Theorem 4.1 proves that

$$\mathbf Z/p^N\mathbf Z\longrightarrow\Lambda/p^N\Lambda$$

is formally smooth for every $N\geq1$. Its proof uses only the Cohen DVR properties and works for every residue field.

In a square-zero test with discrete target $T$ and ideal $J$, continuity of the given map modulo $J$ makes the image of some maximal-ideal power zero. In the Cohen case this puts $p^q$ in $J$ for some $q$, so $p^{2q}=0$ in $T$. Apply the quoted result with $N=2q$ to lift the coefficient map. In the field cases, lift the coefficient field map by its formal smoothness.

Choose arbitrary lifts of the images of the variables. The ideal generated by these lifts, and by $p$ in the Cohen case, has a power contained in $J$, and hence a further power zero. Evaluation of formal series is consequently a finite sum in $T$ once their variable degree is large enough; the lifted coefficient map and variable images define a ring map lifting the given one. The same nilpotence proves its continuity for the full maximal-ideal topology. ∎

Lemma. Lifting a formally smooth complete closed fibre

Let $(A,\mathfrak m_A,k)$ be Noetherian complete local. If a Noetherian complete local $k$-algebra $B$ is formally smooth over $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology, then there is a Noetherian complete local $A$-algebra $C$, formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, with

$$C\otimes_A k\cong B.$$

Proof. Use compatible regular coefficient presentations for the local map $A\to B$ through $k$, obtaining $R\to S$ over $A\to B$. Let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be parameters of $R$, with $t_1=p$ in positive residue characteristic. The ring $\bar S=S/\mathfrak m_RS$ is regular, as is $B$ by formal smoothness over a field. The regular quotient parameter theorem makes the kernel of $\bar S\to B$ generated by part of a regular system of parameters $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$.

Lift these elements to the kernel of $S\to B$. The list $t_1,\ldots,t_d,x_1,\ldots,x_r$ extends to a parameter system of $S$. The preceding parameter-substitution lemma shows that $S/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ is still a power-series ring over its field or Cohen coefficient ring and still contains the images of the $t_i$ as part of a parameter system. Replace $S$ by this quotient. Now $S/\mathfrak m_RS=B$ and $R\to S$ is flat.

The flatness and closed-fibre formal smoothness criterion makes $R\to S$ formally smooth. Put $C=S\otimes_R A$. Since $R\to A$ is a surjection, $C$ is a quotient of the Noetherian complete local ring $S$, and is therefore Noetherian complete local. Formal smoothness passes to $A\to C$ by base change, with the maximal-ideal topology inherited from $S$, and its closed fibre is $B$. ∎

Lemma. Continuous lifting to a complete adic ring

Suppose $R\to S$ is formally smooth for an ideal-adic topology defined by $\mathfrak n\subset S$. Let $T$ be a complete separated adic $R$-algebra, let $J\subset T$ be a closed ideal, and suppose $J^t$ lies in an ideal of definition for some $t\geq1$. Every continuous $R$-algebra map $\psi\colon S\to T/J$ lifts to a continuous $R$-algebra map $S\to T$.

Proof. Choose an ideal of definition $I$ with $J^t\subset I$, and put

$$T_{a,b}=T/(J^a+I^b)\qquad(a,b\geq1).$$

The maps $\psi$ give a compatible first row $S\to T_{1,b}$. Lift successively along the first column to obtain maps $S\to T_{a,1}$. Each column step has square-zero kernel because $J^{2a}\subset J^{a+1}$ for $a\geq1$.

For the rest of the grid use the surjection

$$T_{a+1,b+1}\longrightarrow T_{a+1,b}\times_{T_{a,b}}T_{a,b+1}.$$

Surjectivity follows from the elementary two-ideal fibre-product identity: the two ideals in the numerator quotient have sum $J^a+I^b$. Its kernel is square-zero. Indeed, after quotient by $J^{a+1}+I^{b+1}$ it is contained in the image of $I^b$, whose square is zero since $2b\geq b+1$.

Induction on $a+b$ lifts each compatible pair to the next grid entry by formal smoothness. All maps to these discrete rings are continuous; a pair is continuous because a common sufficiently high power of $\mathfrak n$ is killed by both components. This gives compatible maps at every grid point. Since $J^{bt}\subset I^b$, the diagonal entries $T_{bt,b}$ equal $T/I^b$. Their inverse limit produces an $R$-algebra map $\phi\colon S\to T$.

For every $b$, its reduction modulo $J+I^b$ is that of $\psi$. Closedness gives $\bigcap_b(J+I^b)=J$, so $\phi$ reduces to $\psi$ in $T/J$. Finally, continuity of $\psi$ gives $\phi(\mathfrak n^r)\subset J+I$ for some $r$. Taking the $t$th power yields

$$\phi(\mathfrak n^{rt})\subset(J+I)^t\subset I.$$

Further powers give continuity at every $I^b$. This proves the claim and the compatibility of the lift with the specified topologies. ∎

Lemma. Exterior multiplication is a Koszul homotopy

Let $\varphi\colon E\to R$ be an $R$-linear map, let $e\in E$, and put $f=\varphi(e)$. Exterior multiplication $h(a)=e\wedge a$ satisfies

$$dh+hd=f\,1_{K_\bullet(\varphi)}.$$

Proof. Since $e$ has degree one, the graded product rule gives $d(e\wedge a)=fa-e\wedge da$. Rearranging proves the identity in every degree. It holds for arbitrary modules $E$ over arbitrary commutative rings. ∎

Lemma. A rank-one enlargement of a Koszul complex

For $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $f\in R$, define $\varphi'\colon E\oplus R\to R$ by $\varphi'(e,a)=\varphi(e)+fa$. Then

$$K_\bullet(\varphi')\cong \operatorname{Cone}\bigl(f\colon K_\bullet(\varphi)\to K_\bullet(\varphi)\bigr).$$

Proof. Write $C=K_\bullet(\varphi)$ and let $e_0$ generate the added copy of $R$. The exterior direct-sum formula gives the isomorphism

$$C_n\oplus C_{n-1}\longrightarrow\bigwedge^n(E\oplus R), \qquad(a,b)\longmapsto a+e_0\wedge b.$$

Here $e_0$ is placed on the left, fixing the sign convention. The cone differential is $(a,b)\mapsto(da+fb,-db)$. On the exterior side,

$$d(a+e_0\wedge b)=da+\varphi'(e_0)b-e_0\wedge db =da+fb-e_0\wedge db.$$

This is exactly the image of the cone differential. On a decomposable $b=e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{n-1}$, it says that the first removed factor contributes $fb$, while every other term is minus $e_0$ wedged with the corresponding term of $db$. Thus the equality includes all wedge signs, without a freeness restriction on $E$. ∎

Lemma. Multiplication of the last Koszul entry

Let $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f,g\in R$. The complex $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},fg)$ is homotopy equivalent to a cone of a chain map

$$K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f)[1] \longrightarrow K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},g).$$

For a homological complex $C$, the shift here is $C[1]_n=C_{n+1}$ with differential $-d_C$.

Proof. Apply the rank-one multiplication comparison to $E=R^{r-1}$ and the map sending its basis to the fixed prefix. The cone and shift conventions are the ones in the explicit cone-composition proof. ∎

Lemma. Differential bases and p-bases

Let $k\subset K$ be fields of characteristic $p>0$, and put $C=kK^p$. A family $(u_i)_{i\in I}$ in $K$ is called $p$-independent over $k$ when its monomials

$$u^E=\prod_i u_i^{e_i},\qquad 0\leq e_i<p,$$

with finitely many nonzero exponents, are linearly independent over $C$. It is a $p$-basis when these monomials form a $C$-basis of $K$.

The family is $p$-independent exactly when $(du_i)$ is linearly independent over $K$ in $\Omega_{K/k}$. Every $p$-independent family extends to a $p$-basis, including the empty family. Finally, $(u_i)$ is a $p$-basis exactly when $(du_i)$ is a $K$-basis of $\Omega_{K/k}$.

Proof. Suppose first that the differentials are independent. For each index $i$, extend the coordinate functional on their span to a $K$-linear functional on $\Omega_{K/k}$. Its composite with the universal differential is a $k$-derivation $\partial_i$ satisfying $\partial_i(u_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Every such derivation kills $C$.

If a nonzero polynomial $F$ over $C$, of degree less than $p$ in each of finitely many variables, vanishes at the corresponding $u_i$, choose one with smallest total degree. It cannot be a nonzero constant. A variable occurring with positive exponent has a nonzero formal partial derivative: its positive exponents are strictly below $p$. Applying the associated derivation gives a nonzero polynomial relation of smaller total degree. This contradiction proves $p$-independence.

Next enlarge a $p$-independent family to a maximal one by Zorn's lemma. Unions of chains remain independent because a relation uses only finitely many elements. Let $F=C(u_i:i\in I)$ for this maximal family. Its bounded-exponent monomials span $F$: their span is a subalgebra, and every nonzero element $a$ of it has $a^p\in C^\times$, hence inverse $a^{p-1}/a^p$ in that span. If $v\in K\setminus F$, then $v^p\in C$ and $T^p-v^p$ is irreducible over $F$. Indeed, over an algebraic closure it has only the root $v$; a proper monic factor has the form $(T-v)^r$ with $1\leq r<p$, whose next coefficient $-rv$ would put $v$ in $F$. Thus $1,v,\ldots,v^{p-1}$ are independent over $F$. Adjoining $v$ would preserve $p$-independence over $C$, contradicting maximality. Therefore $F=K$, proving existence and extension of $p$-bases.

For a $p$-basis, evaluation gives the presentation

$$K\cong C[T_i:i\in I]/(T_i^p-u_i^p:i\in I).$$

Reduction of exponents proves surjectivity, and independence of the reduced monomials proves that there are no further relations. A $k$-derivation kills $C$, while arbitrary prescribed values on the $u_i$ respect every displayed relation. The universal property of differentials now says that the $du_i$ form a basis. Extending any $p$-independent family to a $p$-basis proves independence of its differentials. Conversely, if the $du_i$ already form a basis, the established independence criterion makes the $u_i$ $p$-independent; a proper extension to a $p$-basis would add an independent differential to a spanning family. Hence no extension is needed.

We will also use the resulting constant-field test

$$\ker(d\colon K\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/k})=kK^p.$$

In a $p$-basis expansion, the coordinate derivations differentiate the bounded-exponent monomials. For a fixed coordinate, distinct monomials involving it give distinct differentiated monomials with nonzero exponent coefficients. Vanishing of every coordinate derivative therefore leaves only the constant monomial. This proves the test for arbitrary, possibly infinite, $p$-bases. ∎

Lemma. Descent of a vector through intersecting subfields

Let $k\subset K$ be fields and let $(K_\alpha)$ be a nonempty family of intermediate fields such that

$$\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha=k.$$

Suppose also that any two members contain a third member of the family. For a $K$-linear subspace $V\subset K^n$, where $n\geq1$,

$$V\cap k^n\ne0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V\cap K_\alpha^n\ne0\ \text{for every }\alpha.$$

Nonemptiness of the family is necessary here: for an empty family the condition on the right would hold even for $V=0$.

Proof. A nonzero vector over $k$ supplies the forward implication. For the converse use induction on $n$. In dimension one a nonzero $K$-subspace is all of $K$, and contains $1$.

Assume that the assertion holds in dimension $n-1$ and that all the intersections over $K_\alpha$ are nonzero. If $V$ contains a nonzero vector of $0\oplus k^{n-1}$, the conclusion follows. Otherwise apply the induction hypothesis to

$$W=V\cap(0\oplus K^{n-1}).$$

There is an index $\alpha_0$ for which $V\cap(0\oplus K_{\alpha_0}^{n-1})=0$. Every nonzero vector of $V\cap K_{\alpha_0}^n$ has nonzero first coordinate. Normalize one to obtain $v=(1,v_2,\ldots,v_n)$. Subtracting a suitable multiple of $v$ from any other vector in that intersection leaves first coordinate zero, and therefore gives the zero vector. In particular, $v$ is its unique vector with first coordinate one.

Whenever $K_\beta\subset K_{\alpha_0}$, the same normalization of a nonzero vector over $K_\beta$ must produce this $v$. Hence all its coordinates belong to every such $K_\beta$. These refinements have intersection $k$: given any $\gamma$, choose a common refinement of $\gamma$ and $\alpha_0$. Membership in all refinements thus implies membership in every $K_\gamma$. Consequently $v\in k^n$, as required. ∎

Lemma. Formal smoothness forces local regularity

If a Noetherian local $k$-algebra $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ is formally smooth over the field $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology, then $A$ is regular.

Proof. Let $k_0$ be the prime field. The extension $k/k_0$ is separable and thus formally smooth, so composing square-zero lifts shows that $A$ is formally smooth over $k_0$. We can work over $k_0$ instead. The completion comparison for formal smoothness allows passage to $\widehat A$. Regularity of the completion implies that of $A$ by regularity descent under completion, equivalently by flat local descent. Thus assume $A$ complete.

Choose a coefficient field $K\to A$ by Cohen structure. It respects the prime field. If $x_1,\ldots,x_e$ lift a basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, put $P=K[[X_1,\ldots,X_e]]$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$. There is a $K$-algebra isomorphism

$$A/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow P/\mathfrak q^2,\qquad x_i\longmapsto X_i,$$

because both rings are the coefficient field plus their square-zero cotangent spaces. Formal smoothness over $k_0$ lifts this map successively to $P/\mathfrak q^n$, using the square-zero kernels at each step. Its limit is a local $k_0$-algebra map $u\colon A\to P$, inducing the chosen residue and cotangent isomorphisms. The later lifts need not respect the chosen copy of $K$; no such assertion is required.

The map $u$ is surjective. The cotangent surjection and residue isomorphism imply surjectivity on each graded piece of the maximal-ideal filtrations, since those graded rings are generated in degree one. Given an element of $P$, lift its residue and then correct the error in degree $n$ by an element of $\mathfrak m^n$, for $n=1,2,\ldots$. These corrections converge in $A$ and their image is the prescribed element of $P$. Hence

$$e=\dim P\leq\dim A\leq\dim_K(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)=e.$$

The last inequality is the usual parameter bound. Equality proves regularity. The resulting surjection is in fact an isomorphism: its regular local source is a domain of dimension $e$, and quotient by any nonzero kernel element would lower dimension. ∎

Lemma. Separable residue fields give formal smoothness

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a regular local $k$-algebra, with $K/k$ separable. Then $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.

Proof. Complete $A$, using preservation of regularity and the equivalence of formal smoothness before and after completion. The coefficient-field power-series description gives a $k$-algebra isomorphism

$$\widehat A\cong K[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]].$$

The field extension $K/k$ is formally smooth by the separability criterion. Polynomial extension and composition show that $K[X_1,\ldots,X_d]$ is formally smooth over $k$. Passing first to the variable-adic topology and then to its completion preserves formal smoothness by the adic comparison lemmas. This proves the assertion. ∎

Lemma. Multiplication in a rank-one Koszul enlargement

Fix $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $f,g\in R$. On $E\oplus R$, let $\varphi'_a$ be $\varphi$ on $E$ and multiplication by $a$ on the last summand, for $a=f,g,fg$. There is a chain map

$$K_\bullet(\varphi'_f)[1]\longrightarrow K_\bullet(\varphi'_g)$$

whose cone is homotopy equivalent to $K_\bullet(\varphi'_{fg})$.

Proof. The rank-one cone identification identifies these three complexes with multiplication cones on $K_\bullet(\varphi)$.
