The cone-composition lemma supplies the map and the explicit homotopy equivalence. Its proof works for every underlying chain complex, so no projectivity or finite-generation assumption on $E$ is introduced. ∎

Lemma. A power-series description respecting the ground field

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a complete regular local $k$-algebra. If $K/k$ is separable, then there is a $k$-algebra isomorphism

$$A\cong K[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]],\qquad d=\dim A.$$

Proof. The residue-field lifting lemma gives a $k$-algebra section $K\to A$ of the residue map. Choose lifts of a cotangent basis. The power-series evaluation map for this specified coefficient field is surjective by successive homogeneous approximations. The complete proof in Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 6, Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.2 then proves injectivity: a nonzero kernel element in the regular power-series domain would force the quotient dimension below $d$. Thus the isomorphism respects $k$ as claimed. ∎

Lemma. Comparing the cones of two multiplications

Let $A_\bullet$ be any homological complex of $R$-modules. For $a\in R$, write $C(a)=\operatorname{Cone}(a\colon A_\bullet\to A_\bullet)$. Then $C(fg)$ is homotopy equivalent to the cone of a map

$$u\colon C(f)[1]\longrightarrow C(g).$$

We use $A[1]_n=A_{n+1}$ with differential $-d_A$, and

$$\operatorname{Cone}(v)_n=B_n\oplus A_{n-1},\qquad d(b,a)=(d_Bb+v(a),-d_Aa).$$

Proof. First take $A_\bullet=R$ in degree zero. The shifted complex $C(f)[1]$ has terms in degrees $0,-1$ and differential $-f$. Multiplying its degree-minus-one coordinate by $-1$ gives an isomorphic model with differential $f$. Map its degree-zero term identically to the degree-zero term of $C(g)$, and its other term to zero. In these signed coordinates the cone is the two-term complex

$$P_1=R^2\xrightarrow{\ M\ }P_0=R^2,\qquad M=\begin{pmatrix}g&1\\0&-f\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus the displayed matrix uses a specified signed model of the shift.

Define maps $i\colon C(fg)\to P$ and $p\colon P\to C(fg)$ by

$$i_1=\binom{1}{-g},\quad i_0=\binom01,\qquad p_1=(1,0),\quad p_0=(f,1).$$

Direct multiplication gives $Mi_1=i_0fg$, $p_0M=fgp_1$, and $pi=1$. The degree-one homotopy $h\colon P_0\to P_1$ is

$$h=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Indeed,

$$hM=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\g&1\end{pmatrix}=1-i_1p_1, \qquad Mh=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-f&0\end{pmatrix}=1-i_0p_0.$$

This proves the two-term assertion with its omitted homotopy supplied.

For a general complex, the map can be written without any boundedness assumption. Its degree-$n$ component is

$$u_n\colon A_{n+1}\oplus A_n\longrightarrow A_n\oplus A_{n-1}, \qquad (x,y)\longmapsto(y,0).$$

The source differential is $(x,y)\mapsto(-dx-fy,dy)$, so $u$ is a chain map. In the cone of $u$, change the sign of the first coordinate from the shifted summand. The degree-$n$ term becomes

$$P_n=A_n\oplus A_{n-1}\oplus A_n\oplus A_{n-1},$$

with differential

$$d_P(a,b,c,e)=(da+gb+e,\,-db,\,dc-fe,\,-de).$$

The maps and homotopy generalizing the preceding matrices are

$$\begin{aligned} i_n(x,y)&=(0,y,x,-gy),\\ p_n(a,b,c,e)&=(fa+c,b),\\ H_n(a,b,c,e)&=(0,0,0,a)\in P_{n+1}. \end{aligned}$$

The first two commute with the differentials by substitution, and $pi=1$. Substitution also gives

$$(d_PH+Hd_P)(a,b,c,e)=(a,0,-fa,e+gb) =(1-ip)(a,b,c,e).$$

Therefore they are mutually inverse up to chain homotopy for arbitrary $A_\bullet$.

This also explains the tensor-product proof. Totalizing $A_\bullet\otimes_R(R\xrightarrow{a}R)$ gives $C(a)$ after the usual degree signs. Totalization preserves the displayed chain maps, and sends the two-term homotopy to $(-1)^i1\otimes h$ on the summand of $A$-degree $i$: the mixed differential terms cancel, leaving the original homotopy identity. The standard identification

$$A_i\otimes B[1]_j\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)[1]_{i+j}, \qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto(-1)^i a\otimes b,$$

provides the shift signs, and the corresponding cone identification uses the same sign on its shifted summand. Thus the original reduction to a two-term scalar complex and the direct formulas give the same homotopy equivalence. No flatness is needed, since these are actual chain maps and homotopies. ∎

Lemma. A section of a separable residue extension

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a complete local $k$-algebra, without a Noetherian assumption. If $K/k$ is separable, there is a $k$-algebra map $K\to A$ whose composite with $A\to K$ is the identity.

Proof. The separability criterion makes $K/k$ formally smooth. Start with the identity $K\to A/\mathfrak m$. Having lifted it to $A/\mathfrak m^n$, lift further to $A/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$; the kernel $\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$ is square-zero. Choose these lifts compatibly. Their inverse limit is the required $k$-algebra map because $A$ is complete and separated. This is also the continuous complete-target lifting theorem for the discrete source field and the closed ideal $\mathfrak m$. ∎

Marked formal deformation rings

Fix a Noetherian ring $\Lambda$ and a finite map $\Lambda\to k$ to a field. Write $\mathfrak m_\Lambda=\ker(\Lambda\to k)$ and $k'=\Lambda/\mathfrak m_\Lambda$, so $k/k'$ is finite. The ring $\Lambda$ need not itself be local; every local algebra below factors through $\Lambda_{\mathfrak m_\Lambda}$.

The category $\mathcal C_\Lambda$ consists of Artinian local $\Lambda$-algebras equipped with a specified residue-field identification with $k$. Its morphisms are local $\Lambda$-algebra maps respecting these identifications. In $\widehat{\mathcal C}_\Lambda$, the rings are Noetherian complete local with the same residue marking and morphism convention. Completeness always includes separatedness.

Lemma. Cotangent surjectivity for complete marked rings

For a map $f\colon R\to S$ in $\widehat{\mathcal C}_\Lambda$, these conditions are equivalent:

  1. $f$ is surjective.
  2. $\mathfrak m_R/\mathfrak m_R^2\to\mathfrak m_S/\mathfrak m_S^2$ is surjective.
  3. The relative cotangent map is surjective:
$$\mathfrak m_R/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda R+\mathfrak m_R^2) \longrightarrow \mathfrak m_S/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda S+\mathfrak m_S^2).$$

Proof. A surjection with the prescribed residue isomorphism maps the source maximal ideal onto the target one, proving (1) implies (2); quotienting gives (3).

Assume (3), and put $R_n=R/\mathfrak m_R^n$, $S_n=S/\mathfrak m_S^n$. For $n\geq2$, their absolute and relative cotangent spaces are the ones of $R$ and $S$. The Artinian criterion below therefore gives surjections $R_n\to S_n$ for every $n$, including the residue map at $n=1$.

Let $H_n$ be their kernels. Each $H_n$ has finite length as an $R$-module, being a submodule of $R_n$. For a fixed $n$, the images of all later $H_m$ form a descending sequence of $R$-submodules of $H_n$ and hence stabilize. Thus $(H_n)$ is Mittag–Leffler. The exact inverse-limit theorem applied to

$$0\longrightarrow H_n\longrightarrow R_n\longrightarrow S_n\longrightarrow0$$

gives a surjection $R=\varprojlim R_n\to\varprojlim S_n=S$.

There is also a direct completion argument. Once the absolute cotangent map is surjective, the induced maps $\mathfrak m_R^n/\mathfrak m_R^{n+1}\to\mathfrak m_S^n/\mathfrak m_S^{n+1}$ are surjective for every $n$, because the associated graded algebras are generated in degree one over the common residue field. Lift an element's residue and then correct its successive errors using elements of $\mathfrak m_R^n$. The resulting series of corrections converges in $R$ and maps to the chosen element of $S$. The equivalence of the two cotangent tests follows from the same diagram as in the Artinian proof. ∎

Lemma. Cotangent surjectivity for Artinian marked rings

For a map $f\colon A\to B$ in $\mathcal C_\Lambda$, surjectivity is equivalent to surjectivity on absolute cotangent spaces, and also equivalent to surjectivity of

$$\mathfrak m_A/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda A+\mathfrak m_A^2) \longrightarrow \mathfrak m_B/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda B+\mathfrak m_B^2).$$

Proof. If $f$ is surjective, an element lifting a member of $\mathfrak m_B$ has zero residue because the marked residue map is an isomorphism. Thus $f(\mathfrak m_A)=\mathfrak m_B$, proving absolute cotangent surjectivity. The relative assertion is then its quotient.

For the converse comparison, put

$$V=(\mathfrak m_\Lambda/\mathfrak m_\Lambda^2)\otimes_{k'}k, \quad U_A=\mathfrak m_A/\mathfrak m_A^2, \quad W_A=\mathfrak m_A/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda A+\mathfrak m_A^2),$$

and define $U_B,W_B$ in the same way. There is a commutative diagram with right-exact rows

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} V&\longrightarrow&U_A&\longrightarrow&W_A\longrightarrow0\\ \Vert&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ V&\longrightarrow&U_B&\longrightarrow&W_B\longrightarrow0. \end{array}$$

The first map sends $\lambda\otimes c$ to the class of $\lambda\widetilde c$, where $\widetilde c$ is any lift of $c$. Different lifts differ by a maximal-ideal element, so their products with $\lambda$ agree modulo its square. The image is precisely the contribution of $\mathfrak m_\Lambda A$, or of $\mathfrak m_\Lambda B$. This proves the asserted exactness and naturality. If $W_A\to W_B$ is onto, lift the relative class of any element of $U_B$ to $U_A$; its remaining difference lies in the image of $V$ and can be lifted through the identical left column. Hence $U_A\to U_B$ is onto.

Assume that absolute cotangent map is onto. Then

$$\mathfrak m_B=f(\mathfrak m_A)B+\mathfrak m_B^2.$$

Nakayama over the Artinian local ring $B$, applied to $\mathfrak m_B/f(\mathfrak m_A)B$, gives $\mathfrak m_B=f(\mathfrak m_A)B$. The residue isomorphism now says that $A/\mathfrak m_A\to B/\mathfrak m_AB$ is surjective. For the $A$-module cokernel $Q$ of $A\to B$, this gives $Q=\mathfrak m_AQ$. Since $\mathfrak m_A$ is nilpotent, iteration gives $Q=0$, even without invoking finiteness of $Q$. Thus $f$ is surjective. ∎

Supporting proofs and references

The following results supply the lower algebraic and topological inputs used above. Each entry records its precise hypotheses and its proof or complete written source. Any outstanding dependency remains identified at its own entry.

Noetherian spaces and their components

Every subspace of a Noetherian topological space is Noetherian. Such a space has finitely many irreducible components, and each component contains a nonempty open subset of the whole space.

Proof. For a descending chain $F_n$ of closed subsets of a subspace $Y\subset X$, choose closed $Z_n\subset X$ with $F_n=Y\cap Z_n$. Replace $Z_n$ by $Z_1\cap\cdots\cap Z_n$. These new ambient closed sets form a descending chain and still restrict to $F_n$, so ambient stabilization proves subspace stabilization.

The complete finite-decomposition argument is Spectra of rings, Section 4, Theorem 4.3. It works for arbitrary Noetherian spaces: a minimal closed counterexample to finite irreducible decomposition would split into two smaller closed sets, a contradiction. Remove redundant members to obtain the finitely many components $Z_1,\ldots,Z_r$. For each $i$,

$$U_i=X\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}Z_j$$

is open and contained in $Z_i$, since the components cover $X$. It is nonempty because an irreducible $Z_i$ cannot be contained in the union of the other finitely many components without being contained in one of them. The empty space has no components, so the assertion there is vacuous. ∎

Finite-type morphisms from a field

For any scheme $S$, field $K$, and morphism $f\colon\operatorname{Spec}(K)\to S$, these conditions are equivalent:

  1. $f$ is of finite type.
  2. $f$ is locally of finite type.
  3. Its image lies in an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}(R)\subset S$ for which the induced map $R\to K$ is finite.
  4. There is such an affine open in which the image is a closed point $s$, with $K/\kappa(s)$ finite.

Proof. A morphism from a one-point space is quasi-compact: every inverse image of an affine open is empty or a singleton. Thus locally finite type and finite type agree here.

Suppose (2), choose an affine neighborhood $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ of the image, and write $\mathfrak p=\ker(R\to K)$. Then $K$ is a finite-type algebra over the domain $R_0=R/\mathfrak p$. We show that some nonzero $a\in R_0$ has $R_{0,a}$ a field with $K/R_{0,a}$ finite. Apply normalization over a domain to $R_0\subset K$. After inverting a nonzero $a$, it makes $K$ finite over a polynomial subring

$$R_{0,a}[Y_1,\ldots,Y_d]\subset K.$$

A domain over which a field is integral must itself be a field: the inverse of a nonzero element in the larger field satisfies a monic equation, which expresses that inverse in the smaller domain. Therefore the displayed polynomial subring is a field. A polynomial variable cannot be a unit, so $d=0$, and the assertion follows. This is the field-over-domain step needed for the affine neighborhood.

Lift $a$ to $R$. Its image in $K$ is nonzero, so the morphism factors through the principal open $\operatorname{Spec}(R_a)$, and $K$ is finite as an $R_a$-module. This proves (3). Conversely, a finite ring map is of finite type, so (3) implies (2).

For a finite map $R\to K$, the image $R/\mathfrak p$ is a domain over which $K$ is integral, and the inverse argument above makes it a field. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is maximal and $K/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is finite, proving (4). The finite field extension in (4), together with $R\to R/\mathfrak p$, immediately gives (3). This proves all four equivalences without a Noetherian hypothesis on $S$ or $R$. ∎

Stable images in an inverse system

Let $(A_i)$ be an inverse system of sets indexed by a nonempty directed set. Suppose it is Mittag–Leffler: for each $i$, the images in $A_i$ of sufficiently late $A_j$ are constant. Denote that eventual image by $B_i$. Then $(B_i)$ is an inverse subsystem with surjective transition maps and

$$\varprojlim_iB_i=\varprojlim_iA_i.$$

The same assertion holds for inverse systems of groups or modules.

Proof. Fix $i\leq j$. Choose an index $l\geq j$ beyond stabilization indices for the images in both $A_i$ and $A_j$. Every element of $B_j$ is the image of an element of $A_l$, so its image in $A_i$ belongs to $B_i$. This proves that transitions restrict to the $B_i$.

Given $b\in B_i$, the same choice of a sufficiently late $l$ lifts it to an element of $A_l$. The image of that element in $A_j$ belongs to $B_j$, proving surjectivity of $B_j\to B_i$. Finally, every coordinate of a compatible family in the $A_i$ belongs to every later image, hence to $B_i$. Conversely a family in the subsystem is already compatible in the original system. This proves equality of limits. Countability is not needed for this stable-image construction; it is needed for the subsequent general nonempty-limit assertion used in countable Mittag–Leffler exactness. ∎

Intersections of powers in finite modules

Let $R$ be Noetherian, $I\subset R$ an ideal, and $M$ a finite $R$-module. The submodule

$$N=\bigcap_{n\geq0}I^nM$$

vanishes on an open neighborhood of every prime containing $I$. If $I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(R)$, then $N=0$.

Proof. Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 6, Theorem 6.1 proves the stronger statement that one element $1+a$, with $a\in I$, annihilates all of $N$. Its complete proof applies Artin–Rees to obtain $IN=N$ and then uses the determinant form of Nakayama; it also proves the converse description by elementwise annihilators.

For any $\mathfrak p\supset I$, the element $1+a$ avoids $\mathfrak p$. Hence $D(1+a)$ is an open neighborhood on which $N$ vanishes. If $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical, $1+a$ is a unit and annihilates only the zero module. These give the two stated consequences with one uniform annihilator. ∎

The natural long exact Tor sequence

For modules over any commutative ring $R$, a short exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0$$

gives, for every $N$, a natural exact sequence

$$\cdots\longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M')\longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M'') \xrightarrow{\partial} \operatorname{Tor}^R_{n-1}(N,M')\longrightarrow\cdots$$

ending in $N\otimes_RM'\to N\otimes_RM\to N\otimes_RM''\to0$.

Proof. Resolve $N$ by free modules $P_\bullet$. Tensoring the short exact sequence with each $P_i$ is exact, giving a short exact sequence of complexes $0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0$. For a cycle $z\in Z_n$, lift it to $y\in Y_n$. Its differential $dy$ is the image of a unique $x\in X_{n-1}$. This $x$ is a cycle because $d^2y=0$ and $X\to Y$ is injective. Define $\partial[z]=[x]$.

A different lift of $z$ changes $x$ by a boundary from $X_n$. Changing $z$ by a boundary can be lifted by adding a differential to $y$, leaving $x$ unchanged. Thus the map is well defined.

Exactness follows by three chases. If a cycle of $X$ becomes a boundary $dy$ in $Y$, the image of $y$ is a cycle of $Z$ mapping to it under $\partial$. If a cycle of $Y$ maps to a boundary $dz$ in $Z$, lift $z$ and subtract its differential; the result is a cycle coming from $X$. Finally, if $\partial[z]=0$, its lifted differential is the image of a boundary $dx$ in $X$; subtracting the image of $x$ from the lift makes it a cycle in $Y$ mapping to $z$. These are the three kernel-image equalities repeated along the sequence. Degree zero is right exactness of tensor product.

The construction commutes with maps of short exact sequences and with chain maps between free resolutions, because both the lift and its differential commute with those maps. Homotopic resolution maps induce the same homology map, so the sequence and its connecting homomorphisms are natural in both variables. ∎

Reducedness under a flat map of Noetherian rings

Let $R\to S$ be a flat map of Noetherian rings. If $R$ and all rings $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ are reduced, then $S$ is reduced.

Proof. A Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes, say $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$. Their intersection is its nilradical, so reducedness gives an injective map

$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^t\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p_i) =\prod_{i=1}^t\kappa(\mathfrak p_i).$$

Flat tensoring by $S$ preserves this injection. Tensor product commutes with the finite product because a finite product of modules is their direct sum. Hence

$$S\hookrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^t\bigl(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p_i)\bigr).$$

Each factor is reduced by hypothesis. A nilpotent of $S$ maps to zero in every factor, and injectivity makes it zero. If $R=0$, then its unital algebra $S$ is also zero, giving the assertion in the empty-spectrum case. This proves the exact ascent statement used by smooth reducedness. ∎

Exactness of Mittag–Leffler inverse limits

For integer-indexed inverse systems of modules, a short exact sequence remains exact after inverse limit when the kernel system is Mittag–Leffler.

The complete countable directed inverse-limit proof applies at this scope. It proves exactness at the first two terms directly, regards lifts of a compatible target element as a Mittag–Leffler system of nonempty cosets, and uses surjective stable-image transitions along a countable cofinal sequence to choose a compatible lift. No surjectivity of the original transitions is assumed.

The finite-submodule test for an integral element

If an element $y$ of an $R$-algebra $S$ preserves a finite $R$-submodule $M\subset S$ containing $1$, then $y$ is integral over $R$.

The complete determinant proof is Integral extensions: lying over, going up and going down, Section 1, Theorem 1.1. Choose generators of $M$ and express multiplication by $y$ as a coefficient matrix over $R$. Its monic characteristic polynomial annihilates every generator by the adjugate identity, hence annihilates $1$, proving the asserted equation for $y$. The generators need not be a basis. Equivalently, $M$ is faithful for the action of $R[y]$: an element acting as zero kills $1$ and is itself zero.

Additivity of module length

For a short exact sequence $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ over an arbitrary ring,

$$\ell(M)=\ell(M')+\ell(M'')$$

with values in $\mathbf N\cup\{\infty\}$.

Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 3, Theorem 3.3 gives the complete composition-series proof: $M$ has finite length exactly when both ends do, and in that case the lengths add. The same equivalence handles all infinite cases. If either end has infinite length, the middle must also; if the middle has infinite length, the two ends cannot both be finite. Thus the formula retains its full extended-value scope.

Residue fields as composition factors

For a finite-length module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$, every simple factor is $R/\mathfrak m$ for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. The number of occurrences of that residue field is

$$\ell_{R_{\mathfrak m}}(M_{\mathfrak m}).$$

The full proofs are Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 3, Theorems 3.2–3.3 and Proposition 3.4. A nonzero vector in a simple module gives a cyclic presentation, whose kernel is maximal. Localizing a composition series at $\mathfrak m$ retains precisely its factors $R/\mathfrak m$ and kills all the others: for another maximal ideal choose an element in it but outside $\mathfrak m$. The surviving series has simple factors over $R_{\mathfrak m}$, proving the formula and its independence of the chosen series.

Schanuel's lemma and its diagram

Suppose two projective presentations of the same module are given over a ring $R$:

$$0\to K\xrightarrow{c_1}P_1\xrightarrow{p_1}M\to0, \qquad 0\to L\xrightarrow{c_2}P_2\xrightarrow{p_2}M\to0.$$

Then $K\oplus P_2\cong P_1\oplus L$. Moreover, these presentations become isomorphic after adding the other projective module to their first two terms.

Proof. Form

$$E=\{(v,w)\in P_1\oplus P_2:p_1(v)+p_2(w)=0\}.$$

Projection onto $P_1$ is onto with kernel $L$; projection onto $P_2$ is onto with kernel $K$. Both sequences split because their quotients are projective. Consequently

$$K\oplus P_2\cong E\cong P_1\oplus L.$$

This is the fibre-product proof of Projective dimension, Lemma 1.1, with a minus sign in one projection to replace equality by a zero sum.

For the diagram, projectivity supplies $a\colon P_1\to P_2$ and $b\colon P_2\to P_1$ satisfying $p_2a=p_1$ and $p_1b=p_2$. Define automorphisms of $P_1\oplus P_2$ by

$$T=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\a&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Their inverses replace $a,b$ by $-a,-b$. The equalities

$$(p_1,0)T=(p_1,p_2)=(0,p_2)U$$

show that their restrictions identify $E$ with the respective kernels. Using $c_1,c_2$ to identify these kernels gives the commutative diagram

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} 0\to K\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(c_1,\,1)}&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(p_1,\,0)}&M\to0\\ \uparrow\,T|_E&&\uparrow\,T&&\Vert\\ 0\to E&\longrightarrow&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(p_1,\,p_2)}&M\to0\\ \downarrow\,U|_E&&\downarrow\,U&&\Vert\\ 0\to P_1\oplus L&\xrightarrow{(1,\,c_2)}&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(0,\,p_2)}&M\to0 . \end{array}$$

Every vertical map is an isomorphism. Composing the lower vertical maps with the inverses of the upper ones gives the claimed two-row comparison. ∎

Embedding dimension bounds residue-field projective dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$,

$$\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)\leq\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa,$$

where the right side may be infinite.

The full proof is Regular local rings, Lemma 2.1. A minimal generating list of length $e$ defines a Koszul complex mapping to the minimal free resolution of $\kappa$. Comparison modulo $\mathfrak m^2$ makes its degree-$i$ map injective after reduction modulo $\mathfrak m$. The exterior-coordinate map used in the induction is injective in every characteristic: each basis wedge has a coordinate obtained by deleting one of its indices and recording that index, and these coordinates distinguish the wedges. Thus the $i$-th free rank is at least $\binom ei$. In degree $e$ it cannot vanish, which proves the inequality without a characteristic restriction.

Resolutions over a regular local ring

Let $R$ be regular local of dimension $d$. A nonzero finite $R$-module $M$ of depth $e$ has a finite free resolution of length $d-e$. Also $\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq d$, with the supremum taken over arbitrary modules.

These are proved in Projective dimension, Sections 1–4, specifically Theorems 1.5, 2.2, 2.3, 3.1 and Corollary 4.3. A regular parameter sequence gives a Koszul resolution of $\kappa$ of length $d$. Minimal free resolutions and their Tor detection then bound projective dimensions of finite modules. In particular they bound every cyclic quotient $R/J$, since $R$ is Noetherian. The cyclic-module test extends this bound to all modules by a well-ordered generator filtration and compatible projective resolutions; it does not assume arbitrary modules are finite. Finally the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula gives $\operatorname{pd}_RM=d-e$, and a minimal finite free resolution realizes this length.

A finite residue-field resolution is bounded by dimension

If $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ is Noetherian local and $n=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa<\infty$, then $n\leq\dim R$. Regularity is not assumed.

Proof. The Auslander–Buchsbaum formula applies to the nonzero finite module $\kappa$. Its depth is zero, including when $R$ is a field. Therefore

$$n+\operatorname{depth}_R\kappa =\operatorname{depth}R,\qquad n=\operatorname{depth}R.$$

The depth bound for finite modules, applied to $R$ itself, gives $\operatorname{depth}R\leq\dim R$. Combining these equalities and inequality proves the assertion. ∎

Finite length from a finitely generated maximal ideal

Let $\mathfrak m$ be a finitely generated maximal ideal of a ring $R$. If $M$ is a finite $R$-module and $\mathfrak m^nM=0$ for some $n$, then $M$ has finite length. Neither locality nor Noetherianity of $R$ is required.

Proof. Choose generators $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ of $\mathfrak m$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ of $M$. Products $a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_j}v_l$ form a finite generating list for $\mathfrak m^jM$. Its quotient by $\mathfrak m^{j+1}M$ is therefore a finite-dimensional vector space over $R/\mathfrak m$, and its dimension is its $R$-module length. The filtration

$$M\supset\mathfrak mM\supset\cdots\supset\mathfrak m^nM=0$$

has finitely many such layers. Length additivity proves the assertion. If $n=0$, then $M=0$ and the length is zero. ∎

Powers of ideals contained in a radical

If $R$ is Noetherian and $I,J$ are ideals with $J\subset\sqrt I$, then $J^N\subset I$ for some $N\geq1$. In particular, an ideal all of whose elements are nilpotent is a nilpotent ideal.

Proof. More generally, only finite generation of $J$ is needed. Write $J=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ and choose positive integers $d_i$ with $a_i^{d_i}\in I$. For $r>0$, take

$$N=1+\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1).$$

A degree-$N$ product of the generators contains at least $d_i$ copies of some $a_i$; otherwise its degree would be at most $N-1$. Every such product belongs to $I$, and these products generate $J^N$. For $J=0$, choose $N=1$. Applying this with $I=0$ gives the last assertion. ∎

Quasi-finiteness over an intermediate base

Suppose $A\to B\to C$ are ring maps and $C$ is finite type over $A$. If $A\to C$ is quasi-finite at a prime $\mathfrak r$, then so is $B\to C$. No finiteness condition on $B/A$ is required.

The first pointwise argument in the affine Zariski Main proof proves this directly: the same generators give finite type over $B$, and a principal open isolating $\mathfrak r$ in its fibre over $A$ isolates it in the smaller fibre over $B$.

Integral closure near a monogenic quasi-finite point

Let $S=R[X]/I$, let $C$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $S$, and let $\mathfrak q$ be a quasi-finite point of $S/R$. There is $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $C_g=S_g$.

The monogenic part of the affine Zariski Main proof is a complete proof for arbitrary rings. It starts with a relation having a coefficient outside the base prime, puts the leading-coefficient multiple of the generator in $C$, and reduces the degree until that leading coefficient avoids $\mathfrak q$. It does not use the conductor step or the full theorem inductively.

Quasi-finiteness is local at the selected fibre point

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, and let $\mathfrak q$ contract to $\mathfrak p$. For $f\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ and $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$, the map $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ exactly when $R_f\to S_{fg}$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak qS_{fg}$.

The pointwise locality argument in the affine Zariski Main proof gives both directions. The base localization leaves the fibre unchanged; source localization is an open neighborhood of the selected point. Being isolated in that open fibre is equivalent to being isolated in the original fibre, or one may use equality of the local fibre rings and residue extensions.

Quasi-finiteness in a four-ring square

Consider a commutative square $R\to S$, $R'\to S'$, with vertical maps $R\to R'$ and $S\to S'$. Assume $S$ is finite type over $R$ and the induced map $S\otimes_RR'\to S'$ is surjective. If $\mathfrak q'\subset S'$ contracts to a quasi-finite point $\mathfrak q\subset S$ of $S/R$, then $S'/R'$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q'$.

The full four-ring argument in the affine Zariski Main proof constructs the finite-dimensional isolated factor of the original fibre, extends its residue field, and takes its quotient in the new fibre. Its idempotent still selects $\mathfrak q'$, proving the assertion over arbitrary rings.

Strong transcendence rules out quasi-finite points

Suppose $R\subset S$ are reduced rings, $x\in S$, and $S$ is finite as an $R[x]$-module. Assume that every equality

$$u\sum_{i=0}^m a_ix^i=0,\qquad u\in S,\ a_i\in R,$$

forces $ua_i=0$ for each $i$. Then $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at no prime of $S$.

The complete proof is The theorem on formal functions, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.11. Lemma Z.9 passes the coefficient property to a minimal component using a localization zero witness. Lemma Z.10 treats the resulting domains, first by going down over a normal polynomial ring and then by integral normalization and lying over. Lemma Z.8 carries quasi-finiteness through the required quotient and base-change squares. Section 0 supplies polynomial normality over an arbitrary normal domain. These arguments allow infinitely many minimal primes and do not assume finite normalization.

All conductor coefficients lie in the radical

Let $\varphi\colon R[X]\to S$ be finite, and assume $\varphi(R)$ is integrally closed in $S$. Define

$$J=\{s\in S:sS\subset\operatorname{im}\varphi\}.$$

For $u\in S$ and $a_0,\ldots,a_m\in R$,

$$\begin{gathered} u\,\varphi\left(\sum_{i=0}^m a_iX^i\right)\in\sqrt J\\ \Longrightarrow\quad u\,\varphi(a_i)\in\sqrt J\quad(0\leq i\leq m). \end{gathered}$$

The full proof is The theorem on formal functions, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.6, with Situation Z.4 and Lemmas Z.1–Z.5. Monic division first removes a denominator up to an integral element. Localization and an explicit zero witness then clear the leading coefficient. Applying this to a finite module generating list puts a power of the leading coefficient in the conductor. Raising the original relation to a power and descending through its coefficients proves the radical assertion. Neither $\varphi$ nor its restriction to $R$ is required to be injective.

The cotangent space with separable residue

If a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ contains $k$ and $\kappa/k$ is finitely generated and separable, the canonical map

$$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$$

is injective.

The first part of the separable-residue smoothness proof proves exactly this local-ring assertion before using finite type for the smoothness conclusion. It lifts a separating basis and corrects the primitive element by one Newton step in $R/\mathfrak m^2$, producing a residue-field section. The resulting derivation retracts the conormal map. The alternative formal-smoothness lift, and the product-rule identification of the differential fibre before and after quotienting by $\mathfrak m^2$, are also supplied there.

Extracting a root from power coefficients

Suppose $L/K$ is algebraic and separable in characteristic $p>0$, and $\alpha\in L$. If every coefficient of its minimal polynomial over $K$ is a $p$th power in $K$, then $\alpha$ is a $p$th power in $L$. The same conclusion holds whenever $\alpha$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial $P\in K[T]$ with distinct roots and with all coefficients in $K^p$.

Proof. Write $P(T)=\sum_i b_i^pT^i$ and $Q(T)=\sum_i b_iT^i$. In an algebraic closure containing $L$, let $\beta^p=\alpha$. The identity

$$Q(T)^p=P(T^p)$$

gives $Q(\beta)=0$. Frobenius identifies the roots of $Q$ with the roots of $P$, preserving their multiplicities, so $Q$ has distinct roots.

If $\beta\notin L$, its minimal polynomial over $L$ is $T^p-\alpha$. Indeed a nontrivial purely inseparable extension generated by a $p$th root has degree $p$: the minimal polynomial is a polynomial in $T^p$ unless its derivative is nonzero, in which case it is separable and must be linear since $T^p-\alpha$ has only one distinct root. Thus $T^p-\alpha$ would divide $Q$ in $L[T]$, contrary to the distinct-root property. Hence $\beta\in L$. The minimal polynomial in the first assertion has distinct roots by separability, so it is a special case. ∎

The separable part of an algebraic extension

For every algebraic extension $E/F$ there is exactly one intermediate field $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ for which $E_{\mathrm{sep}}/F$ is separable and $E/E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is purely inseparable.

Proof. The elements of $E$ separable over $F$ form a field. To check closure, finitely many such elements generate a finite separable extension: adjoining them successively preserves separability, since their minimal polynomials at each step divide separable polynomials over $F$. The usual count of embeddings in a tower proves separability over $F$; sums, products and inverses then belong to that finite separable extension.

Call this field $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$. In characteristic zero it is all of $E$. In characteristic $p$, the irreducible polynomial of any $\alpha\in E$ has the form $G(T^{p^e})$ with $G$ irreducible and with nonzero derivative: repeatedly remove a common $p$th power from its exponents until this is so. Irreducibility then makes $G$ separable. Therefore $\alpha^{p^e}$ belongs to $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$, proving that $E/E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is purely inseparable. The exponent may depend on $\alpha$, so the argument includes infinite algebraic extensions.

For uniqueness, suppose $F\subset T\subset E$ has the stated properties. Separability gives $T\subset E_{\mathrm{sep}}$. Any $\alpha\in E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is separable over $T$, because its minimal polynomial there divides a separable polynomial over $F$; it is also purely inseparable over $T$. Its minimal polynomial is consequently linear, so $\alpha\in T$. This proves the reverse inclusion. ∎

Primitive elements and intermediate fields

A finite field extension $E/F$ is generated by one element if and only if it has only finitely many intermediate fields. Both properties hold for every finite separable extension.

Proof. Suppose $E=F(\alpha)$, and let $P$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$. For an intermediate field $K$, let $Q$ be its monic minimal polynomial over $K$. Put $L=F(\text{coefficients of }Q)\subset K$. Since $E=L(\alpha)$ and $Q(\alpha)=0$,

$$[E:L]\leq\deg Q=[E:K].$$

The tower formula gives the opposite inequality and then $L=K$. Thus $Q$ determines $K$. It is a monic divisor of $P$ in $E[T]$, and a fixed polynomial has only finitely many monic divisors by unique factorization. There are therefore finitely many possible $K$.

For the converse first suppose $F$ is infinite. A finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ cannot be the union of finitely many proper linear subspaces. For each proposed subspace choose a nonzero linear functional vanishing on it. Their product is a nonzero polynomial in coordinates. A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field cannot vanish on every coordinate tuple, as induction on the number of variables reduces this assertion to the finite root bound in one variable. A tuple where the product is nonzero avoids all the subspaces.

Apply this to the finitely many proper intermediate fields, each an $F$-linear subspace of $E$. An element outside their union generates $E$. When $E=F$, the element $0$ suffices.

If $F$ is finite, so is $E$. Its multiplicative group is cyclic: let $m$ be its exponent, and for each prime dividing $m$ choose an element whose order contains the largest corresponding prime power. Suitable powers of these elements have those prime-power orders, and their product has order $m$ because the orders are coprime. Every nonzero element of $E$ is a root of $T^m-1$, so $|E^\times|\leq m$. The element just constructed gives the reverse inequality. A generator of $E^\times$ thus generates $E$ as a field, proving this case too.

Finally, if $E/F$ is separable of degree $n$, it has $n$ distinct embeddings $\sigma_i$ into an algebraic closure of $F$. This count follows by adjoining finitely many generators and, at each step, extending an embedding through the distinct roots of the next separable minimal polynomial. For infinite $F$, the kernels of the nonzero linear maps $\sigma_i-\sigma_j$ form finitely many proper subspaces. Choose $\alpha$ outside them. Its $n$ distinct images force $[F(\alpha):F]\geq n$, while $F(\alpha)\subset E$ gives the reverse bound. Thus $E=F(\alpha)$. The finite-field case was already proved, completing all assertions. ∎

Transcendence bases with prescribed generators

Let $E/F$ be any field extension. If $A\subset G\subset E$, where $A$ is algebraically independent over $F$ and $F(G)=E$, there is a transcendence basis $B$ with $A\subset B\subset G$. All transcendence bases of $E/F$ have the same cardinality.

Proof. Order by inclusion the independent subsets of $G$ containing $A$. It is a nonempty family, and the union of a chain remains independent because every polynomial relation uses finitely many elements. Zorn's lemma supplies a maximal member $B$. Each $g\in G$ must be algebraic over $F(B)$, since otherwise it could be adjoined. Every element of $F(G)$ is then algebraic over $F(B)$, as it uses only finitely many such generators. This proves the prescribed-basis assertion.

The full finite exchange and arbitrary-cardinality proof is Krull dimension and Noether normalization, Section 1, Lemma 1.3. Its exchange step keeps previously inserted independent elements fixed and proves the needed algebraic-extension independence statement by a determinant. The infinite case assigns finite supporting subsets of one basis to elements of the other and applies the finite bound; reversing the comparison gives equality. It includes finite, infinite and empty bases. ∎

Detecting tensor-product defects in finite subalgebras

Let $R,S$ be algebras over a field $k$. Each of the following properties of $R\otimes_kS$ already holds for $R'\otimes_kS'$ for suitable finitely generated $k$-subalgebras $R'\subset R$ and $S'\subset S$:

  1. it is not reduced;
  2. it has a nonzero zero divisor;
  3. it has an idempotent other than $0$ and $1$.

Proof. For any such subalgebras the canonical map

$$R'\otimes_kS'\longrightarrow R\otimes_kS$$

is injective. It factors through $R\otimes_kS'$, and each of the two maps is injective because every vector space over $k$ is flat.

For (1), express a nonzero nilpotent as a finite sum $\sum_i r_i\otimes s_i$ and generate $R',S'$ by its coefficients. The corresponding element in the smaller tensor product is nonzero, and its required power is zero by injectivity.

For (2), choose nonzero elements $x,y$ in the tensor product with $xy=0$, and include the coefficients of finite tensor expressions for both in the two subalgebras. Their preimages remain nonzero, and injectivity makes their product zero there.

For (3), do the same for the coefficients of the idempotent $e$. Injectivity gives $e^2=e$ in the smaller tensor product and preserves its distinction from $0$ and $1$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis on either original algebra is needed. ∎

Shifted Hilbert functions for an exact sequence

For a Noetherian local ring $R$, an ideal of definition $I$, and an exact sequence of finite modules

$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0,$$

there are $N\subset M'$ of finite colength $l$ and an integer $c\geq0$ such that, for every $n\geq c$,

$$\begin{aligned} \chi_{I,M}(n)&=\chi_{I,M''}(n)+\chi_{I,N}(n-c)+l,\\ \varphi_{I,M}(n)&=\varphi_{I,M''}(n)+\varphi_{I,N}(n-c). \end{aligned}$$

Here $\chi_{I,Q}(n)=\ell_R(Q/I^{n+1}Q)$ and $\varphi_{I,Q}(n)=\ell_R(I^nQ/I^{n+1}Q)$.

The complete Hilbert-function proof constructs $N=M'\cap I^cM$ using Artin–Rees, proves finite colength, and derives both identities, including the boundary value $n=c$ by setting $\chi_{I,Q}(-1)=0$.

Finite colength changes only lower Hilbert terms

Let $R$ be Noetherian local, let $I$ be an ideal of definition, and suppose $Q'\subset Q$ are finite modules with finite-length quotient. If $Q$ has infinite length, the eventual polynomials $\chi_{I,Q}$ and $\chi_{I,Q'}$ have the same positive degree, and their difference has smaller degree.

The finite-colength argument in the Hilbert-function proof proves this for every such inclusion. It chooses $I^bQ\subset Q'$, sets $a=\ell_R(Q/Q')$, and obtains, for $n\geq b$,

$$a+\chi_{I,Q'}(n-b)\leq\chi_{I,Q}(n) \leq a+\chi_{I,Q'}(n).$$

The two bounds have identical leading terms. Infinite length excludes constant Hilbert growth by Nakayama, so the difference has degree strictly below either original degree.

Dimension under surjective prime-chain lifting

Let $R\to S$ satisfy going up or going down, and suppose $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is surjective. Then $\dim R\leq\dim S$, for arbitrary rings.

Proof. For going up, start with a prime of $S$ above the bottom member of any finite strict chain in $R$. Lift its successive steps by going up. Distinct contractions ensure that all lifted inclusions are strict. For going down, choose a prime above the top member and lift the same chain in reverse order. Thus every finite chain length in $R$ occurs in $S$. Taking suprema gives the inequality even when dimension is infinite. The empty spectrum is covered by the convention $\dim0=-\infty$. ∎

A triangular substitution with one highest term

Let $g\in R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ be nonconstant over any ring $R$. There are positive integers $e_1\gg e_2\gg\cdots\gg e_n=1$ for which

$$g(X_1+X_n^{e_1},\ldots,X_{n-1}+X_n^{e_{n-1}},X_n) =aX_n^d+\text{terms of smaller degree in }X_n,$$

where $d>0$ and $a$ is one of the nonzero coefficients of $g$.

Proof. Write $g=\sum_\nu a_\nu X^\nu$ using only its finitely many nonzero coefficients. Choose an integer $B$ larger than every coordinate of those multi-indices and set $e_i=B^{n-i}$. The weights

$$w(\nu)=\nu_1B^{n-1}+\nu_2B^{n-2}+\cdots+\nu_n$$

are distinct by uniqueness of base-$B$ expansions. In the substituted monomial $X^\nu$, its term of highest $X_n$-degree is exactly $X_n^{w(\nu)}$ with coefficient $1$. Every other term has smaller $X_n$-degree, since at least one positive power of a newly added $X_n^{e_i}$ is replaced by $X_i$.

The unique multi-index of largest weight consequently contributes the unique top term of the whole expression, with its unchanged nonzero coefficient $a_\nu$. Its weight is positive because $g$ has a nonconstant term. No coefficient is divided out, so zero divisors in $R$ cause no problem. For $n=1$ the substitution is empty and this is the usual leading term. ∎

Dimension through a prime with a full-support Cohen–Macaulay module

If a Noetherian local ring $R$ admits a finite Cohen–Macaulay module with support $\operatorname{Spec}R$, then every prime $\mathfrak p$ satisfies

$$\dim R=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(R/\mathfrak p).$$

Proof. The complete maximal-chain theorem for full-support CM modules says that every maximal prime chain of $R$ has length $\dim R$. Its proof uses the module itself and does not assume that $R$ is CM.

Choose longest chains in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ and in $R/\mathfrak p$. Their lengths are attained because these Noetherian local rings have finite dimension. In $R$, the first runs from a minimal prime to $\mathfrak p$, and the second from $\mathfrak p$ to the maximal ideal. Concatenate them, counting $\mathfrak p$ only once. No step can be refined, since a refinement on either side would contradict the chosen maximal length; neither endpoint can be extended. The resulting maximal chain has the sum of the two lengths. The cited theorem identifies that sum with $\dim R$. ∎

Specializations from a constructibly closed set

Let $X$ be spectral. If $E$ is closed in its constructible topology, then every $x\in\overline E$ is a specialization of some point of $E$. Consequently a constructibly closed, specialization-stable subset is closed in the original topology. Dually, a constructibly open subset stable under generalization is open. These statements apply in particular to constructible subsets.

Proof. Recall that a spectral space is quasi-compact and sober and has a basis of quasi-compact opens closed under finite intersections. Its constructible topology is generated by those opens and their complements. We first prove the compactness needed here directly from these axioms.

Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on the underlying set of a nonempty $X$, and put

$$Z=X\setminus\bigcup\{V:V\text{ is quasi-compact open and }V\notin\mathcal U\}.$$

This is a closed set. It is nonempty: otherwise quasi-compactness of $X$ would give a finite cover by opens outside $\mathcal U$, whose union cannot belong to the ultrafilter. More generally, every quasi-compact open $W\in\mathcal U$ meets $Z$. If it did not, a finite subcover of $W$ by the excluded opens would give the same contradiction.

If an open set meets $Z$, a basis open contained in it and meeting $Z$ must belong to $\mathcal U$, by the definition of $Z$. For two such opens, intersect their chosen basis opens. Their intersection is quasi-compact and belongs to $\mathcal U$, so it meets $Z$ by the preceding paragraph. Hence $Z$ is irreducible. Sobriety gives its generic point $\eta$. A quasi-compact open $V$ contains $\eta$ exactly when it meets $Z$, which is exactly when $V\in\mathcal U$. Thus every basic neighborhood of $\eta$ in the constructible topology belongs to $\mathcal U$: it is a finite intersection of basis opens and their complements with the corresponding membership choices. The ultrafilter converges to $\eta$ in that topology.

This proves compactness by the ultrafilter criterion. Explicitly, any family of closed sets with the finite-intersection property extends to an ultrafilter; a limit of that ultrafilter lies in every member of the family, since each member is closed. The empty space is compact as well.

Now fix $x\in\overline E$ and take all quasi-compact open neighborhoods $U$ of $x$. Each $E\cap U$ is closed in the compact constructible topology, because $E$ is closed there and $U$ is clopen there. Any finite intersection is nonempty: its neighborhood factor is an open neighborhood of $x$, which meets $E$. Compactness therefore provides

$$y\in E\cap\bigcap_{U\ni x,\ U\text{ quasi-compact open}}U.$$

The basis property says that every open neighborhood of $x$ contains $y$. Equivalently, $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, giving the first assertion.

If $E$ is stable under specialization, this places every point of $\overline E$ in $E$, so $E$ is closed. For the dual assertion, the complement is constructibly closed and specialization-stable, hence closed. Finally, in a spectral space a retrocompact open is quasi-compact, since $X$ itself is quasi-compact; thus constructible subsets, being finite Boolean combinations of these opens, are clopen in the constructible topology. ∎

An affine spectrum is spectral

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-spec-spectral».

For every ring $R$, its spectrum is quasi-compact and $T_0$, has a basis of quasi-compact opens stable under finite intersections, and every nonempty irreducible closed subset has a unique generic point. Hence it is a spectral space.

The second proof of the constructible-specialization criterion verifies these properties from the affine-spectrum foundations and irreducibility theorem. It also gives the complete ultrafilter proof of compactness of the constructible topology and uses that compactness to recover the specialization criterion.

Open and closed sets under specialization

In every topological space, closed sets are stable under specialization and open sets are stable under generalization. A subset is specialization-stable exactly when its complement is generalization-stable.

Proof. Write $x\preceq y$ when $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, so $x$ is a specialization of $y$. If a closed set contains $y$, it contains $\overline{\{y\}}$ and hence $x$. For an arbitrary subset $T$, the implication

$$y\in T,\quad x\preceq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in T$$

is equivalent by contraposition to

$$x\notin T,\quad x\preceq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\notin T.$$

This is precisely generalization stability of the complement. Applying it to a closed set proves the open-set assertion. ∎

Boolean operations on constructible subsets

Constructible subsets of an arbitrary topological space are closed under finite unions, finite intersections and complements.

Here an open $U\subset X$ is retrocompact if $U\cap W$ is quasi-compact for every quasi-compact open $W\subset X$. A constructible subset is a finite union of differences $U\setminus V$ of retrocompact opens. This is the global notion; no Noetherian or spectral hypothesis is imposed on $X$.

Proof. Both $X$ and $\varnothing$ are retrocompact opens. Finite unions of retrocompact opens are retrocompact, since intersecting with $W$ gives a finite union of quasi-compact subsets. For two such opens $U_1,U_2$, first $U_2\cap W$ is quasi-compact open, and then retrocompactness of $U_1$ makes $U_1\cap(U_2\cap W)$ quasi-compact. Thus finite intersections are retrocompact too.

For basic differences,

$$(U_1\setminus V_1)\cap(U_2\setminus V_2) =(U_1\cap U_2)\setminus(V_1\cup V_2),$$

and

$$X\setminus(U\setminus V)=(X\setminus U)\cup V.$$

The right side of the second identity is the union of the two basic differences $X\setminus U$ and $V\setminus\varnothing$. Finite unions hold by definition; distribution proves finite intersections of arbitrary finite unions, and De Morgan's law then proves complements. ∎

Realizing a constructible set as an affine image

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-constructible-is-image».

Every constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is the image of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ for a finitely presented $R$-algebra $B$.

The first proof of the constructible-specialization criterion realizes each basic piece by $(R/(g_1,\ldots,g_m))_f$, then takes a finite product. It supplies a finite presentation for that product using orthogonal idempotents and inverse variables, and handles the empty set by $R/(1)$.

Principal-open images under affine-line projection

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-affineline-open».

The projection $\operatorname{Spec}R[x]\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is open. For $f=\sum_i a_ix^i$, the image of $D(f)$ is the quasi-compact open $\bigcup_iD(a_i)$.

The first terminal case in Chevalley’s polynomial proof proves this formula by identifying the fibre with the localization of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[x]$ at the reduced polynomial. Taking unions proves openness for arbitrary opens.

An affine-line equation with invertible leading coefficient

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-affineline-special».

If the leading coefficient of $g\in R[x]$ is a unit, the image of $D(f)\cap V(g)$ in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a finite union of principal opens.

The second terminal case in Chevalley’s polynomial proof constructs them from the coefficients other than the leading coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $f$ on $R[x]/(g)$. It proves compatibility with residue fields, the nilpotence test, and both directions of the fibre nonemptiness criterion. A constant unit $g$ gives the empty image.

Constructible images of finitely presented closed immersions

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-closed-fp».

For a finitely generated ideal $I\subset R$, the map $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ carries every constructible subset to a constructible subset.

The closed-image reduction at the start of Chevalley’s proof lifts the finite list defining a basic constructible piece and adjoins a finite generating list of $I$ to its closed equations. It then takes finite unions. Finite generation of $I$ is retained.

Constructible images of principal localizations

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-open-fp».

For $c\in R$, contraction from $\operatorname{Spec}R_c$ sends constructible subsets to constructible subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

The localization reduction at the start of Chevalley’s proof clears powers of $c$ from each finite list of defining fractions. It expresses the image as a finite union of sets $D(ca)\cap V(b_1,\ldots,b_m)$, including the case of an empty localization.

Finite principal-open descriptions of constructible subsets

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-constructible».

A subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is constructible precisely when it is a finite union of pieces $D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$.

The initial reduction in Chevalley’s proof identifies retrocompact opens with quasi-compact opens, writes these as finite principal-open unions, and distributes the differences in the definition of constructibility. The reverse implication follows from the same description. This applies to arbitrary rings.

A reduced ring and its minimal-prime fields

For every reduced ring $R$, the canonical map

$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{\mathfrak p\text{ minimal}}R_{\mathfrak p}$$

is injective and all its factors are fields. Moreover, the union of the minimal primes is exactly the set of zero divisors, where a zero divisor means an element annihilating a nonzero element.

Proof. Localization of a reduced ring is reduced: if $(a/s)^n=0$, some denominator $t$ kills $a^n$, hence $(ta)^n=0$, so $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$. For a minimal prime $\mathfrak p$, the only prime of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$. It is therefore the nilradical and is zero. This local ring is a field, and the kernel of $R\to R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\mathfrak p$.

The intersection of the minimal primes is the nilradical: every prime contains a minimal one, and the intersection of all primes is the nilradical. Since $R$ is reduced, this intersection is zero. This proves the asserted injection without any finiteness assumption on the set of minimal primes.

If $xy=0$ with $y\ne0$, some minimal prime avoids $y$, and primality puts $x$ in that prime. Conversely, if $x\in\mathfrak p$ for a minimal prime, its image in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is zero. Some $s\notin\mathfrak p$ then satisfies $sx=0$, and $s\ne0$. Thus $x$ is a zero divisor. In the zero ring the product is empty and equals the zero ring, and both the union and the set of zero divisors are empty. ∎

The field calculation for the Cohen–Macaulay locus

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / lemma-where-CM».

Let $k$ be any field, let $T$ be a finite-type $k$-algebra, and let $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\to T$ be quasi-finite. At $\mathfrak r\in\operatorname{Spec}T$, with contraction $\mathfrak a$, the local map

$$k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]_{\mathfrak a}\longrightarrow T_{\mathfrak r}$$

is flat if and only if $T_{\mathfrak r}$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$.

The proof at the start of the fixed-dimension Cohen–Macaulay fibre-locus lemma establishes both directions. Quasi-finiteness supplies the zero-dimensional local fibre and finite residue extension. The dimension formula converts the point-dimension condition into equality of local dimensions, and miracle flatness gives one implication. For the other, flatness transports a regular parameter sequence and gives the local dimension equality. The argument includes nonclosed points and nonreduced algebras.

Openness of flatness over an arbitrary base

Complete written proof. Native locator: algebra.tex» / theorem-openness-flatness».

For a finitely presented algebra $A\to B$ and a finitely presented $B$-module $M$, the locus of primes $\mathfrak q\subset B$ where $M_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $A$ is open. At every such prime there is $g\notin\mathfrak q$ with $M_g$ flat over $A$.

The full proof is Flatness criteria, dimension and the flat locus, Theorem 6.4. Sections 1, 5 and 6 give its ideal criterion, Noetherian openness and eventual-flatness argument for finite models. The proof of generic freeness in Flat morphisms, §5 supplies the input in Section 5. Theorem 6.4 then passes an actual flat neighborhood from a Noetherian model to $A$. The base ring here is arbitrary; finite presentations are required of both the algebra and the module.

Uniqueness for marked henselian ind-étale algebras

Let $R$ be any ring. Suppose $S$ and $S'$ are henselian local rings, each a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras. Suppose also that specified residue maps $S\to K$ and $S'\to K$ to one field induce the same map from $R$. There is exactly one $R$-algebra isomorphism $S\to S'$ respecting those residue maps.

Proof. Their maximal ideals contract to the same prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$, and both residue extensions are identified with the given $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-field $K$. Apply the full ind-étale evaluation theorem, first with source $S$ and target $S'$ and then with these roles reversed, using the identity of $K$ as residue embedding. It gives unique local maps $u\colon S\to S'$ and $v\colon S'\to S$ with the required markings. Each composite has the same marking as the identity; uniqueness in the same theorem makes $vu=1$ and $uv=1$. That theorem's proof evaluates every étale stage and uses uniqueness to make the evaluations compatible. Thus it applies to arbitrary $R$ and arbitrary common residue extension $K$, as required. ∎

Composition of filtered étale presentations

For maps $A\to B\to C$, assume that $B$ is a filtered colimit of étale $A$-algebras and that $C$ is a filtered colimit of étale $B$-algebras. Then $C$ is a filtered colimit of étale $A$-algebras.

Proof. By the complete finite-presentation factorization criterion, it suffices to factor every $A$-algebra map $P\to C$, with $P$ finitely presented over $A$, through an étale $A$-algebra.

Write $B=\operatorname{colim}_i B_i$ and $C=\operatorname{colim}_j C_j$ with the stated étale stages. Finite presentation first factors $P\to C$ through some $C_j$. The étale descent theorem, part (9) gives a stage $i$ and an étale $B_i$-algebra $D$ with

$$C_j\cong B\otimes_{B_i}D.$$

This is the filtered colimit of $B_{i'}\otimes_{B_i}D$ over stages receiving a map from $i$. Finite presentation of $P$ factors its map once more, through one such algebra $D'=B_{i'}\otimes_{B_i}D$. Étale base change makes $D'$ étale over $B_{i'}$, and composition with the étale map $A\to B_{i'}$ makes it étale over $A$. The resulting $P\to D'\to C$ is the desired factorization. These arguments hold for filtered categories as well as directed sets: the category of arrows out of $i$ is filtered, and every finite diagram can be placed at a common later stage. ∎

Finite algebras and quasi-finite points over a henselian base

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be henselian local.

  1. A finite $R$-algebra is a finite product of henselian local rings, each finite over $R$.
  2. A finite local $R$-algebra is henselian, and its structure map is local.
  3. If a finite-type $R$-algebra $S$ is quasi-finite at a prime $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak m$, then $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is henselian and finite over $R$.
  4. In particular, (3) holds at every prime over $\mathfrak m$ whenever $S/R$ is quasi-finite.

Proof. Use the full henselian equivalences, including finite-algebra decomposition and finite-part decomposition for finite-type algebras. If $S$ is finite and local over $R$, integrality makes its maximal ideal contract to a maximal ideal of $R$, necessarily $\mathfrak m$. The map is local. Every finite $S$-algebra is finite over $R$, so decomposes as a finite product of local rings by the henselian criterion for $R$. The same criterion applied to $S$ proves that $S$ is henselian. Decomposing an arbitrary finite $R$-algebra first and applying this argument to its finite local factors proves (1) and (2).

For (3), the finite-part criterion gives $S=S_1\times S_2$, with $S_1$ finite over $R$ and $S_2$ having no quasi-finite point over $\mathfrak m$. Thus $\mathfrak q$ belongs to $S_1$. Decompose that finite algebra into its henselian local factors as above. The point over $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal of one factor, and localization there is that factor itself. This identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ as finite and henselian. Part (4) follows at once. The finite-part criterion uses the complete algebraic Zariski Main proof already given in the linked henselian argument. ∎

Filtered local limits of henselian rings

A filtered colimit of henselian local rings along local maps is henselian local. If all stages are strictly henselian, so is the colimit.

Proof. Let $R=\operatorname{colim}_iR_i$, with maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_i$. Locality of the maps gives a compatible system of residue fields $\kappa_i$ and embeddings between them. The map

$$R\longrightarrow\kappa=\operatorname{colim}_i\kappa_i$$

is surjective; its kernel consists exactly of classes represented in the stage maximal ideals. A class outside this kernel has a representative that is already a unit at its stage. Hence $R$ is local with that kernel as maximal ideal and with residue field $\kappa$.

Given a monic polynomial over $R$ and a specified simple root in $\kappa$, place its coefficients and that root at one stage. The residue fields embed in $\kappa$, so the root equation and the nonzero derivative already hold there. Henselianity of the stage lifts this simple root, and its image in $R$ supplies the required lift. Thus $R$ is henselian.

If every $\kappa_i$ is separably closed, every monic separable polynomial over $\kappa$ splits there. Indeed its coefficients and a Bézout identity with its derivative are defined at a common stage; the identity makes that stage polynomial separable. It splits into linear factors over the separably closed stage field, and the same factorization holds over $\kappa$. Consequently $\kappa$ is separably closed, proving strict henselianity. The finite-data arguments also cover filtered indexing categories. ∎

Finite presentation over a Noetherian ring

For a Noetherian ring $R$, every finite $R$-module is finitely presented, every submodule of a finite $R$-module is finite, and every finite-type $R$-algebra is finitely presented over $R$.

Proof. Every submodule of $R^s$ is finite, by induction on $s$: projection to the last coordinate has image an ideal of $R$, hence finitely generated, while its kernel is a submodule of $R^{s-1}$. Lift generators of that image and append generators of the kernel. For a submodule of a finite module $M$, take its inverse image under a finite free surjection onto $M$ and then take the images of a finite generating list. This proves the second assertion.

The kernel of a finite free surjection onto $M$ is therefore finite, giving a finite presentation and the first assertion. Finally present a finite-type algebra as $R[X_1,\ldots,X_s]/I$. The complete Hilbert-basis proof in Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 2 makes the polynomial ring Noetherian. Hence $I$ has finitely many generators, giving the finite algebra presentation. These arguments include zero modules and zero algebras. ∎

Finite presentation detected by tensoring with products

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / proposition-fp-tensor».

An $R$-module $M$ is finitely presented exactly when the canonical map

$$M\otimes_R\prod_{\alpha\in A}Q_\alpha \longrightarrow\prod_{\alpha\in A}(M\otimes_RQ_\alpha)$$

is bijective for every family of modules. It is equivalent to test every constant family, and also equivalent to test only the families with every $Q_\alpha=R$, allowing every set $A$.

The full proof appears in the coherence theorem. It compares two cokernels from a finite presentation in one direction. In the other, it first forces finite generation of $M$, then proves that the kernel of a finite free surjection onto $M$ satisfies the product-surjectivity criterion and is therefore finite.

Finite generation detected by tensoring with products

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex» / proposition-fg-tensor».

An $R$-module $M$ is finitely generated exactly when the preceding comparison map is surjective for every family. Testing all constant families gives the same criterion, as does testing only powers of $R$.

The proof in the coherence theorem constructs preimages using any finite generating list. Conversely, take the index set to be the underlying set of $M$ and use the tuple that lists every element of $M$. Any tensor preimage involves only finitely many elements of $M$, and coordinate comparison shows that they generate it. This establishes the criterion for arbitrary modules over arbitrary rings.

Symmetry, sums and the tensor unit

For modules $M,N,P$ over a commutative ring $R$, the following maps are canonical isomorphisms:

$$\begin{aligned} M\otimes_RN&\longrightarrow N\otimes_RM, &m\otimes n&\longmapsto n\otimes m,\\ (M\oplus N)\otimes_RP&\longrightarrow (M\otimes_RP)\oplus(N\otimes_RP), &(m,n)\otimes p&\longmapsto(m\otimes p,n\otimes p),\\ R\otimes_RM&\longrightarrow M, &r\otimes m&\longmapsto rm. \end{aligned}$$

Proof. Each indicated formula is additive in both inputs and balanced over $R$, so the tensor universal property gives a unique linear map. For symmetry the same formula in the opposite direction is its inverse. For sums, the inverse sends $(m\otimes p,0)$ to $(m,0)\otimes p$ and $(0,n\otimes p)$ to $(0,n)\otimes p$, extending linearly. The composites are identities because $(m,n)=(m,0)+(0,n)$. For the unit map the inverse is $m\mapsto1\otimes m$; the identity $1\otimes rm=r\otimes m$ checks the other composite. Pure tensors generate each tensor product, so these verifications prove all assertions, including uniqueness and naturality. ∎

Associativity with a bimodule

Let $A,B$ be commutative rings, let $M$ be an $A$-module and $P$ a $B$-module, and let $N$ be an $(A,B)$-bimodule with commuting left $A$- and right $B$-actions. There is a canonical bimodule isomorphism

$$\bigl(M\otimes_AN\bigr)\otimes_BP \longrightarrow M\otimes_A\bigl(N\otimes_BP\bigr), \qquad (m\otimes n)\otimes p\longmapsto m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

Proof. The right $B$-action on $M\otimes_AN$ is $(m\otimes n)b=m\otimes(nb)$. It respects the $A$-balancing relation because the two actions on $N$ commute. Likewise $N\otimes_BP$ has left action $a(n\otimes p)=(an)\otimes p$. Commutativity of $A$ and $B$ also lets $A$ act through $M$ and $B$ act through $P$ on either iterated tensor product. These actions commute.

Both iterated tensors impose exactly the same additivity relations and the two balancing relations

$$am\otimes n\otimes p=m\otimes an\otimes p,\qquad m\otimes nb\otimes p=m\otimes n\otimes bp.$$

The displayed associativity formula and its reverse therefore descend to the quotients. They preserve both outer actions and are inverse on elementary tensors, which generate the modules. Thus they are inverse bimodule maps, with no finiteness or flatness hypotheses. ∎

Finite algebras

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex / lemma-produce-finite.

Suppose $R\to C\to D$ are ring maps, $C$ is integral over $R$, $D$ is finite type over $R$, and $C_g\to D_g$ is an isomorphism for some $g\in C$. If $g$ is a unit in $C\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, then some $b\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ makes $D_b$ finite over $R_b$. The final general argument in the one-branch étale construction proves this exact statement using the closed image of $V(g)$ under the integral map. No injectivity of $C\to D$ or finite presentation of $D$ is assumed.

Étale lifting of prescribed coprime factors

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex / lemma-factor-mod-lift-etale.

For a monic $f\in R[T]$ and a factorization $\bar f=\bar h\bar i$ into coprime polynomials over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, there is an étale $R\to R'$ with a prime $\mathfrak p'$ above $\mathfrak p$, the same canonical residue field, and a factorization $f=hi$ whose factors have the prescribed reductions and generate the unit ideal in $R'[T]$. The coefficient-Jacobian argument in the one-branch construction proves this, including the Bézout identity, nonmaximal base primes, factors of degree zero, and normalization and restoration of nonmonic factors.

Eight descriptions of a zero-dimensional spectrum

For any ring $R$, put $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$. The following are equivalent:

  1. $X$ is profinite, meaning an inverse limit of finite discrete spaces.
  2. $X$ is Hausdorff.
  3. $X$ is totally disconnected.
  4. Every quasi-compact open subset of $X$ is also closed.
  5. No two distinct prime ideals of $R$ are comparable by inclusion.
  6. Every prime ideal is maximal.
  7. Every prime ideal is minimal.
  8. Every principal open $D(f)$ is closed.

First proof. Conditions (5), (6) and (7) are equivalent: primes lie inside maximal ideals and contain minimal primes, so either endpoint condition excludes strict inclusions. Conditions (4) and (8) are equivalent because principal opens are quasi-compact and form a basis; a quasi-compact open is a finite union of them.

Assume (7). Fix $f\in R$ and a prime $\mathfrak p$ containing $f$. The only prime of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is its maximal ideal, since primes there correspond to primes contained in $\mathfrak p$. Hence $f/1$ belongs to its nilradical. Some power of $f/1$ is zero, so there are $n\geq1$ and $s\notin\mathfrak p$ with $sf^n=0$ in $R$. Every prime avoiding $s$ then contains $f$. Thus $D(s)\subset V(f)$ is an open neighborhood of $\mathfrak p$. Varying $\mathfrak p$ proves that $V(f)$ is open, so $D(f)$ is closed. This proves (7)$\Rightarrow$(8) without reducedness or Noetherianity.

Under (8), distinct primes are separated by a principal open and its complement: choose an element belonging to one prime but not the other, interchanging them if necessary. Both sets are open. Thus $X$ is Hausdorff, and any subset containing those two points is disconnected by this separation. This gives (2) and (3).

A Hausdorff space has closed singletons, so (2) makes every prime maximal, giving (6). If two distinct primes were comparable, their two-point subspace would be connected: every open containing the specialization contains its generalization, preventing a separation into two nonempty opens. Thus (3) implies (5). We have proved the equivalence of (2)–(8).

For completeness, under these conditions $X$ has a basis of clopen subsets and is quasi-compact. Consider all finite partitions of $X$ into nonempty clopen cells, ordered by refinement, and the finite discrete set of cells of each partition. Refinements induce maps between these finite sets. A point of $X$ chooses a compatible cell in every partition. Conversely, a compatible choice of cells has the finite-intersection property: a common refinement of finitely many partitions has its selected cell inside every selected cell in that finite list. Quasi-compactness gives a point in their intersection. It is unique because clopen sets separate distinct points. These inverse maps are continuous, since a condition selecting a cell is a basic inverse-limit cylinder and that cell is clopen in $X$. They give a homeomorphism from $X$ to the inverse limit. Hence (2)–(8) imply (1). An inverse limit of finite discrete spaces is Hausdorff, as a subspace of a product of Hausdorff spaces, so (1) implies (2). For the empty spectrum use the constant inverse system with empty finite space; all the other assertions are vacuous.

Spectral-space proof. The complete affine spectral theorem supplies the spectral axioms for $X$. Under (5) there are no nontrivial specializations or generalizations. Every constructible subset and its complement are therefore specialization-stable. The constructible-closure theorem makes both closed in the original topology. In particular, principal opens are clopen, proving (8) by the spectral route. Conversely, Hausdorffness or total disconnectedness excludes nontrivial specializations, and a clopen principal basis separates points as above. Quasi-compactness and the finite-partition construction then give profiniteness. This retains the second proof through spectral topology. ∎

The element construction of a directed colimit

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex / lemma-directed-colimit.

For a module system over any directed preordered set, take the disjoint union of its modules and identify two elements precisely when their images agree at a common later index. Addition is performed at a common index and scalar multiplication on a representative. The proof of the directed-colimit vanishing criterion checks the equivalence relation, independence of all choices, the module axioms and the universal property. It also proves the exact criterion for a representative to give zero. Neither antisymmetry of the indexing preorder nor injectivity of transition maps is required.

The tensor–Hom adjunction

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex / lemma-hom-from-tensor-product.

For arbitrary $R$-modules $M,N,P$, there is a natural $R$-linear isomorphism

$$\operatorname{Hom}_R(M\otimes_RN,P) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)).$$

The proof of tensor right exactness constructs both maps, checks bilinearity and linearity, verifies that they are inverse, and identifies their compatibility with maps in all three arguments.

The module equalizer on a finite principal cover

Complete proof in this lesson. Native locator: algebra.tex / lemma-cover-module.

For any $R$-module $M$ and any finite family $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ generating the unit ideal, the canonical sequence

$$0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow\bigoplus_iM_{f_i} \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{i,j}M_{f_if_j}$$

is exact, with the last map given by pairwise differences on overlaps. The proof of the principal-cover equalizer establishes this full module statement before its ring specialization. It checks exactness after maximal localization, where one cover member becomes the whole module, and proves the required detection of a zero module by its maximal localizations.

Functoriality of the prime spectrum

A ring homomorphism $\varphi\colon R\to S$ induces a continuous map

$$\operatorname{Spec}S\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}R, \qquad\mathfrak q\longmapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q).$$

The inverse image of $D(f)$ is $D(\varphi(f))$.

Proof. The inverse image ideal is proper because $1$ maps to $1$, and it is prime because a product belongs to it precisely when the corresponding product belongs to $\mathfrak q$. A prime $\mathfrak q$ avoids $\varphi(f)$ exactly when its contraction avoids $f$, proving the formula for principal opens and hence continuity. Contraction under an identity is the identity, and contraction under a composite is successive contraction in reverse order. Thus this construction is the contravariant spectrum functor. ∎

Differentials after quotienting by one more ideal power

For a map $R\to S$, any ideal $I\subset S$ and $n\geq1$, put $S'=S/I^{n+1}$. There is a canonical isomorphism

$$\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS/I^n \ \cong\ \Omega_{S'/R}\otimes_{S'}S/I^n.$$

Proof. The complete quotient differential sequence presents $\Omega_{S'/R}$ as the quotient of $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'$ by the differentials of elements of $I^{n+1}$. The Leibniz rule gives $d(I^{n+1})\subset I^n\Omega_{S/R}$: differentiate a product of $n+1$ ideal elements and each summand still has $n$ such factors. Each element of the ideal power is a finite sum of such products. Tensoring with $S/I^n$ therefore kills this relation map. Right exactness identifies the two remaining terms by the stated isomorphism. No finiteness condition on $I$ or $S$ is used. ∎

Formal smoothness of polynomial algebras

For any ring $R$ and any set $J$, the polynomial algebra $R[X_j\mid j\in J]$ is formally smooth over $R$.

Proof. In a lifting diagram against a square-zero quotient $T\to T/K$, choose in $T$ a lift of the specified image of each variable $X_j$. The polynomial universal property extends these choices and the given map from $R$ to a unique $R$-algebra map from the polynomial algebra. Its reduction is the prescribed map because it agrees on $R$ and all variables. Polynomial expressions use only finitely many variables, so the construction works for arbitrary $J$, including the empty set. In fact it gives a lift against every surjective ring map, without needing the square-zero assumption. ∎

Algebraic residue extensions over a closed base point

Let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ lie above a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$. If $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is algebraic over $\kappa(\mathfrak m)$, then $\mathfrak q$ is maximal in $S$.

Proof. There are inclusions

$$R/\mathfrak m\subset S/\mathfrak q\subset\kappa(\mathfrak q).$$

Every nonzero element $a$ of the intermediate domain is algebraic over the first field. Its monic minimal polynomial has nonzero constant coefficient; solving that equation for $a^{-1}$ writes the inverse as a polynomial in $a$ with coefficients in $R/\mathfrak m$. The inverse therefore lies in $S/\mathfrak q$, making that domain a field. Thus $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. This is also the general intermediate-field argument, and requires neither finite type nor finite degree. ∎

Local dimension at a closed point over a field

If $S$ is a finite-type algebra over a field $k$ and $x$ corresponds to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, then

$$\dim_x\operatorname{Spec}S=\dim S_{\mathfrak m}.$$

Proof. The full dimension-at-a-point formula gives the right side plus $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak m)$. The Nullstellensatz makes this residue field finite over $k$, so that extra term is zero. The component proof of the dimension formula includes reducible and nonreduced algebras and arbitrary ground fields. ∎

The algebraic and topological Jacobson conditions

A ring $R$ is Jacobson if and only if the closed points of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ are dense in every closed subset. Here the algebraic condition means that each prime is the intersection of the maximal ideals containing it.

Proof. First this algebraic condition is equivalent to the corresponding condition for every radical ideal. If $I=\sqrt I$ and $f\notin I$, the intersection-of-primes description supplies a prime $\mathfrak p\supset I$ avoiding $f$. Some maximal ideal containing $\mathfrak p$ then avoids $f$, by the assumed intersection equality for $\mathfrak p$. This proves the radical-ideal equality. The converse follows by taking $I$ prime.

For a radical ideal $I$, put $J=\bigcap_{\mathfrak m\supset I,\ \mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\mathfrak m$. The closed points of $V(I)$ are those maximal ideals, and their closure is $V(J)$: a closed set contains all of them exactly when its defining ideal is contained in their intersection.
