Hence their density in $V(I)$ is equivalent to $V(J)=V(I)$. Both ideals are radical, so the radical-ideal/closed-set correspondence makes this equivalent to $I=J$. This proves both directions, including the empty closed subset, for which the empty intersection is the whole ring. ∎

Finite-type field algebras are Jacobson

Every algebra generated by finitely many elements over a field is a Jacobson ring.

Proof. The full Nullstellensatz proof states that the polynomial algebra over an arbitrary field is Jacobson. A quotient of a Jacobson ring is Jacobson: prime and maximal ideals of $R/I$ correspond to the respective ideals of $R$ containing $I$, and quotienting their intersection equality preserves it. Every finite-type field algebra is such a polynomial quotient. Equivalently, the radical-ideal form of the same Nullstellensatz says directly that every radical ideal of this algebra is an intersection of maximal ideals. ∎

Faithful flatness detected on homomorphisms

An $R$-module $F$ is faithfully flat exactly when it is flat and, for every homomorphism $\alpha\colon M\to N$,

$$\alpha=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \alpha\otimes_R1_F=0.$$

Proof. Flatness identifies the image of $\alpha\otimes1_F$ with $(\operatorname{im}\alpha)\otimes_RF$. If $F$ is faithfully flat, tensoring detects zero modules, so a zero tensored map forces $\operatorname{im}\alpha=0$. The forward implication is automatic.

Conversely, apply the assumed zero-map test to $1_M$. If $M\otimes_RF=0$, its identity tensors to zero, so $1_M=0$ and $M=0$. Flatness therefore preserves homology of every complex and detects whether that homology vanishes. It both preserves and reflects exactness, which is faithful flatness. All modules here may be infinitely generated. ∎

A Tor surjection after a flat pulled-back module

Let $R\to R'\to R''$ be ring maps and let $M$ be an $R$-module. If $M\otimes_RR'$ is flat over $R'$, then the natural map

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R')\otimes_{R'}R'' \longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'')$$

is surjective.

Proof. Choose an exact presentation $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$ with $P$ free, and put

$$T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'),\qquad L=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes_RR'\to P\otimes_RR').$$

There are exact sequences

$$T\longrightarrow K\otimes_RR'\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow0,$$ $$0\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow P\otimes_RR' \longrightarrow M\otimes_RR'\longrightarrow0.$$

Tensor the first over $R'$ with $R''$; it remains right exact. Tensor the second with $R''$; its left injection remains injective because its quotient is flat. Consequently

$$\ker(K\otimes_RR''\to P\otimes_RR'')$$

is exactly the image of $T\otimes_{R'}R''$. The kernel is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'')$ by the original free presentation. All identifications commute with the structural maps, so the resulting surjection is the natural comparison map. No flatness of either ring map was assumed. ∎

The quotient-base Tor comparison

Let $R\to R'$ be a ring map, let $I\subset R$, and put $I'=IR'$ and $M'=M\otimes_RR'$. For every $R$-module $M$, the canonical map

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R'/I',M) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(R'/I',M')$$

is surjective.

Proof. With a free presentation $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$, set $P'=P\otimes_RR'$ and $K'=\ker(P'\to M')$. Right exactness gives a surjection $K\otimes_RR'\to K'$. Write $Q=R'/I'$. Any element in

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',Q) =\ker(K'\otimes_{R'}Q\to P'\otimes_{R'}Q)$$

lifts to $K\otimes_RQ$. Its image in $P\otimes_RQ=P'\otimes_{R'}Q$ is zero, so the lift belongs to $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,Q)$. This proves the comparison surjection; symmetry of Tor gives the order of arguments in the statement.

The free-resolution description makes the same map explicit. Tensor a free $R$-resolution of $M$ with $R'$. It remains exact at degree zero. To obtain a resolution of $M'$ through degree one, add a free summand in degree two mapping onto the missing degree-one cycles, and continue freely in higher degrees. After tensoring with $Q$, degree-one cycles are unchanged and the degree-two boundary subgroup can only increase. The quotient map on homology is the stated natural surjection. This also verifies directly that no flatness or finiteness hypothesis enters. ∎

Intermediate subrings in an algebraic field extension

If $F\subset A\subset E$, where $F,E$ are fields and $E/F$ is algebraic, then the intermediate ring $A$ is a field.

Proof. For $0\ne a\in A$, its minimal polynomial over $F$ has the form

$$a^d+c_{d-1}a^{d-1}+\cdots+c_1a+c_0=0,\qquad c_0\ne0.$$

Solving for the inverse gives

$$a^{-1}=-c_0^{-1}(a^{d-1}+c_{d-1}a^{d-2}+\cdots+c_1)\in A.$$

Thus all nonzero elements of $A$ are invertible. Each calculation uses only one algebraic element, so no finite-degree assumption on $E/F$ is needed. Alternatively, $E$ is integral over $A$ because its monic equations over $F$ are also equations over $A$; the integral-domain field criterion gives the same conclusion. ∎

Noetherianity over a field or the integers

Every finite-type algebra over a field, and every finite-type algebra over $\mathbf Z$, is Noetherian.

Proof. A field has only two ideals. Every ideal of $\mathbf Z$ is principal, so this ring too is Noetherian. The full Noetherian permanence theorem proves that polynomial rings over a Noetherian base are Noetherian and that quotients remain Noetherian. Presenting the given algebra as a quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables proves both assertions. ∎

Differentials in a square with surjective target map

Consider a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc} R&\longrightarrow&S\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\varphi\\ R'&\xrightarrow{\beta}&S', \end{array}$$

where $\varphi$ is surjective. Then $\Omega_{S/R}\to\Omega_{S'/R'}$ is surjective. Its kernel is the $S$-submodule generated by

$$da\quad\text{for }a\in S\text{ with }\varphi(a)\in\beta(R').$$

In particular these generators include $di$ for every $i\in I=\ker\varphi$.

Proof by universal derivations. Let $N$ be the displayed submodule and put $Q=\Omega_{S/R}/N$. For $i\in I$ and $s\in S$, both $di$ and $d(is)$ belong to $N$. The identity

$$i\,ds=d(is)-s\,di$$

therefore shows $I\Omega_{S/R}\subset N$. Thus $Q$ is an $S'$-module. The derivation $S\to Q$, $s\mapsto ds\bmod N$, kills $I$ and descends to $S'$. It kills $\beta(R')$ because every element of that image has a lift $a\in S$ with $da\in N$. It is consequently an $R'$-derivation and gives a map $\Omega_{S'/R'}\to Q$.

Conversely, composition of the universal $R'$-derivation with $\varphi$ is an $R$-derivation on $S$ killing the displayed generators of $N$, so gives $Q\to\Omega_{S'/R'}$. The composites fix every generator $ds'$ or $ds\bmod N$, respectively. They are identities. This identifies $Q$ with $\Omega_{S'/R'}$ and proves the kernel assertion as well as surjectivity.

Proof from presentations. The presentation of differentials has generators $[s]$ and relations for addition, multiplication and the base constants. Surjectivity of $S\to S'$ lifts every target generator and every coefficient. The additive and product relations lift to the corresponding relations upstairs. The additional constant relations are precisely $[a]=0$ when $\varphi(a)$ belongs to the new base image. Two lifts of an element of $S'$ differ by $i\in I$, and $di=0$ is among these same relations. Coefficients differing by $I$ have no further effect, by $I\Omega_{S/R}\subset N$ proved above. Hence quotienting by exactly $N$ gives the target presentation, proving the same result. Both arguments account for the quotient ideal and the change of base. ∎

Associated components of a Cohen–Macaulay module

Let $M$ be a finite Cohen–Macaulay module over a Noetherian local ring $R$. Every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M)$ is minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$, and

$$\dim(R/\mathfrak p)=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M.$$

In particular, there are no embedded associated primes.

Proof. For $M\ne0$, the complete depth bound and component proof are Regular sequences, depth and Cohen–Macaulay modules, Sections 3–4, Theorems 3.1 and 4.1. They give

$$\operatorname{depth}M\leq\dim(R/\mathfrak p) \leq\dim\operatorname{Supp}M.$$

The outer quantities agree because $M$ is CM, so both inequalities are equalities. If $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ were a smaller prime in the support, adjoining it to a chain above $\mathfrak p$ of this maximal length would produce a longer chain in the support, a contradiction. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is minimal. For $M=0$, both the associated-prime and support sets are empty and the statement is vacuous. The historical source for this component statement is EGA, Chapter 0, Proposition 16.5.4. ∎

Associated primes surviving a power quotient

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M$ be finite, and let $x\in\mathfrak m$. If $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ and $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak p+(x)$, then

$$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(M/x^nM)$$

for some $n\geq1$.

Proof. Choose $L\subset M$ isomorphic to $R/\mathfrak p$. The complete Artin–Rees lemma supplies $n\geq1$ with $L\cap x^nM\subset xL$: if its stabilization index is $c$, take $n\geq c+1$. The image

$$\overline L=L/(L\cap x^nM)\subset M/x^nM$$

then surjects onto $L/xL=R/(\mathfrak p+(x))$. Hence $\mathfrak q$ is in its support. Both $\mathfrak p$ and $x^n$ annihilate $\overline L$, so every prime of that support contains $\mathfrak p+(x)$. Minimality of $\mathfrak q$ over the latter ideal makes it a minimal support prime of $\overline L$.

Here is the needed minimal-support fact. For a finite module $N$ over a Noetherian ring and a minimal support prime $\mathfrak q$, the localization $N_{\mathfrak q}$ is nonzero and supported only at the maximal ideal of $R_{\mathfrak q}$. The radical of its annihilator is that maximal ideal; finite generation makes a power annihilate the module. A last nonzero power layer therefore contains a nonzero element killed by the maximal ideal. Represent it by $z/1$, rescaling a fraction by a unit if necessary. For a finite list of generators of $\mathfrak q$, clear denominators in the equations saying they kill $z/1$. Multiplying $z$ by the product of those denominators gives $z'\in N$ with $\mathfrak qz'=0$ and $z'_{\mathfrak q}\ne0$. No element outside $\mathfrak q$ can annihilate it. Thus $\operatorname{Ann}(z')=\mathfrak q$, proving that $\mathfrak q$ is associated.

Apply this to $\overline L$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ retains that annihilator under the displayed inclusion into $M/x^nM$, proving the assertion. The exponent cannot in general be replaced by $1$; the Artin–Rees choice is part of the argument. ∎

Support under quotients and exact sequences

For an arbitrary ring $R$ and module $M$:

  1. If $M$ is finite, then $\operatorname{Supp}(M/IM)=\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(I)$ for every ideal $I$.
  2. A submodule or quotient of $M$ has support contained in $\operatorname{Supp}M$.
  3. An exact sequence $0\to N\to M\to Q\to0$ gives $\operatorname{Supp}M=\operatorname{Supp}N\cup\operatorname{Supp}Q$.

Proof. Localization is exact, so the last two assertions follow by checking whether each localized module is zero. For (1), if $I$ contains an element outside $\mathfrak p$, then $I_{\mathfrak p}=R_{\mathfrak p}$ and the quotient localization is zero. If $I\subset\mathfrak p$, Nakayama for the finite $R_{\mathfrak p}$-module $M_{\mathfrak p}$ says

$$M_{\mathfrak p}/I_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p}=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M_{\mathfrak p}=0.$$

This proves exactly the claimed intersection formula. Finiteness is used only for (1); the other support rules apply to all modules. ∎

Cohen–Macaulayness under a quotient of local rings

Let $R\to S$ be a surjection of Noetherian local rings and $N$ a finite $S$-module. Then $N$ is CM over $R$ if and only if it is CM over $S$.

Proof. Every sequence in the maximal ideal of $R$ acts on $N$ through its image in the maximal ideal of $S$. Its successive quotient modules and multiplication maps are unchanged. Conversely, any sequence from the latter maximal ideal lifts to the former. Thus the possible regular-sequence lengths, and hence depths, agree.

The support of $N$ over $R$ lies in the closed subset defined by $\ker(R\to S)$. The quotient correspondence identifies this support homeomorphically with its support over $S$, preserving all strict prime chains and therefore its dimension. Equality of depth and support dimension is consequently the same over either ring. The zero module is CM under both conventions as well. ∎

Permuting a regular sequence

If $M$ is a finite module over a Noetherian local ring and $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ is $M$-regular, every permutation is $M$-regular. Here regularity includes a nonzero final quotient.

Proof. It suffices to interchange adjacent entries. On the quotient by the entries preceding them, write the pair as $x,y$ and the finite module as $L$. Both elements belong to the maximal ideal, since the final regular quotient is nonzero.

Let $K=\ker(y\colon L\to L)$. Injectivity of $y$ modulo $x$ makes every $z\in K$ equal to $xz'$ for some $z'\in L$. Since $x$ is injective on $L$, the equality $0=yz=xyz'$ implies $yz'=0$. Thus $K=xK$. The module $K$ is finite by Noetherianity, so Nakayama gives $K=0$. Hence $y$ is injective on $L$.

If $xz=yw$, reduce modulo $x$. Injectivity of $y$ on $L/xL$ gives $w=xw'$; cancellation of $x$ then yields $z=yw'$. Thus $x$ is injective on $L/yL$. The final quotient by $(x,y)$ has not changed, so it is nonzero, and the subsequent entries act on the same quotient modules. This swaps the adjacent pair. Adjacent transpositions generate all permutations, proving the result. ∎

An equation good for a chosen maximal regular sequence

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M\ne0$ be finite and CM, and put $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M>0$. Fix an $M$-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_d$. Call $g\in\mathfrak m$ good for this data if

$$\dim\bigl(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g,f_1,\ldots,f_i)\bigr) =d-i-1\qquad(0\leq i<d).$$

Then $g$ is injective on $M$, and $M/gM$ is CM with maximal regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$.

Proof. The full good-element induction occurs inside the second proof of the CM equation lemma. The support quotient formula identifies the definition here with the one used there. For clarity, its induction proceeds as follows.

When $d=1$, the kernel of $g$ is supported at the maximal ideal and has finite length. Multiplication by $f_1$ is injective on it, hence surjective by equality of lengths, and Nakayama kills the kernel. The nonzero quotient $M/gM$ has dimension zero and is CM.

For $d>1$, the good-element identities with $i\geq1$ give the same hypothesis on $M/f_1M$ and the list $f_2,\ldots,f_d$. That quotient is CM of dimension $d-1$ by the regular-element depth and dimension formulas. Induction makes $g$ injective there and makes $f_2,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ regular on $M/(f_1,g)M$. Thus $f_1,g$ is a regular pair on $M$. The preceding permutation argument changes its order, giving injectivity of $g$ on $M$ and of $f_1$ on $M/gM$. The remaining list is then regular as well. The $i=0$ good-element identity and the support quotient formula give dimension $d-1$ to $M/gM$, so this length-$d-1$ list is maximal and the quotient is CM. Nakayama keeps each required final quotient nonzero. ∎

Finite global dimension and uniform regular dimension

Let $R\ne0$ be Noetherian and let $n\geq0$ be an integer. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. The global dimension of $R$, over all modules, is $n$.
  2. Every prime localization is regular local and $\dim R=n$.
  3. Every maximal localization is regular local of dimension at most $n$, and one has dimension $n$.
  4. Every prime localization is regular local of dimension at most $n$, and one has dimension $n$.

Proof. We first establish the uniform local criterion

$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq n \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{gl.dim}R_{\mathfrak m}\leq n \text{ for every maximal }\mathfrak m.$$

One direction holds because localization preserves projective resolutions. Any $R_{\mathfrak m}$-module can be regarded as an $R$-module, and localizing it returns the same module.

For the converse, begin with a finite $R$-module $M$. If $n>0$, choose $n$ finite free terms of a resolution and write its last kernel as $K_n$:

$$0\longrightarrow K_n\longrightarrow F_{n-1} \longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0 \longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.$$

Noetherianity makes $K_n$ finite and finitely presented. The local bound and independence of the last syzygy make every $(K_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ projective. The complete finite-projectivity criterion makes $K_n$ projective over $R$. Thus $\operatorname{pd}_R M\leq n$. For $n=0$, apply that same projectivity criterion directly to $M$, since each $M_{\mathfrak m}$ is projective.

This bounds in particular every cyclic module $R/I$. The full cyclic-module criterion, including its transfinite proof, then bounds the projective dimension of every module, with no finite-generation assumption. This proves the uniform local criterion.

The complete local homological characterization says that a Noetherian local ring of finite global dimension is regular, and its global dimension equals its Krull dimension. Applying the uniform criterion for every integer bound gives

$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R =\sup_{\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\operatorname{gl.dim}R_{\mathfrak m}.$$

This equality includes the value infinity. Also

$$\dim R=\sup_{\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\dim R_{\mathfrak m} =\sup_{\mathfrak p\text{ prime}}\dim R_{\mathfrak p},$$

because every finite prime chain lies below a maximal ideal and localization preserves that chain. Finite integer suprema of these nonempty sets are attained.

Now (1) gives regularity at every prime by localization and the local characterization; the two suprema give (2)–(4). Conversely, (3) and the local characterization give global dimension at most $n$, while the indicated maximal localization gives the reverse inequality. Condition (4) gives the same upper bound and its indicated prime localization gives the lower bound. Condition (2) implies (4) by the dimension supremum. All four conditions are therefore equivalent. A regular Noetherian ring of unbounded dimension does not satisfy these finite conditions. ∎

Global generators of a polynomial maximal ideal

Let $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, where $k$ is any field, and let $\mathfrak m$ be maximal. There are $n$ polynomials generating $\mathfrak m$ in $P$ itself. The local ring $P_{\mathfrak m}$ is regular of dimension $n$.

Proof. By the complete Nullstellensatz, $E=P/\mathfrak m$ is a finite extension of $k$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the image of $x_i$, and set

$$E_i=k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_i),\qquad E_0=k.$$

The algebraic intermediate-ring argument gives $E_i=k[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_i]$. Thus every coefficient of the monic minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$ over $E_{i-1}$ lifts to a polynomial in the preceding variables. Choose such lifts, keeping the leading coefficient equal to $1$, and call the resulting polynomial in $x_i$ $f_i$.

Inductively, quotienting by $f_1,\ldots,f_i$ gives

$$k[x_1,\ldots,x_i]/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\cong E_i.$$

Indeed, after the preceding quotient, the new equation is exactly the minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$ over the field $E_{i-1}$. At $i=n$ the quotient is $E$ with its specified images of all variables, so its kernel is precisely $\mathfrak m$. Hence $\mathfrak m=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ globally.

Moreover,

$$P/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\cong E_i[x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n].$$

These quotients are domains. Their kernels form a strict prime chain of length $n$ ending at $\mathfrak m$: at each step a nonconstant monic polynomial in the next variable becomes zero. The same chain survives in $P_{\mathfrak m}$, giving dimension at least $n$. The full local dimension and parameter theorem bounds dimension by the number of maximal-ideal generators, here at most $n$. Dimension and embedding dimension are therefore both $n$, which is regularity. This argument includes inseparable residue extensions. For $n=0$, $P=k$, the maximal ideal is generated by the empty list and the dimension is zero. ∎

Internal graded Ext: shifts, exact sequences and comparison

Let $S$ be a graded ring and let $M,N$ be graded $S$-modules. Write $M(a)_j=M_{j+a}$. A map of internal degree $b$ sends $M_j$ into $N_{j+b}$; write its group as $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(M,N)$ and take the direct sum over $b$ for $\operatorname{GrHom}(M,N)$. Choose a resolution $L_\bullet\to M$ by direct sums of twists of $S$, with differentials of degree zero, and define

$$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N) =\bigoplus_{b\in\mathbf Z} H^q\bigl(\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_\bullet,N)\bigr).$$

For homogeneous $s\in S_d$, multiplication on the target sends a degree-$b$ map to a degree-$(b+d)$ map. This defines the graded $S$-module structure.

The six properties are as follows.

  1. $\operatorname{GrExt}^0_S(M,N)=\operatorname{GrHom}(M,N)$.
  2. For every integer $a$ and every $q\geq0$,
$$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M(a),N) \cong\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N(-a)) \cong\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)(-a).$$
  1. An exact sequence $0\to N_1\to N_2\to N_3\to0$ gives the graded long exact sequence
$$\cdots\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_1) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_2) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_3) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^{q+1}_S(M,N_1) \longrightarrow\cdots.$$
  1. An exact sequence $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ gives the sequence with reversed first-variable order,
$$\cdots\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_3,N) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_2,N) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_1,N) \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^{q+1}_S(M_3,N) \longrightarrow\cdots.$$
  1. If $S$ is Noetherian and $M$ is finite, the natural map
$$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^q_S(M,N)$$

is an isomorphism after forgetting the grading. If $N$ is finite as well, these modules are finite. 6. For $S=K[t_0,\ldots,t_r]$ over a field and finite $M$,

$$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)=0\qquad(q>r+1).$$

Proof. First justify the resolution construction. Kernels and cokernels of degree-zero maps are computed in each degree, so graded modules form an abelian category. A degree-zero map from a direct sum of twists lifts through a surjection: lift the image of each homogeneous basis element in its specified degree. Such sums are therefore projective. Taking one basis element for each homogeneous generator gives a graded free surjection onto any module. Repeating on its graded kernel produces a resolution. Over a Noetherian ring, a finite module admits one with finitely many basis elements in each resolution term, since each kernel is finite and its homogeneous components generate it.

A map of modules lifts to their resolutions inductively: the image required at the next degree lies in a kernel, the following differential surjects onto that kernel, and projectivity gives the lift. If two chain maps lift the same map, their difference in degree zero lifts through the first differential. After this first homotopy term is chosen, subtract its contribution; at the next degree the remaining difference again lies in the next kernel. Induction gives a homotopy in every degree. All these choices take place among maps of degree zero. Thus the resulting Ext functors and comparison maps are independent of the chosen resolution and are functorial.

For (1), the degree-zero cohomology kernel consists exactly of maps $L_0\to N$ that kill the image of $L_1$. These are maps from $M$, in each internal degree.

For (2), twist the entire resolution by $a$. Its Hom groups satisfy

$$\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i(a),N) =\operatorname{GrHom}_{b-a}(L_i,N) =\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i,N(-a)).$$

These identifications commute with the cochain differentials. Taking cohomology and assembling the degrees gives precisely the indicated negative shift.

For (3), each $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i,-)$ preserves the short exact sequence, by graded projectivity with the corresponding target twist. The connecting map on cohomology is obtained by lifting a cocycle to the middle complex and taking its differential in the first complex. A change of lift changes it by a boundary. This gives the long exact sequence in each internal degree; direct sums are exact, and multiplication by homogeneous elements commutes with the construction. The resulting sequence is one of graded modules with maps of degree zero.

For (4), construct compatible resolutions of the three modules. Choose graded free surjections $L^1_0\to M_1$ and $L^3_0\to M_3$, and lift the latter map to $M_2$. Their direct sum surjects onto $M_2$. Its kernel fits into an exact sequence between the other two kernels: surjectivity on the right follows by correcting a lift by an element of $L^1_0$. Repeat this construction on the kernels. It produces a short exact sequence of resolutions

$$0\longrightarrow L^1_\bullet\longrightarrow L^2_\bullet \longrightarrow L^3_\bullet\longrightarrow0$$

that splits in every degree. Applying $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(-,N)$ therefore gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in the reverse order. The same cocycle-lifting construction gives (4), with the stated variance. Resolution comparison and homotopy show that these are the natural connecting maps.

For (5), use a resolution finite graded free in every degree. An ungraded homomorphism from one such term is a finite sum of homogeneous maps: the images of finitely many homogeneous basis elements have only finitely many homogeneous components in total. Thus

$$\operatorname{GrHom}(L_i,N)=\operatorname{Hom}_S(L_i,N)$$

as ungraded modules for every $i$. This is an isomorphism of cochain complexes. Cohomology commutes with the direct sum over internal degrees because the differentials preserve those degrees, proving the comparison. When $N$ is finite, each Hom term is finite; its kernels and their quotients are finite by Noetherianity. Finally the complete polynomial global-dimension proof bounds ordinary Ext by $r+1$. Applying (5) proves (6).

Historical context. FAC, Chapter III, §4, no. 68, pp. 261–262, uses this internal Hom and Ext convention; agreement with ordinary Hom and Ext requires the stated finiteness boundary. The contravariant sequence and finiteness are inputs to the duality calculations in no. 72, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2, pp. 265–267. The twist by $S(-r-1)$ in §5, no. 77, p. 271, changes internal degree according to (2) and leaves cohomological degree unchanged. These observations preserve the graded meaning of the Hilbert-syzygy bound used there. ∎

Component dimension and closed specializations

Let $S$ be a finite-type algebra over a field $k$, let $\mathfrak p$ be prime, and let $x\in X=\operatorname{Spec}S$ be its point. Then

$$\dim_xX =\max_{\substack{Z\text{ an irreducible component}\\x\in Z}}\dim Z =\min_{\substack{\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p\\\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}} \dim S_{\mathfrak m}.$$

Proof. The full dimension-at-a-point proof establishes the first equality, including that every nonempty open in a finite-type integral component has its full dimension. We prove the closed-specialization equality explicitly.

Write the finitely many irreducible components of $X$ as $Z_1,\ldots,Z_s$. Let $J$ index those containing $x$, and put

$$d=\max_{j\in J}\dim Z_j,\qquad T=\bigcup_{j\notin J}Z_j,\qquad U=X\setminus T.$$

If a closed point $y$ corresponds to $\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p$, every $Z_j$ with $j\in J$ contains $y$: closed sets contain all specializations of their points. The first equality applied at $y$, together with the closed-point dimension formula, therefore gives $\dim S_{\mathfrak m}\geq d$.

The subset $V(\mathfrak p)\cap U$ is a nonempty open in $V(\mathfrak p)$, since it contains $x$. The complete Jacobson argument makes the closed points of $X$ dense in this closed subset. Choose one such $y$ in $V(\mathfrak p)\cap U$. It lies in every component indexed by $J$ and in none of the others. Consequently the same two dimension formulas give $\dim S_{\mathfrak m}=d$ at this particular closed specialization. The lower bound is attained, proving the minimum equality. No irreducibility or reducedness of $S$ was imposed. ∎

Maximal chains in a finite-type field domain

If $S$ is a finite-type integral domain over a field, every maximal prime chain in $S$ has length $\dim S$. In particular,

$$\dim S_{\mathfrak m}=\dim S$$

for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.

Proof. Present $S=P/\mathfrak q$ for $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $\mathfrak q$ prime. A maximal chain in $S$ starts at its zero ideal, ends at a maximal ideal, and is saturated between its endpoints. The corresponding chain in $P$ starts at $\mathfrak q$ and ends at a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$. The complete polynomial prime-chain theorem gives its length as

$$\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak n-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q =n-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q,$$

using the preceding polynomial maximal-ideal calculation. This number is independent of the endpoint and the saturated chain. Finite dimension ensures that a finite chain extends to such a maximal chain. Hence it is the dimension of $S$. Chains below a specified maximal ideal give the same number after localization, proving the local equality as well. ∎

Regular local presentations of a complete intersection

For surjective homomorphisms of local rings $P\to T\to S$ with $P,T$ regular local, the following four conditions are equivalent:

  1. The kernel of $P\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence.
  2. That kernel has a generating list of length $\dim P-\dim S$.
  3. The kernel of $T\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence.
  4. That kernel has a generating list of length $\dim T-\dim S$.

The complete proof is the first comparison in Five local complete-intersection criteria. It uses the CM parameter criterion in both regular local rings, then the parameter generators of $\ker(P\to T)$. One direction lifts generators; the reverse induction removes a parameter whose class remains nonzero in the larger kernel modulo the maximal ideal. This argument has no ground-field assumption.

The native source locator for this result is algebra.tex, lemma-ci-well-defined.

Extending a local-ring isomorphism to principal neighborhoods

Let $A,B$ be finitely presented algebras over a ring $Q$, and suppose a $Q$-algebra isomorphism $A_{\mathfrak a}\cong B_{\mathfrak b}$ is given. There are $t\in A\setminus\mathfrak a$ and $s\in B\setminus\mathfrak b$ such that this isomorphism is induced by $A_t\cong B_s$.

The complete proof is the second comparison in Five local complete-intersection criteria, beginning with a finitely presented map that induces a local isomorphism. After finite denominator clearing, evaluation gives a retraction. Its finitely generated kernel is generated by an explicitly constructed idempotent, which isolates the required component. The final paragraph spreads the given map from finite generators and relations and applies that splitting; it works over an arbitrary common base $Q$.

The native source locator is algebra.tex, lemma-isomorphic-local-rings.

Local dimension at a quasi-finite point

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, and let $\mathfrak q$ lie over $\mathfrak p$. If the map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, then

$$\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq\dim R_{\mathfrak p}.$$

The base ring may be non-Noetherian.

Proof. We use the complete algebraic Zariski Main theorem. Write $B$ for the integral closure of the image of $R$ in $S$. The theorem gives $g\in B\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $B_g=S_g$. Choose finite algebra generators of $S_g/R$ and express them as fractions with numerators $b_1,\ldots,b_t\in B$ and denominators powers of $g$. Then

$$C=R[g,b_1,\ldots,b_t]\subset S$$

means the subalgebra generated by the image of $R$ and the listed elements. It is finite over $R$, by the complete integral finite-type criterion. Localization of the inclusion is injective, and the chosen generators make it surjective onto $S_g$. Thus $C_g=S_g$.

For $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap C$ this gives $C_{\mathfrak r}=S_{\mathfrak q}$. Any finite strict prime chain in $C$ below $\mathfrak r$ contracts to a strict chain in $R$ below $\mathfrak p$, by the full incomparability argument for integral maps. The corresponding localized chain has no greater length than $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$. Taking the supremum proves the inequality, including infinite dimensions.

The original local-base route gives the same conclusion: after replacing $R$ by $R_{\mathfrak p}$, Zariski Main identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ with a localization of its integral closure over that base; incomparability bounds the dimension of the integral closure itself by $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$. If $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian, the local dimension formula instead gives the inequality immediately, because the local fibre at a quasi-finite point has dimension zero. Both routes apply at their stated scopes. ∎

Openness of the quasi-finite locus

For a finite-type ring map $R\to S$, the primes where the map is quasi-finite form an open subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$.

Proof. At any such prime $\mathfrak q$, the finite-algebra construction in the preceding proof gives $g\notin\mathfrak q$ and a finite $R$-algebra $C\subset S$ with $C_g=S_g$. For any base prime $\mathfrak p'$, the fibre

$$C\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p')$$

is a finite-dimensional algebra over the residue field. Its localization at $g$ is again finite dimensional: every element of a finite-dimensional algebra is algebraic, and the inverse of an invertible algebraic element is a polynomial in it. Equivalently, the localization is a quotient of this Artinian algebra by the factors where $g$ is nilpotent.

Every local ring in that fibre therefore has dimension zero, with residue field finite over $\kappa(\mathfrak p')$. These are the quasi-finiteness conditions at its points. Since $S_g=C_g$, they hold at every point of $D(g)\subset\operatorname{Spec}S$. This supplies an open quasi-finite neighborhood of each originally chosen point, proving the claim. No Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ is needed. ∎

Lifting a nonzerodivisor from the closed fibre

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. If the image of $f\in S$ is a nonzerodivisor on $S/\mathfrak mS$, then multiplication by $f$ on $S$ is injective and $S/fS$ is flat over $R$.

Proof. Apply the complete fibrewise injectivity theorem to

$$u\colon S\longrightarrow S,\qquad s\longmapsto fs.$$

Its source is finite over the Noetherian local target ring $S$, its target module is $R$-flat, and its residue map is injective by hypothesis. The theorem proves both injectivity of $u$ and flatness of its cokernel. Its full proof lifts injectivity through all powers, uses Krull intersection, and repeats the argument after every ideal quotient to obtain the Tor flatness test. Thus both conclusions follow at exactly the required scope. If $f$ is a unit, the map is an isomorphism and its zero cokernel is flat directly. ∎

Finitely many algebraic field generators

If $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$ in an extension field are algebraic over $k$, then $k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ has finite degree over $k$.

Proof by adjoining the generators. Put $E_0=k$ and $E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)$. The element $\alpha_i$ remains algebraic over $E_{i-1}$, and its monic minimal polynomial of degree $d_i$ gives the basis

$$1,\alpha_i,\ldots,\alpha_i^{d_i-1}$$

over $E_{i-1}$. Spanning is polynomial division, together with the fact that the polynomial quotient by the minimal polynomial is a field; independence is the minimality of its degree. Products of successive basis elements give a basis for the tower: expand coefficients in the earlier basis to prove spanning, and group by the last basis to prove independence. Hence

$$[E_n:k]=\prod_{i=1}^n d_i<\infty.$$

For the empty list the degree is $1$.

Integral-algebra proof. Choose a monic equation of degree $e_i$ over $k$ for each $\alpha_i$. Reducing powers in each variable shows that the finitely many monomials

$$\alpha_1^{a_1}\cdots\alpha_n^{a_n}, \qquad 0\leq a_i<e_i,$$

span $A=k[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n]$ over $k$. For any $0\ne a\in A$, multiplication by $a$ is injective on this finite-dimensional vector space, since it lies in a field. It is therefore surjective and sends some element to $1$. Thus $A$ is a field, equals $E_n$, and is finite over $k$. This also supplies the finite-integral-algebra deduction used in the prerequisite statement. ∎

Composing specialization-lifting maps

For continuous maps $X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$, if specializations lift along both maps, they lift along $gf$. The same assertion holds for generalizations. Here $u\leadsto v$ means $v\in\overline{\{u\}}$.

Proof. Given $x\in X$ and a specialization $gf(x)\leadsto z$, first lift along $g$ to obtain $f(x)\leadsto y$ with $g(y)=z$. Then lift along $f$ to obtain $x\leadsto x'$ with $f(x')=y$. The composite image of $x'$ is $z$, as required.

For generalizations, start instead with $z'\leadsto gf(x)$. Lift this along $g$ to $y'\leadsto f(x)$ with $g(y')=z'$, and then along $f$ to $x'\leadsto x$ with $f(x')=y'$. Again $gf(x')=z'$. Thus the assertion holds in both directions of the specialization relation. ∎

Images of sets stable under specialization

If specializations lift along a continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$, the image of any specialization-stable subset of $X$ is specialization-stable in $Y$. If generalizations lift, the corresponding assertion holds for generalization-stable subsets.

Proof. Let $T$ be specialization-stable, choose $x\in T$, and suppose $f(x)\leadsto y$. A lift gives $x\leadsto x'$ with $f(x')=y$. Stability puts $x'$ in $T$, hence $y$ in $f(T)$.

For the other assertion, let $T$ be generalization-stable and take $y'\leadsto f(x)$ with $x\in T$. Lift to $x'\leadsto x$ with $f(x')=y'$. This time stability under generalization gives $x'\in T$, again proving that the required point belongs to the image. ∎

Replacing a filtered category by a directed set

Let $\mathcal I$ be a filtered index category, with a set of objects and arrows. There is a directed partially ordered set $D$ and a functor $u\colon D\to\mathcal I$ such that:

  1. For every diagram $M\colon\mathcal I\to\mathcal C$, if $\varinjlim_{d\in D}M(u(d))$ exists, then $\varinjlim_{\mathcal I}M$ exists and the canonical map between them is an isomorphism.
  2. For every diagram $N\colon\mathcal I^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$, if the restricted inverse limit over $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ exists, then the inverse limit over $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{op}}$ exists and restriction is an isomorphism.

Proof. We retain an explicit construction of $D$. Put $\mathcal J=\mathcal I\times\mathbf N$, with a unique arrow $a\to b$ in the second factor whenever $a\leq b$. The category $\mathcal J$ is filtered: choose a common target in $\mathcal I$ and a sufficiently large integer for two objects, and equalize parallel arrows in $\mathcal I$, increasing the integer if needed.

The projection $\pi\colon\mathcal J\to\mathcal I$ is cofinal in the sense of the cofinality theorem. Indeed, for any $i\in\mathcal I$, the category of arrows $i\to\pi(j)$ has the initial object given by the identity into $(i,0)$. It is therefore nonempty and connected.

Call a subcategory finitely generated if finitely many arrows, including identities for its objects as needed, generate all its arrows by composition. Such a subcategory has finitely many objects, although it may have infinitely many composite arrows. Any finitely generated subcategory $F\subset\mathcal J$ admits a cocone in $\mathcal J$. To construct one, first use filteredness to choose arrows from all its finitely many objects to a common target. For each generating arrow, the two resulting arrows from its source to that target can be made equal after postcomposition. Equalize these finitely many pairs in succession; every later postcomposition preserves the equalities already imposed. The resulting arrows commute with all generators, hence with all composites.

Increase the integer coordinate of the cocone vertex beyond every integer occurring in $F$. Denote the new vertex by $t$. There are no arrows from $t$ back to any object of $F$. Adjoin $t$, its identity, and the cocone arrows to $F$. The result $F^+$ is still a finitely generated subcategory: the cocone identities make this arrow collection closed under composition. The object $t$ is its unique final object, since its only outgoing arrow is its identity.

Let $D$ be the set of finitely generated subcategories of $\mathcal J$ having a unique final object, ordered by inclusion. This is a set because $\mathcal J$ is small. It is nonempty, and any two members are contained in the subcategory generated by their two finite lists of generators; the construction just given enlarges that subcategory to a member of $D$. Thus $D$ is directed.

Assign to $F\in D$ its final object $t_F$. If $F\subset G$, there is a unique arrow $t_F\to t_G$ in $G$. These arrows compose correctly, by uniqueness in the larger subcategory, and define a functor $v\colon D\to\mathcal J$.

This functor is cofinal. Every object $j$ is the final object of its singleton identity subcategory. Given two arrows $j\to t_F$ and $j\to t_G$, include these arrows and the generators of $F,G$ in one finitely generated subcategory, and enlarge it to $H\in D$. The arrows from $j$ to $t_H$ through $t_F$ and $t_G$ agree, since $t_H$ is final in $H$. Thus the two objects of the corresponding comma category are joined through $H$. This proves the required connectedness as well as nonemptiness.

Apply the full cofinality theorem first to $v$ and then to $\pi$. It identifies cocones on a diagram over $\mathcal I$ with cocones on its restriction along $u=\pi v$, for every possible target. Therefore a colimit of the latter diagram represents the former cocone functor and proves (1).

For (2), regard $N$ as a covariant diagram $\mathcal I\to\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$. Its colimits there are precisely its inverse limits in $\mathcal C$, with the arrows reversed. Applying (1) in that opposite category gives both existence and the asserted canonical restriction isomorphism. This spells out the inverse-limit assertion as well. ∎

Specialization lifting for closed and open maps

Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be continuous.

  1. If $f$ is closed, specializations lift along $f$.
  2. Generalizations lift when $f$ is open and the following additional conditions hold: the target $Y$ is $T_0$; the source $X$ is Noetherian; and each irreducible closed subset in the source is the closure of one of its points.

Proof. For (1), suppose $f(x')\leadsto y$. The image of $\overline{\{x'\}}$ is closed and contains $f(x')$, so it contains $y$. A point $x$ in this closure mapping to $y$ is exactly the desired specialization of $x'$.

For (2), suppose $y'\leadsto f(x)$ and put $T=f^{-1}(y')$. Every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ has open image containing $f(x)$, hence containing its generalization $y'$. Consequently $U$ meets $T$, so $x\in\overline T$.

The complete Noetherian-space theorem makes the subspace $T$ Noetherian and writes it as a finite union of nonempty irreducible components $T_i$. Therefore $\overline T$ is the union of the irreducible closed sets $\overline{T_i}$. Choose one containing $x$, and let $\eta$ be its generic point. Then $\eta\leadsto x$. Continuity and $\eta\in\overline{T_i}$ give

$$f(\eta)\in\overline{\{y'\}}.$$

On the other hand, $T_i\subset\overline{\{\eta\}}$, so $y'\in\overline{\{f(\eta)\}}$. Thus $f(\eta)$ and $y'$ specialize to one another. In a $T_0$ space this forces equality, since the two points have exactly the same open neighborhoods. Hence $f(\eta)=y'$, giving the required generalization of $x$. All three additional hypotheses in (2) enter the proof. ∎

Cofinality preserves colimits

A functor $H\colon\mathcal I\to\mathcal J$ is cofinal when, for each $j\in\mathcal J$, the category $(j\downarrow H)$ is nonempty and connected. Its objects are pairs $(i,a)$ with $a\colon j\to H(i)$; a morphism to $(i',a')$ is a map $b\colon i\to i'$ with $H(b)a=a'$. Connectedness means that any two such pairs are joined by a finite zigzag of these arrows.

If $H$ is cofinal and $M\colon\mathcal J\to\mathcal C$ is any diagram, then

$$\varinjlim_{\mathcal I}MH\cong\varinjlim_{\mathcal J}M$$

canonically whenever either side exists.

Proof. Fix an object $T$ of $\mathcal C$. Restricting a cocone on $M$ gives one on $MH$. Conversely, let $\lambda_i\colon M(H(i))\to T$ be a cocone on $MH$. For $j\in\mathcal J$, choose $(i,a)\in(j\downarrow H)$ and define

$$\mu_j=\lambda_iM(a)\colon M(j)\longrightarrow T.$$

If $(i,a)\to(i',a')$ is a comma-category arrow, the cocone identity gives

$$\lambda_{i'}M(a') =\lambda_{i'}M(H(b))M(a) =\lambda_iM(a).$$

The same equality holds along an arrow traversed backwards. Connectedness therefore makes $\mu_j$ independent of every choice.

For $c\colon j\to j'$, choose $a'\colon j'\to H(i)$. The composite $a'c$ is a permitted choice at $j$, so $\mu_j=\mu_{j'}M(c)$. Thus the $\mu_j$ form a cocone. At $j=H(i)$ choose $a=1_{H(i)}$; restriction returns $\lambda_i$. Conversely, a cocone originally defined on $M$ is recovered because its naturality forces the formula for $\mu_j$. These constructions are mutually inverse and commute with maps of targets $T$.

Hence the two cocone functors have the same representing objects. Existence of either colimit implies existence of the other, and the resulting isomorphism is the canonical comparison. This argument requires neither filteredness nor any prior cocompleteness of $\mathcal C$. ∎

A full cofinal subcategory of a filtered category

Let $\mathcal J$ be a full subcategory of a filtered category $\mathcal I$. Suppose every object of $\mathcal I$ admits a map to an object of $\mathcal J$. Then $\mathcal J$ is filtered and its inclusion is cofinal.

Proof. Since $\mathcal I$ is nonempty, the hypothesis makes $\mathcal J$ nonempty. For $j_1,j_2\in\mathcal J$, choose a common target in $\mathcal I$ and then a map from that target to some $j_3\in\mathcal J$. The resulting arrows from $j_1,j_2$ belong to $\mathcal J$ by fullness. For parallel arrows in $\mathcal J$, first choose an arrow equalizing them in $\mathcal I$, then map its target into $\mathcal J$. Again fullness gives the needed equalizer arrow within $\mathcal J$. These are the filteredness axioms.

Fix $i\in\mathcal I$. The comma category $(i\downarrow\mathcal J)$ is nonempty by hypothesis. For two objects $a_1\colon i\to j_1$ and $a_2\colon i\to j_2$, filteredness gives a common target for $j_1,j_2$ in $\mathcal I$. Equalize the two induced maps from $i$ by postcomposition, and then map that target into an object $j_3$ of $\mathcal J$. Fullness puts both resulting arrows $j_\nu\to j_3$ in $\mathcal J$, and their composites from $i$ agree. The two comma-category objects therefore have a common receiving object and are connected. The preceding theorem applies, proving cofinality.

The historical reference recorded for this statement is Kashiwara–Schapira, Proposition 3.2.4. ∎

Complete regular rings with a specified coefficient field

A complete Noetherian regular local ring containing a prescribed coefficient field $k$ is a power-series ring over that same copy of $k$, with one variable for each dimension.

The full proof is Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 6, Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.2. Evaluate power series using the specified coefficient embedding and lifts of a cotangent basis. Successive homogeneous corrections prove surjectivity, and the dimension drop for a nonzero kernel element proves injectivity. No perfectness assumption is imposed on $k$.

Coefficient rings and complete local presentations

Every complete local ring has a coefficient ring. If its maximal ideal is finitely generated, it is a quotient of a power-series ring in finitely many variables over a field or a Cohen ring. In positive residue characteristic a Cohen ring may be used even when its map to the target has a nonzero kernel.

The complete construction is Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Sections 4–6, Theorems 5.1 and 6.1, with the prime-field and square-zero lifting proofs in Sections 1–3. Coefficient existence does not require a finite maximal ideal. The finite-variable presentation uses that finiteness hypothesis precisely to choose finitely many parameter lifts. The coefficient image may be a field, a Cohen DVR, or a truncated Cohen ring according to the characteristic and $p$-torsion of the target.

Formal lifting for every Cohen ring

For a Cohen ring $\Lambda$ with residue characteristic $p$, and every $n\geq1$, the map

$$\mathbf Z/p^n\mathbf Z\longrightarrow\Lambda/p^n\Lambda$$

is flat and formally smooth.

Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 4, Theorem 4.1 supplies the complete proof, using the prime-field lifting and flat square-zero base-lifting results of Sections 1–2. Its flatness argument uses cancellation of powers of $p$ in the DVR; induction through $\mathbf Z/p^{n+1}\to\mathbf Z/p^n$ gives formal smoothness. These steps use only the defining properties of a Cohen ring and apply to every such $\Lambda$, including those with imperfect residue field.

Noetherianity of completion along any ideal

If $R$ is Noetherian and $I$ is any ideal, the completion $\widehat R=\varprojlim_nR/I^n$ is Noetherian.

Proof by initial forms. The ideal $I$ is finitely generated and $R/I$ is Noetherian. Thus the complete adic-completion theorem applies. Its proof makes the associated graded ring a quotient of a polynomial ring over $R/I$, chooses finitely many initial generators for an arbitrary ideal, and sums the successively improving coefficients in the completion. It proves this assertion without any assumption on $I$ beyond the finite generation already supplied by Noetherianity.

Power-series proof. Write $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_t)$. Evaluation defines a homomorphism

$$R[[X_1,\ldots,X_t]]\longrightarrow\widehat R, \qquad X_i\longmapsto f_i.$$

For precision, evaluate the terms of degree less than $n$ modulo $I^n$. The results are compatible as $n$ increases, because every omitted monomial evaluates into $I^n$. This constructs the map in the inverse limit, and addition and multiplication commute with it by the same finite truncation calculation.

The map is surjective. Given $a\in\widehat R$, first lift its residue modulo $I$ to $R$. After matching it modulo $I^n$, its error modulo $I^{n+1}$ lies in $I^n/I^{n+1}$, which is generated over $R/I$ by the degree-$n$ monomials in the $f_i$. Lift the finitely many coefficients to $R$ and add the corresponding homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$ in the $X_i$. Induction produces a power series whose evaluation agrees with $a$ modulo every $I^n$, hence equals $a$.

Finally, the power-series ring is Noetherian. It is the $(X_1,\ldots,X_t)$-adic completion of $R[X_1,\ldots,X_t]$: the coefficients of each bounded total degree stabilize uniquely in the inverse limit. The already proved initial-form theorem applies to this finitely generated ideal, whose quotient is $R$. Its conclusion gives Noetherianity of the power-series ring, and its displayed quotient $\widehat R$ is therefore Noetherian. This supplies the evaluation and surjectivity details in the second proof. If $I=R$, the completion is the zero ring and the conclusion is immediate. ∎

Six criteria for universal exactness

Fix an exact sequence of $R$-modules

$$0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\longrightarrow0.$$

The following conditions are equivalent.

  1. Tensoring with every $R$-module leaves the sequence exact; this is universal exactness.
  2. Tensoring with every finitely presented $R$-module leaves it exact.
  3. Whenever finite families $a_i\in A$, $b_j\in B$, and coefficients $r_{ij}\in R$ satisfy
$$f(a_i)=\sum_{j=1}^m r_{ij}b_j\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$

there are $z_1,\ldots,z_m\in A$ satisfying

$$a_i=\sum_{j=1}^m r_{ij}z_j\qquad(1\leq i\leq n).$$
  1. In every commutative square with $m,n$ finite,
$$\begin{array}{ccc} R^n&\xrightarrow{u}&R^m\\ {\scriptstyle h}\downarrow&&\downarrow{\scriptstyle v}\\ A&\xrightarrow{f}&B, \end{array}$$

there is $k\colon R^m\to A$ with $ku=h$. This asks for the upper triangle to commute; it does not require $fk=v$. 5. Every map from a finitely presented module $P$ to $C$ lifts to $B$. 6. The sequence is a directed colimit of split exact sequences

$$0\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow B_i\longrightarrow C_i\longrightarrow0,$$

with each $C_i$ finitely presented and with identity transition maps on $A$. The chosen splittings need not commute with the transition maps.

Proof. Condition (1) immediately gives (2). To deduce (3) from (2), use the matrix map

$$R^m\longrightarrow R^n,\qquad e_j\longmapsto\sum_i r_{ij}e_i,$$

and let $Q$ be its finitely presented cokernel. The tensor presentations identify $A\otimes_RQ$ and $B\otimes_RQ$ as the cokernels of this same matrix on $A^m\to A^n$ and $B^m\to B^n$. The given vector $(a_i)$ maps to zero in the second cokernel. Injectivity of $A\otimes_RQ\to B\otimes_RQ$ forces it to vanish in the first. That means exactly that $(a_i)$ is the image of some $(z_j)\in A^m$, proving (3).

Conditions (3) and (4) are the same after choosing bases: put $h(e_i)=a_i$, $v(e_j)=b_j$, and $u(e_i)=\sum_jr_{ij}e_j$. Notice that this square uses the transpose of the matrix in the preceding tensor presentation.

Assume (4), and take $P$ finitely presented with a map $\varphi\colon P\to C$. Choose

$$R^n\xrightarrow{u}R^m\xrightarrow{q}P\longrightarrow0.$$

Lift $\varphi q$ to $v\colon R^m\to B$ by freeness. Since $gvu=0$, the map $vu$ factors uniquely as $fh$ for $h\colon R^n\to A$. Condition (4) gives $k\colon R^m\to A$ with $ku=h$. Now

$$v'=v-fk,\qquad v'u=vu-fh=0,\qquad gv'=\varphi q.$$

Thus $v'$ factors through $P$ and gives a lift of $\varphi$. This proves (5), with the correction map explicitly specified.

Assume (5). The complete finite-presentation colimit construction writes

$$C=\varinjlim_i C_i$$

over a directed set with each $C_i$ finitely presented. Let

$$B_i=B\times_C C_i =\{(b,c_i):g(b)\text{ equals the image of }c_i\text{ in }C\}.$$

The projection $B_i\to C_i$ is surjective because $g$ is surjective, and its kernel is canonically $A$, via $a\mapsto(f(a),0)$. A lift $s_i\colon C_i\to B$ supplied by (5) yields the section $c_i\mapsto(s_i(c_i),c_i)$. Hence every stage is split exact.

For a transition $C_i\to C_j$, the induced map $B_i\to B_j$ is the identity on the $B$ coordinate and that transition on the other coordinate. It is the identity on the identified kernel $A$. These maps are defined independently of the chosen sections, so incompatible choices of sections cause no problem. Exactness of directed module colimits, with its full proof given above, gives an exact colimit row. Its maps to the original row are the identity on $A$ and an isomorphism onto $C$ at the right. The middle map is consequently an isomorphism: its kernel maps into the left kernel, where the map is injective, and any element of $B$ can first be matched on the right and then corrected by an element of $A$. This proves (6).

Finally, tensor a system as in (6) with an arbitrary module $Q$. Each split sequence stays exact. Tensor products commute with directed colimits by their universal property, and directed module colimits preserve exactness. Passing to the colimit therefore gives the tensor of the original sequence as an exact sequence. This proves (1) and completes all six equivalences. No flatness of $C$ and no finiteness of $A,B,C$ were assumed. ∎

A double complex of resolutions computes the same cohomology

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category, let $K^\bullet$ be a complex, and let $A^{p,q}$ be a double complex with commuting differentials $d_1,d_2$. Assume:

  1. For each integer $n$, only finitely many $A^{p,q}$ with $p+q=n$ are nonzero.
  2. $A^{p,q}=0$ for $q<0$.
  3. Maps $\alpha^p\colon K^p\to A^{p,0}$ commute with the horizontal differentials.
  4. Each augmented column
$$0\longrightarrow K^p\xrightarrow{\alpha^p}A^{p,0} \xrightarrow{d_2}A^{p,1}\xrightarrow{d_2}A^{p,2} \longrightarrow\cdots$$

is exact.

Then the maps $\alpha^n$ into the summand $A^{n,0}$ define a quasi-isomorphism

$$K^\bullet\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tot}(A)^\bullet.$$

Here

$$\operatorname{Tot}(A)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}A^{p,q}, \qquad d|_{A^{p,q}}=d_1+(-1)^p d_2.$$

Only finite direct sums are needed. There is also the symmetric assertion with rows resolving a complex on the axis $p=0$, with $p<0$ vanishing and arbitrary vertical indices.

Proof. The specified total differential squares to zero: the mixed terms cancel because $d_1d_2=d_2d_1$ and the horizontal map increases $p$ by one. Since $d_2\alpha^p=0$ and the $\alpha^p$ commute with $d_1$, their inclusion into the total complex is a cochain map.

We first prove a totalization fact at the full categorical scope. Suppose a double complex $B$ has exact columns and finite diagonals. Fix a degree $n$. Choose integers $a\leq b$ containing every horizontal index of every nonzero term on the three diagonals of total degrees $n-1,n,n+1$. Retain only the columns $a,\ldots,b$, making the horizontal maps out of that interval zero. This is still a double complex; its total complex has exactly the original objects and differentials in those three degrees. In particular, its $n$th cohomology is the same as that of $\operatorname{Tot}(B)$.

The truncated total complex has a finite filtration by the subcomplexes consisting of columns with horizontal index at least $c$, for $a\leq c\leq b+1$. Each successive quotient is a single column, with its degree shifted and its differential multiplied by the fixed sign $(-1)^c$. It is exact. The short exact sequences between consecutive filtration steps and the long exact sequence of cohomology show inductively that the entire truncated total complex is exact. Hence $H^n(\operatorname{Tot}(B))=0$. Since $n$ was arbitrary, $\operatorname{Tot}(B)$ is exact. This argument uses only finite sums, kernels, cokernels and the cohomology sequence in $\mathcal A$; it makes no elementwise argument or global boundedness assumption.

Now form a double complex $B$ by replacing $A^{p,0}$ with $\operatorname{coker}\alpha^p$ and retaining $A^{p,q}$ for $q>0$. The horizontal map descends because $\alpha$ is a cochain map, and the vertical map descends because $d_2\alpha=0$. Assumption (4) makes every column of $B$ exact. Its diagonals are finite by (1). There is a degreewise short exact sequence of complexes

$$0\longrightarrow K^\bullet\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tot}(A)^\bullet \longrightarrow\operatorname{Tot}(B)^\bullet\longrightarrow0.$$

The totalization fact makes its last complex exact. Its cohomology sequence therefore proves that the actual map induced by $\alpha$ is an isomorphism on every cohomology object.

The original spectral-sequence description has the same map: filtration by horizontal index gives

$$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(A^{p,\bullet}),\qquad E_1^{p,0}=K^p,\qquad E_1^{p,q}=0\quad(q\ne0).$$

The induced horizontal differential is $d_K$, so $E_2^{p,0}=H^p(K)$ and all other terms vanish. Higher differentials have no possible nonzero targets or sources on this single row. Finite diagonals make the filtration finite in every total degree; the three-diagonal truncation argument above supplies the needed finite-filtration comparison without imposing a first-quadrant condition. The filtered map from $K$, placed on the zero row, induces these identifications, as the direct cohomology proof has also verified.

For the symmetric assertion, transpose the two indices and repeat the proof. The two totalization conventions are isomorphic: on $A^{p,q}$ multiply by $(-1)^{pq}$. Indeed, conjugating $d_2+(-1)^q d_1$ by these signs gives $d_1+(-1)^p d_2$. On the axis $p=0$ the sign is $1$, so the resulting quasi-isomorphism is exactly the given row-augmentation map. This proves the symmetric variant with the stated canonical map.

Historical source: FAC, Chapter I, §4, no. 27, Proposition 1, p. 220. ∎
